Title: Chinese, North Korean Hackers Adopt ARTEX AI Offensive Framework
Context: The named groups have used the framework to automate various stages of the attack chain, including network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation
Full Text:
Reported cases of ARTEX being used in cyber-attack campaigns:

European Commission Confirms AI-Driven Cyber-Attack Took Systems Offline

Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

Chinese Hacker Deployed AI in Campaign Against South Korean Banks

The ARTEX AI offensive framework is now being widely deployed in cyber campaigns by both allowing both nation-state and cybercriminal groups, new research reports have documented.

The tool has been linked to numerous high-profile incidents in recent months, and more information is emerging about its use.

Microsoft revealed on November 25 that a number of Chinese and North Korean state groups had integrated ARTEX into their toolkits.

The tech giant said it had observed Chinese-nexus actors Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358 leveraging ARTEX in campaigns, in addition to Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK)-linked actors Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.

The named groups have used the framework to automate various stages of the attack chain, including network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation.

Meanwhile, a Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) report, also published on November 25, described the emergence of Agentic Offensive Frameworks (AOFs), such as ARTEX and Cairn, as the “third wave” of AI-driven cybersecurity threats.

It noted that these frameworks have significantly sped up attack chains, in some cases enabling threat actors to reach privileged access in under three hours. The tools have allowed actors to systematically probe attack surfaces, chain vulnerabilities and perform concurrent internal network pivots rapidly.

The CSA added that ARTEX has allowed complex attack chains to be undertaken by low-resourced criminals.

“While these attacks have been theoretically possible before, we have now seen them deployed by threat actors, at scale,” the report said.

Analysis published by Infrawatch on November 24 highlighted more than 130 variants of ARTEX in the wild.

The cybersecurity company observed ARTEX servers rise sharply in early November, after intrusions surged in October.

Read now: FBI Highlights Growing Abuse of AI-Driven Pentesting Framework ARTEX

How ARTEX is Deployed by Attackers

ARTEX is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘Autumn-27’ in July 2026.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

The Microsoft report emphasized that ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques, rather it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques.

However, threat actors using ARTEX can vary network indicators like source IP address or user agent string, especially to bypass static or simple signature-based detection and blocking.

To deploy the tool, Microsoft explained that a threat actor defines the target scope, and a goals model breaks the engagement into objectives that can be verified.

“Planner” and “worker” agents then work together in formulating and executing an attack cycle based on network reconnaissance undertaken on the target.

A reporter agent communicates the attack stages back to the threat actor with reproduction steps and a proof of concept.

Title: Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data
Context: "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said
Full Text: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code. The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information. 1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata. The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said. Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected. 1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions. The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address. The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens. Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult. 1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork. The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords. The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords. Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts. A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®

Title: Most Wanted: The Phishing Kits and Techniques Getting Past Security Controls
Context: Save your spot for the webinar DOMDIFFER: Google's real sign-in page, mirrored from the attacker's browser From August to October 2026, one kit ranked first by breakthrough rate...
Full Text:
Every phishing attack has to get past email security, web filtering, and safe browsing before it reaches an employee. Some kits manage that far more often than others, and those are the kits that security teams need to know about.

At Push Security, we measure this as breakthrough rate: The share of attacks that get past email security, web gateways, and safe browsing to reach the user.

How an attack breaks through

Every browser-based attack starts with a lure, and each control in its path sees only part of the attack:

Email security: Half of the attacks we see never touch email. The lure arrives through a search ad, a chat message, social media, a calendar invite, or a QR code. The rest come from trusted senders and services, so they pass reputation checks.

Web gateways: The pages sit on trusted hosting and are assembled in the browser. The domains rotate every few days, so reputation data lags behind them.

Safe browsing and scanners: Bot checks and cloaking show scanners a harmless page. A new domain isn't on any blocklist yet.

How a phishing attack gets past email, URL, DNS, web gateway, and scanner controls before it reaches the user in the browser.

When the page loads in the user's browser and the user interacts with it, that's a breakthrough. Breakthrough rate counts those attacks, not attempts.

This changes how to read upstream data. A kit with a high breakthrough rate is one that upstream controls are missing. A low count in email or proxy logs doesn't prove that a kit is rare, because the kit may be getting past those controls without a trace.

Our upcoming webinar reveals the five kits with the highest breakthrough rates. Here's an early look at the number one kit.

Save your spot for the webinar

DOMDIFFER: Google's real sign-in page, mirrored from the attacker's browser

From August to October 2026, one kit ranked first by breakthrough rate every month. DOMDIFFER, an AiTM phishing kit that targets corporate Google and Microsoft accounts, broke through 2-4x as often as the next kit each month. DOM mirroring, the mechanism it uses under the hood, also happens to be the newest and fastest-growing way for a kit to relay a sign-in.

We first saw DOMDIFFER in February 2026. DOMDIFFER is our name for the kit (it hasn't yet been linked to a known phishing-as-a-service brand). We believe it grew out of NakedPages, a reverse proxy kit, and the two kits share infrastructure in several places. DOMDIFFER went quiet in the spring, came back over the summer, and has held the top rating since August. Most of its detections in that time came from fake calendar event lures.

New hostnames per month for three NakedPages variants and DOMDIFFER, from our threat intelligence.

One real DOMDIFFER attack starts with a fake Google Voice notification about a new voicemail.

The lure for one DOMDIFFER attack: A fake Google Voice voicemail notification.

The link passes a bot check that turns scanners away. The victim then sees what looks exactly like Google's sign-in page. It isn't a screenshot or a static copy. It's Google's real page, mirrored from the attacker's browser.

Google's sign-in page, mirrored from the attacker's browser by DOMDIFFER.

On the surface, this looks like fairly standard phishing: A notification lure, a bot check gate, then a sign-in page. What makes DOMDIFFER particularly effective lies beneath the surface.

TL;DR: DOM mirroring

AiTM kits relay a sign-in in one of four ways: Reverse proxy, replica page, pixel streaming, and DOM mirroring. In DOM mirroring, the attacker's own browser does the real sign-in. It sends the page's structure (the DOM) to the victim's browser, which rebuilds a working copy. Because a real browser does the sign-in, the kit sends Google genuine browser signals and handles new sign-in steps without needing extra code.

Replica pages are still the most common class, but DOM mirroring is the newest and the fastest growing in 2026. Laurseraph, the main criminal pixel-streaming kit, has switched to DOM mirroring, and kits such as BlueKit and PhantomDOM use it too.

How common each AiTM class is today, with example kits for each.

What the victim's browser gets in each AiTM class, and what relays the sign-in. Orange lines mark an attacker's browser in the middle.

Our research post, From reverse proxies to DOM mirroring, explains the four classes in detail.

Under the hood

DOM mirroring is only part of why DOMDIFFER breaks through security controls. The rest comes from how the kit reaches its victims and stays out of sight of the controls along the way. In the webinar on December 2, Luke will take apart DOMDIFFER and the other four kits in the top five. He'll show how each one works under the hood, and the tricks that get them past controls more often than other kits.

Why controls fall short

Passkeys are worth rolling out, and they stop AiTM phishing where they're enforced. But AiTM is now one payload among several, and attackers are getting creative with how they combine them.

Kits use AiTM interchangeably with payloads that passkeys don't touch. In authorization attacks such as device code phishing, the victim signs in on Microsoft's real page and grants the attacker access. Other kits skip the sign-in page altogether and trick the victim into installing a remote access tool instead.

Kits pick the payload to match the visitor. A Windows visitor might get a remote access tool, a Microsoft account device code phishing, and a Google account AiTM. Some lures now carry two kits at once, so closing one path leaves another open.

Each of these gaps ends the same way: A page loads in the browser, and a user acts on it. In the webinar, Luke will show attackers use these tricks in real attacks.

What the webinar reveals

DOMDIFFER is one of five kits that broke through most often from August to October. On December 2, Luke Jennings will reveal the other four in a live threat briefing. Join the webinar to see:

Title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach
Context: " "Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers
Full Text:
Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

"While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said.

It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts.

As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including -

Names

Email addresses

Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers

1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

"The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security."

"Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."

In this article

A teen and his mom helped find a girl missing for over 500 days

The teens met in the online game Among Us

Talk to kids about in-game chats and what to do if someone asks for help

Here at Malwarebytes, we’re cautious about kids using in-game chats, where they can strike up conversations with people they don’t know. But in one recent case, a teen who had been abducted and held for 521 days managed to contact rescuers via the online game Among Us.

“Jenny” (an alias) was 15 when she met 38-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel online. He offered her money to help him get to Oregon, according to TechSpot.

When they met in Utah in May 2025, Harmel reportedly stole her phone and threw it into the river. Federal prosecutors allege he then took her to his home in Oregon. Jenny said he held her against her will in the basement, physically abused her, and that she tried unsuccessfully to escape.

Rescue eventually came in the form of the online game Among Us, which Jenny accessed via a phone that Harmel gave her. The phone couldn’t make calls, but it had a Wi-Fi connection, which she used to access the game.

In Among Us, players take part in short games set aboard spaceships and on planetary settlements. The crew has to work out who the imposters are before they kill everyone. It’s an anonymous game—you can play without revealing your real name. While playing, Jenny found 16-year-old Landon Tresp and struck up a friendship with him.

A phone that couldn’t call, but could play

After meeting Jenny in the game in the middle of October this year, Tresp said that they “kind of just clicked,” and according to the BBC, the chat moved to the online forum service Discord. There, Jenny told him that she was being held against her will and shared links to news reports about her disappearance.

Mom goes full detective

After two weeks of chatting with Jenny, the boy told his mother, Khristina, on October 31. She immediately jumped into action.

Jenny knew what town she was being held in, but not her address. So Khristina asked her to find a document in the house with a full name on it. Using that information, Khristina searched tax and property records and found a photo of the home on a real estate site. Jenny confirmed it was where she was being held.

Khristina contacted the law enforcement agency working on Jenny’s case, along with Jenny’s mother, who she found on social media. On November 1, when Jenny confirmed that Harmel was out of the house, she coordinated between the girl and law enforcement to help facilitate the rescue.

Harmel was charged in a federal complaint filed in Utah on November 2 with transporting a minor across state lines with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. He made his initial court appearance in Boise, Idaho, on November 4.

What parents and players can do

We often say “talk to your kids about online safety,” but it can be hard to know where to begin. Talk about who they chat with and which trusted adult they can turn to if a conversation makes them uncomfortable or someone says they’re in danger. The Power Up Pact from Ask About Games offers a good framework for a conversation.

Know which games your kids are playing and review the chat settings together, including who can send them private messages.

Title: Following the Cryptocurrency Trail Behind Europe’s Illegal Streaming Industry
Context: See How Cyble Tracks Threats Across the Dark Web Illegal IPTV services, fraudulent storefronts, and the cryptocurrency wallets behind them often surface first on underground...
Full Text:
Overview

Law enforcement agencies from 11 countries have turned their attention to the financial engine powering Europe's illegal streaming industry. Rather than simply shutting down illegal IPTV services one by one, investigators are now tracing the cryptocurrency payments that keep these operations profitable and the people who ultimately pocket the proceeds.

The effort, coordinated by Europol, brought police together with major cryptocurrency exchanges and a blockchain analytics firm. The goal was to map the money flowing from subscribers to the criminal networks behind digital piracy, and to identify who controls the wallets at the end of that chain.

Five Days in Seville Disrupt 57 Illegal IPTV Services

The operation ran for five days, from 16 to 20 November 2026, in Seville, Spain. During that window, investigators worked alongside the cryptocurrency industry to uncover the financial networks supporting illegal IPTV services.

The results were significant. Authorities disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services and identified 321 websites offering copyrighted content without authorization. Together, those websites drew more than 7.3 million visits a year.

So far, investigators have traced more than EUR 26 million in cryptocurrency transactions linked to the services, and that analysis is still ongoing. The market under scrutiny is worth billions of euros annually, with providers selling unauthorized access to premium TV channels, live sports, and films, frequently collecting subscription fees in cryptocurrency.

The Real Cost of the Illegal Streaming Industry

The appeal of illegal IPTV services is easy to understand. For just a few euros a month, subscribers get thousands of TV channels, live sporting events, and premium content, while rights holders receive nothing. Those low prices, however, mask a highly profitable criminal enterprise.

Figures from the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA) put the scale in perspective. Roughly 60 million people across Europe are estimated to use unauthorized IPTV services. Legitimate providers lose an estimated EUR 4.83 billion every year as a result, and governments miss out on another EUR 1.08 billion in uncollected taxes.

That revenue does not vanish. It passes through payment accounts, cryptocurrency wallets, and intermediaries, layers that make it harder for investigators to pinpoint who is really benefiting.

Why Cryptocurrency Didn't Keep Illegal IPTV Operators Hidden

Operators of illegal IPTV services have increasingly turned to cryptocurrency because it allows them to receive and transfer funds across borders quickly. Yet paying in crypto does not make anyone invisible.

Throughout the operation, investigators tracked suspicious transactions across blockchain networks. They searched for links between the illegal services, the cryptocurrency wallets receiving payments, and the individuals controlling them.

This approach reflects a broader shift in how authorities tackle the illegal streaming industry. Taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it, since they can often relaunch under a new name. By tracing payments, identifying beneficiaries, and targeting the financial networks that support these operations, law enforcement aims to make it much harder for criminals to keep profiting from digital piracy.

An International Effort Against Illegal IPTV Services

The operation was hosted at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville and brought together about 40 participants. Around 30 of them were law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain, and the United States.

Europol organized and coordinated the activity through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition (IPC3). The agency provided analytical support, real-time intelligence cross-checks, and a secure channel for participating authorities to exchange information.

Other participants included the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, the AAPA, the cryptocurrency exchanges Binance and Coinbase, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. The intelligence collected will now feed into national investigations, helping authorities identify suspects, disrupt further illegal services, and trace assets tied to criminal activity.

Exchanges Report USD 28.5 Million in Traced Cryptocurrency

Following Europol's announcement on Tuesday, Binance stated that its investigations unit traced more than USD 28.5 million in cryptocurrency across the 57 illegal IPTV networks, describing the effort as a joint Europol and INTERPOL crackdown. According to Cointribune's report on 25 November 2026, this figure corresponds to the more than EUR 26 million cited by Europol, rounded and converted into US dollars in the exchange's statement and later coverage.

Binance said it worked with INTERPOL, Europol, Chainalysis, and national police forces, and that the operation disrupted the 57 services and mapped the 321 associated websites. Alongside the IPTV announcement, the exchange also published broader figures: in 2025, it said it responded to nearly 71,000 law enforcement requests and confiscated USD 131 million in illicit funds. CryptoBriefing separately reported that Coinbase also assisted Europol in the same crackdown.

For market observers, the more telling detail is not any individual token but the scale of data sharing between exchanges and police. Piracy operators used cryptocurrency rails to collect subscription payments, and the case shows that investigators can now routinely reconstruct those flows across multiple exchanges.

Following the Money Behind the Illegal Streaming Industry

The Seville operation signals a change in strategy against the illegal streaming industry. Takedowns alone have limited impact when operators can quickly resurface, so authorities are shifting their focus to the cryptocurrency payments and financial infrastructure that sustain illegal IPTV services.

With 57 services disrupted, 321 websites identified, and more than EUR 26 million in transactions traced so far, the case shows that blockchain activity leaves a trail investigators can follow. As national investigations build on this intelligence, operators who rely on cryptocurrency to stay out of reach may find that the payment method itself becomes the evidence against them.

Title: Data recovery firm co-founder accused of cashing in on ransomware victims
Context: The co-founder of a Florida data recovery firm has been indicted on charges that he secretly paid ransomware gangs while telling victims his company never did
Full Text:
The co-founder of a Florida data recovery firm has been indicted on charges that he secretly paid ransomware gangs while telling victims his company never did.

Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a 52-year-old Colombian national, was arrested in Las Vegas on October 22 and has been charged by a federal grand jury in the District of Rhode Island with three counts of wire fraud, each carrying a maximum of 20 years in prison, the US Department of Justice said.

According to the indictment, the company told ransomware victims it had “sophisticated decryption technology” that could recover their data without a ransom being paid.

Prosecutors allege he had no such technology and instead negotiated with the attackers behind his clients’ backs, paying them and then charging his clients a higher amount so he could keep the difference. He is accused of using the proceeds to buy several properties in Florida.

“As alleged, the defendant preyed on ransomware victims by falsely marketing a solution he did not possess, secretly negotiating with cybercriminals, and profiting from the difference,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles C. Calenda for the District of Rhode Island.

The case against Palacio leans on an undercover operation run in June 2026, when FBI agents posed as a company hit by ransomware and as the ransomware actor holding its data.

Palacio allegedly paid the fake attacker about $6,000 in Bitcoin for the decryption key, then charged the undercover company about $13,260, more than twice the amount he handed over.

Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, described it as a “short-sighted shakedown scheme” in which Palacio is accused of “lying, cheating, and negotiating with cybercriminals to line his own pockets.”

“As alleged, Mr. Palacio Escobar is the proverbial wolf in sheep’s clothing, representing both himself and his company as experts in data recovery, when all the while he was paying the perpetrators of these ransomware attacks, under the guise of helping his clients,” added Docks.

“Anyone who tries to target victims of crime for personal gain should know that justice will eventually find them,” Docks concluded.

Palacio isn’t the first ransomware specialist this year to be prosecuted for turning on the victims who hired him. In July, Angelo Martino, a former ransomware negotiator at incident response firm DigitalMint, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for passing confidential details from his negotiations, including victims’ insurance policy limits, to BlackCat (ALPHV) operators, who used them to push up ransom demands.

Title: 1Password Hacked: Customer Names and Emails Copied, Vaults Untouched
Context: “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker
Full Text:
1Password says an attacker stole customer names and emails through an employee’s GitHub account, but vaults and passwords remained safe.

1Password has disclosed that an attacker got into some of its backend systems. The company posted its update on November 25 and says customer vaults weren’t affected. It also says some customer account data was copied.

“An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password.” reads the update published by 1Password. “Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys.”

An attacker accessed some of company’s backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer data. This affected only some customers and included the names and email addresses they use to sign in. The identity security firm has not said how many customers were affected, a detail also missing from TechCrunch’s report.

The attack started with an employee’s corporate GitHub account. 1Password began investigating on November 19, after detecting signs that someone had accessed the account without permission. The attacker used it to access source code and add malicious code to backend services. These services then downloaded customer-related administrative data. It is still unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s GitHub account.

The copied records include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, and the times each account was created and last signed in. They also hold public keys, which are public by design, and Secure Remote Password parameters, which can’t be used to access an account. The rest is non-secret metadata about 1Password’s internal architecture, such as numeric version and file identifiers.

One item deserves more attention: tokens from emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery. A token only completes the process when it’s paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address.

“The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits.” continues the report. “This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.”

Even so, 1Password changed the code format. It now uses ten letters and numbers instead of six digits. This makes it almost impossible for attackers to guess the code by trying different combinations.

Provisioning invitations are used for the SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning services. A small number of users were in the provisioning process during the incident, and 1Password has contacted them directly. The company also says it found no evidence that anyone used the exposed tokens to take over accounts.

The attacker also accessed more than customer records. They copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, which stores secrets used to run 1Password’s infrastructure. The company says its source code does not contain customer data or user secrets. It has also changed all credentials that may have been exposed.

The company says services, availability and product security weren’t affected. Vaults and the items in them weren’t touched, and neither were the keys that protect them or the account recovery keys. 1Password’s apps and browser extensions weren’t affected either, and it doesn’t store account passwords or Secret Keys.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.” states the report.

To mitigate the incident. 1Password disabled the GitHub account, revoked the stolen token and removed the access the attacker created. It restored clean versions of the affected service, rotated or revoked the internal credentials, tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, and added detections for this kind of attack. It also brought in independent experts to check its containment and remediation.

Several questions remain open; the company hasn’t disclosed how many customers were impacted or whether they’ve all been notified. At this time it is unclear who is behind the athe attacker is, or whether anyone has made demands. The Hacker News also describes the attacker only as unknown.

For customers, 1Password says there’s nothing to update in your account. It does ask you to watch for unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations or account recovery attempts you didn’t start. Phishers read the news too.

Legitimate messages follow a simple rule: only enter your password or Secret Key in the official 1Password app or website. Always open the app yourself or type the website address manually. You only need your Secret Key the first time you sign in on a new device or browser. If someone asks for it at any other time, treat it as suspicious. You can report suspicious messages to support@1password.com.

1Password says it will update its post if it discovers anything new. The company has also published its Security Whitepaper since 2015, giving users more information about how it protects their data.

Title: 1Password Hit by Backend Breach via Hijacked Employee GitHub Account
Context: "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password wrote
Full Text:
Password manager 1Password has suffered a backend breach after an attacker took over a staff member's corporate GitHub account and used it to take customer account data.

The company began investigating on November 19 after detecting signs of the intrusion, it said in an incident post.

"At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password wrote.

From GitHub to Backend Services

With the GitHub account, the attacker reached 1Password's source code and pushed malicious code into backend services, which then pulled administrative records on a subset of users.

Private repository code was also copied, and the attacker got into the company's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) system. 1Password said the source code held no user secrets, but the CI/CD environment contained infrastructure secrets, which it rotated.

Exposed records included customers' names, email addresses, account and user IDs, the dates accounts were created and last signed in, public keys and parameters used by the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol.

Tokens in some invitation, provisioning and recovery emails were also exposed, and those affected, "a small number of users," were told directly. 1Password said a token only worked together with a single sign-on (SSO) login or a code emailed to the account's address.

Read more on GitHub supply chain attacks: New Supply Chain Attack Compromises Tens of Thousands of GitHub Repositories

Vaults Untouched, Codes Lengthened

The keys protecting vaults, account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and its browser extensions were not affected, the company said. It added that it did not store users' account passwords or Secret Keys.

1Password shut down the compromised GitHub account, canceled the token the attacker had stolen and cut off their access. It also rotated or revoked internal credentials that might have been exposed, tightened controls around GitHub, CI/CD and endpoints and introduced new detections.

As a precaution, 1Password lengthened invitation and recovery codes to 10 letters and numbers, up from six digits. It also engaged outside security experts to verify its containment and clean-up work.

The company said customers did not need to change anything in their accounts but should watch for phishing, such as unexpected invitations or recovery requests. Its internal checks found no evidence that exposed provisioning tokens had been used to take over accounts, and the company said it would update its post if anything changed.

Title: 1Password breached through hijacked employee GitHub account, customer names and emails stolen
Context: “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated
Full Text:
An attacker who got into a 1Password employee’s corporate GitHub account went on to copy account records for some of the company’s users and source code from private repositories, the password manager maker disclosed on Wednesday.

“1Password identified a security incident involving some of our backend systems,” the company wrote in a post it plans to keep updated.

“On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” the company detailed.

The post doesn’t explain how the employee’s access was obtained, and it gives no date for when the intruder was detected or shut out.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated.

The keys that protect vaults and the account recovery keys weren’t reached either, with the company reporting that its apps, browser extensions and services kept working normally. “1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys,” it added.

The stolen data

The records pulled down by the malicious code belong to “a subset of our users,” and 1Password hasn’t said how many people that covers or whether individual, business or family accounts were affected. Each record holds the name and email address a customer uses with 1Password, account and user identifiers, the date the account was created and the time of its last sign-in.

The attacker also got the public keys tied to those accounts, which are “public by design” and have “no impact to user security,” the company noted. Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters were taken too, and 1Password maintains these “cannot be used to access your account.”

Another part of the haul affects a smaller group. Tokens from invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails were copied, though a token only works “when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code.”

1Password has since lengthened the code from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters and contacted the small number of users affected. So far, the company has “validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.”

The rest was internal metadata, “version numeric identifiers” and “file numeric identifiers” tied to its internal architecture, which the company lists as non-secret.

The attacker also got into the company’s CI/CD system. “Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets,” 1Password noted. Infrastructure secrets kept in CI/CD have been rotated.

Containment and remediation

The compromised GitHub account was disabled, the token the attacker stole revoked and the access the attacker had set up removed. Internal credentials that may have leaked were rotated or revoked.

On top of that, 1Password said it has tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, added new detections, and brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate the cleanup.

Customers told to stay alert

No action is needed on customers’ accounts, 1Password advised. “We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password,” the post reads, and the warning extends to texts and phone calls that mention invitations or account recovery.

Full Text:
Password management and identity security company 1Password revealed on Wednesday that a hacker stole customer information and proprietary source code. 1Password says customer vaults are not affected.

The company launched an investigation on November 19 after discovering that an employee’s corporate GitHub account may have been compromised.

The attacker used the account to deploy malicious code to backend services and exfiltrate customer records. The compromised customer records include names, email addresses, account identifiers, public cryptographic keys, authentication parameters, account activity times, and non-secret metadata.

In addition, the threat actor obtained source code from private repositories and accessed the company’s CI/CD system, potentially exposing infrastructure credentials.

According to 1Password, the hacker also obtained tokens from emails sent to users for account invitations, provisioning, and recovery.

A “small number” of individuals who were undergoing provisioning or recovery during the intrusion have been notified. However, the company noted that the exposed tokens cannot be exploited on their own and there is no evidence that the attacker hijacked user accounts.

A 1Password representative noted on the company’s community forum that the stolen authentication data included Secure Remote Password verifiers derived from user account passwords and Secret Keys. The verifiers cannot be used directly for authentication, and brute-forcing account passwords would require the associated Secret Keys, which 1Password does not store.

1Password highlighted that customer vaults and the cryptographic keys protecting them were not compromised. “We have no evidence that encrypted vaults were downloaded or accessed,” a 1Password community manager said.

The breach also does not impact client applications, browser extensions, and account recovery keys.

It’s unclear how many users are affected and how the hacker gained initial access to the corporate GitHub account.

In response to the intrusion, 1Password disabled the compromised GitHub account, invalidated a stolen token, replaced potentially compromised infrastructure credentials, and restored clean versions of affected services.

The company said its investigation, conducted with independent cybersecurity experts, is still ongoing. Customers do not need to take any action, but have been advised to watch for phishing attacks that could exploit news of the incident.

Title: More than 4,400 malicious domains are waiting for holiday shoppers
Context: Cybercriminals are positioned to exploit the holiday shopping season through fraudulent storefronts, retailer impersonation, payment fraud and account takeover attacks,...
Full Text:
Cybercriminals are positioned to exploit the holiday shopping season through fraudulent storefronts, retailer impersonation, payment fraud and account takeover attacks, according to FortiGuard Labs’ Holiday Season Cyber Threats Report 2026.

Researchers identified more than 24,000 newly registered domains containing keywords associated with seasonal shopping over a 90-day period, including more than 4,400 classified as malicious. Underground marketplaces are facilitating the trade in stolen customer information, access to e-commerce infrastructure and services that support financial fraud.

Distribution of holiday-related themes across the newly-registered domain dataset (Source: FortiGuard Labs)

Delivery scams and retailer impersonation

Parcel, delivery and shipping terminology accounted for 34.88% of newly registered holiday-related domains, making it the most prevalent theme in the dataset. Other registrations incorporated references to discounts, rewards, gift cards and retail brands.

Attackers can use imitation delivery websites to request payment information under the pretext of missed deliveries, customs fees or delivery rescheduling. Domains referencing DHL, UPS, FedEx and USPS were identified during the investigation.

Researchers identified a fraudulent website impersonating Walmart and advertising Black Friday deals. The storefront reproduced the retailer’s branding, color scheme and product listings to create the appearance of a legitimate shopping destination.

Consumers directed to such websites through advertisements, search results or promotional emails could be tricked into disclosing login credentials, submitting payment information or purchasing products that never arrive.

Fraudulent storefronts do not always rely on impersonating retailers in domain names. Separate research from Doppel found that Black Friday scams began appearing earlier this year, with most confirmed fake pages using web addresses that do not resemble those of the impersonated brands. Approximately one in four lookalike pages were hosted on legitimate platforms such as Google Sites, Blogger and GitHub Pages.

More than 1.7 million retail-related infostealer logs circulate underground

Between August and October 2026, researchers collected approximately 1.72 million infostealer log entries associated with seven major e-commerce platforms from a Russian marketplace. Amazon accounted for approximately 1.49 million entries, followed by eBay with 82,900 and AliExpress with 66,410.

Infostealer malware extracts browser-stored credentials, session cookies, autofill data and other sensitive information from infected devices. Criminals categorize these records by domain, geography and account type, allowing buyers to locate information associated with specific retailers.

“Stolen session cookies may potentially be reused to hijack authenticated sessions, depending on their validity and the security controls implemented by the affected platforms,” the researchers explained.

Stolen credentials and session data could enable unauthorized account access, fraudulent purchases and misuse of stored payment information.

Cybercrime services facilitate retail fraud

Underground forums contain advertisements for subscription-based phishing services, automated payment card validation tools and phishing kits advertised as capable of bypassing MFA.

Criminals are advertising banking credentials, compromised gift card information and access to merchant systems. Fraudulently obtained gift cards can be resold or converted into cash or cryptocurrency.

Researchers also identified an advertised refund-as-a-service operation targeting retailers, food delivery companies, electronics vendors and travel platforms. The operator claims to secure refunds on purchases in exchange for a commission. Such services could exploit return policies and customer support processes.

Communications infrastructure is another component of the underground economy. Listings advertise caller ID spoofing, SMS delivery and bulk email distribution services that could support impersonation campaigns.

Sellers also advertise ready-made social media accounts, advertising campaign management and artificial engagement services. Purchased followers, comments and views could make fraudulent social media profiles and deceptive product advertisements appear more credible.

E-commerce vulnerabilities put retailers at risk

Cybercrime forums contain advertisements for alleged zero-day vulnerabilities, exploit chains and unauthorized access to e-commerce platforms such as Magento, PrestaShop, WordPress and OpenCart.

Access to compromised retail infrastructure could allow attackers to modify checkout pages, deploy payment-skimming scripts, redirect shoppers to fraudulent payment pages and extract customer databases.

Documented exploitation of vulnerabilities affecting Adobe Commerce (Magento) and other web application environments adds to the risks facing online businesses. Security flaws involving remote code execution, unrestricted file uploads and authorization bypass can leave merchant systems vulnerable to compromise.

AI tools enter the holiday fraud ecosystem

Cybercriminals are exploring the use of AI to automate parts of their operations, develop malicious software and produce social engineering content tailored to specific audiences.

One forum user sought an unrestricted LLM capable of generating Romanian-language communications that reflect local financial practices. Such capabilities could make fraudulent messages more convincing to recipients.

Another user described developing an orchestration framework that reportedly coordinates multiple AI agents. The developer claims the framework can circumvent model safety restrictions. Such systems could reduce the manual effort involved in reconnaissance and attack development.

AI-generated videos present another potential avenue for deception. Commercial media generation platforms could be misused to produce fabricated customer testimonials, misleading product demonstrations and advertisements impersonating established brands.

Title: What Two Million Canary Prompts Reveal About AI Supply Chain Security
Context: Qualys detects known vulnerabilities and default credentials in servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM, and AI detection and response (AI-DR)¹, an extension of Qualys EDR to...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

To evaluate the security of the AI supply chain, Dragos seeded approximately two million AI prompts with canary URLs and credentials. The investigation revealed that prompt data was stolen from at least three AI hosting providers and from the system of a Chinese AI lab, which accessed secret URLs from prompts marked for zero data retention. No security team can audit the providers its prompts pass through, whether they are foreign or domestic. Every team can test its own side: the models it calls and what goes into each prompt. Qualys TotalAI maps the models and AI services in use, red-teams any model with a chat completion endpoint (including foreign models), and detects secrets before they reach a prompt.

Inside the Canary Experiment

In a study published on November 19, 2026, a team from Dragos, led by Chief Research Officer HD Moore, sent approximately two million prompts to popular AI services from July through November, tracing around 2,000 request routes. Each prompt carried canary tokens: unique URLs and live AWS keys linked to empty accounts that were fully monitored. If a URL was accessed, it indicated that the system had read the prompt; if a key was used, it showed that someone had stolen a credential.

What the Dragos Canary Study Exposed

Breached Providers

Attackers have stolen prompt data from at least three AI hosting providers, and Dragos reports that these providers were unaware of the breaches until they were notified. In the largest breach, every canary request Dragos sent during several late-October windows was stolen. This included requests that the provider had rejected before any models had a chance to run. Attackers tested the AWS keys, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, attempted to enable Amazon Bedrock models, create Bedrock API keys, and add IAM users. One adversary later used ARTEX, an LLM-driven penetration testing framework, to confirm that the keys were active.

Leaky Routes

AI routers forward requests to pools of hosting providers, and every hop can access the full prompt. A Zero Data Retention (ZDR) setting is intended to ensure that the service an application calls does not retain prompts or responses, yet Dragos found ZDR-marked requests stolen or scraped further down the route. They also discovered instances of marketplace sellers logging prompts and a router quietly forwarding some traffic to these marketplaces.

A Foreign Lab Reading Flagged Prompts

A Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of the prompts sent to its models, including about two-thirds of those marked ZDR; U.S. resellers of its models triggered the same scraper. In a later statement, the lab said an internal security monitoring process extracted and probed the URLs, and that it has disabled that process for forwarded API traffic.

Providers Cannot Be Audited. The Customer Side Can Be Tested.

Every finding turned on one fact: whatever sits in a prompt, from a live credential to customer data or source code, can be seen by every hop on the route. A credential turns that exposure into an intrusion. No model test can show what a provider’s infrastructure does with a request. Security teams can only test their own systems, and Qualys TotalAI answers four questions about this.

1. Which Models and Routes Are in Use?

Qualys TotalAI leverages existing Qualys sensors. Cloud Agents and scanners can fingerprint AI software and GPUs, cloud connectors map managed AI services, Container Security covers AI workloads, and a browser plug-in shows workforce AI usage.

Qualys Container Runtime Security adds evidence about where containerized AI applications connect. Security teams can correlate DNS and outbound TCP events from monitored workloads to track direct connections to AI routers or provider endpoints outside their approved list. For requests routed through a provider, they can use router or gateway records to identify the reported inference provider. Qualys TotalAI enhances this visibility by testing supported model endpoints for sensitive information disclosures.

Self-hosting, which Dragos recommends where affordable, takes third parties off the route but makes the model server the target. Qualys detects known vulnerabilities and default credentials in servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM, and AI detection and response (AI-DR)¹, an extension of Qualys EDR to AI assets, is designed to catch attacks on that infrastructure as they happen.

2. Do The AI Models In Use Leak Their Context?

Red-team tests show what a model gives away under attack. TotalAI evaluates any model with a chat completion endpoint, including foreign models, against 300+ attack scenarios mapped to OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, and the EU AI Act, including 21 sensitive information disclosure checks. A model that discloses a real credential from its system prompt, retrieved documents or tool output proves it sat in the model’s context, where every hop could see it. When a test fails, automated guardrail remediation¹ is designed to push the fix into Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

3. Can a Secret Reach the Prompt?

Guardrails control what a model repeats, not what it was sent: in the largest breach, attackers stole some requests rejected before any model ran. The test that matters is whether a secret can reach the prompt at all, and that starts where secrets live. Qualys scanning detects exposed secrets in container images, CI/CD pipelines, and code repositories. This leak class was responsible for a provider notice in November, where an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public repository. TotalAI MCP scans test the servers that agents source context from for credential exposure. Additionally, MCP tool-call tracing¹ is designed to show what each tool call passes into an agent’s context. Secrets also enter at run time, pasted by users or returned by tools, where static scans cannot see them. Policy-based runtime controls with inline blocking¹ are designed to block or redact secrets before a request exits the organization. A key that never reaches the first hop cannot be stolen further down the route.

4. What Can a Stolen Key Reach?

Qualys analysis of a 2026 intrusion traced an exposed AWS key to a complete cloud takeover in under ten minutes. TotalCloud CIEM shows what each cloud identity can access and flags excess privileges. Its posture checks cover AI services such as Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker, and Azure OpenAI. TruRisk Insights AI attack paths¹ are designed to connect exposed endpoints, excess permissions, and sensitive data into one prioritized path.

What to Do This Week

Map the models and routes in use. Flag any connection to a router or provider that no one approved, as well as any self-hosted model server that can be reached without authentication.

Test the models in use, including foreign ones, after every change to a model or prompt.

Find secrets in code, images, and agent context. Remove them before an agent can load them.

Rotate secrets in prompts covered by any provider or router notice, and give agents short-lived, least-privilege keys.

Hunt for the indicators. Search CloudTrail for ARTEX user agents artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, Bedrock enablement, new Bedrock API keys, and new IAM users.

Dragos also recommends pinning providers and verifying Zero Data Retention on every hop.

Test the Models No One Can Audit

The Dragos study found no new class of vulnerability: exposed credentials and broken privacy promises, moving through a supply chain customers can barely see. No team can audit the provider side. Every team can test the models it calls and keep secrets out of the prompt.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What did the Dragos canary study find?

From July through November 2026, Dragos sent about two million prompts carrying canary URLs and AWS keys to AI services. It found prompt data stolen from at least three AI hosting providers, marketplace sellers logging prompts, and a Chinese AI lab’s systems fetching secret URLs from prompts marked for zero data retention.

Can security teams test AI models they do not host?

Yes, for model behavior: TotalAI tests any model with a chat completion endpoint, including foreign models. What a provider’s infrastructure does with a request is outside what any model test can see.

Does Zero Data Retention protect AI prompts?

Zero Data Retention (ZDR) protects a prompt only at the hop that honors it. In the Dragos study, ZDR-flagged requests were stolen inside breached providers, and their secret URLs fetched downstream. Security teams should verify the route as well as the settings, including what each hop’s retention terms exempt from.

What is AI supply chain security?

AI supply chain security means controlling every service that handles an organization’s AI traffic: models, routers, inference providers, and the agents that build each prompt.

How should organizations secure self-hosted AI models?

Treat model servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM like any other exposed service: patch known vulnerabilities, remove default credentials and require authentication on every API. Qualys publishes detections for specific issues with Ollama, vLLM, and LiteLLM.
