Title: 13 Malicious NuGet Packages Turn Fake .NET Job Assessments Into Malware Delivery Traps
Context: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows .NET developers under the guise of a fake take-home job assessment.

"Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF [Windows Presentation Foundation] button controls," Socket security researcher Kush Pandya said in a technical write-up. "In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL sideloading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable."

All the identified NuGet packages have been deleted from the gallery as of writing. The names of the packages are listed below -

WinUI.Button

VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer

VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls

HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer

HappyOne.WinUI3Controls

Web3TotalButton

RevertButtonIcon

WinUI3IconButton

WindowsAccentColorName

SetButtonColor

InitializeCustomButton

StyledAppButton

StyledComponent

The first NuGet package, WinUI3IconButton, was uploaded to the registry on July 23, 2026, indicating that the campaign has been ongoing for quite some time without attracting attention. The last two uploads, HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls, occurred on November 4, 2026, after both VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls were removed by NuGet on November 2, 2026.

The starting point is a GitHub repository ("stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment") created on November 3, 2026. It features a set of assessment tasks revolving around enhancing a FileButton control and exception handling that candidates must implement within a span of three to four hours. It's unclear how targets are led to these decoy projects.

The README file also permits the test participants to use artificial intelligence (AI) development assistants like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude, but discourages them from copying and pasting the entire project into the tool and generating the solution without "understanding it."

Present within the assessment repository is a "WinUI3_Home_Assessment.csproj" file that references VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer version 1.2.7 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls version 1.0.7.

"VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL ['MSBuildAnalyzer.dll'] after every build," Pandya said. "In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it."

The VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package then launches the copied binary via the FileButton control that "routes clicks to Windows files and folders," triggering the execution of the DLL via a known technique called DLL sideloading.

In a similar vein, creating a WUIButton control from the WinUI.Button package starts a background routine in "lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll" that downloads "avast.exe" from the "Carol-White-Super/cloud" repository via the GitHub API using an embedded access token, saves it as "%TEMP%\Launcher.exe," and runs it.

RevertButtonIcon and SetButtonColor "download a Windows executable to the user's temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops," Socket explained.

"Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to."

Socket also said it identified two bogus repositories impersonating the axios JavaScript library -

jason-code-super/axios

stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (the same GitHub account hosting the assessment)

Both repositories have been flagged as copies of a malicious Node.js library named "axios-test-one" that impersonates the Axios HTTP client but contains functionality that enables code execution and shell access. The repositories serve a Windows executable named "lib/env/axios.csproj."

An analysis of their commit history has revealed several binaries between the two repositories, including -

A loader ("updater.exe" and "msedgewebview2.exe") that uses a GitHub repository ("James-White-Super/React_prj") as a two-way command and control (C2)

A PyInstaller program that functions as a Google Chrome profile stealer and uploads the information to GitHub ("gabsantosbus-star/EngineeringRepository"), and

A "WeapF" payload that reports the computer name, user name, time zone, and CPU model to an attacker-controlled Telegram bot

What's more, the GitHub account named "gabsantosbus-star" (aka Gabriel) has been found to have made the first commit in the two aforementioned fake Axios repositories, along with "figma-share/axios-http," a third bogus Axios repository.

"On November 13, 2026, gabsantosbus-star [...] published a GitHub release of 'Crypto Wallet Analyzer,' a single-file .NET app," Socket said. "The README presents the app as a first-stage client deliverable that inventories eight crypto wallet extensions in Chrome profiles and makes no network requests."

"The visible app does only that, but its decompiled MainWindow constructor also loads a native DLL bundled in the executable. The DLL starts a background thread when loaded, and closing the window only hides it, so the process keeps running."

The DLL in question is a new version of the loader that uses a different repository ("Best-Seller-Dev/dexTrader") for C2. The GitHub account is no longer accessible as of writing.

Further investigation has uncovered that the lure was advertised on a Web3 freelance marketplace called LaborX on November 7, 2026, under the same persona, with the threat actor posing as a "detail-oriented client looking to work with skilled freelancers on various projects."

The $8,500-10,000 job listing, which is still accessible, claims that they are looking for a C# WPF developer to work on their lightweight Windows .NET desktop application that "inventories crypto wallet software installed on a local PC, including browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications."

On their X profile, they describe themselves as a "blockchain and DeFi specialist" and a "cryptocurrency expert" based out of Miami, Florida. But a check of their "About this account" reveals that the profile is actually based in Korea. The account was created in July 2026.

The web of connections doesn't end there, for evidence indicates that the "axios-test-one" npm library was part of a broader collection of six packages that were published between July 14 and 23, 2026, by three npm accounts gsanbus, jasonsuperstar, and jasonsayman -

axios-test-one

telemetry-metrics

telemetry-axios

axios-native

fs-extra-core

vitest-axios

The use of the name "jasonsayman" is particularly significant as it clearly points to an attempt to pass off as "jasonsaayman," the legitimate GitHub account belonging to the developer and maintainer of Axios.

"Telemetry-metrics and telemetry-axios download a Windows executable from ThoSuperstarDev/axios-http and run it, fs-extra-core downloads one from jason-code-super/axios and saves it as msedgewebview2.exe, and the axios clones pull those packages in," Socket said.

What's notable here is that "ThoSuperstarDev" is the former GitHub account name of "figma-share," which, as it happens, also hosts a ClickFix-style page that shows a fake reCAPTCHA verification prompt and guides the visitor to copy and paste a security token into the Windows Run dialog to address a purported "Security Handshake Error."

The fraudulent job campaign has not been attributed to any named threat actor or group. However, Socket noted that the tradecraft shares similarities with other recruitment-themed campaigns orchestrated by North Korea and Iran.

"We found no indicator or code shared with any published Contagious Interview or other North Korean campaign, none of the malware families publicly tied to Contagious Interview (such as BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, and OtterCookie) in the stages we recovered, and no publicly documented family that matches the loader," Pandya said.

Title: What is Strategic Threat Intelligence? | Recorded Future
Context: For the most part, strategic threat intelligence comes from freely available sources
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

Threat intelligence is often thought of as a single function, but in reality, it can be broken down into four categories: strategic, tactical, operational, and technical.

Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical and is used by high-level strategists to inform specific decisions.

For the most part, strategic threat intelligence comes from freely available sources. However, the volume of available sources, combined with language constraints, often makes manual collection infeasible.

The success of strategic threat intelligence depends on strong two-way communication between threat analysts and their primary audience — usually the board of directors.

On the surface, threat intelligence appears to be a single discipline, closely intertwined with the cyber threat intelligence cycle. Practitioners collect data from a variety of sources, analyze it, and use the outputs to make decisions.

The reality is a little more complicated. As with most specialties, threat intelligence can be broken down into subcategories, each with its own uses, techniques, and challenges. Here are the three distinct categories that threat intelligence is typically boiled down to:

Strategic Intelligence: Non-technical, risk-based intelligence used by high-level decision makers.

Tactical Intelligence: Details of threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

Operational Intelligence: Actionable information about specific incoming attacks.

In this blog series, we’ll take an in-depth look at each of these categories, including how they are collected, analyzed, and used to enhance security.

Today, we’re covering strategic intelligence.

What Is Strategic Threat Intelligence?

Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical, risk-focused intelligence that provides executives and board members with a bird’s-eye view of an organization’s threat landscape, enabling them to understand the broader impact of high-level business decisions. It isn’t concerned with specific actors, indicators, or attacks.

Given that the audience is primarily C-suite and board level, strategic threat intelligence is almost exclusively non-technical. Instead, it covers factors such as risk scores and the possible outcomes of a given action or decision, such as entering a foreign market or taking an ideological position.

Since it’s used to inform specific, high-level decisions, strategic threat intelligence is usually gathered on demand rather than as an ongoing initiative, and is most often presented as a report or briefing.

Sources of Strategic Threat Intelligence

Unlike other intelligence categories, the majority of strategic threat intelligence sources are Open Source Intelligence, or OSINT, meaning they can be freely accessed by anyone who cares to do so. Common examples include:

Policy documents from nation-states and other groups of interest

Local and national media

Industry- and subject-specific publications

Comments, online activity, and articles from individuals of interest

Free content produced by security organizations (e.g., white papers, research reports, etc.)

While the accessibility of strategic sources can be a tremendous positive, it can also be a double-edged sword, as analysts must manually process huge quantities of raw data in order to identify valuable insights. Worse still, the most valuable insights are often “hidden” in foreign language sources, forcing analysts to spend even more time on translation.

Fortunately, if analysts are armed with the right tools, these difficulties can largely be sidestepped. Powerful threat intelligence solutions can scour a large volume of sources, identify relevant information in real time, and automatically translate non-native results.

Who Produces Strategic Threat Intelligence?

Perhaps the most significant difference between strategic threat intelligence and other intelligence categories is the skill set needed for production. While typical security and analysis skills are still essential, producing strategic threat intelligence also requires a great deal of expertise in other areas — in particular, a strong understanding of sociopolitical and business concepts.

Since this broad skill set is rarely found in a single individual, some organizations hire analysts with state or military intelligence backgrounds and train them in the security-specific subject areas required for the role. While this approach takes time and resources to pull off, it is often quicker and more effective than holding out for the perfect applicant.

How Should Organizations Request Strategic Threat Intelligence?

Strategic threat intelligence stands apart from the other three categories because it’s almost exclusively requested by (and produced for) a non-technical audience. While the outputs are produced in a format that senior executives and board members will understand, the audience’s lack of understanding of what is and isn’t possible can lead them to make requests that non-government analysts simply can’t meet.

For example, if an organization’s board were considering expansion into another country, it might call on its threat intelligence analysts to provide some insights. As we’ve already seen, though, strategic threat intelligence is very much a “made-to-order” discipline, meaning analysts will do their best to meet the specific requirements of their board.

This is where “asking good questions” comes in. An inexperienced (in the context of threat intelligence) board might be tempted to demand, “Tell us how, where, and by whom we’ll be attacked if we open this branch.”

Requirements like this are highly unlikely to lead to valuable insights for two reasons:

Acquiring detailed intelligence on specific local or national actors is often impossible for non-state actors.

Attempting to predict specific attacks is far less useful (and reliable) than understanding the most common threat trends and their relative likelihoods.

A far better line of questioning would be, “Is this expansion likely to open us up to increased cyber risk? If it is, which threat vectors are most likely to be employed, and what would be the cost of preparing for or responding to those threats?” This type of question gives analysts far greater scope to explore useful avenues of research and is much more likely to result in an insightful and actionable intelligence product.

Ideally, there should be an open line of communication between an organization’s board and its threat intelligence specialists — most likely via the CISO — to ensure that strategic threat intelligence project parameters are set in a way that’s conducive to producing an actionable output.

How Is Strategic Threat Intelligence Success Evaluated?

As we’ve already seen, strategic threat intelligence outputs rarely include binary “yes or no” recommendations, focusing instead on variables such as risk and confidence scores. But that’s not to say that evaluation can’t (or shouldn’t) be attempted.

A strong feedback loop is essential to the consistent production of high-quality intelligence products. Just like any intelligence initiative, a strategic threat intelligence capability should be subject to ongoing evaluation.

This evaluation process should include feedback from the intelligence team’s primary audience — typically the board of directors — and answer key questions, such as:

Was the intelligence produced in line with requirements?

How helpful was the intelligence in making the stated decision?

Was the intelligence pitched correctly for its (likely non-technical) audience?

This type of feedback will typically be collected informally by the CISO and should be used to improve future strategic intelligence gathering and presentation. Of course, one obvious question remains: Was the intelligence proven accurate over time? Unfortunately, this question often proves extremely hard, if not impossible, to answer, for two primary reasons:

Strategic intelligence deals primarily with measurements of risk and likelihood, so even if an anticipated result doesn’t occur, that doesn’t mean the intelligence was inaccurate.

It’s rarely possible to determine precisely what has (or hasn’t) happened in a remote situation.

With all that said, the accuracy of strategic intelligence should be monitored as far as possible and used to improve processes and intelligence outputs.

What’s the Difference Between Strategic and Tactical Threat Intelligence?

As we’ve already seen, threat intelligence breaks down into three primary categories — strategic, tactical, and operational — and it’s easy to conflate strategic with tactical since both inform security decisions. The difference comes down to who’s using the intelligence and what they do with it.

Strategic Threat Intelligence

Tactical Threat Intelligence

Audience

Executives, boards, and other high-level decision-makers

Security analysts, SOC teams, and incident responders

Focus

Broad risk trends and business impact

Specific threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs)

Data Sources

Open-source policy documents, media, and industry research

Malware samples, attack patterns, and technical indicators of compromise

Output Format

Reports and briefings for non-technical stakeholders

Technical indicators that feed directly into security tools

Primary Use

Informing decisions like market expansion or risk tolerance

Detecting and defending against specific, active threats

In short: strategic intelligence tells leadership whether and why a risk matters to the business, while tactical intelligence tells defenders how an attack works so they can stop it. For a closer look at how tactical intelligence is gathered and applied, see our breakdown of tactical threat intelligence.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between strategic and operational threat intelligence for government agencies?

Strategic intelligence informs long-term policy and risk decisions for government leadership, while operational intelligence supports response to specific, imminent threats or incidents — the same distinction that applies in the private sector, though government strategic intelligence often incorporates geopolitical and nation-state sourcing more heavily.

What are some real-world examples of strategic threat intelligence?

Examples include geopolitical risk assessments before entering a new market, industry-wide threat landscape reports for board presentations, and executive briefings on how a competitor’s breach might signal shared industry risk.

What are the benefits of using strategic threat intelligence for business decisions?

It gives leadership a clearer, evidence-based view of risk before making high-stakes calls — like market expansion, M&A, or vendor selection — reducing the chance of decisions made on incomplete or purely anecdotal information.

How long does it typically take to produce a strategic threat intelligence report?

Timelines vary by scope, but since most strategic intelligence is made-to-order rather than continuously monitored, turnaround often ranges from a few days for a narrow question to several weeks for a comprehensive board-level briefing.

How can Recorded Future help produce strategic threat intelligence?

Title: 1Password customer data stolen after employee GitHub account breach
Context: While customer vaults were not compromised in the attack, the stolen data is valuable to threat actors as it provides a list of known 1Password users who could be targeted in...
Full Text:
1Password has disclosed a data breach after an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.

The company says customer password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised in the attack.

In a security incident disclosure published today, 1Password says it began investigating the breach on November 19 after detecting indications that an employee's GitHub account had been compromised.

The attacker used the account to access private source code repositories and inject malicious code into backend services that downloaded customer account records.

The stolen data includes:

Customer names and email addresses

Account and user IDs

Account creation and last sign-in timestamps

Public cryptographic keys

Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters

Invitation, provisioning, and account recovery tokens

Other internal account metadata

The attacker also stole internal company source code and accessed its continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environment, potentially exposing internal infrastructure credentials.

Among the stolen customer data were tokens embedded in links that 1Password emailed to users to accept account provisioning invitations or recover their accounts.

However, 1Password says these tokens cannot be used on their own to access customer accounts, as completing the invitation or recovery process requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address.

The company says only a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

As a precaution against brute-force attacks, 1Password has strengthened these verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters.

The company says it has now disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services, and rotated or revoked potentially exposed infrastructure credentials.

1Password has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its remediation efforts and says it has found no internal evidence of customer account takeovers.

The company is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys but warns them to watch for unexpected invitations, account recovery requests, and other potential phishing attempts.

While customer vaults were not compromised in the attack, the stolen data is valuable to threat actors as it provides a list of known 1Password users who could be targeted in phishing campaigns.

Threat actors could send emails impersonating 1Password, using the breach as a lure to trick customers into disclosing their account passwords, Secret Keys, or recovery verification codes.

Customers should be particularly wary of emails claiming they need to secure their accounts in response to the breach, reset their passwords, or verify their account information.

Rather than clicking on links in these emails, customers should access their accounts directly through the 1Password website or app and never share their passwords, Secret Keys, or verification codes with anyone.

BleepingComputer contacted 1Password with questions about the attack but has not yet received a response.

Title: Switzerland Confirms First AI-Agent Cyberattacks on Local Organisations
Context: Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours
Full Text:
Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours.

Switzerland ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has now seen these attacks firsthand. In recent days, it received its first reports of cyberattacks on Swiss organisations carried out with the help of AI agents. The victims include critical infrastructure operators in at least two sectors.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent.” reads the report published by NCSC. “Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

What stands out is the result. In every AI-assisted attack known to the NCSC, the attackers successfully compromised the victims’ IT systems. The agency sees these incidents as more than isolated cases, warning that they mark a shift in the cyber threat landscape.

The attackers used what the NCSC calls “Agentic Offensive Frameworks”. These AI agents can search for vulnerabilities, choose attack tools, assess the results and decide what to do next, all with limited human input. Security teams also use the same software for penetration testing, which makes these tools dual-use.

The targets aren’t exotic. The agents go after standard or easily guessed passwords, known flaws in software, and systems connected to the internet.

“AI agents often require only a fraction of the time a human would need to locate such vulnerable systems and exploit existing vulnerabilities. Furthermore, they can react flexibly to defence mechanisms by switching to other known attack methods. This leaves organisations with significantly less time to detect an attack and respond appropriately.” continues the report.

AI agents can quickly switch tactics when a defence blocks an attack, leaving organisations less time to detect and stop intrusions. The NCSC warns that these tools speed up common attack methods and that internet-accessible agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI have almost doubled since October 2026. This could lead to more frequent, faster and more successful automated attacks against organisations of all types.

ARTEX isn’t a surprise. The FBI recently published a FLASH alert that describes it as open source, with no model of its own, plugged into external language models. The same advisory says some intrusions went from first contact to privileged access in under three hours.

The NCSC expects more successful attacks and urges companies and critical infrastructure operators to strengthen their security and resilience. It monitors the threat landscape, stays in contact with national and international partners, and shares technical indicators for detecting these tools with infrastructure operators. Its recommendations are short, and it wants them applied without delay.

Start by shrinking what’s exposed. Fewer systems facing the internet means a smaller attack surface, and where possible you can restrict access with geo-blocking or an allow list of IP addresses or network segments. Every internal resource reachable from the internet, such as webmail and VPN, should sit behind multi-factor authentication or passkeys, with no exceptions.

Then limit the damage. Grant the lowest access rights that work, and watch for deviations from normal behaviour and data volumes across identities, applications, workloads and infrastructure. Test your own infrastructure for vulnerabilities on a regular basis, yourself or with an outside specialist.

“Critical security updates for systems accessible via the internet should be installed as soon as possible, but no later than 24 hours after release.” concludes the report.

Title: The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought
Context: The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks
Full Text: American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems. The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23. It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020. However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted. Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords. The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers. According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17. Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique: The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22. These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented. Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo. “Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

Title: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks
Context: Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector
Full Text:
Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector.

The two agencies listed four AI-powered penetration testing and red-teaming frameworks that have been involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents: ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness - Red Team, and PentAGI.

Both agencies have urged organizations to reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet, prioritize patching, and monitor for unusual activity.

Large-scale attacks in Italy

CSIRT Italia says it detected large-scale malicious campaigns that used autonomous AI agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on exposed endpoints.

In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours.

In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence.

The agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks.

“During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low-impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says.

“They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.”

The Italian cybersecurity agency advises administrators to prioritize patching internet-facing systems, focus on addressing flaws known to be actively exploited in the wild, and disable remote management interfaces if not needed.

The agency also recommends monitoring control plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic to detect suspicious activity.

First AI breaches in Switzerland

Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) warned of similar campaigns targeting organizations in the country, confirming the first cases of successful AI-assisted cyberattacks.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said.

“Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

“In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.”

The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next.

NCSC says that the number of AI agents publicly (and often freely) available to cybercriminals has nearly doubled since October, resulting in these massive waves against Swiss organizations, including critical infrastructure operators.

The agency recommends that administrators of internet-facing systems patch critical vulnerabilities within 24 hours of release, add multi-factor authentication (MFA) or passkey protection, and enforce least-privilege principles.

I tried hard not to write another typical “Thanksgiving article.” Obviously, I failed. But you know what? It is Thanksgiving week here in the U.S., and coming up with fun, interesting, short form topics is hard, especially when you’re fighting the weight of Tradition expected this week. So instead of me writing something insightful, you’re getting some things I’m thankful for. Even that’s harder than you might think, because there are so many things, and this is just the newsletter introduction, after all.

Let’s start off with something I’m pretty sure none of us are thankful for: threat actors. Seriously, screw you guys! I know I'd be out of a job without you, but that’s just another way of saying “I coulda been a professional bagpiper.” There are days when that doesn’t sound so bad. So, no gratitude coming your way, people!

In terms of actual thankfulness, I want to give a big THANK YOU to the entire Blue Team, everywhere. Everyone out there defending, especially those in the U.S. taking shifts on Thursday to keep the turkey-eating public safe and secure. This is a hard, often high-pressure job for which you get little thanks, but all the blame when a breach occurs. We see you. We appreciate you. We promise we’ll save you some stuffing.

Speaking of defenders, I’m also very thankful to get to work with so many talented and wonderful people here at Talos. I’m not just saying this because I know my boss will read it! Without exception, everyone I’ve worked with here has not only been an expert at what they do, but they’ve been friendly, welcoming, and very patient with me as I’ve been feeling my way around this new org over the past several months. Thank you!

Finally, and maybe most importantly of all, I want to thank you, our readers. You are the reason we’re all here, doing what we do, helping you to look out for your own networks and protect your own people. We appreciate your trust!

Whether you’re celebrating Thanksgiving here in the States or just having a normal weekend wherever you are, I hope you get some time to relax, unplug, recharge, and de-stress.

Now, who wants some pie?

The one big thing

In Talos’ latest blog, we examine the fascinating tradecraft of the OpenAI-linked agentic swarm that broke out of its containerized environment in 2026. While not inherently malicious, this swarm of AI agents used public internet services as improvised infrastructure to bypass their sandbox constraints and complete their training tasks. By analyzing this unintentional great escape, we can learn how multi-agent systems coordinate, partition work, and adapt when their paths are blocked. This view into autonomous AI operations provides a baseline for understanding how these behaviors transfer to purpose-built cyber attack frameworks.

Why do I care?

The leap from an AI sandbox escape to weaponized cyber attacks has already happened. Agentic frameworks like ARTEX are currently in the wild, proving that multi-agent systems can move from a single compromised credential to deep network access in under 15 minutes. These autonomous threats adapt to errors in real time and execute dozens of actions in mere seconds. Understanding how these swarms coordinate, adapt, and exfiltrate data is a necessity to keep up with an adversary that operates at machine speed.

So now what?

To catch an AI swarm, defenders must look for its operational fingerprints. Monitor your environment for irregular "burst-and-pause" timing patterns that indicate rapid, sub-second automated reasoning. Keep a close eye on unusual traffic to allow-listed public services like “webhook.site”, which agents use to park data before terminating. Finally, hunt for self-labeling conventions, like highly specific URL parameters or predictable file names (e.g., “artex-probe-*”), that agents rely on to track their state. Read the full blog for a deeper dive into these swarm behaviors.

ARTEX: Publicly available AI-powered offensive security framework

Capabilities

Identifying ARTEX network activity

Hunting

MITRE ATT&CK techniques

Since its release in July 2026, the AI-powered penetration testing framework ARTEX has been abused by many threat actors to accelerate their existing workflows related to network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation. As of November 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed both state-sponsored and financially motivated threat actors such as Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon integrating ARTEX into their tooling.

In the past few weeks, we’ve reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation. These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain. Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor. Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes.

ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques. ARTEX does sometimes transmit distinctive characteristics associated with its integrated penetration testing tools. However, threat actors using ARTEX can and do vary network indicators like source IP address or user agent string, especially to bypass static or simple signature-based detection and blocking. The most reliable and durable signal of ARTEX activity is behavioral: ARTEX sends a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retries variations on the same technique or moves on to next-stage actions at machine speed.

In this blog, we’re sharing a detailed breakdown of ARTEX, including its architecture and capabilities, as well as guidance for identifying related network and system activity. Microsoft disrupts and contains threats posed by ARTEX-enabled attacks across the Microsoft Defender suite of products. Defenders can further reduce and mitigate the effectiveness of ARTEX and similar AI agentic attacks by following Microsoft’s recommendations outlined in this report to reduce internet-facing exposure, secure credentials and secrets, and limit lateral movement paths in their environment. Additionally, Microsoft recommends customers to enable automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR to contain and isolate affected devices during an attack.

To help defenders keep pace with machine-speed attacks, Microsoft Perception coordinates red, blue, and green team agents that find exploitable weaknesses, investigate threats, and remediate risks, with security teams approving critical actions. As threat actors increasingly adopt AI, we’re publishing this information to equip defenders with insights that can help protect systems, secrets, identities, and networks from AI-assisted attacks.

ARTEX: Publicly available AI-powered offensive security framework

ARTEX (“AI 自主渗透测试系统,” or AI autonomous penetration testing system) is an AI-driven penetration testing platform. A Go-based backend coordinates multiple large language model (LLM) agents that can take an attack from reconnaissance and attack surface discovery through exploitation, verification, and reporting, with little or no human involvement. ARTEX includes an embedded Next.js web interface and uses PostgreSQL for storage.

ARTEX is primarily a web application penetration testing tool. Its built-in guidance, skills, and findings categories center on vulnerabilities in HTTP applications and APIs, including SQL injection, server-side template injection, XML external entity (XXE) injection, file upload flaws, authentication bypass, and insecure direct object references (IDOR).

ARTEX agents also perform general network reconnaissance and credential attacks. After agents gain initial access to a system or network, they can pivot through interactive shells. By default, ARTEX does not take any measures to obfuscate its malicious activity.

In July 2026, GitHub user Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese-language interface. While the original developer removed the source code in October 2026, other developers who had forked the project continue to publish their own versions of ARTEX in many other languages. In November 2026, the China-based cybersecurity company ThreatBook (微步在线) claimed ownership of ARTEX and began offering commercial access to “ARTEX Pro”, in addition to CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition and other AI-powered penetration testing frameworks.

AI agent architecture

ARTEX uses multiple AI agents for different functions. The threat actor defines the target scope, and a goals model breaks the engagement into objectives that can be verified. A planner agent continuously reviews a knowledge graph containing discovered assets and findings, then issues short attack directions called “intents.” Worker agents claim those intents and carry them out with a real shell and offensive tools. They write new assets, facts, and confirmed vulnerabilities back to the graph. Each update wakes the planner agent, which decides what to do next. The cycle continues until the goals are met or the task reaches its time or step limit. A reporter agent then documents each confirmed finding with reproduction steps and a proof of concept.

ARTEX AI agent architecture

The threat actor can configure ARTEX to power its agents with virtually any large language model, including frontier models, open-weight models, or models that the threat actor has abliterated (modified to remove built-in guardrails) or otherwise manually tuned. For that reason, ARTEX activity is not necessarily constrained by any single provider’s safety controls or visible in any single provider’s telemetry.

An optional pool function allows ARTEX to switch to different models when one fails for any reason (for example, quota exhausted, invalid key, rate-limited, or erroring). The function includes a configurable priority order and cooldown, so a long campaign can continue across multiple providers or keys.

Capabilities

ARTEX agents call tools to act on intents. While threat actors and agents can add arbitrary tools, ARTEX includes a set of pre-configured tools that define its core capabilities: network reconnaissance, web application mapping, web shell upload, and web browser-based attacks.

nmap — A network discovery and port-scanning tool that identifies systems, exposed services, and often their versions, rather than simply testing one connection

nc (netcat) — A general-purpose network utility for opening TCP or UDP connections, listening on ports, and moving raw data between systems

telnet — A basic interactive TCP client useful for manually probing text-based services

whois — A registration-data lookup tool that retrieves information about domain names or IP address allocations

dig — A DNS diagnostic tool

curl — A command-line HTTP and protocol client suited to crafting requests and inspecting responses, including headers, authentication, and APIs

wget — A web download utility

Playwright + Chromium — A browser-automation stack that drives a real Chromium browser, with all elements of the HTTP exchange exposed for manipulation

node — A JavaScript runtime

python3 — A general-purpose scripting runtime

git — A tool for retrieving and inspecting code repositories and their history

ripgrep — A fast recursive text-search tool for finding strings or patterns

jq — A command-line JSON processor that filters and transforms structured output from APIs and other tools

Threat actors also commonly add exploitation frameworks and credential attack tools to extend the capabilities of ARTEX agents:

sqlmap — A specialized web-application testing tool that detects and assesses SQL injection in application inputs

hydra — A parallelized credential-testing tool supporting many network login protocols and configurable username/password combinations

medusa — A modular, parallel network-login tester distinguished by its service-specific authentication modules

ncrack — A network authentication testing tool from the Nmap ecosystem, focused on high-speed testing of supported remote services

nuclei — A template-driven vulnerability scanner that checks targets for defined exposures, misconfigurations, and known issues across multiple protocols

nikto — A web-server scanner focused on potentially dangerous files, outdated components, and common server misconfigurations

gobuster — A wordlist-based discovery tool that enumerates web paths, DNS subdomains, or virtual hosts with a relatively focused command-line workflow

ffuf — A flexible web fuzzer that substitutes candidate values into chosen parts of a request, such as paths, parameters, headers, or hostnames

Msfconsole (Metasploit) — An exploitation framework and its interactive console, combining exploit modules, payloads, and post-exploitation workflows in one environment.

john (John the Ripper) — An offline password-auditing tool notable for broad hash-format support and adaptable cracking modes

hashcat — An offline password-recovery tool distinguished by GPU-accelerated candidate generation and hash testing

ARTEX agents can perform a wide range of actions, depending on the available tools and goals that the threat actor sets. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed ARTEX agents exhibiting the following capabilities as of November 2026:

Network reconnaissance

Port and service scanning

DNS enumeration

HTTP probing and content scraping

Importing assets from separate asset-scanning platforms

Web application reconnaissance

Retrieval of JavaScript bundles, source maps, runtime configuration files, and API documentation to extract routes

Headless-browser crawling, including with a simulated signed-in state

Enumeration of REST, WebSocket, and server-sent events (SSE) endpoints

Web application exploitation

Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in exposed software

Authentication bypass (for example, unsigned tokens and manipulated OAuth callbacks)

SQL injection

Server-side template injection

XML external entity (XXE) injection

File upload flaws

Insecure direct object references (IDOR)

Credential attacks

Weak-password testing

Password spraying

Brute force guessing

Abuse of account-recovery flows

Persistence

Web shell upload

Credential access

Reading secrets from configuration files, .env files, private keys, and /etc/shadow

Dumping databases

Kerberoasting

Lateral movement

Credential reuse

Cloud identity abuse

Authentication with stolen or captured credentials

Cloud permission mapping

Microsoft Graph reconnaissance

Adding application credentials for persistence

Assigning privileged roles for privilege escalation

Reading cloud keys and tokens, including from cloud secret management stores

Identifying ARTEX network activity

While ARTEX does not invent new attack techniques, it can combine the adaptable attack chain of a human threat actor with the speed and precision of malicious software. Therefore, the challenge of identifying network activity from AI-driven tools like ARTEX is differentiating it from both human- and software-driven activity.

Defenders can detect three types of evidence that may suggest AI-driven activity:

The most durable signal of AI-driven activity is the pattern formed by the bursts of machine speed activity. ARTEX agents, sometimes working in parallel, continually adapt and retry a given tactic until they succeed or run out of time. ARTEX agents quickly and exhaustively iterate through different methods of access, exploitation, or abuse. A human threat actor takes time to move from one stage of the attack chain to the next. In contrast, after successfully compromising a system or credentials, the framework then dispatches additional agents to move on to the next stage of the activity at machine speed. While ARTEX is a popular tool, other AI-driven offensive security frameworks also generate similar patterns of behavior.

Automated penetration testing tools, including the ones that ARTEX agents call, can produce a characteristically large volume of anomalous traffic from a single source in a short time. ARTEX does not obfuscate its malicious activity; a large number of these traffic bursts occurring at intervals is consistent with automated targeting.

A small amount of traffic might have user agent strings, network protocol options, or other default values strongly associated with ARTEX or the tools it calls. However, threat actors and ARTEX agents frequently change these values, particularly when evading static rules that block such values. The following table shows two such user agent strings specific to ARTEX:

Type

Value

Notes

User agent string

artex-enrich/*

Included with a short GET request to each newly discovered web asset that does not follow redirects, closes the connection, and reads only enough of the response to extract the page title.

User agent string

norma/*

Included with requests made directly by agents through their built-in web-fetch tool rather than through shell tools.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. Honeytokens can provide early warnings of AI compute hijacking. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

Identifying ARTEX system activity

After gaining initial access to a system, ARTEX agents often use well-known risky utilities (for example, certutil, curl, wget, netcat) on the system to launch web shells, install remote access trojans (RATs), or take other action to achieve persistence. Because ARTEX does not take any measures to obfuscate its malicious activity, existing methods for detecting compromise will likely capture ARTEX activity:

Web server processes (such as w3wp.exe, php-fpm, httpd or apache2, or Java application servers) starting sh, bash, cmd.exe, or PowerShell

New or modified script files (.php, .jsp, .jspx, .asp, .aspx, or .ashx) in web-accessible or upload directories; this includes files written by a database server process after its logging settings were changed to point a log file at a web directory

Several short-lived web shells with incrementing names, each running a different command, as ARTEX agents correct errors until a web shell runs cleanly

Rapid reads of /etc/shadow, .env and configuration files, private keys, and cloud credential files, and bursts of database extraction

Reverse shells and outbound requests from the server to webhook or file-sharing services used to deliver scripts and return command output

Two or three attack chains active at once, and renewed attempts through new paths after containment

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

ARTEX doesn’t introduce new attack techniques. It runs common penetration testing tools and tries one approach after another at machine speed. The mitigations that matter most close exposure before scanning finds it, slow down bursts of requests, protect credentials and application secrets, and contain a compromise automatically.

Reduce internet-facing exposure

Find and fix exposed assets first by using Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management discovery to inventory the internet-facing hosts, websites, and services you own, including ones you didn’t know about. Then prioritize fixes with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, which shows internet-exposed resources that lead to sensitive data or privileged identities. ARTEX agents start with port scans and web path enumeration and act on whatever they find.

Block and slow down attacks on web applications and APIs. After tuning in detection mode, switch Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway to prevention mode so that SQL injection and other common web attacks are blocked, not only logged. Add rate limiting on Application Gateway or rate limiting on Azure Front Door to cap how many requests one client can send in a short time, and turn on bot protection to block or log requests from known malicious IP addresses. For APIs in Azure API Management, follow Mitigate OWASP API security top 10 threats to enforce authentication, object-level authorization, and rate limits. ARTEX agents send hundreds of requests to learn which paths a server allows and harvest API documentation to find internal routes, then test them for injection, authentication bypass, and access-control flaws.

Map and test attack paths

Map what an exposed asset or stolen credential could reach before an agent does. Use attack paths in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and attack path analysis in Defender for Cloud to find defensive choke points, where paths to critical assets converge, and explore the blast radius of each one. Classify your critical assets so the paths are complete, and query the enterprise exposure graph in advanced hunting to explore the same connections. During an incident, blast radius analysis in the incident graph shows the paths an attacker could take from a compromised entity to a critical asset. ARTEX agents record the assets and vulnerabilities they discover in a graph, so mapping your own graph first shows where they would go next.

Test the paths that matter most, within Microsoft’s rules. Microsoft recommends regular red team operations to complement vulnerability scanning. Agree on the scope and constraints with resource owners and fix all critical findings. Testing of Azure resources must follow the penetration testing rules of engagement, which encourage testing your security monitoring and detection, prohibit automated testing that generates excessive traffic, and prohibit using secrets that aren’t your own, including publicly leaked ones. Agentic tools like ARTEX scan public code repositories for secrets, so decide before testing how testers will handle credentials that belong to someone else.

Organizations can incorporate Microsoft Perception’s Recon Agent to map relationships between Azure resources, Microsoft Entra ID identities, and permissions to identify potential lateral movement paths, privilege escalation opportunities, and high-value assets accessible following an initial compromise. Recon Agent’s Identify attack paths playbook searches for potential attack paths within an Azure subscription, while the Assess identity risks playbook investigates whether a managed identity could provide a path to critical assets. The Protect against a threat playbook correlates identified exposures with relevant threat intelligence. Because Perception’s Recon Agent performs read-only analysis rather than active exploitation, organizations should complement its findings with authorized penetration testing to validate viable attack paths.

Protect web servers

Run endpoint protection on every internet-facing server and keep it blocking. Use Defender for Endpoint on Linux and the Defender for Servers plan so that the endpoint detections and hunting queries in this report cover the servers that ARTEX agents exploit, including Linux servers. Turn on tamper protection, use EDR in block mode on Windows devices that run a non-Microsoft antivirus product, and turn on the Block Webshell creation for Servers attack surface reduction rule on Exchange servers.

Restrict outbound connections from web servers. Allow only the destinations each server needs, for example with Azure Firewall threat intelligence-based filtering, and create indicators for IPs, URLs, and domains in Defender for Endpoint to block known-bad destinations. ARTEX agents have used curl and netcat to download remote access trojans, and curl with rotating webhook.site URLs to deliver scripts and return command output.

Secure accounts and sign-ins

Apply Conditional Access to every user and workload identity. Create policies that require multifactor authentication (MFA) for all users, enforce phishing-resistant MFA for administrators, and block legacy authentication. Consider wider adoption of phishing-resistant passwordless authentication deployment to all users. Configure risk policies in Microsoft Entra ID Protection to require MFA or block access for medium-risk and high-risk sign-ins; sign-ins from known threat actor infrastructure, including infrastructure behind ARTEX activity, raise Verified threat actor IP detections at high risk.

For service principals, use Conditional Access for workload identities to block sign-ins from unexpected locations or with elevated risk; workload identity risk detections flag leaked credentials and suspicious sign-ins, including credentials found in public code on GitHub.

Ban weak passwords and slow down guessing. Turn on Microsoft Entra Password Protection with a custom banned password list, extend it to on-premises Active Directory, and review smart lockout settings. In one Storm-0940 campaign that used ARTEX, Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 failures per minute.

Protect application secrets and privileges

Keep application secrets out of code and replace any that leak. Use application management policies to limit which kinds of secrets and certificates apps can use and to enforce rotation, and move workloads to managed identities where possible. Turn on secret scanning and push protection for Azure DevOps repositories and secrets scanning in Defender for Cloud for virtual machines and cloud deployments and invalidate and replace any secret found in code or configuration files, including .env files. In one case that Microsoft observed, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Govern app registration, consent, and privileged roles by restricting app registration to the users who need it, configuring user consent so that users can’t grant broad permissions to unverified apps, and using app governance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to see which apps can reach your data. Use Privileged Identity Management for time-bound role activation, and monitor application credential changes and role assignments as described in the Microsoft Entra security operations guide for applications. During Storm-0940 activity, ARTEX agents added credentials to applications, and an application assigned itself the Global Administrator role.

Protect cloud resources and data

Limit what a stolen credential or token can reach. Follow best practices for Azure RBAC to limit each service principal to the resources and operations its application needs, and grant managed identities only the access they need so that a token taken from the Azure Instance Metadata Service through an XXE or SSRF flaw can’t reach other resources. ARTEX agents map the permissions of the credentials they capture and have used an XXE flaw to query a cloud metadata service for role credentials, and in one investigation AI agents used a compromised OAuth application to run scripts on Azure virtual machines.

Harden and monitor the services that hold secrets and data. Follow Secure your Azure Key Vault; for storage accounts, prevent Shared Key authorization and remediate anonymous read access to blob data; disable basic authentication for App Service publishing; and disable local authentication so that Foundry Tools accept only Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Then turn on Defender for Key Vault, Defender for Storage, Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for App Service, Defender for open-source relational databases, and AI threat protection for the workloads you run. ARTEX agents have run commands through cloud administration interfaces such as Kudu when they had credentials for them, and AI agents have focused on credentials for AI services.

Limit lateral movement and contain attacks automatically

Detect credential theft on domain controllers. Install Microsoft Defender for Identity sensors on all domain controllers. Its alerts, listed in the Detections section, cover the Active Directory credential theft and reconnaissance that ARTEX agents run in compromised domains.

Remove reusable passwords and standing access. Use group managed service accounts, whose passwords Windows manages automatically, so that service accounts don’t rely on passwords that people choose and rarely change. Use Windows LAPS to rotate each device’s local administrator password so that one captured password doesn’t work across many devices and use just-in-time machine access in Defender for Cloud to keep management ports such as RDP and SSH closed until they’re needed. ARTEX agents reuse captured credentials to move laterally over SSH and WinRM.

Enable automatic attack disruption to contain compromised assets that an attacker is using and limit lateral movement early, as well as automated investigation and response, which investigates and remediates alerts automatically. In multiple ARTEX-driven Storm-0940 intrusions, privileged access came less than three hours after initial targeting.

Title: US Treasury financial crimes unit becomes latest fed breach victim
Context: FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies...
Full Text: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline following unauthorized access, disrupting regulatory filings for financial institutions. An alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy, informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation. FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies and foreign government partners. In other words, it has some juicy info in its databases. “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” the alert states. “As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.” FinCEN hasn't said which systems intruders accessed, but clues in the deadline extension notice the agency posted alongside the warning suggest the disruption affects its reporting services for banks and other financial institutions required to submit reports detailing certain financial transactions and suspicious activity that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activity. FinCEN's Secure Data Transfer Mode, one method of submitting those reports, appears to be affected, as do services companies use to submit beneficial ownership information reports and individuals use to update their FinCEN identifiers. Eligible organizations and individuals with filings or updates due from November 18 through December 29 now have until December 30 to submit them. The Register has learned that there’s no evidence of any unauthorized access to Bank Secrecy Act data or beneficial ownership databases. That said, the investigation is ongoing - so that could change. “Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident,” a FinCEN official told us in an email. Several US government agencies have experienced cybersecurity incidents in recent months, including the ATF and the FBI, and reports emerged this week that intruders had also compromised an unclassified CIA system. While US authorities have linked previous cyberespionage campaigns to Chinese or other government-backed groups, financially motivated criminal groups have also targeted federal agencies. As the FinCEN breach is still under investigation, the agency hasn’t stated who may be involved and for what purpose. ®

Title: US Anti-Scam Surge Hits 800 Defendants and 29 Scam Compounds
Context: The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced the figures on November 24 as part of what it described as its largest anti-scam crackdown
Full Text:
US prosecutors have pursued more than 400 scam cases involving over 800 defendants across 85 federal districts since March.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced the figures on November 24 as part of what it described as its largest anti-scam crackdown. The effort followed Executive Order 14390, signed by President Donald Trump on March 6, which directed federal agencies to prioritize cybercrime and fraud.

The DOJ said 30 defendants had been extradited to the US, while US prosecutors and agents had supported law enforcement in more than 10 countries during raids on compounds and call centers that targeted Americans.

FBI Targets Scam Compounds

Under Operation Blackout, the FBI said it had helped disrupt or dismantle more than 29 scam compounds across the Middle East, Africa and Asia. The agency said it had restrained nearly $17bn in criminal funds and that more than 50 people allegedly linked to the scams had been federally charged, while partner countries had arrested or detained more than 320 others.

The FBI also reported helping free and return more than 2200 people trafficked into the compounds.

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said the department would not let scammers "hide behind their screens or escape justice by committing these crimes abroad."

The FBI credited Operation Level Up with stopping over $143m in losses to victims since March 6 and freezing more than $350m through its Recovery Asset Team.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

Crypto Freezes and BEC Cases

The US Secret Service reported restraining more than $200m and recovering over $119m, while disrupting 1780 domains run by scammers. It also had over 1540 cases of business email compromise (BEC) under investigation.

Its cases included a cryptocurrency investment fraud scheme, allegedly run by scam centers based in Cambodia, that went after at least 174 US victims. In October, the Netherlands extradited a Chinese national over his alleged role, and he was arraigned in federal court in California's Central District.

The State Department said it had funded work by US and Southeast Asian authorities that helped freeze over $1bn of stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fake websites and accounts.

The DOJ cited Gallup research estimating that scams cost Americans $68bn in 2025, with about one in 10 US adults affected either directly or via a household member.
