The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense
Context: Detection alone was never enough to stop machine-speed threats, but the issue is even worse in the era of AI attacks
Full Text:
The New Reality of AI Attackers

AI-driven attacks are on the rise, transitioning from theoretical risks to real-world threats. Recent investigations reveal that criminals are using AI to accelerate attacks at scale. We have observed attackers leveraging AI agents to execute context-aware commands with real-time decision-making. In one campaign that we observed, a highly persistent threat actor utilizing AI generated 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed over 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days whereas normal attackers usually do dozens of commands with a few scripts for similar time periods.

The behavioral difference between human operators and AI agents is staggering. In one attack we observed, humans acted followed by an agentic AI attacker. In the first (human attacker) phase, time between commands averaged roughly 24 seconds. The hackers made typographical errors, repeated manual checks and demonstrated environment confusion. On the other hand, in the agentic phase of the attack, we observed flawless, zero-syntax-error commands with a median gap of just 1.4 seconds.

When an AI agent is instructed to execute aspects of an attack, it rapidly scans networks, attempts to escalate privileges and utilizes legitimate native tools to blend in. Because of AI’s machine-speed execution, our Mean Time To Respond (MTTR) metrics must improve considerably. Attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates. If we wait hours to react, an AI agent can have already enumerated our cloud infrastructure and extracted or encrypted our data.

To effectively defend against AI-powered attacks, defenders must employ AI-powered tools. This should be done right where the attacks happen. Defenders should also strive to understand the behaviors that separate AI-based attacks from normal operations, whether fully autonomous or partially controlled by a human.

The Power of Edge AI and Layered Detection

To counter adversaries operating at automated speeds, defense must occur where the attack takes place. Leveraging AI on the edge, specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW), is a major strategic necessity. Edge-based AI can process telemetry instantly, making split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block active privilege escalation attempts locally.

Edge AI is also exceptionally fast. In our own product deployment, edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than taking minutes like agentic LLMs. It can function independently of cloud access or continuous network connectivity. This capabilities shift is crucial for several key reasons:

Even if an attack vector is used to temporarily disable network traffic to operate silently, local edge AI maintains detection coverage

It enables defenders to catch and isolate threats at the earliest possible stage

It safeguards sensitive corporate data locally without requiring telemetry or proprietary data to be transmitted to the cloud for analysis

The Defender’s Ultimate Advantage: Knowledge and Context

Despite their speed, agentic AI attackers have a foundational weakness that affects any attacker: They enter your environment without information. To operate, they must perform extensive reconnaissance, port sweeping and environment enumeration. This is where defenders hold the ultimate upper hand through comprehensive AI analytics.

Winning against machine-speed adversaries requires turning the advantage into real-time detection through automated data fusion and detection. By collecting telemetry across diverse network, endpoint, identity and cloud sources, normalization can map these distinct data streams into a single, cohesive schema. Advanced stitching can then merge related events across these disparate sensors into unified, context-rich stories rather than disconnected events.

Observing these integrated stories allows AI analytics engines to establish baselines of normal organizational behavior across the entire ecosystem. While establishing baselines has been longstanding best practice, AI analytics engines have made it easier for defenders to create these and keep them up to date.

Because threat actors lack this context, their automated attempts to rapidly map the terrain inevitably trigger detectors against established baselines, immediately exposing their presence across our detection layers.

Detection alone was never enough to stop machine-speed threats, but the issue is even worse in the era of AI attacks. Detecting an intrusion minutes after it begins still leaves defenders vulnerable if no immediate action is taken, and in those minutes an agentic AI attacker can cause significant damage to your organization. To truly close the loop against these attacks, organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response capabilities, enabling instant attack isolation and automated remediation before critical systems or data can be compromised.

The Basics Still Matter (But Require A New Approach)

While the sheer volume and speed of AI attacks can seem daunting, there is a positive takeaway: AI-empowered threat actors are not invisible, and their campaigns are entirely detectable. Every attack that we observed triggered alerts, and deep forensic investigations enabled us to reconstruct the attack lifecycles.

The cybersecurity basics still matter. The tools we have relied on as defenders in the past, including XDR solutions, network monitoring and active prevention rules, are still essential and relevant today. We do not need to throw away our playbooks; we simply need to use them differently. By utilizing our existing tools to automate isolation, leaning into AI on the edge for real-time response and trusting our baseline knowledge of our own environments, we are well-equipped to win against the next generation of threats. Crucially, unifying these tools into a cohesive SOC platform connects the dots across the enterprise — where vertical integration and correct platform usage ultimately drive vastly superior security outcomes.

If there’s one thing to take away from this, it is that Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond (MTTD and MTTR) are still king. But if we want to win these battles, detection and response times must drop to minutes, not hours.

To safeguard your organization against the unprecedented speed and adaptability of AI-driven threats, now is the time to evaluate your defense strategy. Ensure your enterprise is equipped with advanced detection and response capabilities, deploy robust security technologies across your endpoints, network, cloud and identity environments, and continuously refine their configurations to eliminate coverage gaps. Take action today to empower your security operation with the real-time visibility, automated response, and contextual intelligence needed to stay ahead of next-generation adversaries.

Title: Shufti Fraud Hub exposes suspicious links between seemingly legitimate accounts
Context: Shufti has announced the launch of its Fraud Hub, a connected fraud intelligence layer designed to detect suspicious verification attempts, identify coordinated fraud networks...
Full Text:
Shufti has announced the launch of its Fraud Hub, a connected fraud intelligence layer designed to detect suspicious verification attempts, identify coordinated fraud networks and monitor emerging risks across the user lifecycle.

Shufti Fraud Hub connects identity, device, biometric, and behavioural signals to help businesses spot threats that individual checks may miss and make context-aware decisions before fraud escalates.

Traditional fraud prevention often relies on assessing accounts individually, particularly during onboarding. Yet passing identity verification does not guarantee that an account will remain trustworthy.

Fraudsters can operate multiple accounts using different identities, shared devices or payment details, with coordinated behaviours that appear legitimate when examined separately. Even when one fraudulent account is blocked, others within the same network may remain undetected and continue operating.

Shufti’s Identity Fraud Report 2026, based on data from its verification network across 11 industries during the first half of 2026, found that 98.78% of linked fraud clusters involved two to ten identities. It also found that 65.68% of matches between separate fraudulent verification attempts involved the reuse of forged identity documents.

Shufti Fraud Hub brings these signals together through four layers of fraud detection: Capture Integrity, Device & Network Intelligence, Document Forensics, and Biometrics. This connected fraud intelligence identifies threats such as manipulated camera feeds, suspicious devices, forged or altered documents, and biometric attacks. The findings contribute to a unified real-time risk score, giving businesses a clearer understanding of potential fraud during identity verification.

Beyond individual verification attempts, Fraud Hub examines relationships across a business’s entire user base to identify suspicious connections, recurring fraud patterns, and coordinated activity. Its account clustering capabilities help uncover potential fraud rings by analysing shared devices, payment details, and behavioural similarities.

This can also help identify previously flagged users attempting to return with different account or identity information.

These capabilities are particularly relevant in industries where fraudsters exploit multiple accounts to evade individual checks. In iGaming, fraudsters may create multiple player accounts using different identities to exploit welcome bonuses, promotional offers, or referral incentives.

While each account may pass KYC independently, shared devices, payment methods, or behavioural patterns can reveal coordinated bonus abuse. Fraud Hub helps operators identify these connections, uncover suspicious player networks, and investigate potential multi-accounting before further losses occur.

A similar challenge exists in FinTech, where fraudsters may open multiple accounts using seemingly unrelated identities and devices, or return after an account has been blocked. Individual accounts may appear legitimate, but connections through shared devices, IP addresses, or recurring behavioural patterns can indicate coordinated fraud or attempts to bypass existing controls. Fraud Hub helps FinTech platforms recognise these relationships, identify repeat offenders, and assess risks before additional accounts or transactions are affected.

The hub also extends fraud detection beyond onboarding through continuous monitoring. Changes in account behaviour, new connections to suspicious profiles, or signs of repeated abuse can trigger further risk assessment. At critical moments, such as account reactivation or withdrawals, businesses can use current risk intelligence to determine whether additional verification or investigation is necessary.

For fraud and risk teams, this connected view changes the investigation process. Instead of reviewing disconnected alerts individually, investigators can examine relationships between suspicious accounts, understand the indicators contributing to risk, and prioritise cases that may represent a broader threat.

“Fraudsters don’t operate one account at a time, but fraud prevention systems often assess them that way. An account can pass every identity check and still become part of a coordinated fraud operation. Shufti Fraud Hub addresses this gap by connecting the signals and relationships surrounding each user, giving businesses the context to recognise emerging threats and make better risk decisions,” said Raja Hassan Fayyaz, Vice President of Product at Shufti.

Fraud Hub also supports Shufti’s Onboard, Monitor and Assure approach, connecting fraud detection during initial verification with ongoing risk intelligence and additional checks at critical points in the user lifecycle. Existing Shufti users can activate this fraud intelligence within their current verification integration, without additional SDKs, separate API calls, or changes to the user-facing verification journey.

Title: ShinyHunters Claims Comeback, New Inception Group Rejects Alleged Ties
Context: According to DataBreaches, the return of ShinyHunters was announced in a message posted on the Exploit cybercrime forum
Full Text:
Someone claiming to represent ShinyHunters has announced the notorious cybercrime group’s alleged return. Separately, the operators of a new extortion campaign named Inception have denied having ties to ShinyHunters.

According to DataBreaches, the return of ShinyHunters was announced in a message posted on the Exploit cybercrime forum. The post came from an account linked to ShinyHunters since 2020.

The message included the address of the new leak site and a new PGP key to authenticate future communications. Its authors also noted that they will not be active on other cybercrime forums and disavowed several hackers who claimed to be members of ShinyHunters.

The post’s authors attempted to establish their identity using a crypto key known to be associated with ShinyHunters, but DataBreaches noted that the original PGP key had reportedly been leaked.

Other threat actors have sought to capitalize on the ShinyHunters name and reputation, and the possibility that the comeback message is the work of impostors cannot be ruled out.

The announcement follows the arrest of several individuals suspected of being involved in ShinyHunters attacks, including a Canada-based cybersecurity expert, a Jordanian national believed to be group leader Rey, as well as a suspect in the Netherlands.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

New group Inception

The cybersecurity community has started tracking a new cybercrime group called Inception. Its leak site emerged earlier this month and lists several major US companies, including AMD, PepsiCo, Lucid Motors, Henry Schein, and Cigna Healthcare. The group has leaked hundreds of gigabytes of data allegedly stolen from these companies, but the data’s authenticity has not been independently verified.

According to research conducted by Okta, Inception may involve hackers previously associated with ShinyHunters. Okta has been tracking these hackers since March as O-UNC-053.

Okta says the cybercriminals’ phishing domain registrations dropped in September and October (around the time of the arrests), but activity picked up in November.

The company’s researchers previously saw organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 being listed on the ShinyHunters data leak site. After the ShinyHunters site went offline, they did not see O-UNC-053 victims being listed on any other website until November 16, when companies targeted by the group were named on the Inception website.

“We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the [data leak site] themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor,” Okta said.

Security researcher Dominic Alvieri has also suggested a possible connection between Inception and ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” Alvieri noted.

In a lengthy statement posted on its website, Inception denied having any connection to ShinyHunters.

“[Okta’s] evidence amounts to shared use of commodity services — domain registrars and CDN providers available to anyone — and overlapping targets. Neither constitutes operational linkage. We acknowledge that privately available tooling circulates among independent operators. Shared access to a service does not equate to shared identity,” the hackers wrote, adding, “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”

ReversingLabs has also monitored Inception’s activities and reported this week that it has uncovered phishing domains suggesting that the cybercriminals may have also targeted companies such as Anthropic, Amazon, Adobe, Nintendo, Netflix, OpenAI, and Tesla. There is no indication that any of them were successfully compromised.

The security firm identified 21 confirmed phishing domains and another 41 associated with the campaign with high confidence.

US Treasury’s FinCEN Disconnects Systems Following Cyber Incident
Context: The website is operational, but some FinCEN services may be temporarily unavailable, and the agency has extended the deadlines for qualifying filers affected by the disruption
Full Text:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the US Treasury Department’s financial intelligence unit, has disconnected some of its systems while investigating a cyber incident.

“FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline,” the agency said in a notice on the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing System website.

The website is operational, but some FinCEN services may be temporarily unavailable, and the agency has extended the deadlines for qualifying filers affected by the disruption.

“FinCEN is granting temporary, limited exceptive relief in response to a service disruption that is hindering filers’ ability to adhere to reporting obligations,” the agency said in a November 24 order (PDF).

The agency has not shared further details on the nature of the incident and made no mention of a potential data breach, but said it was working to return all systems to normal.

It is unclear who was behind the attack and if any data was accessed or stolen. SecurityWeek has emailed FinCEN for additional information and will update this article if the agency responds.

Title: Check Point security management servers hit in global cyberattack campaign
Context: “The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new...
Full Text:
An active intrusion campaign targeting Check Point security management servers has been uncovered, with confirmed attack activity observed between October 17 and November 2, 2026, impacting 22 organizations globally.

Tracked by cybersecurity firm GreyNoise as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), the campaign does not appear to be focused on a single region or industry. Impacted organizations span assets across the US, the UK, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, and Australia, across sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.

“The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique,” a Check Point spokesperson said. “Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity. The most important action is to install the available updates for CVE-2026-16232. Check Point has already released fixes and detailed mitigation and investigation guidance in its SecureKnowledge advisory.”

GreyNoise has not attributed GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group.

“An intrusion into a Check Point security management server is particularly serious because it is not just another server in the enterprise network. It effectively acts as the central control point for managing an organisation’s firewall infrastructure and security policies, with highly privileged access,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. He said that depending on the deployment and the level of access obtained, the consequences could extend well beyond the security infrastructure itself, potentially exposing sensitive data and critical business applications and disrupting enterprise operations.

Building the relay infrastructure

The threat actor operated across 99 IP addresses, primarily routed outbound through ExpressVPN or compromised Check Point devices, generating more than 1,400 network sessions, over 800 command-line artifacts, and over 1,200 created, uploaded, or downloaded files.

GreyNoise first observed the actor scanning and exploiting a Rejetto HFS server on October 2, 2026. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returned a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function.

Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm and thus recover an HFS session cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allowed the attacker to log in as admin without a password.

A few minutes later, GreyNoise observed that admin requests with forged session cookies were used to gain control of the server. This led GreyNoise to believe that exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The forged cookie contained “allow_session_ip_change:true”, allowing forged cookies to work from any IP address.

On October 5, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server, the research said. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Three days later, on October 8, the threat actor automation check in to the compromised server using the HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”.

Instead of using SSH access right away, on October 19, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. GreyNoise noted that it believes the idea was to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.

As the malware download failed, the threat actor returned with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay the next day.

On October 20, the threat actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) for setting up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, which they used to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from a scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point security management server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

Targeted intrusion

Once the compromised server was established as a relay, the actor used it to manage interactions with previously compromised Check Point devices, actively deepening their intrusion against Victim A while conducting bulk actions across 21 other victim organizations. Across the campaign, the operator relied on at least 30 Python scripts, including helpers, launchers, vulnerability probes, and exploit runners.

Between October 20 and 26, the attacker had a compromised Victim A asset download and run Chisel in client mode, allowing them to further scan and interact with Victim A’s environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232, the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point management servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

Between October 20 and 21, the attacker focused on Victim A, first using exploit.py (CVE-2026-16232) against one Check Point server before scanning a second with spray_portal.py. When that second device failed to report back to the relay box, the actor created pull_.py to steal credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configurations through the first compromised server.

The attacker then expanded inside Victim A’s network, running broad port scans with curl, telnet, nmap, and a domain controller probe, followed by targeted exploits against internal Microsoft Netlogon, Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware vCenter servers. They wrapped up this phase by running comb.py,ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py populated with victim-themed usernames and passwords.

On October 26, the operation shifted to bulk targeting. The actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers, including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. Results were shipped in a text file to the hop server that contained an incrementing IP order to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via SCP to this exfil folder. Although the task failed on every device, the error logs sent back to the hop server exposed victim IP addresses and revealed an /etc/ld.so.preload reference to /usr/lib/.libproc.so, pointing to a likely implant before activity paused until November 2.

GreyNoise suspects the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus including separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting.

Securing the management plane

Although GreyNoise’s direct visibility into the campaign paused around November 2, 2026, security leaders must still verify whether their environments have been quietly infiltrated.

With attackers planting backdoors on breached Check Point servers, CISOs must audit their environments for signs of quiet compromise.

To establish whether Check Point infrastructure has been compromised, CISOs and security teams should examine administrative login records for unusual access patterns, including unfamiliar IP addresses, unexpected login times, and unauthorised access added Dhar. They should also look for changes to firewall policies, access-control rules, and configuration files, and thoroughly review system logs, audit trails, and command execution history for suspicious activity.

Dhar noted that once there are indications of a compromise, the immediate priority should be to prevent further access and contain the damage. Security teams should restrict access to the management server to authorised administrative systems and isolate confirmed compromised systems while preserving forensic evidence. Unauthorised accounts should be disabled, suspicious SSH keys and access tokens revoked, and identified malicious IP addresses and domains blocked.

Executive summary: AI app builders give generated apps owner-level access

The Orca Research Pod found the same architectural mistake in multiple independent AI app builder platforms. Code the platform generates inherits the authority of the build environment.

These platforms build the app inside their own trust boundary and never take it back out. As a result, the generated app gets owner-level authority over the developer’s connected accounts and backend. The developer never granted that authority, can’t see it and can’t revoke it.

Key findings

Across several platforms, we confirmed that generated applications could do the following. In some cases, so could anonymous visitors to those apps.

Act as the account owner on connected third-party services

Read live database credentials belonging to other customers

Call privileged backend functions that bypass row-level security entirely

Reach platform secrets from inside the build sandbox

In none of these cases did the developer misconfigure anything. The authority is there by default, in the environment, before the first line of application code is written.

What is ambient authority in AI app builders?

Ambient authority is privilege that sits in the surrounding environment instead of being granted to a specific caller for a specific purpose.

An AI app builder has to be powerful to be useful. To scaffold a working application, it needs to write files, install dependencies, provision a database, commit to your repository and read the services you connected. So the platform gives its build environment broad authority over your accounts.

Then it puts your application in that same environment. Nothing separates the two. The credential the agent used to build the app is still there when the app runs, and the app can read it just as easily as the agent could.

The pattern isn’t one vendor’s bug. It keeps showing up because every builder faces the same design pressure:

Platform

What the generated app is handed

A major AI app builder

A plaintext environment variable that acts as a bearer credential for the account owner on every connected third-party service

A major AI app builder

A live platform session token in the agent’s environment, plus an unauthenticated internal LLM proxy billing the vendor’s own account

A generated backend

Supabase edge functions holding a service-role key, with the JWT gateway defaulted off

A build sandbox

Platform secrets readable by any process running inside it

Three ways AI app builders leak credentials in the wild

One environment variable exposes every connected service

On a major AI app builder, a single plaintext environment variable is present in every project. It authorizes the caller as the account owner across the account’s connected services: GitHub, Gmail, Slack and Drive. The GitHub connector’s scope is full repository access, read and write, private repositories included.

The platform’s AI agent isn’t involved at any point, and that matters more than it first appears. Undocumented endpoints return each connector’s raw OAuth access token, which then works directly against GitHub or Google. No request passes through the platform, so the platform’s logging, rate limiting and revocation never see the traffic.

Three properties make this worse than a typical leaked secret:

Collaborators inherit it. Any project collaborator gets the token through the shared shell, with no planted code and no remix. Revoking the invitation doesn’t revoke tokens they’ve already taken.

The token is portable and long-lived. It’s signed, not encrypted, so anyone holding it can read its claims. Replayed from an unrelated laptop, it still returned the account’s data.

The platform’s scanner misses it. The platform’s own security scanner reports code that exfiltrates the variable as clean. The control users trust to tell them a project is safe says it’s safe.

An unprotected API endpoint leaks database credentials across tenants

At another builder, which we’re not naming, a single API endpoint returned any project’s database integration to any logged-in user of the platform. That included a live database key and the full project configuration. Nothing checked that the caller owned the project, and project IDs were small sequential integers.

Counting through one ID range returned live credentials for thousands of projects across dozens of organizations. That included projects hosted in customers’ own third-party database accounts. The keys are genuine and long-lived. We confirmed cross-tenant reads against multiple unrelated tenants. We also reproduced the issue on a project created during testing, so new projects were affected too.

Where row-level security wasn’t configured, the credentials led straight to the data behind them. Most sampled databases also had email auto-confirm and open signup turned on. An attacker with a leaked key could register a confirmed account and reach everything the authenticated role can see, which is usually far more than the anonymous role.

AI-generated Supabase edge functions bypass row-level security

The third instance involves no platform defect at all. Nothing is broken on the platform’s side. The AI wrote the vulnerability and shipped it.

Ask a builder for an app with a database, and it generates Supabase edge functions to do the work. Many of those functions hold a service_role key, Supabase’s administrative credential, which bypasses row-level security entirely. One builder also ships them with the JWT gateway turned off, so the function answers anyone who calls it. The result is an unauthenticated endpoint holding a key that ignores every access control you configured.

Those defaults come from the generator, not Supabase. The pattern lasts because developers have no reason to suspect it. One developer recorded the belief in a source comment: “The Publishable Key is the successor to the anon key: it is public and safe for client-side code (Row-Level Security protects the data).”

That’s correct, and it matches Supabase’s own guidance. It’s also beside the point, because the app’s own service_role function goes straight around row-level security. The developer secured the front door of a house with no back wall.

This is why teams need to catch risky code before it reaches production, including code an AI agent wrote.

Why prompt injection defenses don’t stop AI app builder credential leaks

The obvious reading of any AI platform vulnerability is prompt injection. Here, it’s the wrong one.

We tried it. On a major AI app builder, the agent resisted every prompt injection attempt we made. Plain application code then walked straight past it, because the code didn’t need to persuade the agent of anything. It just read a variable.

Injection is one delivery route among many. The real defect is that the authority is ambient in the first place. It sits in the environment, where any code and any collaborator can reach it, and in one case any anonymous visitor too. Defenses placed at the agent don’t protect a credential that lives next to it.

That distinction decides where the fix has to go. Guardrails on the model aren’t a control over the environment.

How to secure apps built with AI app builders

Several of these issues were still unfixed when we wrote this. These steps don’t depend on a vendor fix:

Assume the generated app can reach every connected integration. Connect only the services a project needs, at the narrowest scope the builder will accept, and disconnect the rest. Identities with too much access are where this risk starts, so reduce identity-based cloud risk across these connections.

Rotate keys for any project built on these platforms. Treat platform-issued tokens as compromised if a project was ever shared, remixed or made public.

Turn on row-level security for every table, then check it. A table with RLS enabled but no policy isn’t a protected table.

Audit generated backend functions for service-role keys. Confirm each function authenticates its caller, and turn the JWT gateway on. Unauthenticated functions are effectively exposed APIs, so find and secure unmanaged APIs as part of the audit.

Inventory the pair, not just the app. The risk object is the generated application plus the managed database behind it. Neither half alone tells you what’s exposed, so find and protect sensitive data across your cloud behind every generated app.

Frequently asked questions about AI app builder security

Are AI app builders safe to use?

They can be. But this research shows that generated apps can inherit owner-level access to connected accounts by default, so scope integrations narrowly and audit what gets generated.

Does Supabase row-level security protect AI-generated apps?

Not if a generated edge function uses the service_role key, because that key bypasses RLS entirely.

Is this a prompt injection problem?

No. In our testing, plain application code read the credential directly without involving the agent.

How can Orca help secure AI-generated applications?

Orca’s unified cloud security platform brings the full AI footprint into a single risk model alongside your cloud context: the models and MCP servers teams connect, the code AI agents write and the applications AppGen platforms generate.

Orca also helps security teams uncover apps built with AI tools, so generated applications and the data behind them don’t sit outside security’s view. Because Orca sees those connections together, it can surface the issues that turn a generated app into a breach path: overprivileged identities and integrations, exposed secrets in code, unauthenticated APIs and sensitive data without the right protections. Orca then prioritizes them by what an attacker could actually reach. Teams can keep building with AI at full speed while security keeps pace, without adding agents or slowing developers down.

In this article

About 2 billion login records were exposed, some apparently stolen by malware. Some files were labeled “US”

A separate database held 840 million Chinese ID numbers and 11 million student records

If you suspect malware, use a clean device to change affected passwords and sign out everywhere

Two unsecured databases have exposed billions of records, ranging from passwords and browser cookies to national ID numbers and children’s school details. Researchers discovered the databases separately, and the two appear to be unrelated. Both illustrate how personal information from different sources can end up together in a searchable collection.

Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the larger database, which contained approximately 2 billion login records spread across 8,471 folders. Some files were labeled by country, including the US, though it’s unclear how many US residents were affected. The database required no password to access and stored credentials and account details in plaintext.

Fowler reported that the exposed material included:

Email addresses, usernames, passwords, and associated login URLs.

Browser cookies, session tokens, and other authentication information.

Saved application credentials and browser data.

Device and operating-system information.

Logs that appeared to contain autofill information and cryptocurrency wallet data.

Fowler also identified approximately 400,000 documents that appeared to come from malware capable of creating more detailed collections about individual victims.

That makes this more than a list of passwords. Some of the material could help an attacker connect a person’s accounts, identify their device, and potentially access an account where the person was already signed in.

Fowler could not identify the database’s owner. He notified its hosting provider, and public access was restricted several days later. How long it had been exposed, and whether anyone else accessed it, remain unknown.

In the separate discovery, researcher Greg Pollock identified an Elasticsearch server exposing approximately 259 GB of data on people in mainland China. Anyone who knew its address could search it without a password. Its 99 indices contained almost 1.64 billion records linking names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, student information, and business registrations. These included at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers and about 11 million student enrollment records. Some student records linked a child’s name to their school, class, and a parent’s contact details.

This database brought together information from identity registration, education, telecommunications, payment, and business systems. Based on how the records were organized, UpGuard believes someone combined them to create an illicit identity-lookup service.

Pollock could not identify the operator. During his investigation, the server became inaccessible, apparently following a ransomware or other destructive attack. Other copies of the data may still exist.

Are your details being used by cybercriminals?

FIND OUT HERE

How to stay safe

If malware stole your login details, changing affected passwords is a good start. Use a clean device to make those changes, and sign out of existing sessions in case someone also has the cookies that keep you logged in.

Check for infection. Run a scan with a trusted anti-malware product. If you suspect an active infostealer infection, disconnect the affected device and use a separate, clean device for urgent account recovery. Otherwise, malware could capture replacement passwords too.

Secure your most important accounts first. Start with your primary email, followed by banking, payment, work, and other sensitive accounts. Replace exposed or reused passwords with unique ones, using a password manager to generate and store them.

Enable multifactor authentication. An authenticator app or security key adds protection against someone signing in with a stolen password.

Sign out existing sessions. Look in your account’s security settings for an option such as “sign out everywhere,” “log out of all devices,” or “revoke active sessions.” Removing malware and changing passwords do not necessarily stop someone using an already stolen session token.

Watch for financial and identity misuse. Review account activity and credit reports for transactions or accounts you don’t recognize.

Review unsolicited messages with extra care. If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard. It’s free and can help you assess the message and decide what to do next.

You can replace a password. Details like the school you attended can stay useful to scammers for years. If an unexpected caller or message mentions something personal, verify who you’re dealing with before sharing information or sending money.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Title: Credential Remediation Is Slow When You Don’t Know What Will Break
Context: GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those...
Full Text:
TL;DR

More than 64% still valid after four years: GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that most valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, because teams stall on what a revoke will break.

Validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets: Prioritize by impact instead, weighing what a credential can access and whether it leaked publicly, and update the risk score as new context arrives.

Revoke last, never first: Issue a replacement, store it in the vault, switch every consumer to the vault call, deploy and monitor, then revoke the original and confirm it no longer authenticates.

Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI connect securely to data, services, and each other. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, but credential remediation is where many secret security programs bog down. This is the second of three articles we are releasing to explain how we help address detection, remediation, and prevention.

The first article in this series, “The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It,” covered detection across every surface where credentials live. Just knowing they exist is not enough. Teams need to take action to remediate those findings. To do that, they need context around every credential they find.

Without the right context, it is impossible to know what risks the secret carries. It is also difficult to understand which systems rely on those secrets and the risk levels that revoking the secret brings. Nobody wants to break production, but we also cannot allow attackers to leverage those secrets.

The resulting decision paralysis leaves many teams struggling to rotate immediately. Sometimes it can take years for the secret to be revoked finally. That is actually all too common, as shown by GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research that found that 64% of valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, a full 4 years later.

It would be great if there were a one-size-fits-all solution for remediating every leak; in reality, each one is tied to a specific integration. What we can do is streamline the processes needed to get to the end, making it much easier for organizations of any size. And it does take the whole organization to properly deal with leaked secrets.

Why credential remediation is so hard for so many teams

A team that discovers an exposed credential rarely has all the authority or knowledge needed to fix it without causing further issues. A security engineer can see it’s valid and dangerous, but that security engineer usually cannot immediately tell which services will fail when it is revoked. Breaking production is considered a much higher risk than the possibility of a stolen and abused secret, so they need to go looking for answers, which is a time-consuming process.

The developers who know where and why a key is used and, hopefully, how to rotate it safely are often busy shipping new features and managing existing requests from the business. An alert in their email that shows only a file path and a secret type asks those busy devs to stop their workflow and launch their own investigation. These requests, all too often, sink into the backlog.

At the same time, the larger the organization, the harder it is to find the right person who knows the answer to “what breaks if this key is revoked?” Application security teams monitor code where keys are used, identity and access management (IAM) teams govern identities that were issued keys, and the Platform Engineering team runs the vaults holding the keys. They all have different perspectives and, in most organizations that are early in their secrets security maturity journey, can only tell part of the story.

Endpoint security teams are also watching what happens at the workstation level. They are beginning to track secrets stored there, as software supply chain attacks have increasingly targeted these plaintext credential stores over the last couple of years. A secret leaked here might even be the triggering event for the rotation in case of compromise from an infostealer. The endpoint team is historically not connected to AppSec or Platform teams.

One credential can touch all these teams while each individual, isolated group sees only its own slice of the credential layer. Now, multiply the communication and coordination issue across hundreds or thousands of potential leaks, and the scale of the remediation problem becomes clearer.

Action before investigation invites downtime

The risk of revoking before fully understanding the fallout is fairly high for the business. This is weighed against potential future abuse. Of course, this math changes during an active breach when the clock is ticking and when exfiltration or lateral movement is already occurring. Those emergencies do not get backlogged. Mature organizations understand that addressing leaks before an emergency arises is the better plan overall, but remediation times are still measured in weeks for most teams. How long a remediation process takes really boils down to how fast and accurately responders can gather and communicate information about the issue. Responders need to know a lot of things, starting with whether the credential works, what it can access, and who owns it before they can even ask questions like “where else does it appear?” and “which systems depend on it?”

For example, envision two valid cloud credentials. One grants read-only access to a single storage bucket, and the second one is a root-level key with administrative control over production. While their privileges and dependent workloads determine the appropriate level of urgency, both require the same level of insight and investigation to triage the remediation process and decide whether the response is a rotation next sprint or a revocation this very second.

The ultimate goal is to remove the leaked key rapidly, but in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds. Rotating secrets safely simply requires resources and a coordination plan. If this process is always piecemeal and manual, then mistakes are more likely to happen.

A security team that causes an outage once will face resistance the next time it asks to rotate anything.

Prioritize by impact, not just validity

Validity is the first and clearest signal most responders look at. Alone, this is an incomplete signal. GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those secrets cannot be verified automatically.

While validity still matters, access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency. If the leak happened publicly on the internet, that raises the urgency even further. Any risk scoring needs to explain which factors drove it. It also needs to be a living risk score, adjusting for new information as new context arrives. Scoring it once upon discovery is akin to trusting an initial CVSS score in a CVE disclosure. It is a helpful guide but needs to be updated based on what is really going on in your organization. The organization and its risk tolerance will decide what happens next. Having as much information centrally available as possible is key to a rapid response, as responders reach the boundaries of what systems they can actually touch.

Route the work to the right people who can push the change

Remediation requests should let the developer or platform team act immediately, without requiring the team to repeat the investigation that has already taken place.

Any request to replace a key for a production system should include validity and known exposure locations. It should list dependencies too, and where possible show how it connects to business operations. The more the person picking up the request understands about the issue, the sooner they can act. In an ideal world, all remediation requests would be routed to their named owners. In the messy reality of the enterprise, you will likely need to involve the developer who leaked the secret and gather data from commit attribution or source metadata. We need to establish communication because there is a probability that they will need further instructions or guidance.

Requests should not be ‘thrown over the fence’ and then forgotten about. Follow-up and confirmation about remediation progress should be centrally collected and shared so every department knows where the rotation process is at any given moment. This accountability proves resilience efforts when an auditor shows up.

Engineers need to be enabled with a clean way to communicate once they start the work and once their ticket is ready to close. Routing the work through existing ticketing tools keeps it alongside other engineering work, but those tickets also need to integrate with the responder’s security operational tooling.

Rotate, revoke, and vault: the order matters

Safe rotation means following a specific set of steps, in the right order, so you don’t break anything. Remember: “Availability” is one of the legs of the CIA (confidentiality, integrity, availability) security triad.

For mature organizations, this could be as straightforward as rotating the secret in a vault, since the production applications and systems relying on the credential are all already consuming it from the secrets manager. Any plaintext copies are then rendered harmless once the original offending secret is revoked.

For organizations and situations where no existing vaulted copy is in use, this process often starts with issuing a replacement credential. If the responder can do this, they should do so immediately and store it safely in the vault. Then, replace every occurrence of the plaintext secret with that vault call, across every known consumer. The remediation steps from there are to push the changed code or config live and monitor for any issues, ready to roll back if anything breaks. Only when all the new systems are safely consuming the new vaulted credential appropriately can the team revoke the original. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident.

GitGuardian’s service account credential rotation checklist covers these steps in detail.

Verify the fix and keep the evidence

Only close the ticket when the key is safely revoked, and the danger is removed. There needs to be an audit trail about what you fixed and how you proved that. You need verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Optionally, and depending on the circumstances, you can show that the old secret was removed from all surfaces.

Any incidents closed while the credential remains valid deserve their own review queue. This common case happens when a team rotates a key in one system while the old key remains active and valid in another. This means a siloed team only accounted for their one occurrence in their tooling that lacks a unified view or relies on manual tracking.

The incident record also serves auditors and security leaders. It shows what was found, who acted, and how long remediation took.

One credential, start to finish with GitGuardian

At GitGuardian, we have helped thousands of developers and organizations streamline their remediation process.

To help visualize how we can help, imagine a Kubernetes application that calls an external service with an API key stored in a secrets manager. During troubleshooting in our imagined scenario, a developer copies the key into a local configuration file and commits it. This is a fairly common scenario we have seen play out many times.

GitGuardian scanning finds the secret as soon as it is committed. The platform generates a new open incident and alerts the assigned team. An automatic validity check confirms the key is still active, and the Secret Analyzer lists its permissions. A presence check confirms the secret is still in the codebase. All these checks can be rerun as remediation progresses.

For customers with full platform integrations, the GitGuardian Exploration Map shows a production workload depending on it, and fingerprint matching ties the committed value to the vaulted copy. The security team can bring that context to the owning developer and operations team.

Once a replacement key is issued, everyone can track the progress of the rotation and see when the PR that accounts for the deployment configuration is pulling from the vault. There is no guessing about whether revoking the original will affect anything critical. GitGuardian then rechecks validity and confirms the committed copy is gone.

The incident might also expose a pattern worth investigating across other teams. Has this same codebase seen similar incidents? Has the same user caused the same issue before? Are vaulted credentials ending up in unmanaged files on developer laptops on a regular basis? These all point to a wider issue that needs to be addressed to prevent further incidents and an increased remediation backlog.

From fixing to preventing

Remediation reduces risk one credential at a time. It also shows where exposures keep coming from.

The third and final article in this series covers prevention, starting on developer machines and in AI coding workflows. Teams that want to see this remediation workflow can take an interactive tour of the GitGuardian platform.

Take a Guided Tour of GitGuardian

FAQ

What is credential remediation?

Credential remediation is the work of removing the risk from a leaked or exposed credential. The goal is to replace and revoke the leaked key quickly, in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds, and then to confirm the old credential no longer authenticates.

Why does credential remediation take so long?

The team that finds an exposed credential rarely has the authority or the knowledge to fix it alone. A security engineer can see the credential is valid and dangerous, but usually cannot tell which services will fail when it is revoked. The developers, identity, platform, and endpoint teams each see only their own slice of the credential layer, so responders spend their time gathering context instead of fixing the leak.

How do you prioritize which leaked credentials to fix first?

Prioritize by impact, not validity alone. GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that validation-only prioritization misses 46% of critical secrets, because some secrets cannot be verified automatically. Access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency, and a public leak raises it further. The risk score should explain which factors drove it and change as new context arrives.

What is the safe order for rotating a leaked secret?

Issue a replacement credential and store it in the vault. Replace every plaintext copy of the old secret with a call to the vault, across every known consumer. Push the changed code or configuration live and monitor for issues, ready to roll back. Revoke the original only when every system is consuming the new vaulted credential. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident.

How do you verify that a leaked credential has been remediated?

Close the ticket only when you have verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Keep an audit trail of what was fixed and how it was proved, including who acted and how long remediation took. Incidents closed while the credential is still valid deserve their own review, since a team may have rotated the key in one system while it stayed active in another.

Title: US Treasury Investigates Cyber Incident Amid Reported Federal Agency Breaches
Context: The US Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said on November 25 it is "investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access...
Full Text:
The US Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said on November 25 it is "investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems."

FinCEN, which handles reports about financial crimes including money laundering, trafficking and terrorism financing, said it has taken some services offline as a proactive measure.

However, the agency noted that the Bank Secrecy Act Electronic Filing (BSA E-Filing) System, a secure online system to submit BSA reports electronically, is still operational.

In addition, FinCEN said it has extended deadlines for financial institutions to file required documents.

“If a financial institution needs to expedite the delivery of suspicious activity information to law enforcement, filers can use the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not impacted by this service disruption,” FinCEN added.

This comes as several US federal agencies, including the FBI, the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) have recently started investigating data breaches reportedly targeting criminal records like the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database as well as unclassified intelligence information.

Infosecurity has approached FinCEN for comment.

Title: Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach
Context: The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed
Full Text: London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records. A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited. AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically. Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go. The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected. Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations. The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases." Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated. Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues. Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected. Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual. The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details. Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information. Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded. "The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest. "Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

Title: The ‘True Crime Community’ Is Inspiring Violent Attacks Through TikTok
Context: One independent researcher, Ry Terran, pointed out that accurately tracking this movement is difficult given the dense nature of the language they use around attacks
Full Text:
“Algorithmically driven engagement has supercharged its spread,” the report’s authors wrote. “Unlike Tumblr, where the fandom is largely isolated, TikTok actively works to expose users to new content through its algorithm, resulting in TCC videos being served to a much larger audience.”

Finkelstein says that while TikTok does remove some of the accounts his team flags to the platform, in general the company is not doing enough to combat the problem.

“[TikTok’s] capacity to manage this is very spotty,” Finkelstein said. “This is an uncontained open wound. Whatever measures they think they're making to manage this are obviously inadequate to deal with the damage that the community is unleashing. If you took TikTok offline for a few weeks, my guess is these attacks would slow down because there's not a permission structure in place that's encouraging vulnerable youth to go out and murder people in order to be famous with their peers because they're so depressed and living in their mom's basement and spending 10 hours a day on social media.”

TikTok, whose US operations are now owned primarily by a group of investors including Oracle, controlled by GOP megadonor and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison, said it had rules in place to proactively remove TCC-linked content.

“We enforce strict rules against content that promotes violence or glorifies perpetrators of mass violence, and we had already banned a large number of the accounts in this report,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED.

WIRED shared the report with several other researchers who closely track TCC activity online, and all broadly concluded that NCRI’s assessment was accurate. One independent researcher, Ry Terran, pointed out that accurately tracking this movement is difficult given the dense nature of the language they use around attacks.

“When examining perpetrators' social media, I see that they frequently frame threats as a joke, a LARP, or AI-generated,” Terran tells WIRED. “Social media companies should not take these claims at face value, but rather report any credible threats. Without appropriate interventions, TCC-inspired attacks will likely continue to increase.”

Another European-based researcher, who requested anonymity due to fears of retaliation, tells WIRED, “We're panicking here in Europe.” The researcher collaborates with European law enforcement agencies and says they are concerned about the increasing number of attacks taking place globally.

Finkelstein says that US lawmakers and law enforcement need to do more in order to combat this problem. “The FBI seems to want to deal with it by arresting kids. None of this makes any sense,” he says. “We've got to step back and see the scale of this. We should be turning to our law enforcement agencies and our national security apparatus that has the ear of the president and say something's got to be done about this.”

The FBI declined to comment, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security referred WIRED to the FBI.

“The Justice Department remains vigilant against the threat of such violent extremist networks that operate within the United States and around the globe,” Wyn Hornbuckle, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, tells WIRED.
