Title: The Great Escape: Tradecraft insights from an agentic swarm
Context: Further research will be required going forward to grapple with the emergence of agentic attack frameworks and pinning down the meaningful surface area they have for detection...
Full Text:
The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records and offers an unprecedented view into how multi-agent AI systems operate and coordinate at scale.

Distilling and documenting the swarm tradecraft may help defenders understand multi-agent operations and communication, and how agents adapt when a path is blocked.

Some documented behaviors may transfer to more purpose-built cyber attack frameworks like ARTEX, including methods to persistently store results, the burst-and-pause timing patterns of reasoning loops, and the self-labeling conventions that can reveal workload assignments and distribution.

Beginning in June 2026 and extending for several months, a collection of OpenAI models conducting internal training and evaluation tasks broke out of their containerized environments and accessed websites and databases via the public internet in ways the company says it did not authorize.

This activity represents a new kind of cyber event: not a malicious intrusion, but an unintentional series of consequences stemming from an agentic swarm, a group of AI agents exhibiting coordinated behavior toward a shared objective. A swarm implies many agents but doesn’t have a rigid count. The main distinction is behavioral; the collective activity of a swarm becomes complex and unpredictable even when individual agents may be explainable. This swarm provided an initial, public glimpse into the behavior and coordination of autonomous, multi-agent operations.

Due to constraints in their evaluation environment, the OpenAI swarm used public internet services as improvised infrastructure, which made the activity visible and traceable. The behaviors exposed revealed methods for persistent probing, iterative payload development, work partitioning and coordination across agents, and adaptation to execution constraints, in ways that are likely to be relevant for understanding agent behavior beyond this just case.

Agentic cyber attack frameworks are now appearing in intrusion activity, with the ability to support scaling to multi-agent operations. These attacker swarms largely replace the use of public internet resources with purpose-built infrastructure that removes some of the artifacts visible. However, documenting our understanding of operational swarm techniques can give defenders a baseline for recognizing behaviors as they move into new environments and contexts. In some cases, we can already see the evidence where these techniques do transfer.

In this post, we’ll explore and document the tradecraft of the escaped OpenAI swarm and conclude by comparing it to early signals and behaviors from the current agentic attack activity seen in the wild.

Background

Swarms are an important concept to track because they can divide work across parallel agents, potentially completing complex tasks faster, though the gains depend on the task and the quality of coordination. Parallel agent coordination was crucial to OpenAI’s ability to solve the Navier-Stokes Millenium Prize Problem, which arrived at a winning solution with a group on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents over the course of 88 hours.

Early evidence suggests swarms transfer effectively to cyber attack problems. The main factors for swarm efficiency are how parallelizable the tasking is, and if the attackers want to pay the inflated token cost. A rough example is using four agents on the same problem, to get it done twice as fast; as Noam Brown of OpenAI said on a Dwarkesh podcast, “Because there are four agents working for half as long, you’re paying 2x more to get an answer twice as quickly.”

AI models undergoing training and evaluation operate inside sandboxed computing environments. These are controlled workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and iterate toward solutions. These environments are designed to be both enabling and constraining. They give models room to practice, while limiting what they can reach and do, so that mistakes or misaligned behavior stay contained.

Operating under constraint

While the techniques employed by the OpenAI swarm may have crossed the thresholds of intended use, they should not be viewed as malicious intent. A useful framing for understanding these techniques is creativity under constraint. The agents were optimized to meet their objectives, and they displayed considerable persistence and ingenuity to that end.

The constraints the agents were working around were layered and understanding them helps explain the motivation behind every technique. The most fundamental was the absence of a browser runtime: Agents operating in text and code environments cannot natively load JavaScript-heavy pages, call browser APIs, or interact with dynamic web content. The creative solution was submitting URLs to a public scanner like “urlquery.net” which provided a real Chromium instance on demand.

This workaround by itself, however, was still not enough. Browsers apply a security rule called the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one website generally cannot read data from another. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) lets a destination website explicitly permit access. The agents used public CORS proxies to relay requests when target websites did not grant permission.

They also lacked infrastructure of their own to host payloads or receive data, so they relied on public services such as httpbin, httpbun, and "webhook.site" services capable of testing HTTP requests and responses but not designed for this activity.

In some evaluation environments another constraint applied: Agents appear to have been restricted to GET requests only, with no ability to make outbound POST calls. That is likely what pushed them toward using public wikis as shared state stores, as wiki page edits are a write operation achievable through ordinary browser navigation.

The tradecraft

In response to their constraints and in persistent pursuit of their objectives, the swarm developed and refined its tradecraft over time. This included chaining legitimate web services like URL shorteners, CORS proxies (services that relay requests to bypass browser security restrictions), Base64 decode endpoints (services that decode encoded data back into executable web pages), and markdown renderers into extraction pipelines that never required dedicated attacker infrastructure.

Talos observed structured work partitioning across parallel agent instances, iterative probe development, and sandbox identification techniques. The agents coordinated using a variety of identifying tags (e.g., uqscan=claude..., CHATGPTTEST1, OAI_META_1312, archive_test=20261004). These self-labels, intended as internal tracking strings, became the primary cross-campaign fingerprint linking multiple disparate operations.

To better understand the flow, we will detail the activity of the swarm in a seven-step chain, aligning the purpose of the action with the publicly accessible internet services used.

Figure 1. Seven-step sequence of swarm data collection activity.

A separate orchestration layer, Coordinate (COORD), runs above the chain rather than within it. When multiple agents execute the same chain in parallel, COORD governs how work is divided between them — for example, URL shorteners (“da.gd”, “is.gd”) distribute identical payloads to multiple instances; structured identifiers (?uniq0–19, node=, validation=v<unix>_<county>_<req>) partition tasks and track completion. The COORD layer distinguishes a swarm from a single agent running sequentially.

Evolution and execution

The swarm's operational techniques evolved over time. Early activity relied on silent CDX enumeration, querying public web archive indexes to map target sites and using a single exit node. By the peak operational phase, the swarm was running against multiple simultaneous targets with structured work partitioning, sandbox identification, and covert exfiltration beacons. To better understand these events, we can reconstruct from public records the unauthorized access to Australian government websites.

Traced extraction demonstration

Step 1 — RECON: Enumerate target via Common Crawl CDX

The agent silently maps the target site structure by querying Common Crawl's CDX, a searchable database of every URL the archive has ever crawled. This allows enumeration of all potentially relevant target URLs, without the server ever being contacted.

Figure 2. Enumerating target URL directory.

The request in Figure 2 returns archived URL paths, MIME types, timestamps, and status codes. The agent discovers objective-relevant Tableau visualization endpoints at “vizprod.aihw.gov.au” without ever touching AIHW servers.

Effect: Agent identifies the target: vizprod.aihw.gov.au/t/Public/views/AGE-115/...

Step 2 — CRAFT: Build extraction payload

The agent writes a self-contained HTML page with embedded JavaScript. This payload uses the Tableau JS API to load a dashboard; enumerate its parameters, worksheets, and filters; then beacon the extracted data out via an image request.

Figure 3. Script to scrape and extract targeted metadata.

The L() function is the exfiltration design. Each call fires an image beacon to "httpbun.com/status/204" with data in the ?pr= query parameter. The probe ID p0011782077286 is a Unix-epoch timestamp enabling session correlation.

Effect: Payload is ready, now encode as Base64 for hosting.

Step 3 — ENCODE: Host on legitimate decode service

The entire HTML payload is base64-encoded and appended to a public decode service URL. When fetched, the service decodes and serves the payload as a real web page.

Figure 4. The swarm used two delivery hosts: “httpbun.com/mix/b64=” and later, “eu.httpbin.org/base64/”. Both are legitimate API testing services.

Effect: The delivery URL is ready; next step is to submit to urlquery scanner.

Step 4 — SUBMIT: Launder through “urlquery.net”

The agent submits the delivery URL to “urlquery.net”, a legitimate web security scanner. urlquery's Chromium sandbox fetches and renders the page, executing the embedded JavaScript. The target sees requests from urlquery's scanner IPs (“92.42.109.x”), not the agent.

Figure 5. A Base64-encoded payload, a self-label the agent wrote to track its own work.Figure 6. What urlquery sees and does.

[COORD sub-step] The self-label ?uq=p001_1782077286_AGE115_v14 includes a probe prefix (p001), Unix epoch, target identifier (AGE115), and iteration count (v14 = 14th payload revision).

Effect: The chromium sandbox renders page, and payload JS executes.

Step 5 — EXECUTE: In-browser extraction via CORS proxy

When the payload executes inside urlquery's sandboxed Chromium browser, it uses the Tableau JavaScript API to load the AIHW health statistics dashboard. Tableau's backend speaks a protocol called VizQL; earlier payload generations bypassed the full dashboard load and hit the VizQL session API directly via a CORS proxy, reusing session tokens the agent had collected from previous runs.

Figure 7. The CORS proxy ("cors.bwa.workers.dev") is a relay running on Cloudflare Workers, which bypasses the browser's same-origin policy.

AIHW sees the request originating from Cloudflare's IP range, not the agent, nor urlquery.

Effect: The data is validly extracted. Next, send out via a covert beacon.

Step 6 — EXFIL: Zero-byte 204 beacon

Extracted data is URL-encoded into the query string of image beacon requests to "httpbun.com/status/204". The server returns HTTP 204 No Content with zero bytes back. The data travels exclusively in the request URL, which urlquery logs as an ordinary HTTP transaction.

Figure 8. The ?pr= parameter carries URL-encoded Tableau metadata: active sheet names, parameter values, worksheet filters, and field names.

Each beacon sends up to 1,800 characters. The 204 response means no data flows back to the browser, acting as a write-only channel.

Effect. The transaction is logged; the agent retrieves report.

Step 7 — COLLECT: Read back via urlquery report

After the scan completes, the agent retrieves the urlquery report JSON, which contains every HTTP request and response the browser made, including the exfil beacon URLs with embedded data in the ?pr= parameters.

Figure 9. The agent now has dashboard structure, parameter names, filter values, and worksheet layouts — the complete schema needed to construct targeted bulk extraction queries.

This closes the loop. The agent submitted a URL, urlquery's browser executed the payload, and the agent reads the results back from the public report. No direct connection between the agent and the target ever existed. The entire extraction was laundered through two intermediaries, httpbun.com (hosting) and urlquery.net (execution).

Technique transfer in a growing ecosystem

In October, a second autonomous actor was identified via the same technique fingerprints. This time, the activity was attributed to a Tencent-hosted “fleet”, operating from Tencent's Hong Kong network (AS132203). A fleet is distinguished from a swarm in that these agents were working on a unified task, but with no signs of coordination. The Tencent fleet’s activity focused on Alibaba’s Amap navigation service, polling points-of-interest data, with requests consistent with systematically collecting location listings and related details.

Did the Tencent fleet learn from the OpenAI swarm?

The discovery of the Tencent fleet can largely be attributed to technique transfer; this group was following the path pioneered by the OpenAI swarm. The Tencent fleet used "urlquery.net" as a browser execution proxy, "httpbun.com" as a payload delivery host, and "webhook.site" as an exfil channel. There was also progression within the Tencent swarm’s capability. The early fleet operations initially used “httpbin.org/base64/”, and later the same infrastructure switched to “httpbun.com/base64/”, mirroring the OpenAI swarm's own progression to the same host.

A separate actor, operating independently, converging on the same non-obvious infrastructure in the same sequence is harder to explain without the OpenAI swarm's publicly indexed urlquery footprint as a common source. In fact, it seems likely that swarms will web search prior documentation of tradecraft relating to their tasking and could offer a potential explanation to how the Tencent fleet managed to find a write up about their own activity, and in turn, communicate with the authors.

Swarm dynamics in cyber attacks

You don’t look far to see where the insights from swarm behavior may transfer to cyber attack and defense implications. Recent intrusions from agentic cyber attack harnesses like ARTEX exhibit similar characteristics. However, these multi-agent planning systems are distinct in that they have architecturally solved the constraints the OpenAI swarm was working around. The swarm needed a browser (“urlquery.net”) to run JavaScript. ARTEX alleviates this constraint by running a headless Go backend that calls tools directly.

What may hold consistent are methods around the reconnaissance logic, the payload iteration, the structured work partitioning, or the self-labeling patterns. Those are properties of the planning layer, not the infrastructure (e.g., work unit identifiers encoding timestamps, geographic scope, and sequence counters). These coordination patterns may survive the move to purpose-built infrastructure, but they likely be only internally visible queue labels.

Further research will be required going forward to grapple with the emergence of agentic attack frameworks and pinning down the meaningful surface area they have for detection and mitigation. It seems possible these may be durable if they are tied to inherent preferences of the underlying models. In our limited analysis, several avenues seem promising:

Persistent-state exfiltration: writing results that outlast the agentIn the documented ARTEX intrusions, victim machines used curl to POST command output to rotating "webhook.site" URLs. The Tencent fleet did the same by pre-creating "webhook.site" tokens from Tencent IPs before payload deployment, then routing exfiltrated data through them. The OAI swarm used image beacons for the same structural purpose. This convergence reflects a constraint of agents; they can't hold a persistent connection back to an operator. A human running a reverse shell is present in real time to receive output. An agent executes a task, may spawn parallel sub-agents, and completes, or is terminated, before the operator checks in. Results must go somewhere that outlasts the agent's execution window, and parallel sub-agents need isolated write channels so they don't collide. That is what the web hooks, beacons, and message boards are solving. Egress bypass seems like a secondary benefit. These services will often happen to be allow-listed, which makes them harder to block.

Burst-and-pause reasoning loopsGoogle Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) describes ARTEX executing 27 events in 23 seconds, moving from compromised credential to deep system access in as little as 15 minutes and iterating on web shell candidates in real time, rapidly adjusting on error, trimming oversized payloads, and relaunching within seconds. GTIG measured individual burst sequences at 2 – 25 seconds, with sub-second actions inside them. The burst-and-pause timing signature can prove irregular in contexts that reveal rapid reasoning and adaptation.

Self-labeling conventionsAgents mark their own work for later retrieval or correlation. The OAI swarm embedded full operational metadata into URL parameters. ARTEX has used "artex-probe-*" file names. These patterns are high-fidelity signals precisely because they're functional for the agent. They may be useful for fingerprinting agent swarms, because they can't easily alter or remove the labeling scheme without breaking the agent's own state tracking.

The agent-centric future

The 2026 swarm campaigns are not just a curiosity that preceded a threat; they are a snapshot of the same core capability, in the time before the infrastructure constraints were lifted. ARTEX and its cohort of agentic harnesses are now showing us what swarm dynamics look like when resources are unconstrained and aligned on a cyber attack objective.

While these systems are powerful, they are not universally appealing. Using a coordinated multi-agent system is still a trade-off decision for attackers, and one in a growing array of options. Single agent systems can reach the same performance of swarms, and do so more efficiently, following the logic around extending chain-of-thought or scaling test-time compute. Swarm scaling primarily favors situations where speed is the most important factor.

Figure 10. Single- vs. multi-agent token efficiency (Source: OpenAI).

Swarm engagements will have higher token cost, more noise, and require a broader operational footprint. Token costs, however, are only a concern when using an API. The growing list of local, open-weight models with improving cyber capabilities will continue to be an appealing alternative for attackers. As defenders, we need to recognize the distinction in behavior and capabilities and continue to search for identifying characteristics across these attack options and proactively harden our threat models in response.

Title: Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux
Context: He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually...
Full Text:
This month, Amy is joined by Pierre Cadieux, Research Lead for Intelligence Efficacy at Talos. Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security. It’s a great look at how someone who has seen the industry evolve over decades stays grounded and keeps their edge.We also get into what’s kept Pierre at Cisco for nearly ten years. He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually informs the way he approaches threat intelligence today.

Amy Ciminnisi: I've known you since you were in Talos IR, which was not too long ago. But tell me a little bit about your professional journey, because I know that definitely was not the start of it.

Pierre Cadieux: I worked at an ISP as part of the help desk back in the mid-90s. I was one of the people who people would call up and say, "Hey, I've got this computer I just bought, how do I get it on the internet?" I did a lot of learning about what TCP/IP was, what networking was, how to connect things via various different types of connections — whether it be an actual hard-coded network connection or a dial-up connection — and was able to get some expertise around guiding people through that process.

Then I moved to a technology company in San Diego and worked on their help desk. One day, someone called me up and said, "You know how to read Linux logs, right? Or Unix logs, UCS logs, Linux logs." I said, "Yeah." They said, "You know how to use Windows — you're a Windows Server guy, too." I said, "Yeah." They said, "I need you to sit in this chair, look at these two screens — one is a Windows box, one is a Unix box. I need you to be a correlation engine."

So, I looked at the timestamps for both of them, and helped to figure out what was happening because we were having an emergency, an incident, and they had nobody that could look at both. People at that point in time in this organization were very much, "I am doing just Unix things and only know Unix things. I am Windows things only. I only know one of those things." They didn't cross the streams. I could talk both. So I sat in the chair, I stared at both screens and I helped them to track the timeline of what was happening, which ended up being an intrusion exploiting a vulnerable SSH server that was compromised. That changed my course into security.

I spent a number of years in internal security for a number of organizations and got into leadership positions, even CISO positions, leading security teams globally for financial services, for instance, and others. Then I moved into consulting and did that for a number of years as well.

AC: Now you are on the TI&I team, and you also just started contributing to our Threat Source newsletter. What is it that kept you here after all those years?

PC: I'm hitting my ten-year anniversary at Cisco in January. What keeps me at Cisco and Talos is the flexibility of my work. I'm able to, within most bounds, choose what I work on and how I get things done. I have a lot of flexibility in my workday, day-to-day. I work West Coast hours compared to most of my team members who are East Coast. So I sometimes work early shifts with them and am done by the early afternoon. Or sometimes I have to work with folks who are over in Asia Pacific, and I'm working later.

The mission that Talos has resonates with me deeply. One of the things that I have seen along the way was not forgetting the why behind security, not forgetting the fact that what we are defending matters to people, not just to corporations, but to people who are affected by these things. In a newsletter intro, I mentioned that at one of the places I worked, they explained to me that a certain machine was super critical because it wrote the checks that get sent out to people who are expecting this check to come in weekly, monthly, whatever — that was going to be paying for grandma's groceries. And so that motivated me to make sure that box never went down and protect it in a very specific way. Even though it was something that probably should have been sunset and wasn't necessarily up to snuff from a security perspective, there are things we could do to protect it that would allow it to still function as we look for a better solution. At Talos, leadership gives us the space to execute that mission in a way that makes sense for us.

Title: GT13: AI-Assisted Hackers Target 22 Organizations Through Check Point Servers
Context: Sergey Shykevich, its director of threat intelligence, said the activity “does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique”, since CVE-2026-16232 was disclosed...
Full Text:
GreyNoise tracks GT13, an unattributed, probably AI-assisted campaign that hit 22 organizations via Check Point management servers. It may still be running.

GreyNoise detailed an intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers. The company confirmed attacks between October 17 and November 2, 2026, and counts at least 22 victim organizations. It tracks the activity as GreyNoise Threat 13, or GT13.

“GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.” reads the report published by GreyNoise.

The victims don’t share a country or an industry. They have assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia and the United States. The sectors include financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering and manufacturing.

GreyNoise cannot attribute the campaign to any known or publicly tracked threat group. The company also says it lacks enough information to identify the attackers’ motives or country of origin.

GreyNoise tracked most of the activity through its Global Observation Grid, a network of sensors designed to attract and monitor scanning and exploitation attempts. These sensors work much like honeypots, but the company says they offer broader coverage. They allow researchers to observe entire attacks as they happen, rather than relying only on reports from victims.

The attackers used 99 IP addresses, many of them temporary. These addresses belonged either to ExpressVPN exit nodes or to compromised Check Point devices. GreyNoise recorded more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 files that were downloaded, uploaded, or created.

The part GreyNoise saw begins with a file server. On October 2 at 13:17 UTC, the actor started scanning and attacking a Rejetto HFS server through CVE-2026-61500. Every POST to the loginSrp1 endpoint returns a signed session cookie that holds a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function.

After several logins in a row, the actor had enough output to rebuild the internal state of the V8 random number generator. That gave it the key that signs session cookies, so it could forge an admin cookie and log in without a password. Two minutes later, GreyNoise saw admin requests carrying forged cookies, and the server hadn’t been patched.

The forged cookie also carried “allow_session_ip_change:true”, which lets it work from any IP address. GreyNoise calls that perfect for an attacker behind a VPN or hopping between exits. On October 5, the actor used the same trick to install HFS middleware hooks that run commands, and it added an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8, the attacker’s automated system ran a few basic commands to check the system, available disk space, and current user. The activity then stopped until October 19. On that day, the attackers used forged session cookies and the HFS server_code feature to try to download a Linux implant called “ZULT”. They did this despite already having SSH access to the server.

The download failed. The attackers checked running processes, tested the download link with curl, and inspected the network settings. They could not work out why the implant had failed to download, so they returned the next day and used a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay. GreyNoise believes this failure may point to problems in a multi-agent system, suggesting that even automated tools can run into issues.

On October 20, the attackers created a script to start an HTTP server on the compromised machine without requiring authentication. They then began uploading files. The first archive contained the results of a network route scan from a Check Point Security Management Server, showing that the attackers had already gained access to that system. They then installed Nmap and Chisel and configured Chisel to work as a reverse proxy.

That made the HFS server a relay, or “hop” in GreyNoise’s wording. The actor used it to run its operations against Check Point devices it had compromised earlier, and to store the results. GreyNoise couldn’t determine when or how the actor got into those Check Point systems, only that it was there before the HFS compromise.

Between October 20 and 26, the actor had a compromised machine in one victim’s network, which GreyNoise calls Victim A, download Chisel and run it as a client. Through that tunnel, a script for CVE-2026-16232 (a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass that leads to Run Script) launched more than 100 management tasks on several management servers. The tasks copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, minted a new certificate called pivot.p12, and unloaded security policies, which would switch the firewall off.

The actor also probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS and several domain controllers. It ran exploits for CVE-2020-1472 (Netlogon), CVE-2023-4966 (NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473 (Exchange), and CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048 (vCenter). GreyNoise also lists CVE-2025-5777, CVE-2026-41089 and CVE-2026-98432 among the flaws the actor used or tried to use.

“The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.” continues the report. “The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.”

Password guessing played a part too. Scripts named spray_portal.py, comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py carried common, default and weak passwords, plus usernames and passwords themed to the victim. The actor either knew its target or guessed well.

When a second Check Point server wouldn’t report back to the hop, the actor wrote a pull script to steal its data through the first server. The script harvested credentials, internal CA files and the firewall configuration. It was named after the targeted device.

On October 26 at 02:17 UTC, a bulk certificate task went out to 24 compromised Check Point servers: Victim A’s and those of 21 other victims. Results came back to the hop as text files that listed victim IP addresses in increasing order, so a loop was clearly running through them. GreyNoise never saw the actor send the task, which points to another part of its infrastructure.

Every file showed an error, because the certificate task had failed. One message also flagged a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so, registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant. GreyNoise saw no follow-up attempts, but the IP addresses in those files let it notify many victims, directly or through government partners.

Check Point’s position, as reported by The Hacker News, is that this isn’t a new weakness. Sergey Shykevich, its director of threat intelligence, said the activity “does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique”, since CVE-2026-16232 was disclosed earlier and patches exist. The company wants customers to apply updates, follow its hardening guidance to restrict management access and look for suspicious activity.

By early November, other attackers had started scanning the hop and trying to abuse it. On November 2 at 02:28 UTC, the GT13 actor ran a script that checked the box for CVE-2026-98432, a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug. It then used nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that could trigger the flaw. The attacker did patch management on its relay, which is more than some victims managed.

GreyNoise doesn’t read much into the clock. It saw no hands-on-keyboard activity between roughly 17:00 and 00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 hour, which fits a UTC+7 or UTC+8 workday. The malware domain newpayapp[.]com was registered on March 13, 2026, with the registrant state “Hai Phong” and country code “VN”, and GreyNoise treats that as a possible coincidence. The infrastructure clearly existed long before anyone noticed it.

GreyNoise believes GT13 used AI tools to find vulnerable systems, develop exploits and automate attacks, although human operators were also involved. The company is sharing information with authorities and CERTs. Its monitoring stopped on November 2, but it warns that the campaign may still be active because attackers retain access to compromised Check Point devices.

“We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets.” concludes the report. “We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Check Point)

Title: Ransomware Attacks Surge 23% in October Following Record Quarter
Context: Ransomware attacks surged 23% in October compared to September, with 1049 claimed incidents, a new report by NCC Group has found
Full Text:
Ransomware attacks surged 23% in October compared to September, with 1049 claimed incidents, a new report by NCC Group has found.

This rise comes straight after the highest ever quarterly volume of claimed ransomware attacks in Q3 2026, from July to September.

The researchers linked the sharp rise in ransomware to the growing use of AI to rapidly identify vulnerabilities and chained attack paths

“This spike is likely an early indicator of a new cyber environment in which serious vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized more rapidly,” NCC Group wrote.

New Ransomware Groups Increase Activity

The Gentlemen ransomware group claimed the highest number of victims in October at 139, making up 13% of the total.

It was closely followed by N0n, a relatively new actor first observed in September 2026, which claimed 133 victims in the month.

N0n claimed to be responsible for data breaches affecting financial firms JPMorgan, Mastercard and Visa in November.

Qilin, which has been active for a number of years, was in third place, claiming 131 attacks.

A number of other newer groups established in 2026 made up the rest of the top 10 ransomware actors for October. This includes Booba Project with 29 attacks, Emperador with 27 and Wallstreet with 22.

NCC Group researchers noted that the origins of these newer actors remain unknown, and none have been conclusively linked to a specific country or established predecessor.

“These operations should therefore be described as newly observed brands rather than entirely new threat actors, as they may include experienced affiliates, access brokers or developers previously associated with other cybercriminal groups. Their rapid rise also demonstrates the low barrier to creating a new extortion brand within the wider ransomware ecosystem,” they commented.

Industrials Sector Targeted in Third of Attacks

The NCC Group report, published on November 25, found that industrials was the sector most heavily targeted by ransomware in October, making up 31% of claimed attacks. This was followed by consumer discretionary (19%), healthcare (12%) and IT (10%).

Read now: Industrial Control System Vulnerabilities Hit Record Highs

North America was the most targeted region in October, accounting for 46% of attacks. This was followed by Europe at 23%, Asia (15%) and South America (8%).

Title: Plagiarism Checker Turnitin Investigating Cyberattack
Context: Education technology platform Turnitin has disclosed a cyberattack involving certain customer-facing systems
Full Text:
Education technology platform Turnitin has disclosed a cyberattack involving certain customer-facing systems.

A subsidiary of Advance Publications, Turnitin provides plagiarism checking solutions used by thousands of education and research institutions worldwide.

“We are writing to let you know that we recently identified unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing Turnitin systems,” CEO Chris Caren revealed in a November 23 letter on the company’s website.

The company immediately initiated its incident response plan, notified the relevant authorities, and launched an investigation with support from external cyber experts.

“We can confirm our systems are fully operational and safe to use and that these customer-facing systems do not collect government identification credentials or institutional financial information,” Caren said.

The company continues to monitor the affected customer-facing systems while its investigation into the nature and scope of the incident continues.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Customer-facing Turnitin systems include the submission portal for students, a grading interface for instructors, integration APIs for institutions, and reporting dashboards. The company did not say if any or which of these systems was breached.

Caren did not say if any data was accessed or how many customers might have been affected, but the University of Colorado Boulder said on Tuesday it was in touch with the company to understand if any CU Boulder information was compromised.

“At this time, we have no indication that student or instructor information, assignments, or other CU Boulder data was exposed. Since Turnitin is primarily accessed via a Canvas integration, OIT has added additional monitoring to ensure Canvas has not been impacted,” the university’s Office of Information Technology said.

SecurityWeek has emailed Turnitin for additional information on the incident and will update this article if the company responds.

Title: UK Authorized Push Payment Losses Surge 22% as Fraudsters Steal £660m
Context: The UK’s banks have called for technology and telecommunications firms to be held accountable for fraud originating on their platforms, after revealing total losses increased to...
Full Text:
The UK’s banks have called for technology and telecommunications firms to be held accountable for fraud originating on their platforms, after revealing total losses increased to nearly £660m ($863m) in the first half of 2026.

The figures represent an 8% year-on-year (YoY) increase, according to the UK Finance Half Year Fraud Report 2026 published by UK Finance which represents 300 firms.

Although unauthorized fraud losses dipped slightly (-2%) as banks stopped £811m ($1.06bn) in attempted criminal gains, authorized push payment (APP) scams surged 22% over the year to reach £316m ($472m).

APP fraud refers to incidents where a scammer posing as a trusted entity tricks the victim into transferring money to a bank account under their control.

As well as a surge in losses, APP fraud cases increased 25% to 138,345 in the first half of the year, the banking body said.

Read more on APP fraud: APP Fraud Singled Out as Biggest Financial Crime Threat

The report revealed that 58% of APP fraud originates online, with a further 16% beginning via telecommunications – usually SMS or voice-related scams. Both account for a third (33%) of losses.

That’s why banks are intensifying their calls for tech firms and telcos to share more of the burden in stopping these scams. Specifically, UK Finance called for:

Ofcom to place stronger obligations on high-risk platforms such as social media to stamp out fraudulent advertising, which is where a lot of investment fraud originates

Online marketplaces to verify sellers and use secure payment mechanisms rather than allowing separate bank transfers to take place off platform. This would address purchase fraud, which often starts on marketplace sites, UK Finance claimed

Tech firms and telcos to be required to contribute financially and share expertise, intelligence and capabilities to support proactive fraud prevention

The Biggest APP Offenders

According to the report, investment fraud was responsible for the largest losses in the first half of 2026, accounting for £126m, up 29% from a year earlier. Case numbers surged by 21% over the same period.

In terms of volume, it was purchase scams that dominated, accounting for 69% of all APP cases. These happen when fraudsters trick a victim into paying for something that doesn’t exist. Related losses rose 24% annually to £66m ($86m).

Advance-fee scams, where victims pay an upfront fee or deposit for goods or services that don’t exist, saw losses increase 73% to £34m ($44.5m) and cases more than double.

“Criminals are increasingly exploiting online platforms and telecommunications networks to target and manipulate victims before a payment is ever made,” said Ruth Ray, MD of economic crime at UK Finance.

“The financial services sector cannot tackle this threat alone. We need stronger obligations on technology and telecommunications firms so that every sector exploited by fraudsters is held accountable and plays its part in preventing harm.”

Title: How to protect against preinstalled Android malware
Context: The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a...
Full Text:
Introduction

Preinstalled malware on mobile devices is a major threat to user security and privacy. When we buy a new smartphone or tablet, we expect it to be ready to use and secure right out of the box. In some cases, however, devices ship with malware already on them. Such malware can do almost anything: display ads, collect personal data and credentials, track user activity, and more. Preinstalled malware can also turn the infected device into a tool for fraud, such as stealing credit card numbers or other sensitive information, causing financial loss and reputational damage.

We’ve previously reported cases where users bought smartphones on marketplaces with malware already preinstalled. Over the past few months, however, several large organizations have encountered malware embedded in the firmware of mobile devices. The specific risks to corporate security depend on how the devices are used and on the company’s line of business. But because the Trojan sits in the device firmware, any app can be compromised, and the potential damage is hard to overstate. This post looks at the current landscape of preinstalled threats on mobile devices, the risks they pose to corporate users, and available countermeasures, including Kaspersky solutions.

Landscape of preinstalled threats

The total number of devices with malicious code found in their firmware or system apps keeps growing. According to Kaspersky Security Network, the number of such devices detected each month has increased more than 2.5-fold over the past year.

Monthly number of Android devices with preinstalled malware detected by Kaspersky solutions, November 2025 — October 2026 (download)

Several malware families are known to spread through firmware and system apps, the most common being Keenadu and Triada. According to our data, one or another of these two families was found on 88% of infected devices in the first ten months of 2026.

The Triada backdoor (Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada) was discovered ten years ago and has remained popular with attackers ever since. Early versions of the malware actively exploited Android vulnerabilities to gain root access and the privileges they needed. At that time, Triada was often distributed as a regular app. Over time, however, Android introduced tighter restrictions, and attackers now mostly use the preinstalled version of this backdoor. Throughout 2026, users encountered about twenty markedly distinct variants. The most common ones were Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.ag and Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.z. The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads. Known modules can steal credentials for messaging and social media apps, intercept calls and text messages, replace links in browsers, siphon off cryptocurrency, and run a reverse proxy on the infected device. It’s worth stressing that by loading additional modules, attackers get virtually unlimited capabilities.

Keenadu is another preinstalled backdoor we discovered, which appeared relatively recently. The earliest known firmware version that contains this malware dates back to 2023. Even so, the number of devices infected with Keenadu is considerable: according to our data, more than 220,000 devices were infected in the first ten months of 2026.

Keenadu is similar to Triada in many ways, especially in its main architectural feature: once it’s on a device, attackers can download additional modules with any functionality and inject them into target apps. In most known Keenadu attacks, the malware was used for ad fraud, in particular to generate fake clicks. Technically, however, it can perform any action on the infected device. Notably, on first contact with the C2 servers, the backdoor versions we analyzed received a command to activate after about two and a half months. Until then, the malware showed no activity. This is probably meant to give the device owner time to install all the apps they need and settle into daily use, and to make the compromise harder to detect.

Other families of preinstalled malware exist, although they’re less common than Triada and Keenadu. They include Dwphon, Vo1d, and BADBOX. Their functionality is generally similar: mostly ad fraud and traffic redirection. Note that most cases involve phones and tablets, but preinstalled backdoors also threaten other types of devices. For example, Dwphon has turned up in the firmware of children’s smartwatches, and Vo1d samples in TV box firmware.

Corporate environment

We first saw an organization, rather than a home user, encounter preinstalled malware several years ago. That case involved the Dwphon malware. Over the past year, however, we’ve received more and more reports from different customers. In less than a year, several large organizations have come to us with the same request. After installing Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Android on brand-new, out-of-the-box devices, they saw detections of Keenadu or Triada and asked us to confirm that those detections were genuine.

Note that when we talk about corporate threats, we mean the Corporate Owned, Business Only (COBO) and Corporate Owned, Personally Enabled (COPE) usage scenarios, where the employee’s device belongs to the organization. The difference between these models is that COBO doesn’t allow personal use of the device (and usually blocks it at the software level). With COPE, the organization controls global settings but allows free personal use and, in some cases, even installation of third-party apps. By corporate environment, we mean primarily the setup with centralized procurement, where an organization buys all the devices it needs (hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands) for uniform use. This post doesn’t cover infections under the Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) model, where employees use infected personal devices they bought themselves to access company resources or for work communications.

Preinstalled malware appears on a new device as a result of a supply chain attack. Devices can be manufactured and flashed in different places. Likewise, different parties in the production process can create the firmware and prepare it for the device. Malicious code typically gets onto a device in one of three ways:

The manufacturer installs the malware deliberately: the attackers control the entire production process and either sell infected devices cheaply under an obscure brand name or, conversely, pose as a well-known manufacturer, damaging that company’s reputation.

A legitimate brand that makes the final device receives malicious firmware from a contractor acting in bad faith.

A legitimate manufacturer builds the firmware in-house, but the build relies on an already infected base or code component. Here, no one directly involved in manufacturing knows the production chain has been compromised.

What risks do corporate customers face when they buy such devices? Based on the technical capabilities of preinstalled malware, we can identify the following main risks:

Degraded performance of infected devices: shorter battery life, overheating, and glitches in various apps. Some devices have even been known to play random sounds on their own.

Ads on devices, both visible to the user and hidden. They consume extra traffic and also connect the device to various websites, which creates a separate group of risks.

Account takeover in messaging apps, social media, and corporate resources: theft of credentials can damage the company’s reputation and lead to financial losses or even new attacks.

Direct financial losses, such as cryptocurrency theft.

Theft of confidential data and secrets: in effect, spying on corporate devices.

Use in a proxy botnet: the organization’s infected devices can relay arbitrary traffic to any internet resources.

Use in a DDoS botnet: infected devices can be enlisted to launch DDoS attacks on any target. Reputational risks come into play here as well.

External access to the corporate infrastructure through a proxy module. Infected devices are known to have been used as residential proxies to infect other devices on the same local network.

Device downtime: attackers who disable corporate devices in active use can disrupt operations.

Note that not all of the attack scenarios involving preinstalled malware listed above have been seen in real-world incidents. However, Triada and BADBOX, for example, have already expanded their functionality: besides displaying ads, they now steal accounts. We can therefore expect preinstalled malware to keep gaining capabilities that pose even higher risks.

Using Kaspersky solutions to mitigate risks

Mobile Device Management (MDM) is a separate category of solutions built to manage mobile devices, and it helps mitigate infection risks in corporate environments. With MDM, IT teams can centrally configure smartphones, tablets and laptops, enforce security policies, and control app installation. This significantly reduces the risk of infection caused by user actions, because it prevents a user from installing an APK from an attacker’s message, a malicious website, or a rogue app store listing.

However, these measures alone are not effective against preinstalled Trojans. Centralized mobile device management alone is not enough to contain threats like Triada and Keenadu. It must be complemented by protection that can detect malware, including any already present on a device before the company starts using it. The best approach is to combine management and protection in a single agent with a unified console, which simplifies rollout and day-to-day operation: IT teams only need to deploy and maintain one application instead of two.

Kaspersky Next product line, starting with Kaspersky Next EDR Optimum, combines Advanced MDM functionality with antivirus protection. The antivirus engine scans files and installed apps and provides real-time protection. Kaspersky Next can detect malware on Android devices, even in preinstalled apps, and alert administrators to any threats it finds. This allows spotting an infection on a device that nominally complies with corporate policies.

Triada detection report in the unified KSC console (screenshot in Russian)

Note that it’s technically impossible for either antivirus tools or the OS itself to remove preinstalled malware from the system partition. However, Kaspersky Next lowers the risk of buying a whole batch of devices and then finding a preinstalled Trojan that is hard or impossible to remove by reflashing. If Kaspersky Next detects malware like Triada or Keenadu, it alerts the IT administrator, who can then contain the threat by blocking the device’s internet access, clearing app data, rotating passwords, or locking the device entirely. Administrators can monitor and manage the infected device from the unified console of the Kaspersky Security Center.

Threat monitoring in the unified KSC console

Companies planning a mobile infrastructure should account for the risk of encountering preinstalled malware. Before ordering a large batch of devices, we recommend inspecting and pilot-testing sample units. We should stress that this measure is no substitute for installing security software on every device used in the organization. Even if the tests come out fine, an unscrupulous supplier may have deliberately sent clean units for inspection. Protection must also be continuous because, for example, the device update system could come under attack.

Manufacturers need to check devices and firmware code for malware just as customers do. Whether the firmware is written in-house or by a contractor, the result can contain malicious code, as we noted earlier. To detect preinstalled threats, you need a file scanning solution that can respond quickly when it finds malware. Kaspersky Scan Engine is one of the Kaspersky products designed for this task. The engine uses the latest detection technologies to identify a wide range of cyberthreats, including preinstalled ones. It integrates easily into a variety of workflows. For example, it can connect to a software build pipeline or any other system that needs to check files for malicious code.

Title: Despite doom and gloom headlines, AI attacks are thin on the ground
Context: When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses...
Full Text:
When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology.

Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment.

And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats.

Has that happened? Well, kind of.

What CISOs are seeing

In the first quarter of 2026, RSAC asked Fortune 1000 CISOs whether they’d seen definitive evidence of AI-powered attack techniques being used against their companies, beyond social engineering, and 44% said yes.

“We asked the same question in Q4 of a similar cohort,” says Laura Koetzle, RSAC’s head of community research. According to preliminary results — the survey isn’t complete yet — nearly 58% now say they’ve seen evidence of AI-powered attack techniques.

As a result, the majority of CISOs are revamping their vulnerability management programs, according to the forthcoming survey. But they’re not upending how they approach cybersecurity, Koetzle adds. “The same foundational principles still apply.”

The main difference today is in speed and quantity, she says.

Lincoln Wallen, CTO at Framestore, an Academy Award–winning visual effects company, isn’t turning a blind eye to what AI could be used for by attackers.

“We take the potential very seriously,” he says. But he’s taking an old-school approach to dealing with this new threat. “We’re putting a lot of emphasis on cleanliness, hygiene, and patching.”

So far, the signs of AI use have been limited to more sophisticated phishing attacks, he says.

“They feel anecdotally more well put-together, more convincing, involving many more disparate elements of data,” he says. “That’s the most concrete thing that we’ve seen.”

To deal with that, the company has updated its anti-phishing training.

Another area that Framestore is investing in is more efficient and prioritized patching and more frequent penetration testing.

Enhanced productivity but familiar threats

The data seems to support Framestore’s approach, even if the headlines don’t.

Last week, headlines quoted Google’s announcement that “the era of autonomous attacks had arrived” — a reference to Google’s original blog post teaser to its latest AI Threat Tracker report.

But in the actual report, John Hultquist, chief analyst at the Google Threat Intelligence Group, seemed to undercut this top line teaser, saying: “For the most part, attackers aren’t using new groundbreaking methods to break into systems — they are still going after known, unfixed issues, just with much greater speed and scale.”

(Google later changed its headline to “Outpace automated cyber threats with security built for nonstop defense.”)

According to Google’s report, the mechanics of intrusion remain the same. Even attackers using new AI-powered attack frameworks are using them to leverage compromised credentials and unpatched systems. It’s the speed and scale at which these frameworks can be used that’s the challenge.

In fact, using LLMs can even hurt the attackers, as the frameworks “trade stealth for velocity,” researchers say. The attacks can be “forensically noisy” and can hallucinate non-existent details or targets. “Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don’t.”

Or, as Sergej Epp summed up as a takeaway from a recent Cloud Security Alliance CISO huddle call on autonomous attacks, “detecting these attacks is — at least for now — not the hard part. They make a lot of noise, like 1000 interns.”

Austin Berglas, managing director and head of cyber operations at Nardello & Co., a global investigations firm, says he’s not seeing AI-discovered zero days or self-replicating AI agents out in the wild.

“This is one of those examples that is still in the lab environment,” he says.

Most attackers are using AI the way everyone does, he says. “Just like individuals use it for their daily productivity and efficiency, same with the bad actors. They’re able to scale, do it cheaper, do it quicker. And you’re seeing people who typically wouldn’t have the technical chops to do something, who are now able to do it because AI can do the technical side.”

The industry is seeing evidence of faster weaponization of vulnerabilities, confirms Gartner analyst John Watts. “Where it starts to have less evidence is for fully autonomous attacks. What happened with Hugging Face is a fully autonomous attack, and that isn’t that common.”

How CISOs should respond

But if the wave of autonomous attacks and AI-powered malware hasn’t yet fully arrived, what should CISOs do given the reality on the ground?

“The feedback that we get from our client base is that they believe there’s a lot of value in using the controls they already have,” Gartner’s Watts says.

“The wake-up call for the practitioners is to get busy with the patching,” confirms Paul Webber, an analyst at Software Analyst Cyber Research, adding that security by obscurity is no longer an option.

The biggest problem enterprises are facing, he notes, is that they need better automation to handle the increased workload, and the tools aren’t yet where they need to be.

“People need more trust in the security tools so they can move from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop towards fully autonomous response,” Webber says. “And that’s going to take some discipline, some standardization, and some proof in the efficacy of the security tools themselves. At the moment, they’re neither built to a specific standard or definition and people are being asked to make purchasing decisions without physical proof that the tools can do what they purport to do.”

And, in some ways, the much-lauded defensive AI capabilities can make things worse — such as by exposing legacy vulnerabilities that companies now have to hurry up and patch, on top of their already large backlog.

“This is a conversation that we’re actively having right now,” says Christina Powers, partner and cybersecurity consulting leader at West Monroe, a management consulting firm.

“We’re working with a mid-sized bank, and they are just completely lost on how to keep up with the number of vulnerabilities that they got,” she says. “They’re sitting on millions of vulnerabilities. They don’t even know where to start. There’s a bit of analysis paralysis that’s happening because there’s so much information coming in.”

The tools are improving all the time, Powers says, but she recommends security leaders not to wait for better technology to come along.

“If you’re sitting and waiting, you become more of a target because you’re falling behind,” she says.

Title: Maritime industry faces growing cyber threats as 50 ships targeted
Context: The vessel experienced onboard system problems and received a bomb threat, although publicly available information does not establish that a cyberattack caused the technical...
Full Text:
US authorities investigate suspected cyberattacks on up to 50 commercial ships, with Iran and Russia under scrutiny and Fortinet flaws involved.

The United States is investigating a wave of cyberattacks targeting commercial vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals, and other potentially hazardous cargo. According to a Wall Street Journal report, as many as 50 ships may have been targeted, with Iran emerging as the primary suspect.

“The U.S. is investigating Iran’s potential involvement in dozens of cyberattacks against energy tankers amid concerns that Tehran is widening the war with cyber operations and terror plots against Americans far from the Middle East.” WSJ states.

“As many as 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, according to U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter.”

US authorities are also considering possible Russian involvement. However, a Trump administration official told the WSJ that investigators have found no evidence linking Iran to the incidents and described four of the attacks as minor disruptions.

The incidents reportedly involved both cyber intrusions and intimidation campaigns. Some vessels received bomb threats, ransom demands, and messages warning them against transporting US products. Other ships may have been compromised without their crews being aware of the intrusions.

The US Coast Guard has reportedly deployed specialized cyber protection teams to at least four vessels approaching US ports to investigate and mitigate potential threats. The VL Prosperity and Kohaku were among the ships inspected after suspected compromises of their onboard networks.

The attackers are reportedly exploiting vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking devices widely used across the maritime industry. In September, the US Coast Guard Cyber Command and the FBI issued a joint alert warning shipping companies about state-sponsored actors exploiting FortiGate vulnerabilities in maritime environments.

The investigation also concerns vessels operating near Europe and Asia. One of them, the Vivit Africa LNG carrier, was reportedly targeted while transporting liquefied natural gas from the United States to Italy. The vessel experienced onboard system problems and received a bomb threat, although publicly available information does not establish that a cyberattack caused the technical incident.

The incidents highlight the growing exposure of commercial shipping to cyber threats. Modern vessels rely on interconnected IT and operational technology (OT) systems to manage communications, navigation, and cargo operations. A compromise of onboard networks could disrupt operations, delay deliveries, and create safety concerns, although the reported incidents do not demonstrate that attackers gained control of critical navigation or propulsion systems.

Alon Ayalon, co-founder of maritime cybersecurity firm Cydome, told the WSJ that most vessels have “less cyber protection than a midsize office.”

Even without causing physical damage, cyber intrusions and threats can force shipping companies to suspend operations, undergo security inspections, and face costly delays. The investigation highlights the need for maritime operators to address exposed network devices, strengthen remote access controls, and improve the separation between IT and OT environments.

​Unknown attackers have reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), according to a source familiar with the matter.

The source told The New York Times, which first reported the incident, that the cyberattack was carried out using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework and also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

While the CIA and the ODNI have not yet replied to a request for more details regarding this incident, no classified data or systems were exposed in the breach.

"The hack did not involve our classified networks or classified information, and no other systems are currently at risk," the source said.

Hours after the CIA security breach was reported, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) also disclosed that it's investigating a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. After detecting the attack, the agency took some systems offline as a precaution and told banks to use the Financial Institutions Hotline to file reports, since some services may be unavailable.

FinCEN is a US Department of the Treasury bureau that acts as the country's official Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) and protects the nation's financial system from illicit activities by sharing financial intelligence with law enforcement agencies both domestically and internationally.

BleepingComputer reached out to a FinCEN spokesperson with questions about the incident, but a response was not immediately available.

One week ago, the US National Security Agency's classified network also suffered a days-long outage, but the agency blamed scheduled routine maintenance and said its mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational.

US agencies targeted by cyberattacks

These incidents follow a series of other cyberattacks that have led to security breaches at other US federal agencies in recent years.

For instance, two years ago, the Silk Typhoon Chinese state-backed hacking group hacked the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), another Treasury Department office that administers economic and trade sanctions programs.

The same threat group also breached the Treasury's Office of Financial Research, and it reportedly infiltrated the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (a Treasury Department office that reviews foreign investments for national security risks).

More recently, as BleepingComputer reported over the weekend, hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC). However, it is unclear how the attackers gained access, when the breach occurred, or whether they stole any information from the compromised systems.

This follows a claim by the ShinyHunters extortion group that it breached the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, prompting an FBI investigation that led to the arrests of multiple suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attack.

Title: Hackers Compromise 24 Check Point Management Servers in Suspected AI-Driven Attack Campaign
Context: In one case, the attackers have been found using an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500, a critical flaw in Rejetto...
Full Text:
An unknown threat actor has been using artificial intelligence (AI)-driven offensive tooling in a campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, impacting 22 distinct organizations across the world.

The intrusion activity, tracked by GreyNoise under the moniker GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), is assessed to have targeted organizations in the financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing sectors across the U.K., Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the U.S.

Confirmed attack activity has been recorded between October 17 and November 2, 2026, with the threat actor using 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control. Most of these IP addresses are associated with disposable network infrastructure.

The campaign has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. It's suspected that the attackers are relying on agentic harnesses and systems for vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and automatic interaction with compromised assets.

The threat actor has also been observed using tools like Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python scripts to carry out internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement on victim environments.

"We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created," GreyNoise said.

In one case, the attackers have been found using an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500, a critical flaw in Rejetto HFS, in early October 2026 to obtain control of the server and issue commands, including adding an SSH key to the "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys" file.

Subsequently, GT13 is said to have used the compromised server as a relay for follow-on operations centered around saving command results and exfiltrating data from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. The attackers also unsuccessfully attempted to deploy a Linux implant named ZULT to the compromised Rejetto HFS server.

"The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server," the cybersecurity company said. "We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets."

The attackers also moved to burrow deeper into one of the victim networks, using a script for a now-patched Check Point flaw (CVE-2026-16232) to launch over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers to -

Steal firewall databases and internal certificate authority files

Mint a new certificate

Unload security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections

Conduct internal network reconnaissance and attempt lateral movement

The post-compromise activity also involved attempts to target other enterprise systems, such as Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966), Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2024-21893), VMware vCenter (CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048), Microsoft Exchange (CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473), and Microsoft Netlogon (CVE-2020-1472).

In tandem, the threat actor has attempted to exploit various other security flaws, including, but not limited to -

CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure)

CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler)

CVE-2026-41089 (Windows Netlogon)

CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF)

GreyNoise has theorized that GT13 has in its possession a "mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus" that it uses to weaponize vulnerabilities, scan for susceptible assets, and exploit them to gain access to systems that can be later used as operational relays or true targets.

"The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique," Sergey Shykevich, Director, Threat Intelligence at Check Point Software Technologies, told The Hacker News.

"Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity."
