Title: Top corporate cyber-risks related to the human factor and social engineering
Context: A large share of breaches start with exploited vulnerabilities, but attacks that began with an employee mistake hold second place firmly
Full Text:
A large share of breaches start with exploited vulnerabilities, but attacks that began with an employee mistake hold second place firmly. Human risk keeps evolving along with the threat landscape, organizational change, and AI adoption in companies. To see what shifted most in 2026, the SANS Institute surveyed more than a thousand security professionals who specialize in human risk. And they’re nearly unanimous: social engineering attacks are getting more sophisticated and hitting more and more employees, and AI risks go well beyond employees sending data to public LLMs without approval.

Much of the report deals with the security job itself and its difficulties, but we focused on what matters most: what human-risk specialists see compared with what’s actually happening.

The misleading drop in password risk

Just 22% of respondents ranked weak passwords and weak authentication methods as their top risk – putting it in fourth place. Passwords have slid in this ranking for a second year running, creating the false impression that stricter password policies and mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) have improved things.

The reality is more complicated, and two factors matter most. First, part of the “password problem” now gets filed under social engineering. The report lumps everything into that category – from traditional phishing emails to deepfakes. But incident response data shows social engineering becoming more dangerous and more interactive. Employees are increasingly getting calls instead of messages supposedly from the help desk. Sometimes it’s the reverse: the attacker calls the corporate help desk and poses as an employee. Either way, the victim is pushed to reset MFA, read out a one-time code, or enroll a new MFA device, and the password is reset too if needed. The attackers end up controlling the account – having extracted both the password and the MFA. Treating this purely as a social-engineering problem is a mistake, and training rank-and-file employees alone won’t fix it.

Key here are extremely strict procedures for resetting both passwords and MFA – built into security policy. The right takeaway isn’t “we can forget about passwords” but “password policies should improve the way passwords are set”. Above all, the help desk needs training, including outsourced support teams. More on this below in the list of tips.

The second factor is the boom in infostealers. This type of malware steals secrets in bulk from infected computers and personal devices, giving attackers passwords of any length, MFA codes, or authentication tokens and cookies that bypass passwords entirely. That changes what employees need to know about passwords, but not how much it matters. Using unique passwords and keeping work passwords and sessions off personal devices as much as possible remain critical.

An ocean of AI risks

Risks linked to using AI at work have grown for the second year in a row – now firmly holding second place right behind social engineering. “Using AI” sounds simple, but the phrase hides a whole array of very different risks. Some are obvious, while some are easy to miss.

Shadow AI. The experts SANS surveyed say shadow AI is much bigger than shadow IT. More employees are involved, and they use a wider variety of unapproved tools at work. Vague messaging about using AI can add to the chaos. In many organizations, management pushes employees to be “AI-first” and to work more efficiently with AI, while the tools offered don’t suit the employees who have to use them, or managers give no specifics at all and just make demands. As a result employees rush to adopt AI tools they’re already familiar with or ones they’ve just found online. And they check with neither the security nor IT teams first.

Careless sharing of personal data or regulated or confidential information. This is the most obvious risk, and it keeps growing. No amount of training can beat the urge to get more done, and employees will still send confidential information to random AI tools. The only way to prevent incidents regarding confidential/personal data is to move to approved AI tools with built-in filters that strip personal data from inputs.

Weaker critical thinking and conflicts with security policies. This one is less obvious but still very dangerous. Many employees take AI output at face value without checking or questioning it. There are no exact statistics, but the rise of the slang term meat proxy suggests the problem is widespread. The habit of relying on AI means that when an employee hits an unclear IT or security situation, they turn to ChatGPT instead of company policy or a colleague who knows. Incidents related to poisoned AI answers show how dangerous this can be.

Vibe coding. Employees with no development background build internal tools, and sometimes external ones, on their own: dashboards, reports, process automation, and so on. They rely on AI and don’t check the output. The result is often a critically vulnerable application with access to important organizational data. SANS surveys show the practice has spread widely, and these freshly minted coders turn up in almost every department.

Departments that need extra attention

When it comes to how involved regular employees are in security, every department has people who support the process and people who resist it. The SANS report treats this mainly as a matter of office politics: it shows which departments are easier or harder to recruit as allies for security programs. But it also has a clear risk-forecasting angle. Departments in which employees are often targeted by phishing and social engineering, but where engagement with security programs is low, need extra attention from the SOC team. The usual holdouts are finance and operations. In finance, 17% of employees oppose security and 2% support it. In operations, it’s 23% against and 5% in favor. HR and external communications also push back quite a bit, with 13% and 12% opposed and 6% and 7% supportive. The report also lists middle and senior management as separate categories. Senior management is more likely to support security initiatives than obstruct them (21% and 17%, respectively). Middle managers, though, don’t want any security in 17% of cases, and support security initiatives in only 4%.

Tech support staff (service desk, IT support, and similar roles) are a key target of modern social engineering attacks. The statistics don’t list them separately, but, overall, only 10% of IT employees are against security processes, while 28% support them.

How to reduce human risk in 2026

We’ve split the tips below into several sections, each aimed at a different group of employees. For many of these tips, training alone isn’t enough. It’s also essential to update a company’s security policies. Set up approved, filtered access to AI, assign clear responsibility for rolling out AI agents, and formalize how to verify someone’s identity when they ask for a password or MFA reset.

To make training stick instead of staying theoretical, add game mechanics, cyber drills, and repetition – adapted to how fast each person learns. Specialized platforms such as aspersky Automated Security Awareness Platform help roll this out across the whole organization.

What to teach all employees

If anyone contacts you by phone, text, or messaging app, and asks you to share or reset your password or MFA code, or confirm an action – end the conversation. Then contact the company help desk through a channel you already know – even if the caller’s number looks familiar.

No one – not even the IT department – will ever ask for your password or MFA code.

Never approve an MFA request if you didn’t start the sign-in process yourself.

Never paste or run technical commands in the Start menu search bar, Run window, or any other command line if a website, CAPTCHA window, or pop-up message tells you to.

Install software only from approved, official sources. Don’t use cracked software or game mods on devices you use for work.

The same goes for browser extensions. Use only well-known extensions that IT and security teams have approved.

Don’t sign in to work accounts or sync your work browser profile on personal devices.

Use a password manager, and a unique password for every account. Never reuse the same password for work and personal accounts.

Use only approved AI tools, and keep in mind which tool is meant for which type of information. A tool may be approved for business correspondence, for example, but banned for processing customer data.

Never enter customer data or confidential or internal information into public AI services.

Check AI output before you use it. You’re the one responsible for the result.

AI recommendations never override security requirements. If the two seem to contradict each other, call the security team or the help desk and ask for advice.

Don’t use apps, scripts, or agents created with AI at work without sign-off from both management and the security staff responsible for AI deployments.

Report suspicious events – such as strange emails and calls – even if you think you handled them well yourself. These reports can help stop an attack on your coworkers.

What to teach specific groups of employees

User support and IT help desks (including outside contractors)

Never reset a password or MFA during an incoming call. Always call the employee back at the number in the company directory.

Verify an employee’s identity on a video call where they show an ID document. Personal details or a manager’s name given over the phone aren’t enough – since attackers often already have this information.

Before any MFA change or administrator account reset, get confirmation from the employee’s manager through a separate channel. If something seems off, require the employee to show up in person.

If a caller claims to be a vendor employee and asks for access, end the call, then contact the vendor’s account manager using the contact details in the contract with the vendor.

Treat urgency, a caller’s senior job title, or contact outside working hours as warning signs of an attack.

Don’t accept work instructions from colleagues through text messages or other channels not meant for work.

Finance teams, executives, and their assistants

Confirm every payment, change of bank details, or access request by calling back on a number you already know. Do this even if the request came by voice or video call.

Attackers can create voice and video deepfakes of your boss or other managers. Agree in advance with your boss on a few ways to check suspicious requests, such as calling back on a different line or using a code word.

Developers and anyone who builds software with AI (vibe coding)

Review AI-generated code as carefully as you would an intern’s work. If you don’t have the skills to do that, ask colleagues who do.

Never put secrets, keys, or credentials in code or in prompts to AI.

Remember: if you create an AI agent, you’re responsible for what it does. Give it only the minimum permissions it needs, and require human approval for any action that can’t be undone.

For more detailed tips on safe vibe coding, see our separate post.

What to change in your security awareness programs

Drop password complexity rules and regular password changes from your training. Instead, teach people to use unique long passwords and to store them in password managers.

Add simulated attacks to your program – such as voice phishing (vishing) and fake CAPTCHA windows. Include attacks aimed at the help desk.

Never shame employees who fail a simulated attack. Help them understand their mistakes and build confidence instead.

Replace one big annual awareness course with short, regular training sessions. Base them on real incidents and on where your company currently stands on AI adoption.

Run role-specific training for the help desk, finance team, executives, and developers.

Let people report an incident with just one click or call, and publicly thank those who do.

Track the reporting rate for suspicious events and also the time to report, rather than the phishing click rate.

Title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply Chain Attack: How to Secure AI Gateways Beyond Code Signatures
Context: 0 from an attacker-controlled lookalike fork
Full Text:
On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM’s official release pipeline built, signed, and published version 1.107.0 from an attacker-controlled lookalike fork. The v1.107.0 source tag on GitHub was clean, and the compromised images carried a valid signature. The maintainers have since published their root cause analysis and moved to keyless signing, so security teams can now check two things: whether a compromised artifact ever ran in their environment, and whether their deployment policies would catch the next one.

Which LiteLLM Artifacts Were Affected?

All seven litellm==1.107.0 wheels on the Python Package Index (PyPI) were affected, along with the images behind four tags on Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry (GHCR). Times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on October 21, 2026.

Artifact

Tags or files

Exposure window

PyPI wheels

All seven litellm==1.107.0 wheels

11:39 to 13:23

GHCR images

v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, main-stable for litellm, litellm-database, and litellm-non_root

11:46 to 13:51

Docker Hub images

The same four tags

11:46 to 14:20

The source distribution carried a tampered build configuration but not the payload files. Mirrors, caches, and images built on an affected base can extend exposure beyond these windows, so match the digests in the LiteLLM advisory rather than tags.

Would You Be Affected If You Never Imported LiteLLM?

Possibly, yes. The wheels placed cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py in site-packages, outside the litellm package. Python processes these files at interpreter startup, so any Python launch in an affected environment could run the credential collector, including an unrelated pip install. A separate loader could fetch further code from an attacker-controlled server.

The stolen credentials were used quickly. Public research observed Amazon Web Services (AWS) instance-role credentials taken from continuous integration (CI) runners and Kubernetes nodes being validated with sts: GetCallerIdentity and then used to list Amazon Bedrock models later that day.

On hosts, LiteLLM’s advisory points to the startup files above and a detached Python process holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock. For the attack itself, see the maintainers’ official indicators, including the lookalike Berri-AI organization and the attacker’s Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. A missing artifact does not prove a host is clean.

Why Are AI Gateways High-Value Targets?

LiteLLM gives applications one interface to many model providers. A self-hosted proxy can hold upstream provider keys, a proxy master key, virtual keys, and database credentials, often alongside a cloud identity that can call managed model services. The same package on a developer laptop or CI runner exposes something different: source-control tokens, registry and deployment access, and sometimes signing material. Where the package ran determines which credentials were at risk.

What Should You Do If You Installed Or Ran LiteLLM 1.107.0?

Treat the environment as compromised, scope exposure from the artifact that ran, and rotate everything it could reach.

Find every copy that ran. Check direct and transitive dependencies, lock files, build logs, CI runners, developer environments, private mirrors, and image caches. A moving tag may resolve to a clean image today while a cluster or downstream image still runs the compromised build.

Contain and inspect safely. Isolate affected workloads and preserve filesystem, process, network, and identity evidence. Inspect them from a known-clean system, because running Python or pip inside a suspect environment can trigger the payload again.

Follow the credentials. AI gateways concentrate secrets as explained above. From a clean machine, rotate everything the affected process could reach, starting with credentials that can mint tokens or change production. On gateways, that means provider keys, proxy master and virtual keys, and database passwords. For build runners, it means access to source control, the registry, deployment, and signing. Revoke sessions, then review cloud, identity, model-provider, and source-control logs for use after exposure, including GetCallerIdentity calls from workload roles.

Rebuild instead of repairing. Removing the package or retagging an image does not count as recovery. Redeploy from a verified release on clean infrastructure, rebuild downstream images, and confirm the digests actually running. Keep watching the exposed identities after the workload is gone.

How Did Attackers Use a Leaked Key To Reach LiteLLM’s Release Pipeline?

The attackers used a leaked administrative key that was never revoked. In May, a configuration file containing a key for LiteLLM’s internal Agent Platform was committed to a public repository. On October 10, an attacker used it to obtain an organization owner’s GitHub Command-line Interface (CLI) token, then harvested additional maintainer tokens via short-lived workflows. On release day, the owner token overrode branch protection and pointed the staging build at the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm fork. A second stolen token approved production. This incident was separate from the March compromise of versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8.

Why Didn’t Image Signing Stop The Attack?

A signature proves who signed an artifact, not what source that signer built. The official pipeline signed 1.107.0 exactly as it would sign a legitimate release. Public analysis of the image provenance found that it named LiteLLM’s real release workflow as the builder and the lookalike fork as the source repository. A deployment policy that checked the expected source repository and revision, in addition to the signature, had the evidence it needed to reject this release.

LiteLLM rotated its signing key on October 23 and adopted keyless signing from v1.111.0-dev.3 on November 15.

Trust the previous key only for images published before 1.107.0. Verify releases from October 24 until keyless signing began with the rotated key, after checking its fingerprint against LiteLLM’s advisory. Verify keyless releases by the certificate identity and the OpenID Connect (OIDC) issuer, not by a key.

Pin approved digests and package hashes. Give release identities short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials instead of personal CLI tokens, and require independent approval for changes to the build source.

For AI gateways, map each deployment to its owner, model provider accounts, cloud identity, and secrets. Use separate identities per environment and restrict egress, so responders know what to isolate and revoke first.

How Qualys TotalAI Helps You Scope AI Supply Chain Exposure

Qualys TotalAI brings AI software, workloads, and containers into one inventory built on Qualys sensors and connectors. Responders can use it to move from an advisory to a list of assets that need investigation.

Find where AI software runs. The AI Workloads view shows whether AI software is installed, running, or communicating on each host, with binary, arguments, last-seen time, and Qualys Query Language (QQL) search.

See inside AI containers. AI Containers adds installed software, Kubernetes metadata, and linked hosts and containers.

Trace code to deployment. When QScanner runs in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), Code Assets link repositories to the images built from them. Qualys then correlates those images with container, cloud, and Kubernetes inventory to show where the software is deployed.

Prioritize the response. Combine TruRisk scores with what each workload can reach to decide what to isolate and which credentials to rotate first.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Which LiteLLM version should I run?

Run a release other than 1.107.0 that you have verified against LiteLLM’s current signing guidance, and pin it by hash or digest.

Does uninstalling LiteLLM remove the malware?

No. The startup files sit outside the package directory, and stolen credentials stay valid until they are revoked. Rebuild the environment and rotate credentials.

Do images built on LiteLLM need checking?

Yes. Any image built on an affected base image or with an affected wheel carries the payload, whatever its own tag says. That includes builds after the exposure window that pulled from a cache or mirror. Check each image’s base digest and installed packages, not its build date.

Were LiteLLM Enterprise customers affected?

According to the maintainers, customers running the private enterprise release were not affected.

For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 23rd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

The FBI has reportedly experienced a second cyber incident in recent months, this time targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC). The database shares records on fugitives, warrants, criminal histories, and missing persons among US law enforcement agencies. The attackers’ identities, entry method, and potential data exposure were not disclosed by the FBI.

Japan’s RIKEN research institute, which operates one the world’s strongest supercomputers ‘Fugaku’, suspended operations after attackers breached its operations network and tampered with servers between November 10 and 13. The intrusion potentially exposed account information belonging to 4,597 users, including credentials that could provide access to external systems.

The European Commission, the EU’s executive body, has suffered a cyberattack that disrupted internal systems for more than ten days. Affected services included payroll, health insurance, and translation systems. Officials claimed that they contained most of the disruption, and that the attack was assisted by AI tools.

US-based cybersecurity and networking provider Infoblox has confirmed unauthorized access to company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor. The breach reportedly involved sensitive customer data stored in a migration environment. Infoblox stated that its products and services were unaffected and did not disclose the number of customers impacted.

AI THREATS

Check Point Research has demonstrated how differences in capability between AI security filters and underlying language models can enable attackers to bypass safeguards. The analysis describes this limitation as gatekeeper asymmetry, drawing on prompt injection research and examples of security systems failing to recognize malicious inputs.

Researchers analyzed a campaign involving a China-linked threat actor that used the AI-powered Cairn framework against East Asian universities. Autonomous agents discovered and exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in open-source medical imaging software, reportedly obtaining root privileges within approximately 11 minutes. The affected software has since been patched.

Researchers examined TheMailer, an AI-powered phishing kit that uses language models to generate personalized emails and automatically rewrite messages to evade spam filters. Observed activity included a campaign involving nearly 25,000 emails and a target list exceeding 145,000 recipients. The effectiveness of these campaigns remains unverified.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical vulnerabilities affecting PHP 8.2–8.5, including CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2). Under specific configurations, the flaws can enable unauthenticated remote code execution or privilege escalation. Fixed versions include 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. The issues affect PHP-FPM, session handling, and core runtime components.

CVE-2026-129289 is prevented by the “HTTP Non Compliant” protocol anomaly protection. For full protection against this threat, make sure the “Non Compliant HTTP” inspection setting is active on the Gateway.

NGINX has released security updates addressing five high-severity vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123007, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute commands under certain configurations. Researchers estimated that approximately 8.8 million services may remain exposed. Proof-of-concept exploitation has been demonstrated, but no confirmed attacks were reported.

Check Point IPS provides protection against these threats (NGINX Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633))

Oracle and OpenJDK maintainers have released fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Java’s Base64 decoding functionality on certain x86-64 systems. The flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely or crash vulnerable applications.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Memory Corruption PoC (CVE-2026-114938))

Drupal has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-132165, a critical vulnerability in its content management system. Under certain conditions, unauthenticated attackers could exploit the installation process to reinstall Drupal, take control of affected websites, or execute arbitrary code. Fixed versions include Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, and 11.4.13.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has reported a record 2,830 ransomware victims in Q3 2026, claimed by 117 ransomware brands, up from 91 in the previous quarter. The ten largest groups accounted for just 49% of victims, while average ransom payments fell 45% to slightly over $1 million.

Check Point Research has identified a 28% increase in weekly cyberattacks against consumer goods and services organizations ahead of Black Friday 2026. Also, over 4,000 newly registered sales-related domains were found, alongside fake retail storefronts and delivery phishing websites.

Researchers exposed how Russian cyberespionage group Cold Relic exploited a cloud compromise at one US organization to infiltrate another through trusted-contact impersonation. Across both intrusions, attackers stole employee directories, emails, cloud files, and credentials, using the information to develop convincing phishing messages targeting connected organizations.

Title: Agentic Attacks: In The Wild
Context: Wiz Defend includes detections for these patterns and attackers, some of which are outlined both this post and the advisory
Full Text:
Wiz Research has been closely monitoring the evolving role of Agentic Offensive Frameworks in the threat landscape. We first covered this trend in our disclosure of attempts by Storm-0940, a Chinese-state aligned actor, to use ARTEX to conduct supply chain compromises into other software sectors. The next week, we shared the recurring fingerprints of agentic activity based on public and private cases. Then we closed out last month by sounding the alarm on Black October for AI Developer Platforms - linking nine disclosed incidents in an agentic attack trend.

We’ve also worked with our internal partners at Google Threat Intelligence Group in their coverage of Agentic Offensive Frameworks and the Significant Threshold that Agentic Threat Activity has crossed.

There has been explosive growth in successful agentic attacks, just in the last three weeks. Since publishing the Black October post, an additional twenty related incidents have been disclosed by vendors. Wiz’s CIRT has seen a 3x increase in engagement requests, matching the trend across the industry of overwhelming IR demand.

Wiz customers should review the Threat Center Advisory on this topic: AI Agent Frameworks Driving Cloud Intrusions: ARTEX and Related Tooling Indicators. Wiz Defend includes detections for these patterns and attackers, some of which are outlined both this post and the advisory.

Agentic Offensive Frameworks

The activity we’ve observed since late September 2026 uses ARTEX, its public forks and rebrands, and other agentic tools with a similar design.

ARTEX is only one of these frameworks: others seen in the wild include Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike, alongside offensive use of generic harness like Hermes, as well as custom offensive harnesses. ARTEX is open source and has hundreds of forks. Activity attributed to “ARTEX” comes from multiple unrelated operators and should not be read as a single campaign or attributed to one threat actor.

Cases

Wiz Research and CIRT have been hunting, tracking, observing, and responding to a broad set of agentic offensive frameworks attacks, some successful. In addition to the examples we’ve previously shared, we wanted to provide some cases emblematic of what we’re seeing in this new threat environment.

Opportunistic Campaigns Using Agentic Offensive Frameworks

The first pattern we see is broad, seemingly opportunistic attacks by actors who have gone all-in on agentic offensive frameworks. These campaigns are frequently:

Proxied through residential and ISP pools: Requests rotate through commercial residential proxy inventory, often a new exit for every single request. IP-based blocking and IOC sharing do very little.

Noisy: These agents spray passwords, create canary accounts, hammer sign-up and password-reset flows, and probe every available endpoint. They also label their own work: pentest, probe, recon, and incrementing task numbers show up in user agents, resource names and usernames.

Vector agnostic: The same operator will try stolen cloud keys, identity-provider OAuth flows, public sign-up flows, anonymous storage access and CI/CD trust, in parallel and across many organizations.

Once a foothold is found, it is used to explore lateral movement, harvest credentials and exfiltrate data.

We wanted to highlight a campaign, one of a dozen campaigns we’re tracking, which we have named "ARTEX-Harvester." We’ve clustered this campaign based on, among other signals, a distinctive boto3 build, incrementing Intent ID correlation cross-victim, and proxy pool usage overlap.

Between late October and mid-November 2026 we tied it, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organizations. It demonstrates exactly the patterns we highlighted. Almost every request used a different residential or ISP proxy exit - across more than 220 IPs in a single target.

Across the campaign, the same operator attempted:

Abuse of stolen credentials

Anonymous storage probing

Abuse of public sign-up, password-reset and sign-in flows

Identity-provider probing

Among the numerous attempted footholds, one success shows how these attacks progress once initial access is achieved.

Compromised VCS credentials allowed access to private repositories

The attack pivoted from CI to the cloud environment by creating branches that abused CI workload identity trust relationships.

Harvest workflows dumped CI-accessible secrets and Terraform state

Those secrets and repositories were exfiltrated

In parallel, the operator used a stolen service-account token from an application pod. That account could create privileged pods with the node's root filesystem mounted. The operator used that to deploy a "node-level collector" pod, which harvested the kubelet PKI and every projected service-account token on the node. One of those tokens, belonging to cert-manager, could read the ArgoCD secrets, leading to cluster-admin.

Detection

These attacks are far from stealthy. Wiz Issues captured this activity across a variety of rules that are agnostic to the usage of an Agentic Offensive Framework (see below).

Additionally, artifacts were heavily marked with agentic offensive framework self-labeling behavior, including pentest-recon user agents, pentest-* workspaces and pods, and an incrementing task intent counter (pentest-iNNNNNN).

Wiz Sensor caught the behavior within the cluster, including privileged container creation, nsenter, IMDS kube-env queries and drifted scripts reaching for cloud credentials.

Targeted Attacks and Open Directories

One of the more interesting byproducts of agentic offensive frameworks is a trend of poor operational security. ARTEX shipped with its web console exposed to the internet by default, often still on default credentials, and many operators never lock it down: Censys counted more than 1,400 exposed ARTEX consoles in early November.

The result is a steady supply of exposed command-and-control panels and open directories for threat intelligence and security firms to analyze.

Because these frameworks are agentic, those exposures reveal more than attacker actions. They capture the attack as a narrative: operator prompts, planner intents, agent transcripts and the model's own reasoning.

Seeing Both Sides of an Attack

This exposure occasionally grants something rare: both sides of the same intrusion. In some cases, we can pair our telemetry with the relevant attacker’s leaked logs and tools - granting a picture of not just what they did in a single incident, but what they did everywhere else, why they did it, and what they planned next.

Here is one such anonymized case:

Across four days in October, an attacker navigated two AWS accounts and seven EKS clusters:

Initial foothold: a stolen Terraform-runner session read the kubelet kubeconfig, then created a privileged pod and a cluster-admin binding.

CI compromise: remote code execution on the Jenkins controller opened a reverse shell to the attacker's server.

Node persistence: a pod escape put a custom loader on the nodes. It was an ld.so.preload userland rootkit with a DNS-tunnel channel, disguised as a fontconfig service, and had zero detections on VirusTotal.

Credential use off-platform: node, IRSA and Terraform-runner credentials were used from the attacker's own server to read Terraform state and Secrets Manager, and to open SSM sessions.

The attacker’s open directory colors in the details, across over 3,000 exposed files.

It shows activity outside the observed telemetry:

Identity provider: forged admin tokens gave access to 3,392 users and their live session tokens.

Bastion: beacons were pushed to 19 hosts, and the bastion's database was decrypted for 50 SSH private keys.

CI/CD: GitHub Actions secrets were dumped, and the production Jenkinsfile was modified to run before its approval gate, exposing production secrets.

It also shows more about the attacker’s operations:

Command layer: CyberStrikeAI ran the operation. A csai- prefix is on nearly everything the attacker created (csai-escape pods, a csai-pentest-role IAM role, a csai-probe runner).

Operator workspace: an ARTEX checkout sat alongside .claude, .grok and .agents directories. The same server ran ARTEX tooling against several other organizations that month, unsuccessfully.

Reporting: the operator's own auto-generated Chinese language report masks the intrusion as an "authorised red-team pentest" and claims 58 findings.

AI tools as targets: Anthropic API keys were harvested from 50 hosts, and employees' AI coding-assistant session histories were mined for production SSO credentials.

Black October Q4

Finally, let’s revisit “Black October for AI Developer Platforms.”

Since publishing the blog post, disclosed incidents have more than tripled. While insufficient details have been shared to link all these incidents to any single actor, or even agentic offensive frameworks in some cases, there is a clear trend where attackers are using agentic offensive frameworks to target rich sources of LLM access and credentials.

Where victims have disclosed a root cause, the entry points are familiar.

Stolen or leaked credentials (Zeabur, Kernel, Lightning AI, Bitrise)

Exposed or vulnerable services (Chainstack's default-credential Grafana, NEAR AI's SGLang RCE, Northflank's API zero-day)

Tenant-isolation escapes (Railway, Phala, Dokploy).

Increasingly, the way in was an upstream breach: keys and secrets stolen from one platform opened the next.

The impact is just as consistent. Attackers go straight for environment variables and stored customer secrets, prioritizing AI provider and cloud keys that can be validated, resold or burned on LLM usage within hours.

Recommendations

Wiz’s AI Threat Readiness Framework is our blueprint for how to build a security program that can stay ahead of these attacks. Defenders must put AI to work in order to leverage their context advantage against attackers and enable real machine-speed defense against these new tools and tactics.

Detections

The following is a representative subset of generic rules that have been observed in relation to agentic offensive framework attacks:

EC2 Instance Credentials Used Outside Of AWS

ECS Task Credentials Used Outside Of AWS

Unusual GetCallerIdentity Operation

Unusual Mass Access Denied Activity

Unusual Enumeration Activity by IAM User

API Calls From Unusual Country

API Calls by a Known Offensive Tool

Cluster Accessed From an Unusual Country

Unusual Mass Secret Value Retrieval

Attempts To Create Access Token For Multiple Service Accounts

IAM Role Assumed From New or Inactive Account

Model access check behavior tied to previously seen attacks

Azure Application Secret Used After Long Period of Inactivity

GCP Service Account Key Used After A Long Period Of Inactivity

IAM Access Key Used After Long Period of Inactivity

Instance Created Access Token Used Outside GCP

Permission To Impersonate Any Service Account Granted To Member

Wiz has also developed a set of behavioral detections specific to this activity. Among others, these include:

Session or Resource Name Matching an AI Offensive Tool Naming Pattern

AI Offensive Tool Step Counter in Session or Resource Names

Unusual Pagination Pattern by AWS Identity From New ASO

Activity From AI Offensive Tool IP Address Seen In Organization

AI Offensive Tool Activity Detected Via HTTP Endpoint

We note that these rules are expected to be perishable, given the inherent pace of evolution and customization of these tools. Wiz Research continues to develop advanced detection of these attacks based on the behavioral patterns of agent-driven intrusions (their speed, breadth and systematic structure), which persist even as individual tools are renamed, rebranded or customized.

Title: Press play on Elastic Security 9.6, banger after banger
Context: Unlike conventional detections, agentic exploits use natural language to launch attacks, so leaving this data out gives you an incomplete picture of the threat landscape
Full Text:
You’ve clocked in for your shift and just hit play on your 10-hour lo-fi playlist. The caffeine is kicking in, and you’re pumped because the handoff notes from the last shift are really useful. Every case has all the evidence and the rationale behind the disposition, along with the affected hosts and users. Plus, you only have five alerts to review in your queue. This security operations center (SOC) shift is exactly why we built AlertZero, now available as a technical preview in Elastic Security in Elastic Cloud Serverless (Serverless). It’s also coming in early December 2026 to Elastic Security 9.6 for Elastic Cloud Hosted (ECH) and Elastic Self-Managed deployments with an Enterprise subscription or an Elastic Security 9.6 trial license.

AlertZero is big news in Elastic Security 9.6, but there’s a lot more to this release:

Feature

What’s new

AlertZero

Four teams of agents, called Watches, covering alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering, and forensic analysis

Entity Analytics

A refreshed overview, expanded entity resolution, and an AI brief

Ransomware protection for Linux

Elastic Defend’s behavior-based ransomware protection now extends to Linux

YARA memory scanning

Bring your own YARA rules to scan process memory

Automatic Migration

Agentic editing for migrated detection rules

AI detection and response

MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS) support, 143 AI security detection rules, and the Security for AI integration package in technical preview

Grab your coffee, and take a look at what’s new. Where there’s a deeper dive, we’ve linked it.

AlertZero, the agentic layer of Elastic Security

First, explore the four Watches in AlertZero, along with the Workers that perform specific security tasks. Then, learn about proposed actions and the approval process, plus the various model options.

Four Watches for alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering, and forensics

AlertZero covers alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering, and endpoint forensics through four Watches, each of which holds Workers that have specific jobs, such as triaging new alerts or tuning a noisy rule.

Under the hood, each Worker is an AI-powered unit of work that belongs to a Watch. It runs in the background, either on a schedule or in response to events like new alerts, and then analyzes your data and brings you proposed actions. Every Worker is built as a workflow in Elastic Workflows, and each one has its own settings, including its schedule and its autonomy level:

Worker

What the Worker does

What the Worker proposes

Triage Watch’s Alert Triage Worker

Classifies new alerts as true or false positives, with a confidence score for each

Closing alerts that it classifies as false positives

Triage Watch’s Attack Discovery Worker

Groups related alerts into potential attacks, and opens an investigation for each one

Endpoint analysis for attacks that look real or can't be ruled out

Hunt Watch’s Continuous Threat Hunt Worker

Searches your data for activity that matches threat reports, and records any detection gaps it finds

Response actions when your data matches a threat report, and detection gaps for Rule Coverage to review

Detection Watch’s Rule Tuning Worker

Finds rules that keep producing false positives, and determines why

Edits and exceptions for rules that analysts keep closing as false positives

Detection Watch’s Rule Coverage Worker

Reviews the detection gaps that Continuous Threat Hunt records

Enabling, installing, or creating rules to close detection gaps

Forensics Watch’s Endpoint Analysis Worker

Reconstructs the attack timeline on the main host involved, and pulls out indicators of compromise

Isolating a host, or killing or suspending a process

How Workers propose actions and how you approve them

When a Worker thinks something in your environment should change, such as closing a false positive or isolating a host, it writes that up as a proposed action, which lays out what the Worker recommends as a next step and why, based on the context it retrieved. When you open one, you’re in the investigation where the Worker keeps its notes, including the evidence it gathered and the reasoning behind its recommendation, along with the hosts and users involved.

Because an investigation is an Elastic Agent Builder conversation, you can ask follow-up questions before you decide on next steps. Each Worker has up to three autonomy levels (Manual, Assisted, or Supervised) that determine whether a proposed action comes to you for review or runs on its own. When you approve one, the action runs as you, with your privileges, and it’s recorded as your decision. If you decline, the action doesn’t run.

Your Workers, your choice of model

No single model fits every step, and the model you rely on today can change. A provider tightens its guardrails, retires a version, or changes its pricing, and a step that worked starts failing or costing more. Security work runs into this more than most, and when Hugging Face investigated its July 2026 intrusion, the first models its team reached for refused much of the analysis because their guardrails treated reverse engineering an exploit the same as launching one. The team finished the work with an open-weight model it ran on its own infrastructure.

That’s why you choose the models behind your Workers. In Feature Settings, you pick which models do the work, and you can change them as your needs change.

You can use your model of choice, including an open-weight model or one you host yourself, and switching models doesn’t change anything else about how your Workers run.

Entity Analytics gives your hunts and investigations a starting point

The Entity Analytics improvements in Elastic Security 9.6 are generally available (GA) with an Enterprise subscription.

A refreshed Entity Analytics overview with six attention tiles

The refreshed overview brings risk changes, alerts, anomalies, and watchlist activity into one place, so SOC analysts and threat hunters can find the changes that are worth investigating. Six attention tiles (Severely alerting, Newly high-risk, Risk movers, New & alerting, Anomalous, and Watchlisted & alerting) bring forward the users, hosts, and services that changed, each with its trend against the previous period. You can compare periods and see trend lines across 24 hours, seven days, or 30 days, where history is available.

Filter by entity type, risk level, criticality, source, or watchlist, and then inspect the entities that match an attention tile in a searchable entity grid. In the entity flyout, you can switch between resolved identities and individual records, with risk, alerts, anomalies, findings, and observed attributes available for each.

An AI brief on which entities need attention

When your chief information security officer wants a summary of your entity risk posture, you can generate a concise AI brief from your Entity Analytics view, plus a clear starting point for investigation. The brief names what needs attention and shows how key metrics have changed. It also lists up to three entities to investigate first. You can inspect the supporting entity evidence and relevant risk history charts to see why. And you can keep asking follow-up questions in Agent Builder without rebuilding the investigation context.

Entity resolution finds the person behind the logins

Entity resolution already helps you see the person who shows up as a few different accounts across your endpoint, identity, and cloud data, and 9.6 expands these details. For example, if maria.chen in Okta and CORP\mchen in Active Directory share an email address, they show up as one person, with one combined risk view.

Built-in matching rules now also cover Windows and CrowdStrike security identifiers (SIDs), Entra globally unique identifiers (GUIDs), and Microsoft 365 user principal names (UPNs), and email matching is now case insensitive. In Agent Builder, you can inspect resolution groups, link or unlink accounts, and turn built-in rules on or off in plain language. You review the proposed canonical identity and confirm changes before they’re applied.

Elastic Defend adds Linux ransomware protection and YARA memory scanning

Elastic Defend will add several new capabilities in 9.6, including these two:

Ransomware protection parity for Linux, Windows, and macOS

Since your environment runs on more than Windows, your ransomware protection should cover all of it. Elastic Defend is bringing ransomware protection to Linux, GA in 9.6, extending the behavior-based protection that it already provides on Windows and macOS to Linux hosts. So you’ll have one approach across Windows and macOS, as well as Linux, for your servers.

In Prevent mode, Elastic Defend blocks an attack as it happens. You manage the policy in Elastic Security, next to the alerts, investigations, and response, so ransomware prevention, malware protection, endpoint detection and response (EDR), and security information and event management (SIEM) context live together. When something fires, you get an alert with the process and host details that you need to respond to it.

Find the footprints in RAM with your own YARA rules

With adversaries moving in seconds, you need deeper analysis and insight into your hosts. Some malware never touches the disk. It lives in memory, where file scans can’t see it. Elastic Defend scans process memory with YARA signatures, so you can catch threats that hide there. With 9.6, you can bring your own rules and apply custom YARA signatures to match your threat intel. You manage them in a new YARA signatures tab on the Artifacts page, where you apply them globally or to specific policies, and turn on scanning in the Memory threat protection card of the Defend policy. A match creates a Memory Threat – Detected alert with the matched signature name and memory strings, so analysts can see what matched. Custom YARA signatures will be GA in 9.6.

Fine-tune your SIEM migration agentically

Migrating to a new SIEM requires careful planning and execution. We’ve been doing the heavy lifting of migrating your SIEM rules and dashboards to Elastic with Automatic Migration, and we continue to improve that experience.

In 9.6, you can agentically edit your mapped and translated detection rules to fit your environment by adding a rule to chat to start tuning, and you confirm the changes in the same UI.

From chat, you can:

Change the logic of the translated Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL) query by adding a custom index pattern or mapping custom fields into ES|QL. You can also do so by fixing syntax and runtime errors.

Match to a prebuilt rule instead of a custom translated rule.

Get recommendations on alternative prebuilt rules.

Match rules to different integrations.

This works across all supported vendors: Splunk, QRadar, and Microsoft Sentinel.

AI detection and response in Elastic Security

MITRE ATLAS mappings for your detection rules

MITRE ATLAS is MITRE’s knowledge base of the tactics and techniques adversaries use against AI-enabled systems, covering prompt injection, jailbreaks, stolen model API keys, and poisoned agent tools. It’s maintained by MITRE and shaped by real-world observations and research from across industry and academia. It’s modeled directly on MITRE ATT&CK, so the structure will feel familiar: tactics for what an adversary is trying to achieve, plus techniques and sub-techniques for how.

In Elastic Security 9.6, MITRE ATLAS mappings ship with prebuilt detection rules for AI platforms and generative AI (GenAI) tooling, so rules provide the AI-related context out of the box. A new coverage table shows which ATLAS tactics and techniques your rules already address, scored in its own view rather than averaged into your ATT&CK numbers.

140+ new detection rules for AI agents and large language model platforms

AI risk lives in multiple places. A coding agent runs on a developer laptop, the models it calls run in a cloud AI platform, and the keys, guardrails, and agents behind those models are managed through a cloud control plane. The Elastic Security 9.6 rules are organized around the threats that show up in each of those places and the telemetry that Elastic already collects from them.

The new rules cover hijacked coding agents, malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, credentials pasted into prompts, jailbreaks, and stolen API keys across Amazon Bedrock, OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise, Anthropic, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

Security for AI: Prompt injection detection at ingest

GenAI agents can autonomously read files, run commands, call APIs and MCP tools, and send messages, and they frequently do so without explicit user permissions. Threat actors hijack them with methods like prompt injection, which changes an agent’s goals and can lead to dangerous actions in your environment. Unlike conventional detections, agentic exploits use natural language to launch attacks, so leaving this data out gives you an incomplete picture of the threat landscape.

The Security for AI integration package is designed to help counter this. It’s in technical preview starting in Elastic Stack 9.6 with a Platinum or trial subscription, and it adds four small models that score GenAI prompts and responses inside your own cluster as they’re indexed. They look for prompt injection, encoded payloads, obfuscated words, and refusals, and eight prebuilt detection rules act on the results. It supports the AWS Bedrock integration (version 2.2.0 and later) and the OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise integration, including Codex logs, conversation messages, and custom agent logs.

Elastic Security 9.6 and a manageable alert queue

Elastic Security 9.6 is designed to help you get your alert queue to a manageable size and keep it that way, with AlertZero doing the groundwork and Entity Analytics giving your hunt somewhere to start. Plus, it has Elastic Defend covering Linux for ransomware and memory-based threats.

If you’re ready to get started, these and other Elastic Security 9.6 capabilities (except the new Elastic Defend capabilities) are now available in Elastic Cloud Serverless. Elastic Security 9.6 (including those Elastic Defend capabilities) is expected to be available for ECH and Elastic Self-Managed deployments in early December 2026.

Title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right
Context: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data...
Full Text: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization. The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems. The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather important blanks. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers. Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach. More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach. Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems. In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase. Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®

In this article

OXLoader can lead to malware that steals browser passwords and data or gives criminals remote access to a Windows PC

Fake copyright complaints and cracked software activators are among the lures used to spread it

What to watch for in suspicious downloads and how to reduce the risk

We’ve seen an increase in activity involving OXLoader, a loader that installs other malware on a computer. Elastic first documented it in June 2026, when attackers used Google Ads to distribute CASTLESTEALER through OXLoader.

The malware installed varies by campaign. We found OXLoader distributing Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Depending on the payload, attackers could steal saved browser passwords and other data, remotely control the computer, or download more malware.

We found OXLoader in malicious ZIP files disguised as complaint or copyright-infringement notices, as well as fake software activators. One campaign we analyzed used fake activators downloaded from GitLab.

Below, we take a technical deep dive into how that campaign works, including how OXLoader uses DLL hijacking to unpack and run malware.

How to stay safe

Here are a few simple ways to stay safe:

Be wary of emails or links that tell you to run software in connection with copyright infringement or complaints.

Watch for executables with very long names or double extensions, such as .docx.exe or .pdf.exe.

Pay attention when you extract an archive. If some of the files it contains don’t appear, be cautious.

Downloading activators or cracks can compromise your device.

Install Malwarebytes Browser Guard, our free browser extension, to block malicious websites and suspicious downloads.

Use Malwarebytes Premium to block malware in real time, including malicious files.

Overview of the detected campaigns

In this section, we analyze several detected campaigns. In the cases we examined, OXLoader was decrypted either by malicious code embedded in legitimate executables, as in Elastic’s analysis, or through DLL hijacking. DLL hijacking is one of the key new features we observed in these campaigns. The rest of the infection chain is similar to the one Elastic identified.

We identified several DLLs used to decrypt and execute OXLoader, including:

Qt5Widgets.dll

Qt6Core.dll

SDL3.dll

UnityPlayer.dll

ANCUtility.dll

dbghelp.dll

msvcr100.dll

In some cases, we found other DLLs that had been tampered with to launch the malicious DLL. The executables involved were associated with Microsoft applications, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers.

Across different campaigns, OXLoader was distributed using themes related to complaints and copyright infringement. Malicious ZIP files were distributed in several ways. For example, a user might receive an email with an attached PDF prompting them to download and run a ZIP file, claiming there had been “unauthorized copying of brand intellectual property.”

Example of a PDF attached to an email that downloads a malicious ZIP file

When the user runs the executable, the infection chain begins through DLL hijacking, and a fake PDF opens. In this case, WindowsCodecs.dll is the trojanized DLL used to decrypt OXLoader.

The contents of the malicious ZIP file The fake PDF that opens

In some cases, a batch file is present instead of the executable and DLLs. It downloads a ZIP file containing the malicious DLL from different websites or hosting providers. The batch file’s content is similar to the one analyzed by Elastic. These files have long names, for example:

Photo_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Product_Review_Order_Front_Back_PDF.bat Form_Video_{ RANDOM NUMBERS }_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat Case_Form_Video_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat

In other cases, OXLoader was distributed through ZIP archives named Evidence_of_Violation.zip, downloaded from Google Sites. These websites used different titles and graphics.

Google Site used to distribute the malicious archive

In this case, WinWord.exe is renamed with a double extension, such as Travel_Point_Conditions.docx.exe or evidence_of_violation.docx.exe. OXLoader is then executed through DLL hijacking using the malicious DLL msvcr100.dll.

Example of one of the malicious archives

Finally, in the campaigns analyzed in this post, OXLoader was distributed through fake activators and cracks for popular software, downloaded from GitLab.

Malicious activators hosted on GitLab that distribute OXLoader

Technical analysis of OXLoader

In this campaign, users download software activators from GitLab, triggering the infection chain.

Stage 1: DLL hijacking

The archive downloaded by the user contains several legitimate DLLs, along with a legitimate executable from Take-Two Interactive Software, which is used to perform DLL hijacking using the UnityPlayer DLL. The manifest.json contains encrypted shellcode, which is decrypted and injected into another legitimate DLL.

The extracted archive with the malicious DLL

The DLL at address 0x18054485b contains a jmp instruction that calls the code responsible for decrypting the remaining code at 0x1807a3372. This decryption code differs across the cases we analyzed.

The call to the decryption function The self-decryption function

The code is heavily obfuscated using opaque predicates, control flow flattening (CFF), and mixed Boolean arithmetic (MBA). We therefore used the Sogen emulator to trace the main functions that execute and identify the malware code that called them.

Partial Sogen execution with some functions related to anti-analysis and language checks Termination of the malware if a virtualized environment is detected (Sogen output)

The values ​​used by the remaining functions are decoded using two functions:

The function at the address 0x1807a2282 decrypts the data ​​using the following formula: input1 ^ (input2 + 0x33fda).

The function at the address 0x1807a2624 is responsible for decrypting an 8-byte chunk; this function is called multiple times by other wrappers to decrypt the complete strings.

The decrypted strings

The anti-analysis and language checks we observed are similar to those identified by Elastic, with the minor addition of a check using WNetGetResourceParentW to detect virtualized environments.

Description

Value

Invalid values to detect virtualized environments

Pass invalid values ​​using the functions WNetAddConnection2W and WNetGetResourceParentW and check if the LastErrorValue is ERROR_BAD_NET_NAME (67) and ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS (487)

CPU-count

NumberOfProcessors greater than or equal to 3

Display Refresh rate

Executes a PowerShell command and it checks if the result is equal to or greater than 20 Hz

Geographical location

GetUserGeoID compared with 5 (Azerbaijan), 7 (Armenia), 29 (Belarus), 137 (Kazakhstan), 130 (Kyrgyzstan), 152 (Moldova), 203 (Russia), 228 (Tajikistan), 247 (Uzbekistan), 238 (Turkmenistan)

UI-Language

GetUserDefaultUILanguage compared with 0x419 (Russia)

The refresh rate is obtained using this PowerShell command:

powershell "Get-WmiObject Win32_VideoController | Select-Object -ExpandProperty CurrentRefreshRate"

It’s possible to bypass the anti-analysis checks by patching the function 0x1807999c2. Otherwise, if an analysis environment is detected, the system is shut down via a cmd command, or jumps to an invalid address.

The necessary files are then copied to a randomly named folder in ProgramData. In this case, the files were:

C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\ fl studio pro.exe C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\unityplayer.dll C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\manifest.json C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\awindows.storage.dll

A cmd command is executed to add a RunOnce registry value and executes the extracted main executable.

Title: AlertZero in Elastic Security: Every alert answered. Every decision yours
Context: Attack Discovery passes attacks to Endpoint Analysis for a closer look at the hosts involved, and Rule Coverage works from the detection gaps that Continuous Threat Hunt records
Full Text:
Most security operations center (SOC) teams we talk to describe the same problem. There are more alerts than people to work them, so the queue decides what gets looked at, and threat hunting and detection rule tuning keep slipping to the following week. And most of the time that an alert eats up isn't spent deciding what to do with it; it’s spent digging up context first, like whether this rule has fired on this host before and what else was going on around it. We built AlertZero to do that digging for you, so your analysts can spend their time on the calls that really need them. Starting today, with Elastic Security 9.6, AlertZero is available in technical preview in Elastic Cloud Serverless and is expected to be available for ECH and Self-Managed deployments in 9.6 in early December.

In October 2026, we offered an early look at AlertZero, where we followed one suspicious login from the first alert, through the evidence gathered in an investigation, to a proposed host isolation waiting for an analyst's approval. Today, we’re giving you the full breakdown on what’s in the technical preview release: the six Workers and what each one proposes, how much they can do at each level of autonomy, how to choose models, and how to get started in both written and video form.

What’s inside AlertZero: 4 Watches and 6 Workers

Let’s start with an overview. AlertZero covers four areas of SOC work: alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering, and endpoint forensics. Each Watch covers one of these four areas, and they hold the Workers that do that work. A Worker has one specific job, such as triaging new alerts or tuning a noisy rule.

Under the hood, each Worker is an AI-powered unit of work that belongs to a Watch. It runs in the background, either on a schedule or in response to events like new alerts, and then analyzes your data and brings you proposed actions. Every Worker is built as a workflow in Elastic Workflows, and each one has its own settings, including its schedule and its autonomy level.

AlertZero deep dive video

Here’s a video overview, where Elastic’s James Spiteri, Senior Director of Security Product Management, and Jackie McGuire, Senior Director of Security Product Marketing Management, show you AlertZero.

Why we build Workers and Watches this way

AlertZero builds every Worker as a workflow of deterministic steps, and it calls a model only where judgment is needed. That split does four things:

Lookups and checks run as code, so they behave the same way every time.

You can check the model’s conclusions against the evidence, because it works from data pulled from your own environment.

Cost stays down, since model calls go only to the steps that need judgment.

Nothing changes in your environment based solely on the model’s recommendation. A Worker’s AI steps can only read your data, and every change is carried out by deterministic steps. Its autonomy level decides which of those wait for approval.

To see how a Worker reached a result, you can open the run and follow each step it took. When a Worker thinks something in your environment should change (for example, that a false positive should be closed or a host should be isolated), it writes that up as a proposed action. The proposal lays out what the Worker wants to do and why, along with what it found. The level of autonomy (Manual, Assisted, or Supervised) that you’ve assigned the Worker dictates how it proceeds. At Manual, it waits until someone on your team approves or declines it.

How the Alert Triage Worker classifies alerts

Now that we’ve covered the basics, let's look at what happens inside a run of the Alert Triage Worker, one of the two Workers in the Triage Watch. Every Worker is a workflow made of deterministic steps that run as code and AI steps that call a model only where judgment is needed.

On each run, the Alert Triage Worker picks up new alerts and starts with the same steps that an SOC analyst would follow before deciding whether to close an alert or escalate it, or possibly to dig deeper. It looks up how past alerts from that rule were closed and how common the activity is in your environment. It also looks up what the rule is designed to detect. Those lookups are deterministic, so no model is involved.

Only once the evidence is assembled does the Worker pass it to a model, and it does so in a single AI step, deciding whether each alert looks like a true or false positive and how confident it is with that determination. The Worker's deterministic steps then take over again to record the verdict and, for confident false positives, to propose closing them.

How AlertZero Workers hand off work to each other

You can run any combination of Workers. A team that mainly wants help with triage and noisy rules, for example, can run Alert Triage and Rule Tuning without turning on Attack Discovery or Endpoint Analysis. The false positives that Alert Triage flags count toward Rule Tuning, which looks for the rules that keep producing them and proposes fixes. Other Workers also hand work to each other in the same way.

Attack Discovery passes attacks to Endpoint Analysis for a closer look at the hosts involved, and Rule Coverage works from the detection gaps that Continuous Threat Hunt records. If you turn off one side of a handoff, the other keeps running but has less context to work with. Response actions in this release, whether they come from Endpoint Analysis or Continuous Threat Hunt, run through Elastic Defend, which Endpoint Analysis also needs to investigate hosts.

AlertZero autonomy levels: Manual, Assisted, and Supervised

Every Worker has an autonomy setting with up to three levels. At Manual, anything that a Worker proposes waits for someone on your team to approve it. Assisted applies only to Rule Tuning and Rule Coverage. At that level, they start looking into a rule or a coverage gap without asking first, although any change they come up with still needs approval. Supervised goes the furthest: the Worker approves its own proposals and acts on them, and afterward, you review what it did.

Whatever its autonomy level, every Worker can tag and annotate the alerts it reviews and can open investigations without preapproval. The rest depends on the level you set.
