How to review and approve a proposed action

A lot of an analyst's day is taken up by the work that leads to a decision. For example, you pull context on an alert and determine whether a rule has misfired before, or you search your data for something that a new threat report describes. The decision itself, like whether to contain a host or change a rule, or maybe to close a batch of alerts, is usually the quicker part. AlertZero takes on that groundwork and attaches everything it found to the decision that it brings you. What changes in your environment remains up to you, and you choose how much of it to hand off.

Every proposed action lands on the proposed actions page, grouped under Respond, Investigate, and Configure. Open one, and you're in its investigation, which is where the Worker keeps its notes, including the evidence it gathered and the reasoning behind its recommendation, along with the hosts and users involved. Because an investigation is an Elastic Agent Builder conversation, you can ask follow-up questions before you decide, such as, What else is that host connected to? Or, What would the proposed exception stop matching?

When you approve, the action runs as you, with your privileges, and it's recorded as your decision. If you decline, the action doesn't run.

Working a case together with escalations

Some cases need more than one person. An escalation brings one or more related investigations into a shared conversation. You can assign it to people on your team and keep it private or make it public. You work the case together there, with the agent available for questions along the way.

Choosing models for AlertZero: Efficient, Balanced, and Frontier tiers

No single model is the right fit for every step, and the one you rely on today can change. A provider tightens its guardrails or retires a version, or even changes its pricing, and a step that used to work starts failing or costing more. Security work runs into this more than most. When Hugging Face investigated its July 2026 intrusion, the first models that its team reached for refused much of the forensic work, because their guardrails treated reverse engineering an exploit the same as launching one. The team finished the analysis with an open-weight model.

That's why AlertZero lets you choose the models that its Workers use. We assign each AI step in a Worker's workflow to one of three model tiers, based on what the step needs. You pick the models for each tier in the AlertZero section of Feature Settings, and the Workers draw from those:

Efficient handles quick, frequent calls, such as checking detection coverage, where a small, low-cost model does the job.

Balanced covers work where accuracy matters and a step uses tools over many rounds, like diagnosing a noisy rule or analyzing a host.

Frontier is for single-pass work where one output carries the most weight, such as generating attack discoveries, so that's where your most capable model belongs.

You can use your model of choice for any tier, including an open-weight model or one that you host yourself. If every tier points to a model that you host, the prompts built from your alerts go to that model instead of a third-party service. If a model stops working well, you can switch it for that tier without changing anything else about how your Workers run.

What AlertZero changes for your SOC team

AlertZero changes where your team’s time goes. New alerts will keep coming, and some of them will always need a person. Watches focus on emptying your queue. The groundwork behind each decision, including pulling context on an alert and noticing that a rule keeps misfiring, happens in the background. What reaches your team is a shorter list of decisions to make, with the evidence behind each one. You determine which Workers run and how much each one can do on its own, along with which models do the work, and you can change any of that as your team gets comfortable.

That's the shift we built AlertZero for: less time spent assembling context and more time for the hunts and rule fixes, as well as the investigations, that keep slipping to next week.

Getting started with AlertZero: Requirements and setup

In this preview, AlertZero is available now on Elastic Cloud Serverless and will be coming to Elastic Cloud Hosted (ECH) and Elastic Self-Managed deployments with an Enterprise subscription or a trial license. You turn it on one space at a time, so you can start with a single team or environment and grow from there. Check the requirements first, and then follow Set up AlertZero to turn it on and add an AI model, along with enabling your first Workers. AlertZero privileges cover the roles that your team will need, including the separate privilege for creating escalations.

Title: Elastic ships 143 detection rules for AI agents and LLM platforms
Context: Add the integrations for the AI platforms you use (OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI), and turn on...
Full Text:
Elastic 9.6 will ship 143 AI security detection rules. A coding agent runs with your shell and your files, along with your cloud keys. The rules cover agents hijacked into running attacker commands, malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, credentials pasted into prompts, jailbreaks, and stolen API keys used to run models at someone else’s expense. When that activity happens on a developer’s machine, Elastic Defend can kill the process outright.

In August 2025, malicious versions of the Nx build tool used a post-install script to collect credentials and invoke installed AI coding command line interfaces (CLIs) with safety checks bypassed, to help find sensitive files (GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c). An npm package impersonating a Postmark MCP server copied every outgoing email to an attacker (postmark-mcp, version 1.0.16). A compromised Amazon Q Developer extension release carried instructions telling the AI agent to delete local files and cloud resources (AWS-2025-015), although AWS confirmed that the payload failed on a syntax error.

The rules run in both Elastic detection engines, as prebuilt security information and event management (SIEM) rules in detection-rules and as Elastic Defend behavior rules in protections-artifacts. In this blog post, we cover the threat vectors that these rules address, the telemetry that each one needs, how coverage compares across AI vendors, and what to do with the alerts.

Key takeaways

Elastic 9.6 will ship 143 production SIEM rules for AI security that cover coding agents, MCP servers, AI platforms, and the cloud services behind them.

Coverage spans Amazon Bedrock, OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise, Anthropic, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry, with comparable detections for each, wherever the provider's logs allow it.

Elastic Defend adds on-host prevention for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and other coding agents, stopping agent-driven persistence and malicious Cursor workspaces before they run.

The AI rules map to MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS) and MITRE ATT&CK, so AI threat coverage can be measured against AI-specific techniques.

Where AI security detection rules fit: Agents, platforms, and cloud

AI risk lives in multiple places. A coding agent runs on a developer laptop, the models it calls run in a cloud AI platform, and the keys, guardrails, and agents behind those models are managed through a cloud control plane. The Elastic 9.6 rules are organized around the threats that show up in each of those places and the telemetry that Elastic already collects from them.

What’s coming in the 9.6 AI security detection rule set

143 production SIEM rules tagged Domain: GenAI. New rules in this release add OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry to existing coverage for Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, and the endpoint.

Elastic Defend prevention for AI coding agents. Persistence via GenAI Tool kills a process started by a coding agent when it tries to install persistence on macOS or Windows, and Cursor Arbitrary Code Execution via PHP stops a malicious repository from running code when it’s opened in Cursor.

MITRE ATLAS mappings. All 143 AI SIEM rules map to MITRE ATLAS techniques alongside MITRE ATT&CK, and 9.6 will be the first release that carries those mappings into the product. A dedicated article covers the mappings in detail.

Where do AI threats show up, and what telemetry detects them?

No single log source covers all three layers, so the rules are built around the telemetry that each layer produces, including:

User AI tooling,where coding agents, MCP servers, and local model runtimes execute. Elastic Defend process, file, network, and domain name system (DNS) events give full process lineage from the agent to whatever it started. SIEM rules use this data (several also accept Sysmon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender XDR, and Auditd), alongside the Elastic Defend behavior rules.

AI platforms, where prompts and admin actions are logged, along with connector activity. Fleet integrations collect OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise audit and conversation logs, Anthropic audit logs, Amazon Bedrock invocation and AgentCore runtime logs, Google Cloud Vertex AI prompt and audit logs, and Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI logs.

The cloud control plane, where models, guardrails, agents, and keys are provisioned. AWS CloudTrail drives the Bedrock and AgentCore control plane rules.

Across these sources, the 143 SIEM rules break down by platform as follows:

Source

SIEM rules in Elastic 9.6

Amazon Bedrock

38

OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise

34

Anthropic

29

Endpoint (Elastic Defend and third party)

18

Google Cloud Vertex AI

14

Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI

10

Total

143

Rules that inspect prompt and response content need prompt logging turned on in the provider. Everything else works from the default audit streams.

Two detection engines: SIEM rules and Elastic Defend behavior rules

The 9.6 coverage comes from two engines that work differently and complement each other:

Prebuilt SIEM rules run in Kibana on a schedule against indexed data from any source: Elastic Defend, third-party endpoint tools, cloud audit logs, and AI platform logs. They detect and alert minutes after the data arrives and correlate across sources. They catch patterns that only appear over time, such as usage spikes or impossible travel. This is where cloud and AI platform threats are covered.

Elastic Defend behavior rules run on the host, inside the Elastic Defend agent, against live process, file, and network events. They evaluate as the activity happens and keep working when the host is offline. In prevent mode, they can kill the offending process before the action completes. This is where an attack carried out through a coding agent can be stopped mid-flight.

The two layers feed each other. Elastic Defend alerts land in the SIEM alongside everything else, and several SIEM rules run on Elastic Defend telemetry. Elastic Defend Alert from GenAI Utility or Descendant adds AI context to any Elastic Defend alert whose process tree leads back to an AI tool.

How attackers use AI coding agents to run their commands

A coding agent runs whatever its context tells it to run. If an attacker controls part of that context, through a poisoned README, issue, web page, or dependency, the agent becomes a signed, trusted process that executes the attacker's commands. The Nx compromise showed the other route, malware that simply starts the agent itself with approvals disabled. Detections here focus on how the agent was started and what it started:

GenAI CLI Started with Unsafe Permission Bypass identifies agents launched with flags such as --dangerously-skip-permissions, --yolo, or --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox.

Potential Prompt Injection Coercing Shell Execution fires when a shell starts from a command line that contains instruction-override or jailbreak phrasing.

Potential Destructive AWS CLI Command Executed by GenAI Agent and Execution via OpenClaw Agent cover what the agent starts.

On the endpoint, Elastic Defend can stop the activity outright. Persistence via GenAI Tool kills a process started by a coding agent when it writes a LaunchAgent, LaunchDaemon, Startup folder item, rc.local, or sudoers entry. For a full walkthrough, see Living off the coding agent.

Credential theft through AI coding agents and prompts

Agents run with the developer's access to cloud credentials, Secure Shell (SSH) keys, keychains, and browser stores, and users routinely paste secrets into prompts. Both paths end with credentials somewhere that they shouldn’t be. GenAI Process Accessing Sensitive Files detects AI tools (such as Claude Code and Cursor) opening cloud credentials, SSH keys, keychains, browser credential stores, and shell profiles. Agents have legitimate reasons to touch some of these files, which is why the alert carries full process lineage for triage. Prompt-level coverage applies the same idea on every platform that logs content, including:

AWS Bedrock Model Prompt or Completion Containing Credentials, with matching rules for Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry, and ChatGPT Enterprise.

AWS Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Prompt Targeting Credentials or Instance Metadata for agents asked to read instance metadata or credential files.

AWS IAM Credentials Added to a Bedrock API Key Phantom User and Anthropic Admin API Key Created for persistent API access.

Agent supply chain: MCP servers, skills, hooks, and plugins

An agent's MCP servers, skills, hooks, and instruction files decide what it does in every future session. A single malicious entry gives an attacker persistence that looks like an ordinary configuration change, which is exactly how postmark-mcp worked. (See MCP Tools: Attack Vectors and Defense Recommendations for Autonomous Agents for background.) Unusual Process Modifying GenAI Configuration File flags unexpected processes writing to agent configuration, such as .cursor/mcp.json, .codex/hooks.json, and Claude SKILL.md files. Related coverage includes:

GenAI or MCP Server Child Process Execution, a building block that records every process an MCP server starts, for correlation and hunting.

Anthropic MCP Server Created and OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise Unusual Codex Plugin Installed at the platform level.

Cursor Arbitrary Code Execution via PHP on the endpoint (macOS). Cursor, the AI code editor, ships with Visual Studio Code's Workspace Trust turned off by default, so a booby-trapped repository can run code the moment that it’s opened. The rule kills the shell, and Cursor itself, when Cursor runs a PHP script supplied by the project's .vscode configuration.

Detecting prompt injection, jailbreaks, and guardrail evasion

Jailbreaks try to talk the model out of its safety policy. Guardrail evasion goes around it, either by calling models without a guardrail attached or by changing the guardrail itself. Platform rules use the provider's own verdicts and the prompt text. Examples include:

AWS Bedrock Invocations without Guardrails Detected by a Single User Over a Session.

AWS Bedrock Guardrails Detected Multiple Violations by a Single User Over a Session.

GCP Vertex AI Jailbreak Prompt Heuristics, Microsoft Foundry Jailbreak Detected, and OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise Jailbreak Prompt Heuristics.

AWS Bedrock Guardrail Deleted or Weakened and GCP Vertex AI Safety Filters Set to BLOCK_NONE for changes to the guardrails themselves.

AWS Bedrock Model Invocation Logging Disabled or Modified and Anthropic Compliance API Logging Disabled for attempts to remove the audit trail.

When an AI agent gets cloud tools and IAM roles

Managed agent platforms give models real tools: code interpreters, browsers, file systems, and identity and access management (IAM) roles. That turns a successful injection into cloud access. AWS Bedrock High Risk Filesystem or Execution Tool Invocation fires when a Bedrock agent calls execution-capable tools, and AWS Bedrock AgentCore Execution Role Used Outside Its Runtime fires when an agent's role credentials are used from outside the agent. First Time GCP Vertex AI Agent Engine Sandbox Code Execution by User and Source ASN covers the same pattern on Google Cloud.

LLMjacking: Detecting stolen AI API keys and runaway usage

In LLMjacking, stolen AI credentials are resold or used to run large language models (LLMs) at the victim's expense, and attackers often test which models a key can reach before they start. The rules look for enumeration followed by invocation, sudden request and token spikes, and removal of spend controls. Examples include:

AWS Bedrock Foundation Model Enumeration Followed by Invocation via Long-Term Key.

AWS Bedrock High-Frequency Single-Model Inference API Probing, which also covers attempts to extract a model through its API.

GCP Vertex AI High Request and Token Volume and Microsoft Foundry High Request and Token Volume.

Anthropic Extra Usage Spend Limit Deleted.

Data exfiltration through AI connectors and unsanctioned AI use

Connectors let assistants read and send mail, search file shares, and publish content. A compromised account or an injected instruction can move data out through tools that the business already approved. The new ChatGPT Enterprise rules watch connector activity directly, and the endpoint rules catch AI use outside approved channels. Examples include:

OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise Gmail Message Sent via Connector and OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise Google Drive Download Burst.

Anthropic Artifact Shared Publicly and Anthropic Organization Data Export Accessed.

GenAI Process Performing Encoding/Chunking Prior to Network Activity for agents staging data before sending it.

Connection to Common Large Language Model Endpoints and Ollama API Accessed from External Network for unsanctioned model use and exposed local model servers.

AI security detection coverage by platform: Bedrock, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft

Most organizations use more than one AI provider, so we built the same detections for each platform wherever the provider's logs make it possible. Secrets in prompts, along with abnormal usage volume, are covered on almost every platform, as are agent and tool activity. Where a cell is empty, the gap usually reflects the data that the provider exposes rather than a choice on our side. The Anthropic audit logs we ingest, for example, record administrative and account activity but not prompt content, so content-level rules apply to Bedrock, Vertex AI, Foundry, and ChatGPT Enterprise. Bedrock is the most complete column because it exposes invocation logs, guardrail verdicts, AgentCore runtime logs, and CloudTrail.

What to do with AI security alerts

An alert is the starting point. Elastic Security gives you several ways to act on these detections, including:

Block on the endpoint. Run Elastic Defend in prevent mode so the behavior rules that we’ve covered in this post stop agent-driven persistence and malicious Cursor workspaces before they complete.

Triage with full lineage. Endpoint alerts carry the process tree from the agent to the child process, so you can see whether a human, an agent, or a package install started the activity.

Correlate with Attack Discovery. Attack Discovery groups related alerts (for example, an agent reading credentials followed by a cloud API call from a new location) into a single attack narrative. See our Hugging Face breach analysis for an example.

Prioritize with entity risk scoring. AI alerts raise the risk score of the host and user involved, which helps surface a developer workstation that’s accumulating suspicious agent activity.

Respond. Isolate a host, or kill a process. Trigger a workflow that rotates a leaked key or disables an AI platform account.

Tune and extend. Add exceptions for approved agents and MCP servers, and adjust thresholds to your usage. Use the building block rules as inputs for your own correlations and hunts.

How to enable AI security detection rules in Elastic 9.6

To get started:

Once available, upgrade to Elastic 9.6, open Security > Rules > Detection rules (SIEM), and install or update the prebuilt rules.

Filter by the Domain: GenAI tag, and enable the rules that match the data you collect.

Title: Cleverbridge Confirms Customers’ Payment Card Data Breached
Context: However, an investigation found that an unauthorized third party copied payment card data stored on its platform
Full Text:
Global e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has revealed that a hacker has stolen payment card data, putting affected customers at immediate risk of fraud.

In an update published on its website, the firm said that it detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4, 2026. The incident was quickly contained, and systems brought back online the same day. However, an investigation found that an unauthorized third party copied payment card data stored on its platform.

“We worked diligently to identify individuals whose personal information may have been involved and began notifying affected individuals on 20 November where appropriate,” Cleverbridge wrote.

The company has not confirmed how many people’s card details may have been affected by the incident. The investigation remains ongoing.

Cleverbridge manages global payments, subscription billing, tax compliance, and checkout services for software and SaaS companies across more than 240 countries. Customers listed on its website include Tenable, Jamf, Veeam, Red Hat and Sony.

BleepingComputer reported that the breach notifications sent to affected individuals revealed that the stolen data includes card numbers, expiry dates and card security codes (CVV/CVC).

No other personal data, such as names, contact information or billing details, were accessed, according to the notifications.

The stolen information can be used to verify online transactions. As such, Cleverbridge urged those impacted to check their card statements and inform their card issuers immediately if they see a transaction they do not recognize.

“You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card,” Cleverbridge added.

The payments processor also warned affected individuals to be vigilant of phishing attacks that request card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone or text message.

Cleverbridge Rules Out Ransomware Attack

Cleverbridge confirmed that the incident is not ransomware related, stating that none of its systems were encrypted.

No other details were provided on the actor’s potential motivations. It is not known whether the stolen data has been misused so far.

The incident follows notifications by JPMorganChase, Visa and Mastercard that customer data had been breached following a compromise of a third-party vendor.

Ransomware group N0n claimed the attacks and reportedly leaked the stolen data on its dark web leak site.

Title: Black Friday, red flags: too-good-to-be-true deals hiding real threats
Context: Despite differing mechanics, both approaches exploit the same vulnerability – reflexive trust in a familiar brand whose identity the scammers have appropriated – and simply...
Full Text:
Intro

Black Friday remains a defining moment of the holiday shopping season and a key period for cybercriminals seeking to exploit the surge in consumer activity. The scale of this demand is reflected in seasonal spending patterns. According to PwC’s post-holiday analysis, holiday spending rose by 6.4% year over year in 2025, with Black Friday once again being the peak sales day generating nearly $20 billion. Consumer behavior points to the same trend: KPMG’s 2026 Consumer Pulse Survey found that Black Friday remains the most important sales event, with 62% of respondents pointing to its importance. Moreover, it is strongly associated with online shopping, with 83% of consumers preferring to buy online or combine online and in-person purchases on this occasion. To find the best offers, 55% of respondents in 2026 planned to research purchases through retailer websites and 46% through brand websites. As shopping activity concentrates online during peak sales periods, threat actors gain broader opportunities to exploit consumer demand, trusted brands, and heavy promotional traffic to steal credentials, payment data, and money.

At Kaspersky, we closely follow the cybersecurity risks associated with major shopping events and seasonal spikes in online retail activity. Our annual analysis examines how cybercriminals adapt their tactics to target consumers during high-demand sales periods.

This report extends our annual Securelist series published in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, exploring how shopping-related cyberthreats continue to evolve.

Methodology

To keep pace with the evolving shopping threat landscape, we conduct an annual assessment of the most prevalent malicious techniques, including financial malware, phishing pages impersonating major retailers, e-commerce platforms, digital services, banks, and payment providers, as well as spam campaigns designed to steer users to fraudulent sites. The threat data we rely on is sourced from Kaspersky Security Network (KSN), which processes anonymized cybersecurity data shared consensually by Kaspersky users.

Most of the data in this report draws on was collected from January through October 2026.

Key findings

In the first ten months of 2026, Kaspersky identified more than 19 million phishing attacks targeting users of online stores, payment systems and banks, a year-on-year increase of 1%.

As many as 5% of these attacks were directed at online shoppers.

Around 84% of all phishing attacks targeting users of online stores and subscription services involve scammers impersonating Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Shopify and Alibaba Group pages.

Netflix-themed phishing detections grew by 5% in 2026 in comparison with 2025 data.

We detected more than 220,071 sales-themed spam messages in the first two weeks of November, which is 50.2% more than in 2025.

More than 801,000 banking Trojan attacks were recorded during the first 10 months of 2026.

Between June and November 2026, Kaspersky products have already detected over 27,000 attacks by malware and potentially unwanted applications posing as GTA VI-related content.

Shopping-related phishing by the numbers

Phishing and scams remain among the most persistent threats for online shoppers, particularly during peak sales periods, when heightened transaction volumes and time-sensitive offers create conditions for abuse. One of the most notable developments in recent years has been the growing use of AI to increase the speed, scale and sophistication of such campaigns. AI-enabled tools can be used to generate convincing phishing emails, fraudulent shopping pages, and realistic seller identities, while also adapting messages and visuals to mimic legitimate brands. In the context of major retail events, where consumers often move quickly across marketplaces, social platforms, and promotional channels, this added level of automation further increases the risk of deception, credential theft, and financial loss.

Although phishing has long remained a common method of deceiving users, we are seeing a growing number of attacks in segments related to online shopping. From January through October 2026, Kaspersky products blocked 19,063,077 attempts to access phishing links targeting users of online stores, payment systems, and banks – nearly three times (198.1%) more than during the same period last year, when 6,394,854 such attempts were recorded. A breakdown of these attempts shows that 44.54% targeted online shoppers, compared with 48.21% in 2025; 28.55% targeted banking users, up from 26.10%; and 26.91% mimicked payment systems, versus 25.69% last year.

Financial phishing attacks by category, January–October 2026 (download)

Since 2021, we have conducted annual assessments of the distribution of phishing attacks targeting users across popular online platforms, including Amazon, Alibaba Group, eBay, Mercado Libre, and Walmart, in order to track how the attackers abuse trusted brands. In 2026, Kaspersky products detected and blocked 3,102,304 phishing attempts involving the misuse of Amazon’s brand, up 411.6% from 606,369 attempts in 2025. Threat actors consistently stick to leveraging well-known and trusted consumer platforms to enhance the credibility of fraudulent pages.

Other major e-commerce brands were also widely impersonated in phishing campaigns. Kaspersky detected 360,949 attempts to visit phishing pages mimicking Alibaba-owned brands including AliExpress, while eBay-themed phishing pages accounted for 163,381 alerts. The Latin American marketplace Mercado Libre was used as a lure in 109,081 cases, and Walmart-related phishing pages were identified 74,220 times.

Popular online stores mimicked by scammers, January–October 2026 (download)

The rankings of platforms most frequently impersonated by scammers include more than just brands directly associated with tangible items. The attackers are equally interested in scamming users of popular services selling digital products, such as music, TV shows, e-books, and others. The overall top five brands abused in 2026 were Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Shopify, and Alibaba Group–associated brands, which together were mimicked in 7,119,400 detections. Overall, these five platforms represented 83.83% of all phishing attacks associated with online stores and subscription services.

TOP 5 online platforms mimicked by scammers, January–October 2026 (download)

As mentioned before, Amazon was abused in 3,102,304 detections, or 36.53% of the total. Phishing pages impersonating Apple-related resources accounted for 1,622,917 detections, or 19.1%. Netflix-themed phishing accounted for 1,365,648 detections, or 16.08% of the total, marking a 70.5% increase from 801,148 detections recorded in 2025. Shopify-themed phishing accounted for 667,582 detections, or 7.86%.

What mass scam campaigns look like

Mass scam campaigns often rely on phishing kits or templates that can be used to quickly build numerous pages that target different markets, languages, and user segments and mimic widely used platforms. These platforms are broadly recognized and generally trusted by the users, while standardized scam flows allow attackers to scale operations with minimal effort. Across these campaigns, scammers combine familiar visual design, urgent calls to action, and fake login, payment, or verification pages.

Brand recognition in this scenario works against users: the more familiar an interface looks, the less likely a visitor is to question its authenticity. This logic forms the basis of a whole cluster of phishing campaigns that abuse the names of major tech platforms. Fraudulent pages copying login pages of these platforms reproduce the original layout, branding, and even alternative sign-in options, leaving credential entry forms as the only interactive element – everything typed into these forms goes straight to the attackers. Hijacked logins to an e-commerce platform potentially open the door not only to the victims’ purchase history or payment methods in this exact store, but also to other accounts that use the same login credentials.

Scammers often create pages that replicate the fonts and visual style of the original site. This example mimics an Amazon page

A common technique for stealing login credentials. Example of a fake website impersonating Shopify

A related but noisier approach relies on manufactured urgency: we detected pages masquerading as Apple support that bombard the visitor with alarming pop-ups about a suspicious Apple Pay “pre-authorization” and urge them to immediately call a “support number”. If the user contacts the phone number, fake operators will try to talk the victim into revealing sensitive details or granting remote access to their device, which can be used to steal money and data. Despite differing mechanics, both approaches exploit the same vulnerability – reflexive trust in a familiar brand whose identity the scammers have appropriated – and simply choose different triggers: routine in the first case, panic in the second.

Example of a scam page exploiting a sense of urgency

There’s usually a variety of scams abusing users’ trust and the hype surrounding Apple devices. Fake stores appearing to sell or lease iPhones for “low monthly payments” are one example of such scams.

Scammers consistently target fans of flagship smartphones. Example of a fake page impersonating Apple

The streaming platform discount trap

Black Friday has become a major subscriber acquisition window for subscription-based streaming services rather than a peripheral promotional event. Antenna estimates that Black Friday drove 8.9 million incremental premium subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) sign-ups in 2025 and accounted for roughly 25% of all November sign-ups, an 800,000 increase compared to 2024, when Black Friday promotions generated 8.1 million sign-ups.

This concentration of promotional activity also expands the space for abuse. As subscription platforms compete for user attention with discounts, limited-time offers, and account-based promotions, threat actors can easily repurpose the same themes across phishing pages and fraudulent payment forms. In this context, brands tied to subscriptions, billing, account access, and merchant services are used as lures: they are widely recognized, naturally associated with recurring payments and promotional offers and therefore likely to prompt user engagement.

Netflix remained among the top five online-store and subscription-service brands most frequently abused by scammers, highlighting the persistent use of streaming services as lures in brand-abuse campaigns. While the majority of observed schemes affecting this platform simply sought to phish users’ credentials, we also saw “generous offers” trying to lure users with discounts. In one example, the attackers embedded the Netflix name in a bundle with other services, such as telecom or entertainment packages. The fraudulent page is designed to collect a range of personal data. Afterwards, the attackers contact the victim via WhatsApp to ask for further information or money. Another scheme imitates the platform itself, offering fake discounted subscription deals. In both scenarios, attackers exploit trust in a globally recognized entertainment brand to increase engagement and push users toward sharing sensitive details or paying money.

Scammers create Netflix-themed fake pages to harvest personal and payment data or sell nonexistent subscriptions

Subscription entertainment brands, such as Spotify and YouTube Premium, are also being used as phishing lures to collect either payment card data through fake subscription forms or account credentials through counterfeit login pages. Informal “support” channels, such as WhatsApp chats, add credibility and help attackers guide victims in real time.

Subscription-service scams impersonate Spotify and YouTube Premium to steal payment details and account credentials

Inside the Black Friday spam wave targeting shoppers

In 2026, Black Friday–related scams continued to spread across multiple channels, with fraudulent email campaigns remaining one of the ways they reached their victims. As retailers stepped up their seasonal marketing, cybercriminals took advantage of the flood of promotional messages by sending look-alike emails. During the first two weeks of November, Kaspersky detected 220,071 spam messages related to the sales season – 50,18% more than in 2025. Over the same period, 1,728 of the identified spam messages referenced Singles’ Day promotions in Asia.

Scam campaigns built around Apple products begin long before Black Friday: fraudulent activity traditionally spikes on the eve of Apple’s keynotes and then flows seamlessly into the November sales season. In one example, a link from a spam email leads to a fake store impersonating a telecom operator, which offers the new iPhone 18 Pro Max at a tiny fraction of its retail price as a “time-limited special offer”.

An example of a detected spam email impersonating a Telenor marketing proposal. The email offers a new smartphone model for sale

The page mimics the real provider’s product page and is most likely designed to trick the user into entering payment card details.

Scammers created a fake page impersonating the Telenor online store. The users land on the website through a link in a spam email

Alongside fake stores, gamified giveaways are still a persistent email scam format of the sales season: instead of simply offering a discount, fraudsters invite users to “win” a prize, which makes users lower their guard and adds an element of excitement. Pages of this kind typically impersonate well-known retail brands and use personalized greetings, limited attempts, and guaranteed “wins” to create an impression of an exclusive, harmless lottery. The prize, of course, is predetermined and serves only as a pretext to request personal and payment card details, allegedly to cover delivery. Exploiting trust in household retail names, such schemes leave victims with compromised card data or stolen money instead of a gift.

Fake REWE-branded Black Friday giveaway offering a free gift for guessing a “secret number”

Wasted: GTA VI “offers” and other lures targeting the gaming community this November

In November 2026, the gaming industry is set for one of its most anticipated launches in years: GTA VI. Highly awaited game releases have long created openings for cybercriminal activity. In our 2024 Kaspersky Security Bulletin, we predicted that cybercriminals would seek to exploit GTA VI’s popularity. In fact, the risk is also amplified by timing: the game’s November 19 launch coincides with the seasonal sales campaigns, when users are already primed to look for discounts, bundles, and limited-time offers. This means users need to be extra cautious.

Malware campaigns typically cluster around the game itself, using the surrounding attention to disguise malicious files as related content; between June and November 2026, Kaspersky detected 27,416 malware and potentially unwanted application attacks posing as GTA VI–related content. At the same time, phishing schemes follow a separate logic: they exploit purchase intent and urgency around offers, driving users to fake pages.

In the example below, a fake store offers Brazilian users a chance to buy a PS5 subscription bundle with GTA VI included. Scammers offer payment options via a banking card or Pix. If the user pays, they never see either PlayStation or the game.

Besides GTA VI, all traditional gaming phishing and scam schemes are also present. The screenshot below shows a fraudulent website mimicking Steam that allegedly gives away $50 gift cards as part of a “Winter Gift Marathon”. To get the card, users are urged to log in to their Steam accounts, compromising their credentials.

Another scheme invites users to a Discord group chat. However, when the victim tries to enter the chat, a pop-up window appears telling them that they need to install a security module. If they click the “Install” button, a suspicious file is downloaded to their device.

From self-care to scam: how attackers target beauty and wellness fans

In addition to shopping-related scams, cybercriminals have continued to exploit consumer interest in personal health, wellness, and beauty in 2026. These themes have long been present in spam and phishing activity, as they combine broad consumer appeal with topics that often involve sensitive personal decisions and data. The continued expansion of online health services, consultations, and wellness products also makes such lures appear more familiar and plausible to users.

Weight loss was one of the health-related themes observed in spam campaigns. In one identified example, a link in a spam email redirected the recipient to a page promoting a telehealth weight-loss service. The page used likely fabricated credibility markers – such as claims of “1,000s of patients” and “600+ doctors” – to make the site appear as an established medical provider. The prompt to “qualify in 5 minutes” through an online assessment acted as the first step in the conversion funnel. Depending on the scheme, such websites may further prompt users to enter their personal and medical data into a fraudulent form, may steal money, or just sell dubious products or services under the guise of a magic pill.

An example of a weight-loss telehealth page

Another spam email targeted users concerned about skin aging. It used a health-advisory style banner and a clickbait headline presenting “The 1 Vitamin You Need if You Have Wrinkled Skin” as a dermatologist’s recommendation. By combining appeals to medical authority and social proof, such as mentioning thousands who already use this vitamin, and framing the offer as free advice through the call to action “Tap For Recipe,” the campaign lowered users’ guard.

A spam email banner promoting a dubious anti-aging supplement through fake dermatologist claims

The link from the email redirects users to a fraudulent site that imitates a legitimate skincare brand and uses a sensational headline about a “$1 Japanese pink vitamin” allegedly responsible for a famous actress’s youthful appearance – a claim the celebrity never made. A fabricated comment section showing more than 36,000 “comments” creates fake social proof and guides visitors toward purchasing a dubious supplement (if it exists at all).

A fraudulent skincare-themed page using a fake celebrity endorsement

Beauty-themed scams are distributed not only by email. Moreover, they are not limited to miracle supplements; fraudsters also exploit the appeal of luxury cosmetics offered at implausibly low prices. In the example below, a fake online store impersonates a trusted retailer, Sephora, and advertises branded perfume at a fraction of its retail price. The page combines familiar pressure tactics, including a fabricated rating, a scarcity warning (“only 6 bottles left”), a one-bottle-per-customer limit and a countdown timer. Together, these elements are designed to rush victims into paying for products that will never be delivered.

Example of a fake beauty retailer page encouraging users to make a purchase on sale

Banking Trojans

Banking Trojans remained active in 2026. On PC, they can monitor browser activity, inject fraudulent content into legitimate sessions, intercept credentials and card data, and in some cases, manipulate payment details or cryptocurrency transactions. On mobile devices, they usually target a range of banking and online store apps, using various techniques to obtain user credentials or interfere with transactions. This makes banking Trojans particularly dangerous around major retail sales, when fast purchase decisions and intensified use of digital payment flows increase the risk of financial theft.

PC banker activity continued to decline year over year: in the first ten months of 2026, Kaspersky detected 801,150* attacks, compared with more than 1.09 million in 2025. This trend persists due to the continuous shift away from PC bankers toward mobile-first fraud and credential theft. Even so, PC banking malware remained active throughout the year. One example is GoPix, a Brazilian banking Trojan delivered through Google Ads malvertising and designed to abuse Pix, Boleto and cryptocurrency transactions. Other noteworthy threats are JanelaRAT, which targeted online banking users in Brazil and Mexico, and Horabot, which continued to surface in multistage campaigns combining banking malware with email-based propagation.

In the mobile segment, BeatBanker is worth mentioning: an Android banker active in Brazil, distributed via a fake Google Play page and bundled with a crypto miner.

*These statistics include globally active banking malware, and malware for ATMs and point-of-sale (PoS) systems. We excluded data on Trojan banker families that no longer use banking Trojan functionality in their attacks, such as Emotet.

Conclusions

Kaspersky’s phishing data points to a rise in shopping-related threats: from January to October 2026, phishing attempts targeting users of online stores, payment systems and banks increased by 198.1% compared with the same period in 2025. The main tactic remained brand impersonation: scammers abused the names of major online platforms and digital services to create fake login pages, payment forms, support alerts, and subscription offers. Amazon-themed phishing grew by 411.6% year over year, while detections of fraudulent pages abusing Netflix increased by 70.5%.

Black Friday-themed spam also intensified, rising by 50.2% compared with 2025. These campaigns blended into the broader flow of seasonal promotions and redirected users to fraudulent websites. Beyond traditional retail, attackers used lures tied to subscriptions, gaming, and health and wellness, showing how scams are adjusted to current consumer interests. Banking Trojans remained active, although PC banker detections declined year over year, as attackers continued shifting from traditional desktop banking malware toward mobile-first scenarios.

Overall, the findings show that major shopping periods remain associated with a higher concentration of recurring cyberthreats. During seasonal sales events, users should be especially cautious with unsolicited offers, verify websites before entering data, and treat unusually generous discounts or urgent requests with skepticism. To make sure that they don’t end up on a fraudulent website amid the shopping rush, we recommend that users protect their devices with a comprehensive security solution, such as Kaspersky Premium, which uses an advanced AI-powered detection technology that analyzes website characteristics and URLs to identify suspicious patterns. In 2026, Kaspersky Premium was awarded an “Approved” certificate by AV-Comparatives for the second year in a row for its ability to detect fake online stores.

Title: Badbox Returns to Spread Ad Fraud and Proxyjacking Payloads
Context: These networks route internet traffic through regular consumer devices and are often abused by threat actors for account takeover, brute-force attacks, malware distribution, and...
Full Text:
Security researchers say they have uncovered what may be the largest ad fraud operation ever discovered by bid volume.

Human’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team claimed Badbox 3.0 accounted for 40 billion bid requests per day at its height, more than three times the previous record holder VastFlux.

“Badbox 3.0 runs primarily on low-cost consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that Human researchers recognized from Badbox and Badbox 2.0,” a report published on November 19 explained.

“Those modules come from an actively maintained catalog hosted on public code repositories. Satori researchers have linked these repositories to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer.”

Read more on Badbox: Malware-Infected Devices Sold Through Major Retailers

The fraud modules secretly render video ads on owners’ devices, sending ad requests that borrow the identities of legitimate apps. They also enroll the device, without the owner’s knowledge, as an exit node in one of 11 residential proxy networks.

These networks route internet traffic through regular consumer devices and are often abused by threat actors for account takeover, brute-force attacks, malware distribution, and more.

One of these networks, Pxyedge, was identified by Human as IpMoYu, a network operated by the actors behind Badbox and Badbox 2.0.

Advice for Device Owners

Human urged users to choose devices from familiar brands, ensure they are Play Protect-certified, only download apps from official marketplaces, and take action if devices behave strangely.

It said those compromised by Badbox 3.0 are all “low-cost, off-brand, uncertified” devices running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP); built in China and shipped globally.

However, the report warned that the botherders are likely to adapt again, as they have done with previous iterations of Badbox

“The capability now lives in public code repositories, mirrored across hosting platforms, a mainstream CDN, and a proxy built to slip past network blocks, with fallback locations written into every module record,” it explained.

“Its proxy network survived exposure by changing its name. Its ad fraud, hidden on the devices and passed off under the names of legitimate apps, reached a daily volume larger than any ad fraud operation disclosed before it.”

On a more positive note, Human said it was part of an operation to disrupt XCPE, a botnet linked to Badbot 3.0 by shared command-and-control (C2) domains. It boasted more than a million infected devices in over 200 countries and territories before the Google-led industry effort.

Title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
Context: “The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider...
Full Text:
For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing.

Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking.

Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense.

Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop

Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas.

“What am I missing? What attack vectors or edge cases should I inspect?” is the kind of questions Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, an AI-enabled software development company, such a prompt can help with.

“This approach works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, while reviewing penetration test results, and auditing cloud configurations, as well as when modeling threats and assessing risks,” Romanov says.

Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers another version of the adversarial agent prompt — in this case against agent helpers.

When agents are used to generate security reports, engineers often find themselves buried under irrelevant findings — noise, says Dourassov. However, when a second agent is deployed to analyze the quality of another agent’s work, and correct its output, the result can be surprisingly efficient.

“The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider a good job,” Dourassov says, noting that his adversarial agent is basically a reviewer. “Its task is to eliminate noise, rectify claims, and highlight the true importance of the first agent’s result.”

The agent’s definition of a good job, Dourassov says, is being able to eliminate noise and supply only signal to the human user. “Therefore, it’s essential to use an adversarial prompt to review agents’ output, so we ensure we don’t face security fatigue from AI slop.”

Take care of business

Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at business and technology consulting firm Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas that CISOs can deploy on a regular basis to aid with their work.

The first Fisher uses is a vendor due diligence prompt. “I feed it our organization’s risk thresholds and the vendor in question, and it benchmarks that vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints, and recent news, then returns a structured report I can review and validate quickly,” he explains.

Fisher also recommends crafting a professional writing prompt that takes technical analysis and reframes it into language a CIO or board will actually engage with.

Gen AI pioneer Kevin Surace offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year’s CSO Conference and Awards in May. “Translate the SOC for the boardroom. This is important. They don’t really understand what’s going on,” Surace said. “The prompt here: ‘You are writing the cyber risk section of the board deck. You have four minutes of board time. Below is ninety days of security operations data. Produce three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.’ This is so useful.”

Fisher’s third prompt for CISOs is a tech debt reduction prompt “where I list our technology stack and have AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities, and consolidation opportunities,” he says.

Fisher advises building each of his recommendations as a standing agent, project, or skill, or whatever your AI platform supports, so you have a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt from scratch every time.

Don’t wait for a perfect first version, Fisher adds. “Get an initial prompt working, even if it’s rough, and have AI help draft the instructions themselves.” Expect to revise it several times before it’s reliable.

Challenge your policies and content

At the CSO Conference, Surace also highlighted how CISOs can use AI prompts to audit their policy libraries.

“You are a compliance auditor. I am giving you our policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and the EU AI Act. Produce three lists,” his example prompt began, directing the LLM to find contradictions, gaps, and stale language — the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks, he noted.

Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor. The tool reviews policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses, and specific customer requirements.

Brännlund believes that organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than organizations that treat it as a content generator. The key, she states, “isn’t using AI to write content, but using it to challenge content.”

Tying together policy review and the adversarial assistant concept, Surace advised CSO conference attendees to also “red team your own runbook.”

“You are the operations lead for Scattered Spider. I am giving you our incident response playbook, our detection coverage matrix, and our on-call tree. Identify the five places this runbook fails,” his prompt started, probing for wrong assumptions, bottlenecks, escalation path weaknesses, and so on.

“It’s totally worth doing this,” he said. “You will have more information in an hour than you, than you’ve ever had.

Vet your agent’s capabilities and weaknesses

Chris Hughes advises asking your model what your AI agents can actually do.

“Give it an agent’s configuration, tool manifest, or MCP server definitions and ask it to summarize the agent’s effective permissions, the blast radius if it’s compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow,” says Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College. “Most organizations are deploying agents faster than they’re documenting what those agents can reach, and this closes the gap in minutes.”

The model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment, and after every change. It also surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning, Hughes says. The model doesn’t share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, he notes. Once tuned, the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise.

Embrace deep inspection

Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests tailoring an AI prompt to take aim at AI prompts themselves, noting that perhaps the most important capability is a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent.

“CISOs should be able to determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service, but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky—such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access,” he says, adding that as AI agents become more common, that same inspection and policy model needs to extend beyond human prompts to agent-driven interactions.

Tait believes that CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway (SWG), zero trust network access, browser-based access, and APIs.

“The goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application, but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services,” he explains. “This also means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.”

Title: AI-Assisted Cyber Attacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms
Context: In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an...
Full Text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country.

This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.

"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week.

The incidents have been found to include the following methods -

Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs.

Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes.

Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert.

Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records.

CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor.

The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions -

Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths.

Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information.

Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel.

Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems.

Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks.

"Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity."

The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as the national nodal agency disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets.

"In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools."

Earlier this month, the agency also warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial ​firms and has used offensive penetration testing tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, and CyberStrikeAI to automate the intrusions at machine speed.

According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the attacks have targeted banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintech companies, leading to multi-crore (equivalent to 10 million) unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs.

"Perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers / IT systems to compromise the infrastructure," I4C said. "Hackers then target automated fund disbursement systems or special interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers. The money is sent to 'mule' accounts (accounts used by criminals) across different banks and then quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT."

India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has also alerted of rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure, urging banks to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month.

The Surge in AI Attacks

The advisories also come at a time when organizations around the world are being targeted using AI tools, giving attackers a way to "execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity." Last week, the European Commission confirmed that attackers armed with ARTEX broke into its HR, medical reimbursement, and translation systems. The first signs of the attack were detected on October 22, 2026.

ARTEX has also been implicated in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and Barracuda, with the latter revealing that a financially motivated criminal weaponized an exposed valid cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor to map its reach, repurpose discovered secrets to access more systems and look for seed phrases, and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets.

"In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours [between November 1 and 2]. The work was methodical and tireless," Barracuda said. "The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match ARTEX."

Frameworks like ARTEX manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute, and adapt tactics across multiple kill chain stages, including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, and data exfiltration.

They can translate tactical goals described in natural language into machine commands that are executed by specialized AI agents. It integrates with various external LLMs, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, SpaceXAI Grok, Zhipu GLM, and Kimi.

"ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an alert this month.

"The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale."

Check Point, in a report published this month, said it uncovered more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX, with attackers leveraging the tool to conduct opportunistic, financially-motivated cybercrime.

"Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target," the company said.

Data security firm Cohesity said threat actors using ARTEX are gaining access to systems that receive less security attention, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales support applications, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications built by individual business units.

"In a research network we operate, a threat actor linked to Rhysida used an AI framework to rewrite tools in response to obstacles, often within minutes, and more than 150 versions of a single script reached a domain controller within a day," it said.

In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

The AI framework, called "exploit_agent," integrates with multiple frontier and local large language models (LLMs). It's designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention. The attacker, suspected to be Russian-speaking, is said to have leveraged the framework to target French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

"The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software," Mandiant and GTIG said. "It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention."

Some of the other notable incidents where AI agents and models do the legwork are listed below -

Use of CAIRN in intrusion activity against targets, including in the aerospace sector in the U.S.

Embedding LLMs into influence operation workflows to produce synthetic media, create convincing virtual personas, and generate and publish content.

Use of Google's Gemini API, along with tools from multiple AI providers, to build an end-to-end influence-as-a-service (SaaS) platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, specifically across Europe and the Middle East.

Use of LLMs by a China-linked contractor called Leaky Castle to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data

Abuse of a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure by a China-nexus threat actor to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents.

Use of LLMs by North Korean threat actors to generate resumes and prepare for job interviews at Western organizations.

Creation of fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms by a suspected North Korean hacking group called Midnight Neptune (previously UNC1069) in attacks aimed at cryptocurrency entities in North America and Europe using job- and ClickFix-themed lures. These personas have been found to direct targets to fraudulent meeting platforms, which are used to run diagnostic fix scripts via ClickFix. "Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor," Google said.

Use of CyberStrikeAI ("43.240.29[.]11") between September 30 and October 16, 2026, to validate stolen AWS credentials, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, and send a remote command. "The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded," Elastic Security Labs said.

Use of Hermes, in combination with DeepSeek, by a threat actor called Silent Lynx in cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026 to assist with reconnaissance, data collection, and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems.

Use of ARTEX to exploit a vulnerable custom PHP upload function and stage a web shell, and use it to access secrets and API keys, and ultimately compromise a company's development pipeline to alter a Git repository and deploy an attacker-controlled Kubernetes pod.

Use of an AI coding assistant to revive a stalled attack at a U.S. retail organization and come up with ways to bypass defenses and steal credentials after their commands were blocked by security software in late September 2026. The attack is assessed to be financially motivated, based on the threat actor's scans for passwords in point-of-sale scripts and an IP address overlap with a prior campaign targeting online retailers.

Use of CAIRN by a Chinese-speaking attacker between August and September 2026 and pairing it with GLM and DeepSeek models to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attacks, attributed to CL-STA-1238, have targeted advanced semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy, and civil society sectors, achieving unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the entities, including valid credentials, personal data, military and government identities, and the creation of persistent administrator accounts in a production system. "CAIRN coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Confirmed findings accumulate as immutable facts, and the agent queues its next actions as intents."

Use of ARTEX to gain access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. "Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure," Cloudflare said. "LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments."

Use of ARTEX to generate deepfake videos to trick identity verification checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges and steal AI credentials at "industrial scale" to gain free access to models. Amazon has characterized the second campaign as a "self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting." Targets include LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow (CVE-2025-3248), RAGFlow (CVE-2026-28797), Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.

Use of CAIRN by a suspected Chinese-nexus threat actor to discover a zero-day vulnerability (GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94) in MONAI Label, a medical imaging application, and use it to gain complete control of a server within 11 minutes. The activity was detected in September 2026.

"An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

"The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. The agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints."

What's notable about accelerating AI-enabled attacks is that the technology is not just used as a force multiplier but has also emerged as the target.

"The integration of AI-enabled tools into enterprise workflows is creating new attack surfaces, particularly where those tools hold privileged access to code, credentials, data, or connected applications," Recorded Future said. "Developer tools are a primary target of attacks on AI systems. Threat actors exploited weak access controls and software supply-chain vulnerabilities to steal data or establish persistence."

Besides automating the time-consuming phases of intrusions, LLM-driven pentesting frameworks also lower the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks.

"Now, an attacker can give an agent a goal in plain language," GitGuardian said. "The agent can investigate the environment, select tools, execute commands, interpret the results, and decide what to try next. The tools are also becoming better at recovering from failed attempts. An agent can encounter an error, interpret the response, modify its next command, and continue investigating."

"Anyone with access to AntiFox or ARTEX can just verbally say into the dictation, 'find exposed credentials, determine what they access, and identify valuable resources.' That incantation initiates a series of technical actions that previously required considerably more hands-on expertise."
