Title: Node2Shell and eMudhra: One Attack Chain?
Context: The malicious input would arrive through an outbound connection the application already makes, without the attacker needing to exploit its authentication mechanism
Full Text:
What you will learn

How a forged eMudhra certificate could deliver a malicious Brotli response, which conditions must hold, why simpler paths to the decoder exist and how code execution would put application credentials at risk.

Part 2: Following the attack path

In the first part of this series, we looked at two unrelated security incidents: Node2Shell, a memory corruption vulnerability in Google's Brotli decoder, and the eMudhra certificate authority compromise, which exposed private keys that should never have been recoverable.

The question is what happens when we put them together.

Node2Shell allows specially crafted compressed data to corrupt memory when an affected application decompresses it. The eMudhra compromise could allow an attacker to impersonate a trusted HTTPS service if the client still accepts certificates issued through the compromised keys.

One vulnerability affects how an application processes data. The other effects how it decides who to trust. Could the second provide a way to deliver the first?

It's technically plausible under specific conditions, but there's no public demonstration of the combined attack and the forged certificate may not even be necessary.

From a trusted connection to a vulnerable decoder

Consider a Node.js application that connects to an external API using the built-in fetch() function. The application establishes an HTTPS connection, validates the server certificate and automatically decompresses Brotli-compressed responses.

Now consider an attacker who can redirect that connection and recover one of the compromised eMudhra intermediate CA keys. If the client still accepts a certificate chain involving that key, the attacker could impersonate the external service.

The application might complete the TLS handshake without detecting the substitution. But the response would now be controlled by the attacker.

Instead of ordinary API data, the impersonated server could return a malicious Brotli-compressed response. When fetch() decompresses it, the vulnerable decoder could encounter the same memory corruption issue demonstrated by Imperva.

The malicious input would arrive through an outbound connection the application already makes, without the attacker needing to exploit its authentication mechanism.

Hypothetical attack chain combining eMudhra certificate impersonation with Node2Shell. Each stage requires specific conditions, and no combined attack has been publicly demonstrated.

Would the attack actually work?

Several conditions would need to be met.

The attacker needs control over the connection path or another way to redirect the request. Recovering a CA private key alone doesn't provide that control.

The client must still trust the forged certificate. Browser protections don't necessarily apply to server-side applications, but Node.js and other runtimes have already introduced changes to certificate validation.

The application must process the response using an affected Brotli decoder. Node.js fetch() provides one entry point, but not every HTTP client handles compressed responses the same way.

The second and third conditions can overlap. The October 21 Node.js release addressed both the decoder and certificate trust issues, so older runtimes may still have both problems, depending on their certificate configuration.

Reaching the decoder also doesn’t guarantee remote code execution. Imperva demonstrated RCE on Node.js 24.22.0 running on Linux arm64, but it required multiple attempts. Public exploit code now exists and CISA lists the flaw as exploited, but whether the result is a crash or successful code execution still depends on the build, architecture, runtime protections, and application behavior.

The individual mechanisms are documented, but we haven't tested the combined chain, and there's no public evidence that the compromised eMudhra keys have been used to deliver Node2Shell.

Does the attack even need the certificate?

Often, no. Node2Shell doesn't depend on the eMudhra keys. Applications accepting Brotli-compressed request bodies may expose the decoder directly to external clients. Applications fetching data from attacker-controlled servers or compromised upstream APIs could also receive malicious responses without a forged certificate.

PowerShell 7 provides another example. Microsoft's guidance confirms that Invoke-WebRequest and Invoke-RestMethod automatically decompress HTTP responses by default. This creates a potential entry point when the commands process Brotli-compressed responses from an attacker-controlled or compromised server.

The forged certificate adds value in a more specific situation.When the attacker needs to impersonate a trusted HTTPS service, can redirect the connection and the client still accepts a certificate issued through the compromised keys.

It's a possible delivery path, but not the only one, and not necessarily the simplest.

The problem is bigger than Node.js

CVE-2026-111497 affects Google's Brotli decoder, which is used across multiple runtimes, libraries and applications. Microsoft released fixes for .NET, PowerShell 7 and Visual Studio in late October. Python's brotli and brotlicffi packages also required updates, while Java applications using brotli4j and products built on Envoy and Istio have been identified as affected.

The exposure differs between products. In .NET, for example, automatic Brotli decompression isn't enabled by default for ASP.NET Core requests or HttpClient responses. An application must enable those paths or explicitly use the Brotli APIs.

An application accepting compressed requests may expose the decoder to unauthenticated clients. An HTTP client that decompresses responses requires the attacker to control the server or the response. The important question isn't just whether a vulnerable library is present, but where it's called and who controls the input.

Patching also depends on how the library is packaged. Some applications use the operating system's Brotli library, while others bundle or compile their own copy. Java's brotli4j includes native Brotli code, and self-contained .NET applications or containers may need to be rebuilt.

Updating the system library won't necessarily fix every application using it.

What does this mean for identity security?

If the combined attack worked, the result wouldn't stop at impersonating a trusted service. It could also lead to code execution inside the application.

A forged certificate doesn't automatically expose application credentials. It may allow service impersonation or interception of information sent over the connection. But if malicious content delivered through that connection leads to code execution, the attacker could potentially access API tokens, service-account credentials and other secrets available inside the process.

Whether the malicious data arrives through a forged certificate, an HTTP request or a compromised upstream server, successful code execution puts the identities available to that application at risk.

The next target could be the access the application already has. There's still no demonstrated attack combining the eMudhra keys with Node2Shell. But the analysis shows that an attacker may have simpler ways to reach the vulnerable decoder without relying on certificate impersonation.

In this article

A ransomware group leaks files linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customers

The data may include emails, phone numbers, and travel or dining bookings; no card numbers have been reported exposed

Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing

Customer information linked by researchers to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase has appeared after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. The companies report no impact to their payment networks.

On November 19, the companies acknowledged incidents involving third-party providers. JPMorgan told Reuters:

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

But “no payment data” doesn’t mean “not useful to criminals.” Knowing your name, email address and which financial services you use can give a scammer a convincing opening line.

Visa said it was aware of the claims and that they were associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard said an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited number of email addresses associated with a particular card-benefit program.

Cybernews researchers say similar formatting suggests the data came from the same third-party provider. The provider and its role haven’t been identified, but it may handle card benefits such as dining, reservations, or loyalty programs, rather than payment processing. The leaked records appear to relate to those extra services.

A ransomware group calling itself n0n has claimed responsibility and published data it says it stole.

What information was exposed?

The answer depends on the company and on whether we are talking about company disclosures or researchers’ analysis of the purported stolen files. The leaked data has not been independently verified.

The companies have disclosed the following:

JPMorgan Chase: Marketing data held by vendors, potentially including some customer names and email addresses.

Visa: An incident at an Asia-Pacific service provider. Visa says its systems were not affected and there is no indication that payment data, such as card numbers, was affected.

Mastercard: A limited number of email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. Mastercard described this as non-payment information.

The n0n leak site lists JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard and claims their data was published after the ransom deadline passed on November 16.

Screenshot of n0n leak site, November 20, 2026

Researchers at Cybernews reported additional details from the leaked datasets:

JPMorgan: Roughly 16,000 customer email addresses, some phone numbers, identifiers described as account IDs, and more than 100 employee email addresses.

Visa: A dataset involving more than 6,000 premium customers, with fields including names, email addresses, phone numbers, messaging-app information, and booking details such as dates and addresses.

Mastercard: Data posted by n0n includes marketing information related to customers in North America, the Middle East, and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses, according to Reuters.

How to protect your accounts

If you’re concerned your information may be involved, these steps can help protect your accounts and identity:

Verify messages independently. Open your bank’s official app, use a website address you already know, or call the number on your card or statement. Do not use a link or phone number supplied by someone claiming to be investigating the breach.

Never read out a login or payment-verification code to an unexpected caller. Those codes can be the missing piece that allows a criminal to access your account. Enter them only when completing an action you initiated through the genuine service.

Do not transfer money to “protect” it. A caller who tells you to move your savings into a “safe account” is trying to steal them. Hang up and contact your bank independently.

Verify any offer of breach support before enrolling. JPMorgan says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.

Consider a credit freeze as a separate identity-protection measure.

Title: Mail Bombing Attacks Fuel IT Helpdesk Impersonation Scams
Context: FIRE said that there are some indications that these attacks are likely an AI Agent setup, where the agent is instructed to crawl every webpage available for newsletter...
Full Text:
Cybercriminals are conducting large-scale “mail bombing attacks”, followed by IT helpdesk impersonation in order to compromise user accounts.

Fortra Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) are tracking the campaign, which involves inboxes being deliberately flooded with emails.

In an update on the campaign, published by FIRE on November 19, the researchers noted that mail bombing does not require access to a target mailbox. Rather a target’s inbox is flooded with subscriptions after an attacker has submitted a target email address to newsletter, registration and other signup forms across unrelated websites.

This email flood can interrupt activities like customer service and routine correspondence, as well as obscuring account alerts, payment notifications and other messages that may require attention.

FIRE said that there are some indications that these attacks are likely an AI Agent setup, where the agent is instructed to crawl every webpage available for newsletter subscription boxes.

Mailchimp and its transactional service, Mandrill, were the most frequently observed delivery services, followed by Amazon SES and SendGrid.

“In the attacks observed so far by the FIRE team, the average email delivery of a mail bombing attack is at a peak of 10k messages per active campaign, around 1k emails per day,” Fortra said.

FIRE said it has also detected phishing attempts during these mail-bombing waves, which are harder to detect among the wave of otherwise legitimate emails.

The mail bombing campaign has been followed by vishing calls in which contact is made by the threat actor through Teams.

“In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality, attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both,” the researchers explained.

Fortra said that these mail bombing campaigns can be difficult to detect because individual subscription emails can appear entirely normal and may not contain malicious links.

Meanwhile, allowlist exceptions can make containment harder when they cover delivery platforms carrying the flood.

Security Teams Advised to Monitor Email Volumes

Fortra recommended that security teams monitor email volume per recipient against the normal baseline. Investigate bursts involving many unrelated senders, subscription wording and mailing-list headers.

Security teams should also confirm the scope and duration directly with the email delivery provider.

During FIRE’s investigation, Mailchimp advised that senders could request temporary subscription blocking for a specified recipient. Mailchimp also documents a separate automatic control that restricts an address from joining additional audiences for 24 hours after rapid repeated signups.

Fortra did not attribute the campaign to a particular group.

Title: Catching Ransomware: Introducing encrypts-files and Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486
Context: Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the...
Full Text:
When we search for ransomware samples during an investigation or detection test, we usually want to answer a direct question: Did this file actually encrypt user documents when executed?

Modern ransomware families implement file encryption in many different ways. While commodity builders may call standard operating system cryptographic APIs, contemporary Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) payloads written in Rust, Go, C++, or .NET frequently embed statically linked AES, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA, or custom intermittent encryption routines that never touch OS crypto libraries. At the same time, benign installers, browsers, and updaters legitimately use cryptography and write thousands of temporary files during normal execution.

This week, we rolled out three updates across VirusTotal and Google Threat Intelligence to identify malware that encrypts user files:

New encrypts-files Tag Across Windows and macOS Sandboxes: A cipher-agnostic behavioral trait (behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) and file-level search tag (tag:encrypts-files) emitted across CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only when dynamic analysis confirms real encryption of user documents.

Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486 Gating in CAPE Sandbox: Previously, generic CAPE file-churn signatures mapped high-volume file deletes, overwrites, or moves directly to T1486. Newly scanned CAPE reports now require verified user-file encryption before emitting those T1486 mappings, cutting CAPE-only daily T1486 hits from 1,039/day (78.5% with 0 AV detections) to 0 on benign files and reducing false positives across platform-wide T1486 volume by 97.6% (from 7,238 to 171 files per day).

Real-Time VirusTotal Livehunt Support: Real-time YARA-X matching on sandbox reports via vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES.

Figure 1: High-level overview of how CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage verify user-document encryption before emitting tag:encrypts-files and gating CAPE T1486.

How Cipher-Agnostic File-Encryption Verification Works

Across CAPE Sandbox (Windows), Zenbox (Windows), and macOS Mirage (Apple Silicon), each sandbox environment contains realistic user documents across standard user profile directories.

During and after detonation, our sandboxes apply three verification gates before emitting encrypts-files (and before CAPE emits generic T1486 mappings):

Content Destruction and Entropy Verification (Cipher-Agnostic): Rather than hooking OS cryptographic APIs, each sandbox inspects modified user-file content on disk using format-aware verification tailored to its platform. Depending on the file type and sandbox, checks evaluate destroyed file structures, elevated entropy, or non-text byte patterns alongside corroborating ransomware behaviors without relying on a single fixed entropy threshold. Because verification evaluates the resulting files on disk, it catches AES, ChaCha20, intermittent encryption, and XOR ciphers alike.

Coordinated Ransomware Extension Renames: Many ransomware families read original user documents, write encrypted copies under a uniform new extension (for example, .k404, .lkd, .INC, .BLWZ, or .heartbreaker), and delete the originals. Our sandboxes correlate reads, writes, moves, and unlinks across user directories to confirm coordinated encryption renames across user documents.

Benign File-Churn Exclusion Guards: Self-extracting archives, software installers, compilers, browser caches, and logs are explicitly excluded when they only generate routine temporary or application files rather than encrypting user documents. Similarly, dropping a README.txt file or calling crypto APIs alone never triggers encrypts-files without corroborated document encryption.

Real-World Ransomware Caught in Action

Across 328,257 newly submitted unique files (405,469 total files including rescans) analyzed in CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage since November 17, tag:encrypts-files matched 55 files and surfaced in-the-wild and validation payloads across Windows executables, Python scripts, DLLs, compressed archives (ZIP and RAR), and a rescanned Apple Silicon macOS binary with zero benign software false positives across all 55 manually reviewed matches (alongside 0 benign false positives across 9,976 random CAPE reports and 400 macOS Mirage runs in pre-rollout backtesting). Below are three examples you can inspect on VirusTotal.

1. Catching Zero- and Low-Detection In-the-Wild Lockers: The .k404 Campaign and lkd.exe

Static signatures often lag behind script-based or freshly compiled lockers. In an active .k404 extortion campaign submitted on November 17-18, Python locker fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354 (system_update.pyw) was flagged by 0 out of 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis, while companion PE binary 3dd45ab8e2f9c1af773a75221d792fb78870764419170e9c9c5941160364c700 (K404T_Fidye.exe) had 10 / 75 detections and separate Windows locker a8c2402ef3ae115300f5428712ccb0b5461f4a2f14b5bfdfbe08d5ad86bd3087 (lkd.exe) had 3 / 75 at the time of analysis.

Figure 2: VirusTotal Behavior report for undetected Python locker system_update.pyw (fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354, 0 / 59 AV on GUI at capture), showing encrypts-files, T1486, and Desktop user files encrypted with the .k404 extension.

When detonated in Zenbox, system_update.pyw runs under pythonw.exe from AppData\Roaming\WindowsSystemUpdate\, self-deletes, and rewrites Desktop user files into .k404 ciphertext, while K404T_Fidye.exe and lkd.exe encrypt user documents in CAPE Sandbox using .k404 and .lkd extensions alongside k404t.txt and read_me_restore.txt ransom notes. In CAPE Sandbox, verified encryption sets both tag:encrypts-files and T1486. Note that Zenbox, macOS Mirage, and third-party sandboxes (such as Dr.Web vxCube or VMRay) keep their own rule-level T1486 mappings, so a file can carry T1486 from another sandbox rule without tag:encrypts-files.

2. Enterprise RaaS & High-Speed Windows Encryptors: INC Ransom and BlackWizardLock

Modern Windows ransomware families optimize encryption speed using asynchronous I/O and multi-threaded directory queues. In sample d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645 (INC Ransom), CAPE Sandbox captures the payload binding user files to Windows I/O Completion Ports (IOCP), rewriting user documents into .INC files, and dropping INC-README.txt across directories.

Similarly, sample 98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e (BlackWizardLock) executes unpacked payload code from dynamically allocated memory, stages temporary .~BLWZ.tmp files, overwrites user documents with .BLWZ extensions (such as bitaddress.pdf.BLWZ and cover-letter-uidev.docx.BLWZ), and presents a full-screen Russian extortion lock screen that directs victims to @seedware on Telegram and threatens to destroy the Master Boot Record (MBR) after five wrong key attempts.

Figure 4: BlackWizardLock (98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e) Behavior report showing encrypts-files, T1486 impact, and user documents encrypted into .BLWZ files.

3. Native Apple Silicon macOS Ransomware: Heartbreaker (Historical macOS Sample Rescanned in macOS Mirage, 16 / 75 AV at Analysis)

While native macOS ransomware is rare in the wild compared to Windows, re-analyzing historical macOS samples validates Apple Silicon coverage. Sample 6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18 (first submitted in May 2025 and rescanned in macOS Mirage) is a self-signed 64-bit ARM64 Mach-O binary detected by 16 out of 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

Figure 5: Native macOS Heartbreaker ransomware (6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18) Behavior report in macOS Mirage showing encrypts-files, T1486, and user files in Downloads encrypted to .heartbreaker.

When detonated on bare-metal Apple Silicon in macOS Mirage, the binary installs a persistent LaunchAgent (/Users/admin/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist), drops /Users/admin/Desktop/README.txt, and encrypts user documents in /Users/admin/Downloads/ into Invoice_INV-2026-0842.pdf.heartbreaker and Vendor_Payment_Schedule.xlsx.heartbreaker. What This Signal Does Not Catch

tag:encrypts-files is a high-precision confirmation signal, not an exhaustive recall filter. A missing tag does not mean a sample is benign or lacks ransomware logic. Automated sandbox runs will not emit the tag in several common scenarios:

Samples that require command-line arguments or passwords: Affiliates often guard execution with a runtime flag (such as LockBit 3.0 builds that require -pass <key> to decrypt their payload).

Sandbox evasion, user-interaction gates, or long sleeps: Samples that exit on VM checks (DETECT_DEBUG_ENVIRONMENT), stall past the analysis window (LONG_SLEEPS), or wait for specific locales or clicks never reach their encryption loop.

Unreachable command-and-control key servers: Families that fetch an encryption key from an offline C2 server before touching local files abort prior to file modification.

DLLs with custom exported entry points: Standard rundll32 detonation executes DllMain, which misses DLL lockers that require calling a specific named or ordinal export with structured arguments.

Network-share-only targets or executable file infectors: Samples configured to encrypt only SMB shares, niche database extensions absent from the VM, or parasitic .exe infectors (such as Virlock and Neshta) do not encrypt user documents on the local profile.

Safe ransomware simulators and analysis timeouts: Tools that only encrypt their own newly created test files rather than user documents, as well as samples that time out before reaching their encryption loop, do not trigger the tag.

Practical Security Use Cases & VirusTotal Intelligence Queries

Security teams can use tag:encrypts-files (or behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) immediately across VirusTotal Intelligence Search and the v3 REST API to streamline four common workflows:

Building Clean Ransomware Validation Corpora for EDR and Storage Defense: Endpoint protection engineers, NAS/SAN storage security teams, and purple teams need fresh samples guaranteed to perform real disk-level file encryption when testing ransomware rollback and anomaly-detection sensors. Filter directly on samples verified to encrypt user documents across operating systems and architectures:

All confirmed file-encrypting samples: entity:file tag:encrypts-files

64-bit Windows PE encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:peexe tag:64bits

Archive, script, and non-PE file encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files NOT type:peexe

macOS Mach-O encryptors (low in-the-wild volume): entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:macho (note: 20 of the first 55 tagged files match NOT type:peexe, mostly ZIP/RAR archives plus .pyw scripts and DLLs)

Uncovering Evasive or Newly Emerged Ransomware Families: Combine dynamic encryption proof with low static antivirus detection thresholds to catch novel packers, custom Go or Rust lockers, or targeted affiliate builds before broad signature coverage arrives:

Low-detection file encryptors (< 10 AV detections): entity:file tag:encrypts-files p:10-

Rapid SOC Triage and Impact Prioritization: During incident response, seeing behaviour_tags:crypto on a suspicious binary only tells an analyst that cryptography libraries were linked or called. Seeing encrypts-files paired with T1486 confirms destructive file-encryption capability immediately, enabling faster containment and backup isolation decisions.

Confidential Detonation in Private Scanning: When triaging sensitive incident samples that cannot be uploaded to the public corpus, you can detonate them in Private Scanning to run the same CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage checks inside an isolated tenant.

Real-Time Hunting with VirusTotal Livehunt and YARA-X

Beyond retrospective search, you can receive real-time IOC Stream notifications whenever newly submitted or sandbox-analyzed files exhibit verified document encryption by pairing VirusTotal Livehunt with the vt YARA-X module.

1. Core Livehunt Rule: Verified ENCRYPTS_FILES Trait

The rule below matches any file whose sandbox behavior emits vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES. Because CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only emit this trait after verifying user-document encryption, ANDing T1486 adds no extra precision:

import "vt" rule HUNT_Ransomware_EncryptsFiles { meta: description = "Detects files verified to encrypt user documents in sandbox execution (ENCRYPTS_FILES trait)" author = "Google Threat Intelligence" date = "2026-11-17" reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt" condition: for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : ( trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES ) }

2. Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting

To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the 0/75 system_update.pyw script and 3/75 lkd.exe binary above), add a vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious threshold:

import "vt" rule HUNT_Evasive_Ransomware_LowAV_EncryptsFiles { meta: description = "Alerts on low-detection files (< 10 AV engines) verified to encrypt user documents in sandboxes" author = "Google Threat Intelligence" date = "2026-11-17" reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt" condition: vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious < 10 and for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : ( trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES ) }

Two practical tips when authoring Livehunt behavioral rules:

Prefer vt.behaviour.traits over vt.metadata.tags for immediate behavioral matching: Livehunt evaluates dynamic rules as soon as sandbox reports finish (vt.behaviour.traits), so checking vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES matches directly on the normalized sandbox report without waiting for downstream file-tag indexing.

When (if ever) to query T1486 in Livehunt: Do not AND T1486 onto ENCRYPTS_FILES rules, because vt.behaviour.mitre_attack_techniques aggregates across every sandbox (including broader Zenbox and third-party mappings) and adds no precision over the trait. Only add a case-insensitive technique.id iequals "T1486" check in separate rules when you want broader T1486 hits from third-party sandboxes that do not emit ENCRYPTS_FILES.

Try It Out and Share Your Feedback

Title: Suspected North Korea-Aligned Group Hides C2 on Solana Blockchain
Context: A financially motivated threat group has hidden its command-and-control (C2) server addresses on the Solana blockchain and deployed malware built to survive removal attempts
Full Text:
A financially motivated threat group has hidden its command-and-control (C2) server addresses on the Solana blockchain and deployed malware built to survive removal attempts. Cisco Talos said the group used the Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), an infostealer and a cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker.

Cisco Talos detailed the activity in research published November 18. It tracks the group as UAT-12643 and assessed with low confidence that it was a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT).

Talos based its assessment partly on earlier use of Overlord by UNK_DeadDrop, a cluster it described as likely North Korean, and on a Solana C2 technique previously linked to North Korea's Lazarus Group. It noted that other actors had used both.

How Overlord RAT Stays Hidden

The operators stored encrypted C2 addresses, which tell infected machines where to get instructions, in memos attached to transactions from a Solana wallet they controlled. The Go-based Overlord RAT checked that wallet for updates, so the operators could switch servers without redeploying the malware.

Overlord also resisted removal. Trying to terminate it crashed Windows with a Blue Screen of Death, and it planted itself in the Windows Recovery Environment, the part of Windows used to repair or reset a PC, which Talos said ensured "the implant survives a full system reset."

Talos identified 35 commands. Beyond surveillance, including keylogging, screenshots and webcam and audio capture, they covered file and process control, script execution, movement through internal networks and in-memory plugin delivery.

Read more on blockchain C2: Six npm Packages Read C2 Addresses From Ethereum Wallet

Targets Include Gamers and Cryptocurrency Holders

Talos said the lures and payloads pointed to three groups of targets: cryptocurrency holders, people with gaming accounts and users of internet phone software. Lures included a fake financial statement, a tampered Viber installer and files named after an internet phone app.

The actor also used Good Game, a publicly available Python infostealer that collected browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets and gaming-related information. Talos said the campaign actor was not its developer. The stealer searched files for keywords in English, French, Spanish and Portuguese, which Talos said pointed to possible victims in Europe.

The toolset also included a clipboard hijacker that swapped copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses for ones the attackers controlled. Talos did not see how the malicious files reached victims and gave no victim count.

An operational security mistake also left the actor's file server publicly reachable, Talos said, giving researchers a view of its toolset and C2 settings.

Title: ROMULUS ClickFix Attacks Deliver RAT That Can Spy on Users and Control PCs
Context: "As attackers continue to change the applications and loaders used to distribute their payloads, the underlying malware architecture provides a more consistent way to identify...
Full Text:
Threat actors have been observed using the ROMULUS ClickFix malware delivery platform to deliver a previously undocumented remote access trojan (RAT) that shares similarities with CNCMachineRMS.

"ROMULUS likely operates as a delivery service, distributing CNCMachineRMS and Legion Loader through separate chains while retaining ClickFix and signed binary sideloading techniques," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker, Nevan Beal, and Andi Ursry said in a report.

ROMULUS was first publicly documented by Forescout Research last month, describing it as a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures to distribute malware families like Legion Loader (aka Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper).

Attacks involving ROMULUS have also leveraged ChatGPT Custom GPTs as a pathway to direct unsuspecting victims to malicious sites that employ ClickFix lures to deliver a RAT payload by means of DLL sideloading.

Interestingly, CNCMachineRMS has also been delivered via another malware loader called BabaDeda Loader through ClickFix attacks that employ DLL sideloading involving the legitimately signed IBM SPSS IDE executable.

The latest findings from Blackpoint Cyber indicate that ROMULUS is distributing CNCMachineRMS alongside LegionLoader through separate infection chains.

One of the payloads delivered through the ClickFix activity associated with ROMULUS is a malicious MSI installer ("IconEdit2Turb.msi") that's executed using "msiexec.exe" by means of a PowerShell command. The installer masquerades as Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool, while initiating a DLL sideloading chain to run a malicious DLL ("I++u.dll").

The DLL is designed to decode and run embedded shellcode responsible for launching CNCMachineRMS. It's worth noting that the RAT malware is the same final implant also distributed via the aforementioned ChatGPT Custom GPT lures.

The trojan enables remote desktop control, screen streaming, microphone and camera capture, file management, and system reconnaissance. It's also equipped to run additional payloads on demand. Communication with attacker-controlled infrastructure takes place through DNS over HTTPS (DoH).

"As attackers continue to change the applications and loaders used to distribute their payloads, the underlying malware architecture provides a more consistent way to identify related activity and understand the threats being delivered," Blackpoint Cyber said.

The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of ClickFix-style campaigns that -

Combine ClickFix with EtherHiding on more than 70,000 compromised websites to run JavaScript that interacts with a Polygon smart contract to fetch additional JavaScript that renders a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA prompt and ultimately deliver malware ("slaiclind").

Use fake Zillow apartment-review pages that serve a fake verification prompt to install NetSupport RAT on visitors' Windows computers.

Employ a JavaScript-to-WordPress attack chain called TRUST#GRAFT that employs an unknown initial access method to inject JavaScript into WordPress sites that serves a fake Cloudflare verification prompt and then fingerprints the visitor and checks if the request is from an already authenticated WordPress administrator browser before uploading a malicious PHP plugin named Web Media Optimizer that's capable of injecting remote JavaScript into public pages and copying itself into the "mu-plugins" plugins directory for persistence.

Use a sponsored Google search result for the keywords "amazon business" to a spoofed Amazon login page ("orders-amazon[.]com[.]advancedfences[.]com") with an embedded ClickFix command that uses the Window's built-in finger utility to initiate a multi-stage attack chain that leads to the deployment of the NetSupport Client remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool and a version of Lumma Stealer.

Abuse Google Ads to direct users to an Anthropic Claude shared chat that stages a fake "Download Claude" page with ClickFix commands to trick Mac users into running a malicious command on their Terminal, resulting in the deployment of Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS) stealer.

Use a typosquatted domain that employs a "House Wiring Scheme" theme ("veriffication-redirect[.]com") to serve a fake Cloudflare verification prompt, which utilizes clipboard manipulation to trick users into running a malicious command on the Windows Run dialog, which then retrieves next-stage Python payloads via DNS TXT records. This includes a previously unreported trojan called CrocoRat, along with a broader theft workflow targeting web browsers, stored credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and seed phrases on standalone systems.

Directly contact targets via phone and convince them to open compromised WordPress sites that serve ClickFix lures to deliver malicious payloads via trojanized MSI packages masquerading as 3D PDF Maker Smart, Bitwarden VPN, and ESET Sysinspector, and execute them via DLL sideloading.

Use a ClickFix variant called TerminalFix that instructs users to open Windows Terminal and run a command to deploy a Python-based tunneling implant using Lorem Ipsum Loader. The activity is being tracked as STAC4924.

Use Google search ads for "claude mac" to a Bing search result, which then directs the victim to a compromised retail website before landing on a fake Claude download page. The bogus landing page employs another ClickFix variant called InstallFix to get Mac users to copy and run a malicious command on their Terminal. The crafty Google Search-to-Bing redirect and cloaking technique has been codenamed Adception.

Use fake Cloudflare verification prompts on bogus sites mimicking gaming marketplace DMarket, Microsoft Office authentication in Czech ("login.microsoftofice[.]cz"), and U.K. retailer Howdens ("updates.howclens[.]com") to deliver CrashHandler RAT and remote access malware, including one that abuses the Stripe API as command-and-control (C2) to receive instructions and send back stolen information.

In a report published last week, Huntress revealed that ClickFix broadened its scope beyond simple script or loader delivery into sophisticated attack chains that establish persistence, support lateral movement, and enable reconnaissance and credential theft, in some cases using steganographic tricks to hide malware and reconstruct them on the infected host.

"Threat actors are using increasingly elaborate delivery methods, including browser-cache-seeded chains and executables reconstructed from data hidden in PNG files," Huntress researchers said.

Title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
Context: Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet),...
Full Text:
The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them.

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide.

A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required.

There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets.

“Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush, Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post. “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.”

Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do

WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025.

WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository, and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take.

The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address.

This meant an attacker merely had to supply an address. Theoretically, if they opened a pull request and pointed an InstallerURL software installation package at their own server, “the trap was set,” Harush explained.

Microsoft’s automated Azure DevOps validation pipeline would then attempt to fetch the URL, but the attacker’s server would intentionally return an error. This added a validation error label to the pull request.

The moderator’s internal script would respond to that label by running a CheckInstaller routine which would send a HEAD request to the attacker via an authenticated HTTP helper, whose job is to automatically attach credentials or tokens to outgoing HTTP requests and handle authorization errors. Then all the attacker had to do was check their logs and extract the moderator’s official GitHub token, which was “casually” handed over.

But the token is not merely a repository-scoped credential, it is a full identity credential, meaning whatever that Microsoft employee can do on GitHub, the token can do.

Harush explained: “It is like a courier stapling your house key to every parcel that has your name on it, because most of them are destined for your own address.” But if a stranger uses your name and changes the address to one they control, “your key is delivered directly to them.”

Armed with this key to Microsoft’s internal environment, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests, and slip in backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages, all under a highly trusted, official Microsoft badge.

They could also access and write to every other Microsoft repository the moderator had access to, modify GitHub Actions workflows across those repositories to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and exfiltrate corporate secrets.

There is a precondition for this attack: At least one moderator has to have the triage tracker running in a continuous background loop, which it is designed to do as it waits for work.

Underlying model ‘fundamentally flawed’

Harush pointed out that Microsoft’s C# version of the tool, in the same directory, did not share the flaw; as such, it would have offered safer authentication. Microsoft has since patched the PowerShell vulnerability, safely scoping the authentication mechanism to ensure that users’ tokens are only attached when a request host is an authorized GitHub endpoint, such as api.github.com, github.com, or raw.githubusercontent.com.

Harush noted, however, that the underlying credential model is “fundamentally flawed,” and that relying on Classic PATs is a “severe liability.”

Cycode advises binding credentials to destinations, rather than functions; auditing every internal tool that handles maintainer credentials; and ensuring that headers are conditionally applied based on the target host, “not unconditionally stapled by a wrapper function.” Treat all user inputs as hostile, validated hosts before credentials are attached, and deprecate classic PATs.

“The blast radius of a leaked token must be limited to one repository and the bare minimum permissions,” Harush said. “A leaked token should never mean a leaked corporate identity.”

He emphasized, though, that WinGet moderators are doing exactly what’s asked of them: Using automated tools to manage a “flood of community submissions” and make their jobs easier. “But automation does not just remove the human who would have clicked the malicious link; it removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.”

Scripts are a soft spot

The WinGet flaw was a near miss, but “a very serious one,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Exploiting it would have let an attacker publish malware with “Microsoft’s seal of approval.”

This means attackers could have pushed tampered installers to anyone who ran an install or an update, reached into any other Microsoft repositories the moderator could touch, and hijacked the build machinery to steal more secrets.

And the damage would have looked like routine work. An IT team scripting a standard software rollout would have installed the attacker’s code on every machine, and the logs would have shown an approved package from an approved source.

“The attack would have been a Trojan horse delivered by the mail carrier everyone trusts,” Dickson said.

Enterprise security teams should learn that their own scripts are a soft spot, he pointed out; internal tools, bots, and automation get production-level keys and hobby-level review. CISOs should inventory every script and bot that holds a token, and answer important questions: What could this key do in the wrong hands? Where is it allowed to go?

Additionally, he advised replacing broad, long-lived tokens with narrow, short-lived ones, and binding every credential to the specific services that need it, which is exactly how Microsoft fixed this problem. “Also, enterprises should stop trusting public registries blindly,” Dickson said.

Ultimately, security teams should review their automations the way they review their people, he said. “A script that runs in a loop around the clock with a moderator’s keys is, in effect, a moderator who never sleeps and never questions anything.”

Title: AI Joins the Industrial Attack Workflow
Context: The recent cyberattack on French refrigerators and our tracking of the malicious AI framework ARTEX show that threat actors are increasingly using AI to accelerate attacks,...
Full Text:
The recent cyberattack on French refrigerators and our tracking of the malicious AI framework ARTEX show that threat actors are increasingly using AI to accelerate attacks, expand their reach, and improve their effectiveness. GreenJuliett, the group behind OT cyberattacks similar to those in France, has begun incorporating AI into its operational technology (OT) attack chain. Understanding the scale AI offers financially motivated and state-sponsored threat actors helps us see it as more than a tool: it’s something that can fill an operator’s role, even while humans remain in control.

On October 11 and 12, 2026, someone changed the defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at more than 700 retail locations in France. This resulted in fires, damaged equipment, and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros, highlighting the physical impacts of attacks against operational technology (OT). On November 9, France attributed the attack to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC). We track activity that likely belongs to an element of Shahid Kaveh as GreenJuliett.

GreenJuliett (also known as CyberAv3ngers and Bauxite) builds infrastructure aimed at internet-facing PLCs. And while that work continued through at least October 30, despite repeated public reporting on the group, the target set began to widen. Between August and October, we observed GreenJuliett-linked infrastructure scanning, or attempting to exploit, Fortinet FortiGate firewalls, edge devices that protect OT networks, in Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. Our network data suggests the group is also working to add internet-of-things (IoT) and CCTV devices to its list.

While we have not independently tied GreenJuliett infrastructure to the refrigeration attacks, over the past three months, we have seen the group continue to target PLCs (programmable logic controllers), which are similar to the internet-exposed controllers the refrigerators in France used. We have also observed that AI is now part of how they work.

From Accounts to Infrastructure

In October 2024, OpenAI banned accounts it assessed as belonging to CyberAv3ngers. The operators had used ChatGPT to research default credentials for PLCs, compile lists of electricity companies and common PLCs in Jordan, and draft scripts against industrial protocols (such as Modbus TCP, a control protocol that allows PLCs to communicate quickly on local networks).

However, in 2026, the picture is different. In October, we found a configuration for LiteLLM (an open-source gateway that puts multiple AI models behind a single interface, suggesting a team-sharing model for access), alongside self-hosted chat applications built for Persian-language users, on infrastructure we assessed as likely used by GreenJuliett-linked operators. We also observed servers in the group's anonymization network communicating with infrastructure that hosts Anthropic's Claude.

While we have not confirmed specific instances of misuse in this research, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported publicly on detecting and disrupting misuse by Iranian government operators. AI shortens the time it takes to identify vulnerable device types and write targeting scripts, and GreenJuliett has moved it from individual accounts into its operating environment.

Title: Third-Party JavaScript Is Part of Your Attack Surface: Lessons from a Recent Supply-Chain Attack
Context: Start Trial References Newsweek, Cyber attack hits 178 major websites Qualys, How Web Malware Detection works Qualys, Web Malware Detection Qualys TotalAppSec product page
Full Text:
In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript. Most of those organizations never deployed bad code. The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service.

The attackers did not break into those websites. Instead, they exploited a weakness in the vendor’s platform to gain administrative control of some customer accounts, then modified the JavaScript those customers delivered through the vendor. The vendor’s CDN served the altered code to every visitor of an affected page.

Researchers who analyzed the injected code found it running on many organizations’ websites. It was built to steal payment card details typed into on-page forms, tamper with cryptocurrency transactions, and send readable cookies to attacker-controlled servers.

The lesson extends beyond one vendor: modern websites run code their owners did not write and often do not track.

The hidden risk of third-party JavaScript

Analytics, personalization, advertising, consent management, chat, and A/B testing all depend on external scripts. Each <script src> that points to another host lets that host run code in your visitors’ browsers with the same privileges as your own code. It can read and change the page, watch form input, read cookies not marked HttpOnly, and send data out.

That is why a third-party supply-chain compromise is different from an application compromise. The attack did not require any change to the affected organizations’ source code, servers, or pipelines. The malicious file was served from the vendor’s own CDN, with the vendor’s valid certificate, from a host every affected site already trusted. Code review and server-side monitoring had nothing to catch. One weakness in a shared platform reached many organizations in a single day.

What Content Security Policy can and cannot do

Content Security Policy (CSP) tells the browser which sources may load scripts and receive data. In this incident, the injected code loaded its main payload from an attacker-controlled domain, so a strong CSP could block it.

But much depends on the word strong. Most affected sites had either no CSP or one that still let the payload run. Allowlisting the vendor’s domain made no difference, because the malicious code came through that host. Protection came from a restrictive script-src that did not allow the attacker’s domain. ‘unsafe-eval’ let an inline fallback copy of the payload run, and ‘strict-dynamic’ extended trust to scripts the compromised snippet inserted. A tight connect-src limited exfiltration but could not stop wallet-address swapping inside the page.

Reducing third-party script risk: guidance for every organization

These practices apply to any organization that runs external JavaScript on its website.

Know what runs on your pages. Keep an inventory of every third-party script, the pages that load it, who owns it internally, and why it is needed. Include scripts added through tag managers.

Load less, especially on sensitive pages. Remove scripts that no longer serve a purpose, and keep analytics, marketing, and testing scripts off payment, login, and account pages unless they are essential.

Enforce a strict Content Security Policy. Allow only the script and connection sources each page needs, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’ and ‘unsafe-inline’, use nonces or hashes where you can, and enable violation reporting. Roll out changes in Report-Only mode first.

Keep payment entry out of reach. Hosted payment fields, served in an iframe from your payment provider’s domain, cannot be read by scripts running on your own page.

Protect cookies and sessions. Mark session and authentication cookies HttpOnly so injected scripts cannot read them, and set Secure and SameSite as well.

Pin or self-host what rarely changes. Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) for third-party files that change infrequently, or host them yourself. Scripts that change often, such as tag managers and testing tools, need monitoring instead.

Hold script vendors to a high standard. Ask providers how they secure customer accounts and code changes, and how quickly they notify customers of incidents. On your own accounts with them, enforce MFA or SSO and limit who can publish code.

Watch for changes. Monitor third-party scripts for new code, new network destinations, and unexpected behavior. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.

Plan your response. Know how to disable a third-party script quickly, and keep web, CDN, and CSP logs long enough to investigate an incident.

How Qualys TotalAppSec helps identify exposure

1. Assess Content Security Policy: QIDs 150206 and 150207

QID 150206 – Content-Security-Policy Not Implemented flags applications that send no CSP header, which leaves no browser-enforced limit on where scripts can load from.

QID 150207 – Content Security Policy Insecure Configuration flags weak elements: ‘unsafe-inline’, ‘unsafe-eval’, wildcard sources, a missing default-src, and missing or invalid reporting configuration. This incident showed the effect of one of these directly, when ‘unsafe-eval’ let the inline payload run.

A QID 150207 finding does not mean a given policy would have allowed this particular attack. That depends on the full policy, including script-src, trusted sources, and nonces or hashes. Treat these findings as starting points for a policy review. Reporting matters as well. The vendor’s first investigative recommendation was to review CSP violation reports, and sites without reporting had none to review.

2. Discover external JavaScript dependencies: QID 150545

QID 150545 – JavaScript Library Loaded via External Server reports out-of-scope JavaScript libraries found during crawling, including the page, library version, and external URL. It does not judge whether a library is malicious. Its value is visibility: an inventory of external scripts is the basis for deciding which vendors to trust and which hosts a CSP should allow.

3. Find applications that serve known malicious scripts 533507 (new)

We have released QID 533507 – Known Malicious Script Reference Detected. This unauthenticated check sends an HTTP GET request and inspects the response body for a script src referencing known malicious scripts.

Use it to inventory which applications load known malicious scripts and to prioritize the applications handling payments or cryptocurrency for CSP review.

Detecting malicious content with Qualys Web Malware Detection

TotalAppSec shows where you are exposed and how well your controls are configured. Qualys Web Malware Detection asks a different question: is malicious content present? Qualys Web Malware Detection combines heuristic analysis (signature rules for patterns such as encoded JavaScript); behavioral analysis (visiting the site with a vulnerable browser and watching for unexpected file writes or processes); reputation checks of pages, referenced URLs, and remotely loaded resources against public blacklists; and antivirus scanning of downloaded scripts and files. Three detections relate directly to third-party script risk:

QID 207003 – A Match to a Known Virus was Detected: a file written to disk during page rendering is identified as malicious by a virus scanner.

QID 208000 – Content was Loaded from a Remote Malicious Page: a page loads scripts, iframes, or images from a blacklisted domain.

QID 208001 – A Link to a Malicious Page was Found: a page links to a domain on one or more blacklists.

Reputation-based detection depends on a domain being blacklisted at scan time. Attacker infrastructure is often new: Report URI found this campaign’s primary domain was registered the morning the attack began. Continuous scanning, alongside preventive controls such as CSP, is paramount for that reason.

Together, these findings give three different views. A script reference (QIDs 533507, 150545) shows where you depend on someone else. A weak control (QIDs 150206, 150207) shows how much damage a compromised dependency could do. Malicious content (QIDs 207003, 208000, 208001) is evidence that something harmful is present.

Recommendations for security teams

Follow the actions in the vendor’s report. Confirm which pages ran the snippet during the exposure window, review CSP violation reports and outbound requests against the published indicators of compromise, and keep your web, CDN, and CSP logs. The vendor and Report URI published different indicators, so check both.

For every organization:

Inventory third-party scripts. Use QIDs 533507 and 150545 to see which applications load external JavaScript, and from where.

Restrict trusted sources. Remove unneeded scripts, especially from payment, login, and personal-data pages.

Implement CSP and assess it continuously. Resolve QID 150206 and 150207 findings, keep script-src and connect-src restrictive, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’, and test changes in Report-Only mode.

Monitor third-party script changes. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.

Investigate malicious content. Treat Web Malware Detection findings as triggers for investigation.

Remove unauthorized scripts and remediate. Restore known-good code and rotate secrets stored in readable cookies.

Reassess after remediation. Rescan to confirm that fixes are in place.

Conclusion

The incident here did not require breaching a single customer’s application. It required one weakness in a platform those applications trusted. Securing a web application means having visibility into both the code you write and the external scripts you allow to run in your users’ browsers. Title: How AWS Security Incident Response triages your security findings
Context: If you send third-party detection findings to Security Hub CSPM from tools such as CrowdStrike, Trend Micro, or Lacework, their threat detection findings are also ingested
Full Text:
AWS Security Incident Response continuously triages the threat findings from Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub CSPM, but most of that work never shows up as a case. If cases are all you look at, it’s hard to tell whether the service is working at all, and that’s the question I hear most often when I help customers onboard. The Proactive response dashboard gives you a high-level view of this activity, and this post takes you behind the numbers to show what happens to an individual finding.

In this post, I walk you through what happens to a finding after it’s ingested by the service, what gets triaged, where each finding is sent, and how a triage decision becomes a case. I then show you how to confirm triage is working day-to-day, so your team can focus on the findings that require attention. The process flow is shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1: AWS Security Incident Response triage flow, from ingestion through to one of three outcomes

Ingestion

AWS Security Incident Response ingests threat findings from GuardDuty through Amazon EventBridge rules that are automatically deployed to your accounts during the onboarding process.

If you send third-party detection findings to Security Hub CSPM from tools such as CrowdStrike, Trend Micro, or Lacework, their threat detection findings are also ingested. Each of those findings must carry complete payload information such as resource ID, account ID, timestamp, and threat details. GuardDuty findings are ingested directly, so these findings aren’t re-ingested through Security Hub CSPM and there’s no duplication.

Triage

The service triages findings that indicate an active threat, such as compromised credentials, cryptomining, or data exfiltration. These represent activity that’s underway or has already occurred.

Posture and compliance findings aren’t triaged. A misconfiguration or a failed benchmark check reflects the state of your environment rather than an active threat, so those findings remain for your team to address through your existing remediation process.

Outcomes

For each threat finding, the service runs an automated triage process. It evaluates the finding payload, related AWS activity from AWS CloudTrail and Amazon VPC Flow Logs, AWS threat intelligence, and the context you provide about your environment. The service then maps the finding against a profile of known-good activity. What fits the profile is treated as expected, and what doesn’t is flagged for a closer look.

What happens next depends on that outcome. A finding is sent to one of three places:

Archived, no action needed – Automated triage or an AWS Security Incident Response engineer confirms the activity is benign or expected. The finding is archived in GuardDuty, with no case and no customer contact.

A proactive case is opened – Triage can’t confirm the activity is benign. This is either Unconfirmed Activity (the service needs you to confirm whether it’s expected) or Inappropriate/Unintended Activity (confirmed activity that needs your action). A proactive case is opened, your incident response team is engaged, and the finding stays Current until it’s resolved.

Retained for your review, no case – Posture-related findings, such as overly permissive policies, configuration, or missing encryption, aren’t threats. By design, they stay Current without archiving and no case is created.

When a proactive case is opened, you respond to it in the AWS Management Console for AWS Security Incident Response under Cases, where you can communicate directly with the team, share context, and resolve or reopen the case. Timely responses also help the service learn your environment, which helps reduce false positives over time. For the full workflow, see Responding to an AWS generated case.

The preceding outcomes use GuardDuty terms, because it’s the primary source. Third-party findings ingested through Security Hub CSPM follow the same triage logic, but their disposition shows as a workflow-status change rather than archiving. The finding moves from NEW to NOTIFIED when triage begins, which removes it from the default Security Hub CSPM view. If triage clears it as benign, it moves to SUPPRESSED. Otherwise it stays visible for your review.

Because only benign findings are archived, it’s normal to see many findings in Current, and that isn’t a sign the service missed them. Across customers, less than 1 percent of ingested findings result in a customer-facing escalation. Most are handled automatically, without a case.

Credential exfiltration finding example

Suppose GuardDuty generates an UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding: temporary credentials created on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance were used from an IP address outside AWS. Triage cross-references the payload against what it knows about your environment.

Cleared – The external IP belongs to a corporate virtual private network (VPN) range that your workloads regularly call through, and the service has seen this pattern before. The finding is archived in GuardDuty.

Escalated – The IP is in a hosting-provider range with no prior association to your accounts, and the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role has never made calls from outside AWS. The service creates a proactive case, notifies your incident response team, and an engineer investigates whether the credentials were compromised.

Same finding type, two outcomes. The difference is context, and context is what triage builds by observing your environment over time.

How triage sharpens over time

The service builds a profile of what’s normal in your environment. It learns the IP ranges and domains you trust, and the IAM principals and behaviors your workloads rely on. When your team routinely connects from a known VPN range, or a specific IAM role runs nightly batch jobs, the service recognizes those patterns and measures new findings against them. Early on, engineers investigate more findings by hand as they learn your environment. Within a few weeks, automated triage handles most of those decisions on its own.

Triage is dynamic. A finding treated as expected today can be re-evaluated tomorrow if the context changes, so the service can still catch a real threat that reuses a pattern it formerly treated as safe. You can shape the profile by submitting known-good activity, such as trusted IP ranges or authorized scanning tools, through an AWS Support case. For details, see Submit known-good activity.

Archiving versus suppression

It’s possible to conflate the two mechanisms, so it’s worth separating them:

Archiving is the primary mechanism. When automated triage or an engineer determines a finding is benign, the service archives it in GuardDuty. The finding then stays there for 90 days.

Suppression rules are less common and work differently. A suppression rule acts on future findings. When the service identifies a recurring pattern of expected activity, it might create a GuardDuty suppression rule that automatically archives matching findings so they don’t generate new alerts. Suppressed findings aren’t sent to your configured export, such as an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket or SIEM. When the service creates a rule, your incident response team is notified, and you can view and manage it in the GuardDuty console under Suppression rules.

A healthy deployment typically shows many archived findings and few or no suppression rules. That’s expected, and it means the service is handling findings dynamically rather than relying on static filters.

How to see what triage is doing

Triage runs on its own, and the service gives you a few ways to confirm it’s working.

Proactive response dashboard

The Dashboard page in the AWS Security Incident Response console has a Proactive response section. It counts how many findings were ingested, triaged, investigated, and escalated over the timeframe you select, the last 7, 30, or 90 days.

The Overview leads with two figures. Noise reduction is the share of ingested findings that automated triage resolved without opening a case, so you can see for yourself how much volume never reached your team. Time saved estimates the analyst hours that automation returned to you, counted as one hour for each ingested finding.

Below that, Finding evaluations breaks those stages down:

Ingest – Threat findings collected from your detection sources

Triage – Findings evaluated automatically to decide whether the activity is expected

Investigation – Findings automated triage couldn’t confirm, passed to an AWS Security Incident Response engineer for a closer look

Escalation – Investigations raised as a case when a genuine risk was detected or the activity couldn’t be confirmed as expected

A flow diagram on the dashboard shows how those findings move from their sources through triage and investigation, with branches for the ones closed as false positives and the ones still in progress. For more, see Viewing proactive response metrics.

Monthly report

The monthly report is the periodic companion to the dashboard. AWS Security Incident Response emails it to your incident response team a week or two after each month closes. It opens with the accounts monitored, findings processed, and investigations, then lists each investigation and its status, the triage flows that show the checks run for each finding type, and the context the service has learned about your environment, such as the trusted networks it now recognizes as normal.

Archived findings in GuardDuty

For a quick confirmation outside either view, open Findings in the GuardDuty console and filter to see Archived. That list also includes findings archived by you or by suppression rules, so look for the threat findings AWS Security Incident Response archived after triage. Each one is a finding that the service cleared as benign so your team didn’t have to.

Conclusion

AWS Security Incident Response continuously evaluates your threat findings so your team can spend its time on confirmed threats rather than alert volume. Findings that are evaluated as benign are archived automatically, the ones that need a response become proactive cases, and posture issues stay in Current for your team to handle.

Cases show only a small part of that work. When I deliver AWS Security Incident Response to customers now, I walk them through the triage flow in Figure 1, the Proactive response dashboard, and their monthly report, so they can see how triage works end to end.

To get started, see the onboarding guide. Setup takes about 10 minutes. For more information, see the AWS Security Incident Response product page or the User Guide.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Anatoliy Kochetov

Anatoliy is a Technical Account Manager and AWS Security Incident Response SME. He works with AWS Enterprise customers, providing ongoing support and technical guidance to help them build secure, resilient solutions using AWS best practices.
