Title: Hardening GitHub Actions Against Insider Threats
Context: Several of the largest incidents of 2026 fall into this category, and they didn't need to exploit a vulnerability to gain access
Full Text:
Part one of this series covered attackers with no credential for your organization, who reach the pipeline through a pull request, a dependency or a third-party action. Those controls are largely deterministic. Pin an action to a commit SHA and a retagged action cannot run.

This post covers the other half, and it behaves differently. Here the attacker presents a valid credential. Either a maintainer's account, token or session has been stolen, or a person with legitimate access is acting against the project.

Several of the largest incidents of 2026 fall into this category, and they didn't need to exploit a vulnerability to gain access.

To GitHub, npm, and your cloud provider, the attacker's requests were indistinguishable from normal work. No input validation would have rejected them, because nothing about them was malformed.

That changes what the controls in this post can promise. They cannot prevent every maintainer account takeover — chapter 10's phishing-resistant factors do break one common entry route, but nothing here stops a credential that leaks some other way. What these ten chapters do is shrink the blast radius, raise the number of independently protected things an attacker must compromise, and shorten the time between the first malicious action and revocation.

Read this half as containment and detection rather than prevention, and treat the revocation drill in chapter 19 as essential rather than optional.

The threat model. A phished or malware-infected maintainer, a stolen personal access token, OAuth token, SSH key or session, or a departing insider. They push a workflow to a new branch, publish a release, add a deploy key, relax a ruleset, flip a repository public, or approve their own deployment — every one an ordinary operation performed by an authenticated principal. What works against that: phishing-resistant factors, no standing privilege, two independent humans on the release path, and fast revocation.

The organizing principle is a single question: how many separately protected things must be compromised for a malicious release to ship? One account should never be enough — and “separately protected” is the key phrase. If one administrator can reach the credentials for all three accounts, they are really just a single point of failure.

The LiteLLM incident in October 2026 shows why that qualifier matters. The attacker appeared as three accounts — one overrode the protection, one approved the release, one deleted the evidence — but the completed investigation describes a single cascading compromise rather than three breached boundaries. A publicly committed administrative key exposed an organization owner's GitHub CLI token, and that access was used to plant workflows and take the other engineers' tokens. The owner's token could have removed the approval restriction outright; splitting the work across accounts appears to have served detection avoidance rather than being necessary to defeat the gate. So the number to raise is the count of independently protected credentials, not of identities: two approval accounts whose tokens the same compromised administrator can read are one. That is why this post starts at the account and its credentials rather than at the pipeline.

Where your team is too small for genuine separation, lean harder on chapters 15 and 19: a staged release that a human must approve under a security key, and an alert that fires the moment a configuration event looks wrong.

Chapter 10: Make the Accounts Themselves Hard to Take Over #

The mistake

Treating "we have 2FA" as settled because everyone uses an authenticator app.

App codes and SMS are phishable in real time. A proxy login page relays the code to the real site inside its validity window, and the attacker ends up with a live session. The second mistake is leaving 2FA to individual choice rather than enforcing it at organization level. The third is long-lived browser sessions that survive a password reset.

Observed in the wild

npm author Qix, 8 September 2025, is the cleanest case. No code bug, no misconfiguration — an email from npmjs.help, a look-alike domain registered three days earlier, warning that the maintainer's two-factor setup was out of date, and a cloned login page that captured the credentials and the code typed into it. With the account the attacker published malicious versions of chalk, debug and more than a dozen related packages, together two to three billion downloads a week. npm removed them within about ninety minutes. From the registry's point of view, every one of those publishes was the maintainer. Counts vary between sources, from eighteen packages to around twenty-five.

What to do

Require phishing-resistant factors. WebAuthn security keys or passkeys are bound to the origin, so a proxy page cannot relay them. This is the control that breaks the entry flow above, and TOTP is not a substitute — a relayed code is exactly what the cloned page collected. Enroll at least two keys per maintainer so a lost key is not an outage. GitHub will not enforce it for you: its Only allow secure two-factor methods setting counts authenticator apps and the GitHub Mobile app as secure alongside passkeys and security keys. Where you have an identity provider, enforce phishing-resistant authentication there; on GitHub alone this stays a team policy you verify by inspection.

Enforce at organization level, not per person. Without enforcement you discover the gaps during the incident.

Shorten the session. Use SSO with conditional access where you have it, cap session lifetime, and revoke active sessions on any role change or suspected compromise. A stolen session cookie needs no second factor at all.

Treat recovery codes as credentials. They are a 2FA bypass by design. Store them where you store secrets.

Narrow the publish path. npm 2FA on publish helps, and trusted publishing (chapter 14) is better still. Keep in mind that trusted publishing proves which workflow in which repository published. It does not prove the published content is good. Neither closes the maintainer's own interactive route to the registry; chapter 14 covers what the package settings do and do not close. And as long as releases publish straight from CI, an unattended pipeline reaches every consumer at once: whoever can influence what it runs — through a workflow edit, a dependency or an action — reaches the registry with it. Use staged publishing where the ecosystem supports it (chapter 15); where it does not, consider an approval-gated alternative to publishing from CI.

Security keys do not defeat device-code phishing, where the attacker initiates an OAuth device flow, sends the victim the user code, and the victim enters it on the real site and completes their own genuine MFA. Nothing is relayed, so no authentication method blocks it, FIDO included. Blocking the device flow is effective but breaks legitimate CLI and developer tooling, so most teams carry this risk and compensate with chapter 11 and chapter 19.

Note also what 2FA does not reach at all: a personal access token, an SSH key or a deploy key authenticates with no second factor, from anywhere, for as long as it lives. That is the next chapter.

Configuration

# Org Settings -> Authentication security # [x] Require two-factor authentication for everyone in your organization # [x] Only allow secure two-factor methods # NB: "secure" here includes authenticator apps and GitHub Mobile, # not passkeys and security keys only. There is no security-key-only # setting; enforce phishing-resistant auth at the IdP if you have one. # [x] Require SAML SSO authentication (if you have an IdP)

# Verify enrolment rather than assuming it. This lists members with no 2FA # at all - it does not report which factor anyone enrolled, so it cannot # prove security-key or passkey coverage. gh api /orgs/acme/members --paginate --jq '.[].login' > all.txt gh api '/orgs/acme/members?filter=2fa_disabled' --jq '.[].login' > no2fa.txt # What an org owner can revoke (GHEC with SAML SSO), and what they cannot: # People -> (user) : the member's active SAML session, through # their linked identity. Not a sign-out of # their GitHub account. # Authentication security : Revoke SSO authorizations - removes a PAT or # SSH key's access to THIS org. The credential # itself survives and still works elsewhere. # "Delete keys and tokens" does destroy it, # but is Enterprise Managed Users only. # That is organization containment. Account-wide revocation belongs to the # account holder, or an EMU admin; chapter 11's token sweep is separate.

Chapter 11: Remove Standing Privilege and Long-Lived Tokens #

The mistake

Classic personal access tokens with repo and workflow scope and no expiry, created once for an automation job and never revisited.

They outlive the task, survive a password reset, are unaffected by 2FA, and sit in plaintext in ~/.npmrc, ~/.netrc, CI variables and shell history. The organizational version is granting broad write or admin roles permanently because narrowing them is inconvenient.

A subtler one: assuming offboarding closes everything. Removing a member revokes their organization access, but a deploy key belongs to the repository rather than the person, so it survives their departure untouched.

Observed in the wild

This is what the malware is built to collect: the tj-actions payload scanned runner process memory specifically for personal access tokens, npm tokens and private keys.

GhostAction ran on nothing else. Reporting indicates initial access came from personal access tokens lifted from infostealer logs, and from a phishing site harvesting OAuth tokens carrying repo, workflow and read:org. In none of these did the attacker need the victim's password.

What to do

Set an organization PAT policy, both halves. Require approval for fine-grained tokens that access the organization, and separately restrict classic PATs. This catches people out: classic tokens are not subject to the fine-grained approval flow, so by default any classic PAT reaches organization resources with no approval at all. Two settings, two tabs.

Cap token lifetimes. The organization default maximum for fine-grained tokens is 366 days, which is weak for this purpose — a year is long enough for a stolen token to outlive the incident that leaked it, so set it to the shortest period your workflows tolerate. Classic PATs carry no maximum-lifetime requirement by default, though an organization can enforce one; that they default to none is a second reason to restrict them outright.

Restrict which third-party OAuth Apps can reach the organization. App access restrictions are on by default for new organizations and let owners approve each app individually. This is the control that counters a phishing site harvesting an OAuth token — a flow a security key does not stop, because the victim completes a genuine authorization. Enabling restrictions on an existing organization revokes every previously authorized app and SSH key, so plan the rollout rather than clicking it on a Friday. One exception matters here: GitHub's own privileged OAuth apps, GitHub CLI among them, can still reach organization data despite these restrictions, and the authorization of such an app lands in the user's security log rather than the organization or enterprise audit log. That is a gap in seeing the app authorized, not a cloak over every repository operation later performed with its token — but it is the credential class the LiteLLM chain ran on.

Replace personal tokens in automation with a GitHub App, scoped to the repositories and permissions it needs. Installation tokens are short-lived and the App does not disappear when a person leaves.

Audit who can write workflows. A token-authenticated push to .github/workflows/ needs workflow scope or Workflows: read and write, and most automation has no reason to hold either. Withholding it narrows that credential rather than closing the path, though: SSH keys and deploy keys are a separate write route that these scopes do not govern, so inventory them alongside the tokens.

Inventory deploy keys and SSH keys separately from members, on a schedule. They are the credentials offboarding misses.

If your organization is owned by an enterprise, the enterprise policy wins and you cannot loosen it locally. Worth knowing before planning a rollout the enterprise has already decided.

Configuration

# Org Settings -> Personal access tokens -> Fine-grained tokens # Access: [x] Require administrator approval # Maximum lifetime: 30 days (default is 366 - lower it) # # Org Settings -> Personal access tokens -> Tokens (classic) # [x] Restrict access by personal access tokens (classic) # SEPARATE SETTING - the approval flow above does not cover classic PATs

# Standing inventory: the keys offboarding does not remove. Both halves # need their page limits raised, or the inventory quietly stops short of # whatever you are looking for. for r in $(gh repo list acme --limit 5000 --json name --jq '.[].name'); do gh api --paginate "/repos/acme/$r/keys" \ --jq ".[] | {repo: \"$r\", title, read_only, created_at}" done # Apps and their permissions, including who can write workflows gh api --paginate /orgs/acme/installations --jq '.installations[] | {app: .app_slug, workflows: .permissions.workflows, contents: .permissions.contents}'

Chapter 12: Lock Down Who Can Change Workflow Files #

The mistake

Protecting only the default branch.

Branch protection and CODEOWNERS fire on pull requests into main. A direct push to refs/heads/anything-else is unreviewed, and an on: push trigger written into the attacker's own YAML runs it on that branch at once. The second form of this mistake is treating CODEOWNERS over .github/workflows/ as the control. It requires review on a pull request; it does not restrict who may push.

Observed in the wild

Shai-Hulud, 2025–2026. Using stolen tokens the worm pushed a workflow file into victim repositories, triggered it on push, enumerated every repository secret with ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}, uploaded them as an artifact, then deleted the branch and the workflow to cover its tracks. No pull request was ever opened, so no review control saw any of it.

GhostAction, 2025–2026. A campaign built on nothing else. The attacker authenticates with a stolen maintainer credential, reads the repository's existing workflows to learn which secret names it references, then pushes a new workflow — often under a commit message posing as a security improvement, such as "Add Github Actions Security workflow" — that hardcodes those names and posts the values to a fixed address. GitGuardian put the first wave at 817 repositories and 3,325 stolen secrets, and a second wave through September 2026 at 772 repositories. Figures vary between sources. No vulnerability was exploited at any point.

LiteLLM, 21 October 2026. Branch protection rejected an unauthorized modification to the private release workflow because it had not passed the required pull request and status check process. Five seconds later a credential associated with a privileged developer account overrode those protections and applied the modified workflow.

The protection was configured correctly and fired correctly. It was defeated by an account that held bypass rights, and five seconds indicates a scripted, pre-planned override rather than exploration.

What to do

No single setting covers this. Layer five, in this order.

A push ruleset restricting .github/workflows/**. This blocks the push itself, at the server, on every branch including ones that do not exist yet. Bypass restricted to a named team. Two things to plan for. Push rules need at least a GitHub Team plan, are available for private and internal repositories only, and extend across the repository's fork network — they are not available on public repositories. And a restricted path blocks ordinary workflow edits as well as hostile ones, so pick the bypass setting deliberately: an empty list freezes the path for everyone, while a named team keeps authorized changes possible and becomes the control you are then relying on.

Keep the bypass list empty, or as close to empty as the organization allows. Branch protection does not apply to repository administrators by default, which is the mechanism behind the LiteLLM override. This is the layer that would have mattered there, and it has to be set before the incident, not during it.An empty bypass list only constrains who walks through the rule, not who can edit or disable it. An organization owner can change the organization ruleset itself; for that tier there is no configuration answer here, only chapter 19's alerting on ruleset changes.

Branch rulesets, scoped to what each rule is for. Require a pull request and Code Owner review on the default and release branches, where merges actually happen — applying them to every branch taxes ordinary work and does nothing against a planted workflow, which never opens a pull request. Add Restrict deletions on all branches: the worm deleted its branch to hide, and this blocks that. Prefer organization-managed rulesets, which combine restrictions and stop repository administrators weakening them; multiple rulesets apply to the same branch at once, so these can be two.

Token scope hygiene. A token-authenticated push to .github/workflows/ requires workflow scope on a classic PAT, or Workflows: read and write for a GitHub App. Withholding it narrows that credential rather than closing the path — SSH and deploy keys are the other route, which is why chapter 11's inventory of them matters here too.

Block Actions from creating and approving pull requests. A workflow that can approve its own pull request removes the human from the merge step, which is how a planted change reaches the branch a release later runs from. GitHub's guidance is that allowing workflows “or any other automation” to create or approve pull requests is a risk wherever the result gets merged without oversight. The setting exists at enterprise, organization and repository level; turn it off at the highest level you control.

Because the push ruleset is unavailable on public repositories, detection fills the gap there. Alert on any push touching .github/workflows/** that did not arrive through a merged pull request, on branch deletions shortly after a workflow run, and on the string toJSON(secrets) anywhere in the repository — no legitimate workflow serializes the entire secret set. Chapter 19 covers the alerting.

Configuration

# 1) Private/internal: Settings -> Rules -> New ruleset -> New push ruleset # Enforcement: Active # Bypass list: @acme/platform-security (empty = applies to everyone) # Push rules -> Restrict file paths: # .github/workflows/** # .github/actions/** # 2) New branch ruleset # review, where merges land # Target branches: Default branch, release/* # Rules: Require a pull request before merging # Require review from Code Owners # 3) New branch ruleset # deletion, everywhere # Target branches: All branches (fnmatch **) # Rules: Restrict deletions # blocks the cover-tracks step

# Audit which credentials can write workflow files at all gh api --paginate /orgs/acme/installations --jq '.installations[] | select(.permissions.workflows == "write") | {app: .app_slug, workflows: .permissions.workflows}'

Chapter 13: Turn On Workflow Execution Protections #

The mistake

Treating "can open a pull request" as equivalent to "can run our CI."

By default any actor whose event matches a trigger starts a run. Teams also leave workflow_dispatch broadly available on deployment workflows, so anyone with write access can deploy regardless of who reviewed the code.

Observed in the wild

The PyTorch runner compromise turned on exactly this gap. Approval was gated on previous-contributor status, so the researchers landed a one-character typo fix, became previous contributors, and then triggered workflows on self-hosted runners. Cryptomining abuse of workflow_dispatch and fork pull request triggers on public repositories is the volume case rather than the headline one.

What to do

Configure execution protections at enterprise, organization or repository level, under Settings then Actions then Policies. Two rule types combine:

Actor rules control who may trigger: named users, repository roles, GitHub Apps, Copilot, Dependabot. This separates who contributes code from who runs CI.

Event rules control which events may trigger: push, pull_request, pull_request_target, workflow_dispatch.

The September 2026 general availability added three things worth using. Workflow file targeting lets deploy.yml be restricted to a release team while CI workflows stay open to all contributors. Insights show how rules would evaluate before you enforce them. A REST API manages rules as code.

Where you have it, roll out in evaluate mode first, read the insights, then enforce — the same sequencing GitHub is using for its own pull_request_target default. Evaluate is a GitHub Enterprise Cloud option, so on other plans the choice is between not having the rule and enforcing it directly; stage that by targeting a few repositories before widening the policy.

One limit to plan around: execution-protection insights are surfaced for enterprise accounts. Organizations and repositories can configure and enforce rules, but the cross-repository reporting view is an enterprise feature.

A date. GitHub already adds a default event policy blocking pull_request_target on public repositories that have no applicable policy of their own, and enforcement of it begins 2 December 2026. If a public repository depends on that trigger, add an explicit event policy before the date. Actions policies are available on all public repositories, so plan is no obstacle — but they exist only at enterprise, organization and repository level, so a personal account has to set one on each repository.

Configuration

Repository: acme/payments-api Rule A workflow: .github/workflows/deploy.yml events: workflow_dispatch actors: team:release-engineering mode: enforce Rule B workflow: .github/workflows/ci.yml events: pull_request, push actors: any mode: enforce Rule C workflow: .github/workflows/renovate.yml events: pull_request_target # explicit allow, before 02-Dec-2026 actors: app:renovate mode: enforce

Chapter 14: Replace Publish Tokens With OIDC Trusted Publishing #

The mistake

Storing NPM_TOKEN, PYPI_API_TOKEN or static cloud keys as repository secrets.

A publish token stored as a secret is a bearer credential that remains usable until it expires or is revoked, subject to its restrictions, for anyone who reads it once. The secondary mistake is exposing it to jobs with no business publishing: a test job with NPM_TOKEN in scope means any dependency's postinstall script can read it.

Observed in the wild

Nx s1ngularity. The stolen artifact was a static npm token, and stealing it once was enough to publish. That is precisely the primitive the Shai-Hulud worm consumed at scale, harvesting credentials from developer machines and CI and publishing infected versions of every package its victims maintained.

What to do

Configure trusted publishing on the registry, bind it to the specific repository, workflow file and environment, and delete the stored token. npm trusted publishing with OIDC reached general availability on 31 July 2025; PyPI has offered the equivalent since 2023. The workflow requests an OIDC token with id-token: write and never handles a long-lived secret.

npm now supports multiple trusted publishing configurations per package, from September 2026, for projects releasing from more than one workflow, and opt-in dist-tag permissions so a publisher can be restricted from moving latest.

Trusted publishing proves which workflow in which repository published. It does not prove the published content is good. And it removes the need for a stealable credential rather than removing the credentials themselves: configuring a publisher revokes nothing, so every existing token stays valid until you sweep them. Be exact about what the package-level Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens setting then does. It closes the token route — granular access tokens cannot publish, whatever their bypass-2FA setting — and it leaves both other routes open. Trusted publishing is untouched, because it uses OIDC rather than traditional token authentication. Manual publishing remains as an additional route, requiring interactive 2FA. Chapters 12, 13, 15 and 16 are what stop a compromised workflow from abusing the identity it leaves behind.

Scope the permission itself, too. id-token: write applies to the whole job, so a build step sharing that job can request the same identity, and --ignore-scripts does not stop code that runs during the build. Grant it on a narrow publish job that runs no project code, and keep the install and build in a separate job. That protects the credential boundary; it does not establish that the artifact passing between the two is safe, which is what the build's own review path is for.

For cloud deploys the same pattern replaces static AWS, Azure and GCP keys. Since 15 July 2026 new repositories get immutable identifiers in the default OIDC subject claim — repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:…, not available on GitHub Enterprise Server — so a recycled namespace cannot inherit a trust policy written for the original repository. The names stay in the subject alongside the IDs, so a policy matching the full string still needs updating after a rename. Repositories created before that date keep the previous format unless you opt in, and renames and transfers after it move to the new one, so check which format each trust policy is written against.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: a long-lived, replayable bearer credential - run: npm publish env: NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}

# Hardened: build and publish are separate jobs, and only the publish # job can mint an OIDC token. permissions: {} jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: read # no id-token here steps: - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> with: { persist-credentials: false } - uses: actions/setup-node@<sha> with: { node-version: 24 } - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts - run: npm run build # third-party code runs HERE, not in publish - run: npm pack # the exact tarball that will be published - uses: actions/upload-artifact@<sha> with: { name: package-tarball, path: "*.tgz" } publish: needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: release # scopes the trusted publisher binding permissions: id-token: write # minted here, and nowhere else steps: # No checkout at all: the privileged job never holds project source, # so it needs no contents: read either. - uses: actions/download-artifact@<sha> with: { name: package-tarball, path: out } - uses: actions/setup-node@<sha> with: node-version: 24 registry-url: <https://registry.npmjs.org> # Publishing the prepared tarball, not a working directory: npm runs # prepublishOnly only for directory publishes, so no project code runs # here at all. --ignore-scripts keeps that true if this ever changes. - run: npm publish ./out/*.tgz --ignore-scripts

Chapter 15: Gate Releases Behind npm Staged Publishing #

The mistake

A tag push that runs straight through to a live, installable version with no human in the loop.

Teams reason that since OIDC removed the stealable token, the path is safe. But an injected or modified workflow still runs as the trusted publisher, and the resulting package is indistinguishable from a real release.

Observed in the wild

Nx had roughly four hours of malicious versions live before anyone noticed. The team's own postmortem lists trusted publishing plus manual release approval as the remediation.

TanStack shipped 84 malicious versions through an automated release path.

What to do

Staged publishing went generally available on 22 May 2026 and needs npm CLI 11.15.0 or newer. The workflow runs npm stage publish, which uploads the tarball to a stage queue instead of the registry. A maintainer with publish access then approves it, which requires a 2FA challenge.

OIDC tokens issued through trusted publishing cannot approve from the stage queue. That is what preserves the human gate even when the CI identity itself is abused. Staged versions generate the same provenance as direct publishes, and can be configured to be approvable only once malware scanning completes.

Then close the bypass. Set the trusted publisher configuration to stage-only, which makes the registry reject a plain npm publish from that workflow. Without it, an attacker who modifies the workflow simply drops the stage and publishes directly. Note the scope of that: stage-only constrains that CI publisher. A maintainer publishing interactively from their own account is a separate route, left open by design and gated by the 2FA prompt from chapter 14's package settings rather than by the stage queue.

The equivalent elsewhere. PyPI has no staging queue, so use a GitHub Environment with required reviewers (chapter 16) in front of the publish job. For container registries, push to a staging tag and promote after verification. The LiteLLM release was a PyPI one, so an environment approval stood in for staging — which is why chapter 16, not this chapter, enforces that gate.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: live to every consumer, no human gate - run: npm publish

# Hardened: lands in the stage queue, waits for a human - run: npm stage publish

# npmjs.com -> package -> Trusted publisher -> "Stage only" # A plain `npm publish` from this workflow is now rejected by the registry. # # Maintainer, from a 2FA-enabled account: # npm stage list # approve in the npmjs.com UI or via CLI # (an OIDC token cannot give this approval)

Chapter 16: Require a Second Human at the Deploy Boundary #

The mistake

Keeping production credentials as repository-level secrets, so every workflow in the repository — including one added on a branch nobody watches — can reference them.

Then, having moved to environments, adding required reviewers and leaving Prevent self-review off. A maintainer who triggers a deployment and approves it themselves has added a dialog box, not a control, and that is precisely the configuration a compromised account walks through.

Observed in the wild

Repository-scoped secrets are the common amplifier across the pwn-request incidents. In Nx the npm token was reachable from the compromised workflow because nothing scoped it to a gated environment.

LiteLLM, 21 October 2026 shows the limit of this control rather than its absence. The project had an approval gate, and at 11:11:18 UTC a credential associated with a second developer account satisfied the production approval. The completed investigation describes that credential as having been taken using access the attacker already held, so the gate was never independent of the account it was meant to check. An approval gate is worth the independence of the credentials behind it.

Prevent self-review stops one identity approving its own run. It does nothing against two.

What to do

One environment per deployment target, with secrets attached there rather than at repository level. A workflow job cannot access environment secrets until a reviewer grants approval.

Required reviewers plus Prevent self-review, shipped October 2023. Without that toggle the rule is self-service.

Disable Allow administrators to bypass configured protection rules. By default, administrators can bypass the protection rules and force a deployment to the environment, which makes the reviewer requirement above advisory for anyone holding admin. Configure the environment to disallow bypassing for all deployments to it. Title: The internet needs a nap (and you do, too)
Context: A vulnerability is not an outage, and an outage is not automatically an attack
Full Text:
“Not everything that is faced can be changed; but nothing can be changed until it is faced.” — James Baldwin

Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I had planned to write about one thing. The week, apparently, had other plans.

I can start with conversation on the most viral cybersecurity news of the week. So obviously I had to go with PHP... oh wait, Java. Let’s type this up... wait, Outlook, Apple? The NSA? As soon as I start to type nginx comes pounding on my door. It’s the kind of news cycle that makes me wonder if the internet is trying to tell us something. I think it just wants everyone to stop asking it for things for a few hours, and can you blame it?

These are different events with different causes. A vulnerability is not an outage, and an outage is not automatically an attack. But they all arrive in the same place: someone’s queue, someone’s pager, someone’s overflowing calendar. The headlines might be viral and “new,” but the work they create is not.

For all of us, the work starts with knowing what is in the environment. Which systems run PHP or Java? Where is nginx deployed? Who owns those devices and services? Are they still supported? Are they properly admin’d? In every environment there is an application that everyone knows is important, and no one is quite sure how to patch it without breaking something else (or everything else). Isolating these devices and applications and getting them into the modern era is a challenging lift, but it’s beyond time and a big part of “know your environment.”

Then there’s the telemetry. A new vulnerability or a service disruption can make ordinary activity look strange, and strange activity can disappear into the noise when everyone is busy chasing the latest alert. Teams need time to understand what “normal” looks like in your own network and ensure that your tools are being leveraged to their full potential by your smart people. Because people still have to decide what it means and what to do next.

“Patch faster” isn’t an answer, and it’s not realistic for anyone.

The new normal is a steady stream of things that demand attention, each one landing on systems and people already carrying too much. The answer is still the same unglamorous work: Know your environment, keep it as up to date as possible and watch it carefully for the anomalies, and most importantly give the people doing the work enough room to do it well.

“Every quality that made a person more valuable than a database was a product of experience.” — Ted Chiang

The one big thing

Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of "Java4Shell" (CVE-2026-114938), a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. This flaw can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) when a malformed Base64 input is sent to affected Java Virtual Machines. The vulnerability impacts OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support enabled. While we haven't observed in-the-wild exploitation yet, the vulnerability has already been successfully tested against a suite of Java applications.

Why do I care?

This vulnerability requires a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI, which includes commonly deployed hardware from both Intel and AMD. Because of this, there is a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems spanning both on-premise and cloud environments. Furthermore, as additional targets are tested and confirmed, that attack surface is likely to grow, and we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.

So now what?

Defenders should apply the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, you can mitigate the threat by starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled using "=XX:UseAVX=2". Keep in mind this mitigation is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command and will likely fail to start.

Deploy the Snort rules and review the Splunk detections mentioned in the blog to help detect malformed Base64 data and suspicious post-exploitation indicators. We will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and provide updates accordingly.

Top security headlines of the week

Optimizely hack turns world's biggest websites into malware dispensers BBC, Zoom, HSBC, and GitLab among those caught up in supply chain attack targeting visitors' crypto wallets, credit cards, and iPhones. (The Register)

NGINX2Root: New remote code execution vulnerabilities in nginx require urgent patching nginx2root is a collection of five critical CVEs, the most impactful of which allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. (Xint)

NIST finalizes post-quantum cryptography guidance, GAO offers a reality check NIST laid out a technical road map to guide organizations through the process in its recent "Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards" report. The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) cautions that federal agencies are not prepared to meet deadlines. (Dark Reading)

Microsoft rules out cyber attack in outage, warns of phishing campaignThe outage disrupted access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook, and possibly affected Teams, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Phishing emails posing as Microsoft 365 service notices referenced the real outage incident and threatened to delete held messages. (SecurityWeek)

Criminals attack French postal operator subsidiary, grab contact details of 22M people Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer. According to Maileva, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year. (The Register)

Police arrest 15 over £1.5M “we'll recover your losses” scam targeting elderly City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. (The Register)

Can’t get enough Talos?

Talos Takes: Using public blockchains for malware command and control Attackers are moving away from centralized infrastructure that is easy to seize or block. By leveraging public blockchains, threat actors are building highly resilient C2 channels that operate on top of legitimate, decentralized networks.

The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure.

Title: Nvidia adds possible hack to list of very bad things under investigation
Context: “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson said
Full Text: Finding a new CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information. The embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson said. “We continue to monitor the situation." The ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.” The post also included a countdown, ending November 28. While we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026. The actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments. According to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts. In February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®

In this article

A fake Tesla livestream used an Elon Musk deepfake to push a crypto scam

Coinbase says it blocked $4.7 million in attempted transfers

A giveaway that asks you to send crypto first to get more back is a scam

Coinbase says it stopped about $4.7 million in attempted payments to a fake cryptocurrency giveaway. The scam didn’t rely on breaking into customers’ accounts. It persuaded them to send money themselves.

Imagine you’re watching a Tesla event on YouTube when Elon Musk appears with an unexpected offer: send cryptocurrency to the address shown, and you’ll get twice as much back. A QR code makes it easy to pay, while the livestream pressures you to act before the offer disappears. You open your crypto app, enter the payment details, and prepare to confirm.

According to Coinbase, that is exactly what happened when a fake Elon Musk livestream prompted hundreds of its customers to attempt payments to scammers. The customers were logged in and approving the payments themselves. That made the transfers look authorized, even though the customers had been tricked into sending money. Coinbase describes this as a central challenge in detecting the scam.

Reportedly, Coinbase’s automated scam defenses prevented roughly $4.7 million—about 91% of the money involved in those attempted payments—from leaving customers’ accounts. That is money the company says it prevented from being sent, not money recovered after it was stolen. Coinbase hasn’t said how much ultimately reached the scammers.

Using Elon Musk’s image for this type of scam is not new. Deepfakes can make these scams more convincing. A deepfake is an image, video, or audio recording created or altered with AI to make it seem like someone said or did something they didn’t.

Scammers may need only a photo or a shockingly short clip of the real person to create a convincing deepfake. That’s not hard to find when you want to impersonate a public figure like Elon Musk.

How to stay safe

The best advice in cases like this is the usual one: if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

To avoid a fake cryptocurrency giveaway, you don’t need to decide whether every movement or syllable in a video is AI-generated. The payment request itself should be a clear warning.

Don’t send cryptocurrency to “unlock” a larger cryptocurrency payout. Promises to multiply the amount you send are a red flag.

Don’t treat an on-screen wallet address or QR code as proof that an offer is legitimate. Coinbase warns against sending funds to addresses displayed in videos, livestreams, or messages.

Close the offer and go to the company’s official website or account yourself, rather than using links supplied by the promotion.

Take payment warnings seriously. Pause, read the explanation, and discuss the offer with someone you trust. Or ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard if no trusted person is around.

If you already sent cryptocurrency

Cryptocurrency payments typically can’t be reversed, so there’s no guarantee of recovery. But don’t blame yourself or feel stupid; act quickly to limit further losses:

Preserve the evidence. Keep transaction records, receipts, screenshots, messages, and details of the livestream or website. Contact the exchange or service you used immediately and report the scam. In the US, you can report it to the FTC through ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Stop communicating with the scammers. Don’t let further messages persuade you to make another payment. It is not uncommon for fake giveaways to demand additional payments to supposedly process the first transfer.

Watch out for recovery scams. That FBI agent sending you a DM is just as fake as the Elon Musk in the deepfake video.

For more advice about what to do when you’ve been scammed online, read our blog Been scammed online? Here’s what to do.

Title: How to protect a company from attacks through AI agents | Kaspersky official blog
Context: Instead of risking detection by using specific malware, attackers can now just send an agent plain text prompts and make it do what they need, such as find secrets on the...
Full Text:
The risks of using AI at work have been known for a while, but new evidence keeps piling up. With AI agents that employees set up to perform actions on company computers, the situation only continues to worsen: attackers are already targeting them. Instead of risking detection by using specific malware, attackers can now just send an agent plain text prompts and make it do what they need, such as find secrets on the computer, or send information somewhere external. Every useful skill of an AI assistant becomes an opportunity for the attacker.

It’s not enough for security teams to keep track of which AI tools are in use. They also need to watch the tools’ permissions, instruction sources, connected components, and actual actions. But it doesn’t require adding more security products to do it. Familiar tools can handle many of these tasks: application control, web filtering, EDR, file analysis, and up-to-date threat intelligence. A detailed description of the relevant protection mechanisms can be found in Securelist’s guide to safe deployment of AI agents. That article is packed with technical details, but here, we’ll walk through the main risks of corporate AI, and the traditional security measures that help minimize them.

An assistant nobody approved

Shadow AI refers to AI services and apps that employees use without approval from the company’s security and IT departments. The app or service itself is usually legitimate, but the organization doesn’t know what data it processes, where it sends that data, or what actions it can perform.

To prevent the use of such tools, a registry of approved AI apps and online services should be created and maintained. To restrict access to AI services that security policy doesn’t allow, Kaspersky endpoint security, managed through Kaspersky Security Center can be used. The restriction is applied by the Application Control module, which has an AI Tools category. It can be run in a mode that blocks prohibited apps (denylist), or in a stricter mode that allows only explicitly approved ones (allowlist). Access to web-based AI services is managed by a similar tool: Web Control. For approved services, it should be explicitly specified which types of data can be processed in them. The service providers’ contractual commitments on data protection should also be explicitly checked.

Fake installers instead of AI

This threat is only indirectly related to AI, but we’re mentioning it because attackers loved it so much in 2026. A user searches for a link or installation instructions for an AI agent, clicks an ad, and lands on a page that looks almost identical to the developer’s real website. The page tells the user to copy a command into Terminal — and the result is predictable. In March, we described a version of this scam that uses fake Claude Code and OpenClaw installation pages: instead of a useful tool, users got an infostealer.

Several levels of protection against these attacks — known as ClickFix — should be used. Installation packages and instructions for approved tools should be used through the corporate catalog. Web filtering and anti-phishing mechanisms should help block known fake pages, while endpoint protection should detect malicious payloads and suspicious launch chains.

Excessive agent permissions

Desktop apps, such as the official ChatGPT app, are often seen as the same chatbot in a separate window. In reality, they’re full-fledged AI agents that can work with files and run programs within the permissions they’ve been given. In practice, an agent often has all the privileges of the current user. If action confirmation and isolation are also turned off, a mistaken or malicious instruction can have very serious consequences.

In September 2026, researchers described the hijacking of an active AI assistant session at a SaaS provider. First, the AI agent recommended infected software from the PyPI repository, and then installed it on its own. The attackers got hold of GitHub OAuth tokens and used them to spread the Shai-Hulud worm further.

Last year’s s1ngularity attack is an even more striking example. The malicious script searched for installed AI tools and launched them in a mode that skips confirmation prompts. The agents were told to look for SSH keys, .env files, and crypto wallets. There was no need to hack the model to do this.

This makes a local AI agent an extremely powerful weapon in living-off-the-land attacks. To spot an agent being used for the wrong purpose, its launch parameters, access to credential stores, and child processes should be monitored closely.

To counter this threat, Kaspersky NEXT EDR Optimum users have access to special rules that detect dangerous launch modes. A separate group of rules tracks agent access to files with credentials, tokens, and keys. Depending on the situation, the response can include terminating the AI agent process or even isolating the host.

Dangerous MCP servers

The MCP protocol allows to connect extra tools and data sources to AI applications. For example, an MCP server can search for documents, call APIs, or work with files. However, the sandbox and restrictive policies that apply to the AI agent don’t extend to MCP. That makes connecting an MCP server about as risky as installing a new software component.

In February 2026, cybersecurity experts discovered the SANDWORM_MODE campaign. The McpInject module placed a malicious MCP server in a hidden directory, and added it to the configurations of Claude Code, Cursor, Continue, and Windsurf. The tool descriptions contained injected instructions to search for secrets, such as SSH keys and cloud credentials.

To keep MCP risks under control, an organization needs to maintain an allowlist of MCP servers, monitor changes to their configurations, and limit network connections. Local servers should be vetted like any executable software, and remote ones — like external services with access to corporate information.

Kaspersky EDR has special rules to detect suspicious MCP server scripts that are created or modified in hidden and temporary directories. Such a location doesn’t prove a component is malicious, but it’s a good reason to check where it came from and which process installed it.

Malware that calls LLMs directly

Attackers have learned to use LLMs to generate code and scripts on the fly, requesting what they need straight from the infected system. Google’s reports describe two malware families — PROMPTSTEAL and HONESTCUE — that were found in real-world attacks. The former queried a model through the Hugging Face API to get Windows commands; the latter received C# code from Gemini and compiled it in memory.

From a network monitoring perspective, in both cases the connection goes to a legitimate AI service. That’s why it’s not enough to look at the destination address alone: it’s essential to know which process opens the connection and what it does with the response.

A practical measure is to allow access to model APIs only for the applications and workflows that truly need it, and to investigate any unexpected requests together with endpoint events.

In Kaspersky EDR, two rules can help to spot unusual applications connecting to known external language model APIs and detect local model files. Finding them doesn’t mean a device is infected, but it can help uncover an AI tool that nobody accounted for.

Malicious skills

An agent’s capabilities are often increased with ready-made skills: sets of instructions, scripts, and helper files. Installing them effectively adds one more supply chain that the security team has to manage.

In February 2026, researchers found 341 malicious skills in the ClawHub catalog. Many of them suggested users install so-called necessary components, which, if they did, in actual fact saw them run the AMOS infostealer. Later, Unit 42 described additional ways to bypass security checks that the attackers used, such as inflating the package size to exceed scanner limits.

Skills, along with their related scripts, components, and archives, should be checked before they’re handed over to an agent. This can be done with Kaspersky Scan Engine, built directly into the extension onboarding process, and by adding the standard checks of the package source, version, and contents.

How to limit the impact of an attack

Detection and response are essential, but Secure by Design AI implementation should reduce potential damage even before protection kicks in.

Least privilege. Whenever possible, run the agent under a separate account or in an isolated environment. Limit access to project directories and only the services the agent needs. A ban written as a text instruction is no substitute for isolation.

Credentials outside the agent’s reach. Don’t keep long-lived tokens and keys in configuration files the agent can read. Whenever possible, use a secrets vault, short-lived credentials, and an intermediary service that strictly performs the requested operation without revealing the secret to the agent.

Verified dependencies. Download skills, packages, and models through an internal repository or a controlled proxy. Pin approved versions, and compare checksums against a trusted reference.

Restricted outbound connections. Allow access only to the model APIs, MCP servers, and other resources that the agent really needs. Don’t forget about child processes: blocking the agent’s main process won’t help much if the shell it launches still has unrestricted internet access.

A dedicated response playbook. After a compromise, check the configuration of agents and development environments, event handlers, and connected MCP servers. Revoke affected tokens and active sessions, and replace any keys that may have been exposed.

An approved alternative instead of a flat ban. Give employees an approved AI tool, clear rules for handling data, and a fast process for approving new features. Otherwise, even a policy that looks strict on paper will only push people toward shadow AI.

Title: Typosquatted Domains Impersonate AI Platforms to Deliver ClickFix Attacks
Context: Researchers at Island discovered nearly 200 typosquatted domains impersonating dozens of AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, and...
Full Text:
Researchers at Island discovered nearly 200 typosquatted domains impersonating dozens of AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

“One Claude typo, cloude[.]ai, ended at a ClickFix lure that runs a hidden PowerShell command fetched from a decimal-encoded IP address,” the researchers write. “The gate behind it serves 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers and enterprise software. Other AI typos led to fake ‘Security Check’ pages serving Net Guard, a Microsoft Store-signed app. The package matches the Store’s own hash, and inside it is browser-hijacking malware that changes the visitor’s existing browser and can run remotely supplied scripts through DevTools. A third route led to a search-hijacking browser extension, one of 30 built from the same kit. Thirteen have since been removed, and the 17 still listed show 972,000 declared users between them.”

Typosquatting isn’t a new technique, but attackers are taking advantage of current trends to mimic increasingly popular AI tools.

“ChatGPT draws the most lookalikes in our set, 25, from chatgpy[.]com to chtgpt[.]com,” Island says. “Claude follows with 18 and DeepSeek with 16, among them deepseel[.]com and deeepseek[.]com. Runway has 12, including runawayml[.]com, and Perplexity, Lovable, and Character.ai have 11 each, with names such as perplixity[.]ai, lovabe[.]dev and charactor[.]ai. The list reaches well past chat assistants: giemini[.]com, griok[.]com and mistrial[.]ai for Gemini, Grok and Mistral, notbooklm[.]com for NotebookLM and mauns[.]im for the agent platform Manus. Some lookalikes imitate the companies themselves, such as opnai[.]com and anthropiv[.]com, for people who type the company instead of the product.”

Title: Spying on Governments with Zero Lines of Malware: A Custom SoftEther Bridge in Webworm’s Toolkit
Context: Introduction For a threat actor, the perfect malware is one they don’t have to write, and already does all they need
Full Text:
Introduction

For a threat actor, the perfect malware is one they don’t have to write, and already does all they need. One example of this is shown by the China-aligned APT known as Webworm, which has been known to deploy the open-source SoftEther VPN into the networks of compromised governmental organizations to maintain low-profile, long-term access.

After this was publicly documented and defenders could keep an eye out for this tactic, the actor presumably started thinking of ways to make their covert access stealthier. In this post, we share our analysis of what we believe to be a so-far unknown custom SoftEther-based tool, which implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools, and which we attribute to Webworm with moderate confidence. We additionally provide guidance and tooling for detecting its presence on a system and extracting the configuration(s) associated with it.

Technical analysis

To illustrate how the tool works, we will use the only public sample of this tool we are aware of, which can be found in our IoCs list (90e7…).

The sample is a Windows PE32+ file targeting the x64 architecture. Based on cleartext strings and constants in the binary, we identified it as a (modified) build of the SoftEther VPN Bridge executable, specifically version 4.44, build 9807. Similarly, the PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb. As such, the tool doesn’t hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions.

The first and most trivial change the threat actor implements is in the PE metadata. Here we learn that the OriginalFileName of this binary is netcapa.exe, and it brands itself as “Network Monitor Software” published by a company named “Network Systems Solutions Inc.“. The only field unchanged against the stock SoftEther executable (vpnbridge_x64.exe) is the Version, which reads 4, 44, 0, 9807.

Next, we wanted to identify any functionality added or modified by the threat actor. The SoftEther bridge alone is a powerful tool to maintain remote access to a compromised network, but we wanted to know if perhaps there was a backdoor to give the threat actor direct command execution on the infected host. For that reason we checked out the corresponding tag in the public “SoftEtherVPN_Stable” repository on GitHub and compared it to the decompiled sample.

Internal rebranding

The rebranding apparent in the exposed metadata extends into internal strings used in debug banners, service names, registry keys, the contents of the server’s HTTP 401 error page, or firewall rule names, where occurrences of “SoftEther VPN” are replaced by “NtMonitor VPN”.

However, the renaming is inconsistent; for example, the service name used by the entry point is still SEVPNBRIDGE, and many registry key paths still reference the “SoftEther Project”.

Network stealth

Stock SoftEther VPN Mayaqua/Network.h defines HTTP endpoints used by the protocol:

HTTP_VPN_TARGET "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi"

NtMonitor replaces these endpoints with much more innocent-sounding names, in particular:

HTTP_VPN_TARGET "/update/alive.cgi" HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 "/update/picture.cgi"

A client initiating a connection to a SoftEther VPN server will send a handshake request to HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 along with a "watermark", i.e. a byte pattern proving that the client is speaking the correct VPN protocol. Otherwise, the server answers with a decoy HTTP response.

NtMonitor changes the upstream GIF watermark with a custom byte pattern (a truncated PNG file showing the Windows logo), so that stock SoftEther clients and servers cannot handshake with this build, and NtMonitor's own peers cannot be fingerprinted with the well-known stock GIF watermark.

Embedded resource archive

As the threat actor probably realizes, a SoftEther resource archive named hamcore.se2, which sits next to the executables in the installation directory and is required to be present at runtime, provides a straightforward detection opportunity for unauthorized installations. We think that, for this exact reason, the actor chose to reduce the contents of this archive to a bare minimum, package the archive inside the bridge executable itself (as a PE resource), and implement a custom resource directory walk to load the archive at runtime. As a side effect, this increases the binary’s size by about 1.5 MB compared to the official build.

Encrypted configuration

Another weak point (for the attacker) in stock SoftEther is that its configuration is stored on disk in plain text in a well-recognizable format. The actor changes its name from vpn_bridge.config to setting.conf and modifies the configuration loader to handle custom-encrypted files that start with the magic bytes RCEN in ASCII. The rest of the encrypted file has a simple format and includes the encryption key. A Python script to decrypt such files with the actor’s custom RC4-like cipher is available on the Rapid7 Intelligence GitHub repository.

Attribution and interpretation of findings

Beyond the changes described above, we did not identify any additional malware functionality. Clearly, the threat actor prioritizes stealth above raw capability. It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther’s detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it. At the time of our analysis, only one anti-virus vendor detected the sample on VirusTotal, although it has been public since January.

This aligns well with the TTPs previously reported for Webworm by ESET, and such attribution is further supported by indicators in decrypted configurations Rapid7 Intelligence has access to. In all of the cases, the VPN is configured to bridge (“cascade”) a remote network into the local one; furthermore, in cases that were not likely deliberate tests, the remote IP address was located inside AS 20473 belonging to The Constant Company, LLC, which (also including its subsidiary, Vultr) has been associated with Webworm on many occasions in the past.

Considering this attribution, we can put together some important takeaways: Quite likely, we are looking at a new evolution in the tooling used by Webworm, a China-aligned APT whose activity is known to focus on governmental organizations, especially in Europe. Earlier this year, ESET already noted this group to shift away from custom malware to dual-use tools such as SoftEther VPN, but now we are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint.

Detection guidance

To detect this particular variant of Webworm’s tooling, we provide a list of IoCs and a YARA ruleset on our public GitHub repository. If you have the ability to inspect TLS traffic in your organization, one of the most reliable detections you can deploy right now is to look for POST requests to /update/picture.cgi with Content-Type: image/jpeg and a request body starting with and 89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a 00 00 00 0d 49 48 44 52 (initial bytes of the custom PNG watermark).

Although the samples we have seen all use the same NtMonitor branding internally (despite the PE metadata differing across samples), this is the easiest change for the threat actor to implement next. Similarly, the HTTP endpoints and watermark can be swapped out trivially. As such, we recommend defenders in the government sector to familiarize themselves with intrinsic SoftEther VPN behavior in order to stay one step ahead of when the threat actor decides to update the tool next.

Technique Name

Comment

T1587.001

Develop Capabilities: Malware

The actor is maintaining their own fork of SoftEther VPN used for malicious purposes.

T1027.013

T1140

Title: KPMG Canada client documents accessed in cybersecurity breach, accounting firm says
Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
Context: We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States
Full Text:
Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.

Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.

These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year.

Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups.

Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026.

In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings.

Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks

Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period.

State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information.

On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second.

Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle

Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone.

Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data.

Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools.

Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks.

PHP vulnerability

On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability.

On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend.

Recommendations

Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted.

Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations:

Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff.

Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure.

Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default.

Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority.

Title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
Context: Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4
Full Text: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations. Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time. "What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said. Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday. The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®
