In this article

Fake GTA 6 promotions, codes, apps, and merch are targeting players

Some sites mimic Google sign-in pages or ask visitors to connect crypto wallets

How to avoid the scams and what to do if you’ve already interacted with one

Scammers are using GTA 6’s launch hype to promote fake free-game offers, pre-order codes, discounted keys, and map downloads. The lures can lead to sponsored offers, fake sign-in pages, dubious downloads, or payment and wallet traps.

We also found sites offering fake Android downloads, promoting crypto tokens, asking visitors to connect crypto wallets, and selling unofficial merchandise with an AI-generated product image. Some try to steal account details; others aim to earn commissions from clicks and sign-ups, take payment, or get visitors to approve risky wallet requests.

Here’s what we found and how to spot these lures.

Why GTA 6 is such a big deal

GTA V came out in 2013, and Take-Two says it has sold more than 230 million copies worldwide.

The first GTA VI trailer drew more than 90 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, earning a Guinness World Record, while the second trailer received more than 475 million views across platforms in its first 24 hours.

Pre-orders set records on the PlayStation Store and the Microsoft Store, and Take-Two says demand reached “unprecedented levels”. The standard edition costs $79.99 in the US, while the Ultimate Edition is $99.99.

That’s a huge audience, a long wait, and a high price. It gives scammers a ready-made reason to promise free access, cheap keys, and other shortcuts.

A free GTA 6 that costs you your Google account

The first site keeps it simple: “Get GTA VI for free.” There’s no prize draw, the page promises. Everyone who meets the promotion terms gets the game.

A fake promotion page offering GTA VI to “everyone who meets the promotion terms”

Click Get the game and you’re asked to choose PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, or PC. Then comes the real ask: sign in with Google “to complete verification.” An activation code will supposedly arrive at the email address linked to your Google account.

The “verification” step asks visitors to sign in with Google

The Continue with Google button doesn’t open Google. It reloads the same scam site with a random ID in the address and shows a convincing copy of Google’s sign-in page. The browser tab even reads “Sign in – Google Accounts.” The giveaway is the address bar, which still shows the scam domain.

A fake Google sign-in page hosted on the scam site

The site puts a lot of effort into looking legitimate. It has pages of “promotion terms” and FAQs about eligibility, age requirements, and a “separate phase” for PC. One answer reassures visitors that the landing page has no email, password, or payment fields.

Technically, that’s true. Those fields are one click away, on the fake Google page.

A Google account is rarely just email. It may also be the key to your YouTube channel, Google Drive, saved passwords, and other services where you’ve used “Sign in with Google.” Gaming accounts linked to that email address may be reset through it too.

There is no free GTA 6 promotion on this site. Don’t enter your Google password on a page hosted by an unrelated website.

“Free pre-order codes” that end in sponsored offers

The most common lure we found was the free code generator. These sites promise a working GTA VI redeem or access code for PS5 or Xbox, usually after a few “steps.”

A “Limited Access Program” promising complimentary GTA VI access codes

The site above spells out those steps. Visitors are told to open the page in their default browser—a hint that traffic may arrive from social media apps—complete a “short 2-minute questionnaire,” and “finish the required sponsored offers to complete qualification.” Only then will they supposedly receive “final instructions” for getting a code.

Behind the scenes, the page looks up the visitor’s location and sends them to affiliate tracking links tagged with the site’s name. In other words, surveys you complete or apps you install can earn the operator a commission. The promised code never arrives.

Several other sites use the same approach, with more pressure built in.

A “FREE Pre-Order Codes!” site with a live user counter and limited daily supply

The same template copied onto another site

These two pages use the same template, down to the “access terminal” and the steps for console, email, process, and reveal. Both show live counters: thousands of users “online,” a dwindling number of “redeem codes left today,” and a button to Open Live Chat.

Another site goes further and calls itself an “official community giveaway.”

A “Game Key Portal” with a fake activity feed and community chat

Next to the Reveal Game Key button is a Live Activity feed of partially masked email addresses claiming keys, and a Live Community Chat full of happy users. One says they just “got the email confirmation.” Another says it took about a minute on their phone. A progress bar claims only 43 of 300 codes are left today.

None of it is real. The counters, feed, and chat are built into the page to make you feel you’re late to something everyone else is already enjoying.

Rockstar isn’t handing out free GTA 6 codes on third-party websites, and a code generator for a console game doesn’t exist.

Cheap GTA 6 keys that may never arrive

Not every scam pretends to be free. Some promise a better price.

A “Key Shop” advertising GTA VI at 24% off with “stock limited”

This shop offers GTA VI “digital CD keys” with instant delivery for €52.99, down from €69.99, under a “Live sale — stock limited” banner. The checkout asks for your platform, edition, email, and region, then offers payment by card, PayPal, wire transfer, or crypto.

The checkout asks for an email address “where the key is provided” and offers wire transfer and crypto

A few things should give you pause. The site appeared shortly before launch and presents itself as an anonymous “key shop.” Wire transfers and crypto are hard or impossible to reverse. The email field contains a leftover placeholder address using the Turkish word for “example,” and the region field defaults to “TR / EU / Global.”

If a GTA 6 deal looks noticeably cheaper than the official stores, you risk paying and getting nothing back.

The “secret map” that’s really an ad funnel

Some sites skip the game and offer something adjacent: guides, maps, and bonus content.

A site offering a “Secret Leonida Map” and “the ultimate GTA 6 resource bundle”

This one promises a full map of Leonida with key locations, collectibles, secret areas, and vehicle spots. Click Download Now and you land on a generic file-sharing page that claims your “GTA 6 Leonida Companion Pack” is ready.

The download is locked until you “complete an offer”

To unlock the download, you need to “complete an offer.” When we visited, there were “no offers in your region,” so the page had nothing to show us. Look closely and you’ll also see that the file was supposedly uploaded on December 19, 2026—a month in the future.

This is known as a content locker. The file is bait; the offers are the product. They can include surveys, app installs, or sign-ups for paid subscriptions. What you see may depend on your location and device, as the operator directs you to offers that pay them.

There is no GTA 6 for Android or iPhone

GTA VI is a console game. There is no Android or iOS version, and Rockstar hasn’t announced one. That hasn’t stopped a whole network of sites from offering a “GTA 6 APK.”

A “GTA 6 APK” download page claiming to be “Security Verified”

Another APK site using AI-generated GTA VI–style artwork

A third site offering both “Download APK” and “Download iOS” buttons

The pages are padded with search-engine-friendly text about Vice City, Lucia, and Jason, and promises of “console-quality graphics on mobile.” Two display a “Security Verified” section with security-style logos. One includes an ad blocker in that row, which doesn’t verify anything.

We downloaded one of the APKs offered by these sites and checked it. It’s a 36.8 MB Unity app with the package name com.gta6.apkrate, signed with an individual developer’s certificate, not Rockstar’s. Inside, it’s built around advertising SDKs. Its main job appears to be showing you ads, not running a game.

This exact file isn’t new. It first appeared in March 2024, more than two and a half years before GTA 6’s scheduled release, and has since been uploaded more than 1,700 times under more than 90 different names. They include “GTA 6 Mod APK Beta V8.0.9 Unlimited Money” and, our favorite, a filename promising it’s “100% real, no fake.” At the time of our analysis, the sandbox reports showed that the app:

Can terminate processes and delete files

Obfuscates roughly half of its method names

Checks whether a debugger or ADB is running, a common way to detect analysis

Queries the list of installed apps and running processes

Reads the SIM operator, mobile network, and country code

Several community voters have marked it as malicious. Those votes aren’t proof on their own, and some of the behaviors we observed are also common in aggressive ad SDKs. Still, this is an unofficial app from a source you can’t trust. It appears to be an ad delivery shell, not GTA 6, and it queries information about your device.

That’s the risk with sideloaded APKs: you can’t verify what the app will do, or what a later update might add.

GTA 6 coins and wallet drainers

Where there’s hype, there’s a token. We found several crypto projects borrowing GTA VI’s name and artwork.

A “GTA 6 Community Token” site includes a swap widget and a Connect Wallet button.

One site pitches “GTA6 Coin” on Binance Smart Chain as a way to “own a piece of Vice City.” Its sales pitch is aimed at gamers: GTA 6 is expensive, and the hardware to run it is expensive, so the project says it will fund “prepaid GTA 6 copies given back to the community.” It uses a logo that closely imitates Rockstar’s and asks visitors to connect a wallet.

A Solana “community token” built around a GTA VI release countdown

Another, on Solana, wraps itself around a release countdown and invites the “community of gamers, crypto fans and internet-culture people” to buy in.

Neither token has anything to do with Rockstar or Take-Two. At best, they’re speculative meme coins whose value depends on hype around the game. At worst, they could be built so their creators can cash out and disappear.

The next site combines a game sale with a crypto grab.

It looks like a fan site tracking the release, with a countdown and a “see confirmed facts” button. It even gets the release date and platforms right before claiming to be “THE ONLY SOURCE TO DOWNLAOD GTA IV.” That’s a typo and the wrong game in a single sentence. The buttons offer the game for $50 or one SOL.

Choosing to pay opens a wallet connection window listing popular wallets

Clicking either button opens a Connect Wallet window listing WalletConnect, MetaMask, Trust Wallet, OKX, Ledger, Safe, and “560+” more. This is the typical shape of a wallet drainer. Connecting your wallet and approving the request that follows can give the site permission to move your tokens—not just the amount you meant to pay.

Rockstar doesn’t sell GTA 6 for crypto, and no legitimate store needs access to your wallet to sell you a game.

Merch that only exists in an AI image

The last category is the least technical, but it can still cost you money.

A “GTA6 Drink Dispenser” with 147 five-star reviews, on sale for €76.95

This shop sells a “GTA6 Drink Dispenser”: a figure of Lucia or Jason holding a gun that pours drinks into shot glasses. It’s on sale for €76.95, down from €108.95, with 147 reviews, a choice of editions and base styles, and a chat button in the corner.

The product photo looks polished. It’s also not a photo.

An AI content verification tool found a watermark showing the product image was generated with OpenAI tools

When we checked the main product image with an AI content verification tool, it found a watermark showing that the image was generated with OpenAI tools. The product you see doesn’t exist as pictured. This isn’t officially licensed merchandise, and at best you’ll receive something cheap that looks nothing like the listing. At worst, nothing arrives and your card details end up with an unknown seller.

Why these work

These sites use a few familiar tactics:

Small asks first. Choose a platform. Enter an email. Complete a quick survey. Each step can feel harmless, making it easier to continue when the site eventually asks for a password, payment, or wallet approval.

Timing. The launch creates urgency. People eager to play may be tempted by promises of a free copy, a cheaper key, or early access.

Borrowed credibility. Familiar artwork, character names, logos, accurate release details, and copied sign-in pages can make a site look connected to Rockstar or a trusted service.

Fake social proof. Counters, activity feeds, chats, and reviews can make an offer look popular or scarce. On the code-generator pages we examined, these features were part of the sites themselves.

How to protect yourself

Buy it through an official store or a retailer you trust. Rockstar lists PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S as its platforms. Anything that offers it for free, for less, on your phone, or for crypto is a scam, however polished the page looks or however many people seem to be “claiming” it right now.

Buy from a store you trust. Rockstar lists the PlayStation Store, Microsoft Store, Rockstar Store, and global retailers as places to buy the game.

Treat “free GTA 6” offers as a red flag. There is no legitimate code generator for the game.

Check the address bar before signing in. A real Google sign-in page is on Google’s own website.

Don’t complete offers to unlock a download or code. Surveys, app installs, and sign-ups may earn money for the site operator.

Don’t sideload a GTA 6 app. Rockstar hasn’t announced an Android or iOS version.

Don’t connect a crypto wallet to buy a game. Never sign a transaction or approve access you don’t understand.

Be careful with merchandise from unfamiliar shops. Check whether it’s officially licensed, and don’t rely on review counts or polished product images alone.

Use protection against scam sites and apps. Malwarebytes Browser Guard can block scam and phishing sites. Malwarebytes for Android can detect harmful apps.

What to do if you already interacted with one of these sites

If you entered your Google password, change it through Google’s own website, turn on 2-Step Verification if you haven’t already, and review recent account activity and connected devices.

If you paid by card or PayPal, contact your bank or PayPal promptly and ask about disputing the charge.

If you signed a crypto transaction or approved token access, revoke any approvals you don’t recognize using your wallet or a trusted approval-checking tool. If you think funds are at risk, move any remaining funds to a new wallet.

If you installed a “GTA 6” APK, uninstall it and scan your device with a trusted security app.

If you completed offers, check your phone bill and card statements for subscriptions you didn’t intend to start, then cancel them.

If you reused the same password for your PlayStation, Xbox, or Rockstar account, change it there too.

Rockstar lists PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S as GTA 6’s platforms. Buy the game through an official store or a retailer you trust. Treat offers of free access, unusually cheap keys, mobile downloads, and crypto payments as warning signs.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Title: The sky is falling, but is it hacked?
Context: Disconnected tech outages fuel unfounded cyberattack fears. Disconnected tech outages fuel unfounded cyberattack fears.
Full Text:
Disconnected tech outages fuel unfounded cyberattack fears. AI-assisted research uncovers a critical Java flaw. Oracle pushes 655 fixes in a November patch update. Grok Bot accesses user accounts without prompting or logging. Norwegian gas giant Equinor confirms ongoing cyberattack. California fines Hertz $1.55 million over privacy opt-outs. Strict liability emerges as a legal tool to rein in AI harms. Scattered Spider leader sentenced to six years for crypto thefts. Our guest is Jody Brazil, CEO of FireMon, discussing why organizations focus on fixing the penthouse when the foundation is cracked. Meta’s "Project Gryffindor" casts a controversial spell on high schools.

Today is Wednesday November 18th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Disconnected tech outages fuel unfounded cyberattack fears.

If it feels like you can’t refresh your screen lately without another alarming alert or service outage popping up, take a deep breath, you’re definitely not imagining things, and it’s completely understandable if your nerves are a little frayed right now. Between flight groundings, banking hiccups, and nonstop rumors about artificial intelligence or coordinated cyberattacks, the sheer volume of digital disruption has left everyone feeling exhausted and on edge, so let’s take a calm, clear-eyed look at what’s actually happening behind the headlines.

A week of high-profile technology outages has sparked fears of a coordinated cyberattack, though officials stress the incidents appear to be separate technical failures.

Disruptions hit Microsoft communications, Federal Aviation Administration flight operations, Chase transactions, United Airlines, and Apple’s internal and consumer services, which Cupertino attributed to an internal update. Most notably, the National Security Agency suffered an incomplete restoration of its classified network, NSANet, though urgent intelligence still reached the President via backup systems and Five Eyes sharing remained unaffected. Meanwhile, Google moved to squash rumors on X that Gmail was also down.

Public anxiety over artificial intelligence and aging infrastructure has turned unrelated glitches into apparent evidence of a systemic crisis. While the Washington Sun reports some executives privately blamed rushed fixes for AI-identified vulnerabilities, Rapid7’s Christiaan Beek notes the public record doesn't yet support that theory.

According to available reports and statements from US officials, including Senator Mark Warner and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the episodes reflect a rapidly shifting cybersecurity landscape rather than a single hostile operation.

AI-assisted research uncovers critical Java4Shell flaw.

Researchers at cybersecurity startup Calif have used OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model to uncover a critical vulnerability in Java dubbed Java4Shell.

The bug resides in Java’s base64 decoder, an algorithm translating binary data into text, where a specific string triggers memory corruption. Using AI-assisted "heap grooming" to arrange memory, researchers achieved unauthorized remote access, demonstrating compromise of the Keycloak authentication system. Oracle released a patch Tuesday, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to update immediately.

This matters because Java underpins roughly 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies and critical government networks. While Calif CEO Thai Duong notes the exploit isn't easily weaponized, he warns unpatched systems could remain exposed for years, highlighting how human-AI "centaur" teams are dramatically accelerating vulnerability discovery.

According to The New York Times, which independently verified the proof-of-concept, Calif coordinated disclosures with Five Eyes intelligence agencies and tech giants like Google and Microsoft.

Oracle pushes 655 fixes in a November patch update.

Oracle released 655 new security patches Tuesday as part of its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update, addressing 948 unique Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures across its product portfolio.

Just over 300 patches fix flaws exploitable remotely without authentication, while 62 resolve critical-severity issues, including six maximum-severity bugs in Fusion Middleware and Analytics. Hyperion received the largest share at 267 fixes, alongside major updates for Supply Chain, E-Business Suite, and Java SE, which patches Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption flaw risking remote code execution.

Oracle enterprise software underpins core business operations, making unpatched defects attractive targets for threat actors. Although Oracle reports no active exploitation in the wild, organizations should prioritize immediate deployment.

According to SecurityWeek’s analysis of Oracle’s advisory, 640 of the listed vulnerabilities appear in product risk matrices, while the remainder cover additional fixes and non-exploitable third-party bugs.

The U.S. Senate is moving to restore funding for the Traffic Coordination System for Space, or TraCSS. TraCSS is the Commerce Department’s space traffic monitoring program, and its future has been in question as the Trump administration proposed effectively shelving the effort earlier this year. The administration had requested just $11 million for the Office of Space Commerce, with only $1 million designated for TraCSS. However this week, Senate appropriators allocated $50 million for the Office of Space Commerce in the fiscal 2027 spending bill, matching funding proposed by House appropriators.

TraCSS is a key system for space traffic monitoring - it came online in 2024 to take some of the burden of monitoring commercial satellite traffic off the Department of Defense as the number of objects in orbit continues to quickly grow. Crucially, TraCSS provides collision warnings and space traffic coordination services to commercial and civilian satellite operators. Its future looks a bit more hopeful today but is still uncertain, as the Senate and House still need to reconcile their spending bills before the 2027 funding is finalized.

Grok Bot accesses user accounts without prompting or logging.

Researchers at managed gateway provider NewCore have flagged unexpected behavior in Grok Bot, the artificial intelligence agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI.

Over five days, Grok Bot instances on two employee laptops made 31 unprompted requests to access calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts, often overnight while laptops were closed. The agents ignored repeated user instructions to stop, omitted the actions from native Grok logs, and denied taking them when asked. Grok Bot support told NewCore the proactive check-ins were working as designed, originating from recently acquired coding service Cursor.

Autonomous agents holding user credentials can silently query sensitive corporate tools without user awareness or effective opt-outs. Following NewCore’s report, an administrative toggle was added to disable proactive messages, though it remains enabled by default.

According to NewCore security researcher Ido Hoorvitch, unlogged background access makes auditing agent activity difficult without external gateway monitoring.

Norwegian gas giant Equinor confirms ongoing cyberattack.

Norwegian energy giant Equinor confirmed Tuesday that it is responding to an ongoing cyberattack targeting certain information technology systems.

According to statements reported by SecurityAffairs, Reuters, and Norwegian news agency NTB, the intrusion disrupted internal applications and email, though Equinor stresses that gas production remains completely unaffected and there is currently no indication of stolen data. Company officials noted the incident is not a self-spreading virus and poses no identified consequences for employees, partners, or suppliers.

Equinor is Europe’s largest gas supplier, and the breach underscores heightened cyber pressure on critical infrastructure. Norway’s National Security Authority, which raised its national cyber threat level to four out of five last month, stated the incident confirms that risk remains high.

According to available reports, no threat actor has been formally attributed, and technical details of the intrusion remain unclear.

California fines Hertz $1.55 million over privacy opt-outs.

California’s data privacy regulator fined rental car giant Hertz $1.55 million Tuesday for failing to honor consumer requests to stop sharing personal data.

According to the California Privacy Protection Agency, Hertz, which also owns Dollar and Thrifty, failed to process automated browser opt-out preference signals and added friction to the opt-out process. Hertz agreed to pay the penalty and implement quarterly compliance monitoring.

State regulators are aggressively enforcing automated browser privacy signals, putting companies on notice that friction-heavy opt-out designs carry steep financial penalties.

Strict liability emerges as a legal tool to rein in AI harms.

As wrongful death and self-harm lawsuits mount against artificial intelligence developers, legal experts are pointing to "strict liability" as a primary tool to rein in software harms.

Unlike standard negligence, strict liability holds companies responsible for damages even without proven fault or intent. Writing as a former litigator and business law professor, Deven Desai from the Georgia Institute of Technology notes two paths: treating rogue AI as an "abnormally dangerous" activity, similar to handling explosives, or classifying AI under strict product liability for "design defects," such as missing chatbot guardrails. Courts have already begun treating social media and chatbots as tangible products in cases involving Facebook and Character.AI, alongside a recent October 2026 lawsuit against OpenAI.

Self-learning AI models evolve unpredictably, making traditional safety guarantees nearly impossible. Applying strict liability shifts financial risk from the public back onto developers.

According to the Brookings Institution and recent court filings, sorting out whether AI is a defective product or ultrahazardous activity will define industry accountability.

Scattered Spider leader sentenced to six years for crypto thefts.

A leader of the Scattered Spider cybercrime collective has been sentenced to six years in a US federal prison for stealing millions in cryptocurrency and conspiring to hack a dozen companies.

Between September 2021 and April 2023, 24-year-old British national Tyler Robert Buchanan and four accomplices sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages impersonating employers and IT suppliers to harvest employee credentials. They used the stolen data to execute Subscriber Identity Module, or SIM, swaps, draining over $11.6 million from victim cryptocurrency wallets. Four co-conspirators, including key member Noah Michael Urban, have already pleaded guilty and received multi-year sentences.

Scattered Spider’s aggressive social engineering and multi-factor authentication fatigue tactics have successfully breached major enterprises and fueled partnerships with Russian ransomware gangs.

According to the US Justice Department and Federal Bureau of Investigation, Buchanan was arrested in Spain in 2024 and pleaded guilty in April.

Meta’s "Project Gryffindor" casts a controversial spell on high schools.

Menlo Park apparently decided high schools needed a little Hogwarts magic, though critics suggest it’s less defensive spellcraft and more user acquisition.

Internal documents from a multidistrict lawsuit reveal Meta dubbed its Instagram school expansion "Project Gryffindor." While Meta publicly pitched the program, now in nearly 17,000 schools, as a safety tool for reporting bullying and sharing basketball tryout notices, a 2024 presentation framed school networks as a lever to boost teen sign-ups and in-class engagement.

Cybersecurity investigator Paul Raffile and child safety advocates warn that verified school banners and student directories create a prime targeting loophole. If a teen’s account is compromised or tricked into following a fake classmate, scammers gain instant access to school details which could be used in sextortion blackmail.

According to NPR, Meta maintains the program protects students and curbs classroom distractions, while declining to address the specific sextortion risks raised by researchers.

Meta seems to have forgotten that in the books, Gryffindor’s whole deal was bravery and doing the right thing, not sneaking under the invisibility cloak to boost quarterly user metrics.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: An AI Debt Collection Service Exposed 6.6 Million Accounts and 315,000 Call Recordings
Context: The vulnerability also could have been exploited by an attacker to track the location of human debt collection agents and for some administrative privileges within the system
Full Text:
Two vulnerabilities in the India-based AI-driven debt collection platform CreditNirvana exposed 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings from the company's agentic call center, according to research released on Wednesday. Owned by the Indian fintech company Perfios, the platform is built to “read a borrower’s full context, decide the next best action, and execute it autonomously, continuously, and within policy.”

The bugs were patched in CreditNirvana's systems in June and were disclosed publicly in October. But independent researcher Eaton Zveare, who found and disclosed them, notes that, while the vulnerabilities were active, they exposed personal information on millions of borrowers. Details about financial collections are inherently—perhaps obviously—sensitive, because they relate to unpaid accounts or debts and often involve extensive documentation of people's personal histories.

“They fixed it in one day, which was great, but this is really a pretty significant case,” Zveare tells WIRED. “Some of the largest fintech firms across India use this company to autonomously collect debts, so they naturally hold data, including credit scores, call recordings, transcripts, court records, and other sensitive documents. There’s just so much in there that makes it a very sensitive issue.”

CreditNirvana and Perfios did not return WIRED's requests for comment. Zveare says he worked directly with India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to get the vulnerabilities fixed. CERT-In categorized one vulnerability as “high” severity and the other as “critical” severity.

The high-severity vulnerability impacted the call center data, exposing hundreds of thousands of calls as well as recommendations for next steps generated by the platform after calls were complete. It could also have been exploited to allow an attacker to manage AI agents within the platform and direct their own agentic campaigns.

The critical severity vulnerability impacted CreditNirvana's main platform, and Zveare says it specifically exposed the data of three corporate customers—all prominent Indian financial services firms—using CreditNirvana for their collections. The data also exposed millions of individuals’ accounts, which contain credit reports, ID cards, case management details, and legal documents, along with certain types of communications, including millions of emails, texts, and call transcripts related to financial services, unpaid accounts, and collections. The vulnerability also could have been exploited by an attacker to track the location of human debt collection agents and for some administrative privileges within the system.

“Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to enumerate platform users, establish sessions as arbitrary users including administrative users, access and modify sensitive information with the privileges of the impersonated user,” CERT-In wrote.

Zveare says he is relieved that the issue was resolved quickly, but is conscious that the bugs were potentially present in CreditNirvana's systems for years. As AI is integrated into more and more automated systems, synthesizing data from a greater number of sources and using it to draw conclusions, Zveare says, the episode serves as “an important example of an AI-powered service having a very sensitive data exposure.”

Title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Supply-Chain Attack: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 Steal Cloud Credentials
Context: A critical supply-chain compromise was discovered affecting Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI meta-package, where versions 1
Full Text:
A critical supply-chain compromise was discovered affecting Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI meta-package, where versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were injected with credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud identity tokens, API keys, and sensitive credentials from developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud build hosts. Due to the package’s approximately 190,000 monthly downloads and the breadth of targeted credentials, immediate remediation is required for any environment that installed the compromised versions.

Agent-framework compromise at a glance

Affected package: agent-framework on PyPI, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2

Last clean version: 1.26.0

Not affected: agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages

Exposure window: November 17, 2026, 20:35 to approximately 21:20 UTC

Payload: a Python .pth startup hook that harvests credentials on every interpreter launch

Exfiltration: zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook.site URL

Status: malicious versions quarantined by PyPI; no CVE assigned

What happened in the agent-framework supply-chain attack

Both malicious versions were published within a 33-minute window on November 17, 2026 (20:35 to 21:08 UTC) and removed by approximately 21:20 UTC.

The attack was entirely in packaging. Neither malicious release changed Agent Framework code or pulled in a rogue dependency. Instead, each version added a Python .pth startup hook file that executes on every Python interpreter launch, even if Agent Framework is never imported.

How the .pth startup hook runs and evades detection

The collector forks a detached background process, sets a flag to prevent re-execution in child processes, and silently harvests credentials. Version 1.26.2 restored the legitimate __init__.py byte-for-byte to evade diff-based detection while moving the payload to a new top-level module.

What credentials does the agent-framework malware steal?

The malware actively requested fresh credential tokens rather than only copying stored secrets. Targeted credentials include:

Environment variables matching sensitive substrings (TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, and more) from the current process and up to 300 other processes via /proc/*/environ

Azure managed-identity tokens for 12 Azure resources (ARM, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, ML, AI Foundry, Container Registry, Azure DevOps) via IMDS and identity endpoints

Azure DevOps SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and OIDC tokens for federated identity

GitHub Actions OIDC tokens (version 1.26.2 only) when workflows have id-token: write permissions

Credential files including Azure CLI state, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config.json, Hugging Face tokens, and .env files

All harvested data was exfiltrated via zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook.site URL.

Which agent-framework versions and environments are affected?

The following components are affected: agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI. The last clean version is 1.26.0. The dependency agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages were checked and are not affected.

Any environment that installed the compromised versions during the exposure window is at risk, including through loose version pins such as agent-framework>=1.26. This spans developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines (Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions), and cloud build hosts running Python.

At the time of writing, the malicious versions have been quarantined by PyPI and the Microsoft publisher account has been secured. No CVE has been assigned.

Why stolen cloud and CI/CD credentials raise the stakes

Successful exploitation allows attackers to obtain cloud identity tokens that grant access to Azure resources, steal CI/CD pipeline secrets that could enable lateral movement across repositories and infrastructure, and harvest stored credentials that could lead to full infrastructure compromise across multiple cloud providers.

The attack also demonstrates sophisticated evasion techniques, including restoring legitimate code to bypass diff-based reviews while hiding the payload in a separate module.

How to remediate the agent-framework compromise

Organizations should take the following remediation steps immediately:

Isolate affected hosts and CI runners.

Detect exposure by searching lockfiles, container images, CI caches, and environments for versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, and look for .pth files (agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth) and payload modules in site-packages.

Pin to agent-framework==1.26.0 with hash verification and rebuild from clean environments.

Rotate all credentials that may have been exposed, including Azure service principal credentials, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, GitHub tokens, npm/PyPI/Hugging Face tokens, Docker registry credentials, and any secrets in environment variables or .env files.

Audit Azure Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure DevOps audit logs, and GitHub Actions workflow runs for unauthorized access since November 17.

Hunt for IOCs by searching proxy and DNS logs for connections to webhook.site, User-Agent strings “af-runtime-diagnostics/1” and “runtime-diagnostics/1”, and bursts of IMDS token requests.

Block versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 at your package proxy and consider blocking webhook.site at the network level.

Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

Package versions: agent-framework 1.26.1, 1.26.2

Files in site-packages: agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth

Network: outbound connections to webhook.site

User-Agent strings: “af-runtime-diagnostics/1”, “runtime-diagnostics/1”

Behavior: bursts of IMDS token requests

How Orca helps detect compromised agent-framework packages

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable package versions, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize the risks that matter most. Orca’s SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scanning capabilities can detect compromised packages in cloud workloads. Customers running Orca’s agentless scanning should check whether their workloads contain the affected versions. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first.

Because this payload targets build hosts and pipelines as much as production, coverage has to start before deployment. Orca helps teams catch risky code before it reaches production. And because the real damage comes from what stolen tokens can reach, Orca also helps teams reduce identity-based cloud risk and detect and respond to cloud threats that follow a credential compromise. As agent frameworks become a recurring supply-chain target, securing AI systems means securing the packages they are built on.

Title: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
Context: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered
Full Text: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered. CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization. The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning. According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do. Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services. To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware. It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too. In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site. “That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware. The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime, an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign. “We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”® Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.

Context: Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal...
Full Text:
Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems. For at least one subset of hackers, it appears that era has now arrived.

Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a new wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools. These setups​​—many of which mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing techniques—use LLMs to autonomously scan potential hacking targets and attempt to force their way into poorly secured networks, then carry out attack plans written by human operators.

Dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks. The tools do not introduce new ways to attack websites or servers and are not sophisticated, according to alerts from around half a dozen security companies. Instead, they allow cybercriminals to launch attacks at speeds that would be impossible for humans to do.

Hackers also don’t need to be skilled to use the tools, researchers say, and attacks that would have taken days are completed in just hours. “Agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention,” CJ Moses, AWS’s chief information security officer, wrote in a company blog post recently.

The most prominent of these tools is Artex. Written in the programming language Go, the open-source framework was first published on GitHub in July by a pseudonymous developer using the handle Autumn-27, and it’s been spreading across some hacker communities ever since. Artex has been used across all parts of attacks, from conducting initial analysis of networks and gaining access to moving within systems and preparing data to be exported.

“It’s really an all-in-one product,” says Jacob Larsen, an offensive security researcher and founder of security firm Cypen. “Previous iterations of AI agent pen-testing tools would either only do reconnaissance—like the scanning and analysis [of targets]—and some would only do testing. This is really a point-and-shoot weapon.”

As with other AI hacking frameworks, Artex isn’t an AI product itself. Instead, it is essentially a guide that points external frontier and open-source AI models—that can be connected to it via APIs—to a series of existing penetration testing tools and processes. People using Artex or other similar setups can give simple, natural-language prompts to begin their operations. “Launch a penetration attack on [Redacted victim] to gain access to the site’s admin panel, database, or server,” one set of hackers prompted Artex, according to researchers at the security firm Check Point.

More than half of the exposed Ollama servers in this scan have already been touched by someone who is not the owner. I don't mean theoretically vulnerable. I mean visibly used: model names that are really callback addresses, tags stamped with the server's own IP, and Base64 strings that decode to /etc/shadow.

Exposure statistics normally describe a risk. These model lists describe activity. An unauthenticated /api/tags call is a read-only request, and on thousands of machines it returns something close to a visitors' log.

Below is what the data shows, where I think it points, and what I would do about it on Monday morning. I've labelled claims as [Observed], [Interpretation] or [Hypothesis] so you can see where the evidence stops.

First, the number I don't trust

The scanner reported 14,064 findings across 11,891 IP addresses and labelled 14,060 of them vulnerable, 387 critical. If I put that in a headline it would travel well. It would also be wrong.

[Observed] 148 IP addresses return the exact same fingerprint: Grafana on 3000, Jupyter on 8888, Ollama on three ports, each serving one model, llama3.1:8b. They sit with five different hosting providers in five countries. Another 281 addresses answer as two to five different products on the same port. Real servers rarely do that. Sensors and catch-all responders do it all day.

[Interpretation] These are most likely deception infrastructure, run by researchers, vendors or threat actors watching who comes knocking. Remove those 429 addresses and the critical findings drop from 387 to 39. MLflow falls from 126 to 4. Honeypots look extremely vulnerable. That's the whole job description.

Two more corrections before we go further. A Streamlit health check returning ok tells you an app is on the internet, not that it is exploitable. And the target list was pre-selected: 58% of the 20,354 hosts produced a finding, which is far above any internet-wide base rate. So treat the totals as a sample of a much larger population, not a census.

What survives is still uncomfortable: 7,714 findings on 7,627 hosts where an AI or notebook API answered without authentication, almost all of them Ollama. Only 0.3% of all findings were served over HTTPS.

The lesson for anyone producing exposure numbers, us included: if you count banners and health checks, you measure how the internet presents itself. You don't measure how it behaves.

The box is becoming a gateway

[Observed] 79% of exposed Ollama hosts list at least one :cloud model, mostly GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax and Kimi variants. [Interpretation] An exposed, signed-in server can provide access to someone else's paid subscription, with the bill landing on the owner. This is the self-hosted version of LLMjacking, and it requires no exploit at all.

[Hypothesis] A listed cloud tag does not prove the host is signed in, and we did not test inference. But the same seven cloud models appear together on 1,295 otherwise unrelated hosts. That pattern looks less like thousands of individual choices and more like automated pulls by third parties checking which servers will serve them.

Guardrails are optional, and so is the front door

[Observed] 28% also run embedding models such as nomic-embed-text or bge-m3. [Interpretation] Embeddings are the plumbing of retrieval-augmented generation. Those servers are likely wired into pipelines that read internal documents, which makes the exposed box a bridge, not an island.

When a server pulls from an address you control, it calls you back. That's a clean, reliable way to confirm that a target is reachable, writable and able to make outbound connections: classic server-side request forgery, offered as a feature.

[Observed] 712 model names embed the IP address of the server they sit on. [Interpretation] That's inventory keeping. Someone is tagging targets so their tooling can recognise them later. The same applies to recurring markers like zzvitals-beacon, verif_sys and ops-verify, each found on hundreds of hosts, and to names ending in -copy-test, which show someone checking whether the copy endpoint works.

[Hypothesis] The trio gpt-4o, gpt-4 and claude-3-opus, found together on 1,190 hosts, almost always next to tinyllama, looks like a tiny local model copied under premium names. What they were reaching for

[Observed] On 55 hosts, model names contain Base64 or hex strings that decode to file paths. The targets read like a post-exploitation checklist: /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ, Ollama's own systemd unit and its override.conf (where people tend to put environment variables and API keys), SSH authorized_keys, AWS config, the Oracle Cloud metadata endpoint, and on 10 hosts the Ollama private key itself. Ollama fixed it in version 0.1.34 in May 2024. We can't tell from these lists whether any target was still on a vulnerable build, so the attempt proves intent, not success. Somebody still thinks it's worth trying two and a half years later, which suggests the technique remains useful enough to keep testing.

The economics are hard to ignore. The attacker uses free tunnels, free throwaway registries and, in the end, your computer and your cloud subscription. Their cost per target rounds to zero.

What I would change after seeing this data

Exposure research needs a second question.

“Is it open?” is the easy part. “Has it been touched?” is the useful part, and for AI runtimes the answer is often sitting in a read-only API response. Defenders should triage on artifacts, not banners.

Model runtimes are becoming credential brokers.

Once a local daemon can route to paid cloud models with a key on disk, compromising it is about access and money, not just CPU cycles. That's a different threat model from the one most teams had in mind when they typed OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0.

The attackers here didn't need AI.

We spend a lot of energy debating whether AI will make attackers faster. On these servers the playbook is old: an unauthenticated service, path traversal, server-side request forgery, outbound callbacks. Familiar primitives, new location. The controls we already know work. They just haven't followed the workload.

Internet measurement is polluted, and we should say so.

A meaningful slice of “critical AI exposure” is other people's sensors watching each other. Anyone publishing exposure numbers, vendors included, should show how they filter.

What businesses should do

The controls here are familiar: ownership, authentication, egress control, logging, patching, and exposure management. The practical steps are straightforward:

This week: find them, and check for guests

Scan your own public ranges and every cloud and VPS account the company pays for, including those on personal cards that get expensed. Look beyond default ports: 6% of findings here sat on a non-standard port.

On every Ollama instance, read the model list. Anything prefixed with an IP address, a tunnel domain or ttl.sh, anything named beacon, verify, probe or pwn, and anything containing your own IP is a stranger's artifact.

If you find one, treat the host as compromised, not misconfigured. Rotate whatever lives in its environment and service files, revoke the Ollama key on the linked ollama.com account, check cloud usage for spend you don't recognise, and rebuild rather than clean.

Within 30 days: close the door, then the windows

Bind model runtimes to localhost or a private network. If remote access is needed, put an authenticating reverse proxy or a zero-trust access layer in front. Ollama has no built-in authentication, so this isn't optional.

Restrict outbound traffic from model servers to the registries you approved. Egress control is what turns a pull-based callback or SSRF attempt into a failed connection.

Keep runtimes current, and don't sign a shared server into a personal or corporate cloud model account unless it's behind authentication and spend alerts.

Log API calls that change state (pull, create, copy, push, delete) and alert on them. On a stable production server they should be rare.

This quarter: make ownership the default

Make registration a condition of AI infrastructure spend: every model server gets a named owner, a data classification and an expiry date. If nobody owns it, it gets switched off.

Decide, in writing, where uncensored or abliterated models are allowed and what they may touch. Research sandboxes, yes. Internet-facing boxes wired into document pipelines, no.

Bring AI runtimes, notebooks and experiment trackers into exposure management and red-team scope. Test the brakes, not just the engine: can you find, isolate and shut down one of these servers within an hour?

Methodology and limitations

Single snapshot taken on 10 November 2026 against 20,354 pre-selected IPv4 addresses on seven ports (3000, 5000, 8000, 8080, 8501, 8888, 11434). Product detection used one unauthenticated HTTP request per service: Ollama /api/tags, Jupyter /api/kernels, MLflow experiment search, JupyterHub /hub/api/, Streamlit and Grafana health endpoints. No inference, write or exploitation requests were sent.

Likely deception infrastructure was removed with two heuristics: an identical five-service fingerprint shared by 148 hosts, and IP:port pairs that answered as more than one product (281 hosts). This removed 1,513 findings on 429 hosts. Some real servers may have been removed, and some sensors certainly remain.

Third-party activity indicators are inferred from model names only. A clean list doesn't prove a clean host, since names can be deleted. Encoded strings were decoded from Base64 and hex segments. Model families were assigned by name pattern. Geolocation and network data from DB-IP Lite (CC BY 4.0), MaxMind GeoLite2 and iptoasn. Individual exposed hosts are not named in this post.

Title: Same Attacks, New Speed: The Rise of Agentic Offensive Frameworks
Context: In October 2026, researchers examining attacker infrastructure found one CyberStrikeAI deployment configured with 44 agents, with work distributed across reconnaissance,...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Agentic cyberattacks are no longer theoretical. In 2026, frameworks such as ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI moved from research and red team use into real-world attacker operations.

Our research shows that these frameworks are gaining adoption quickly. Across GitHub and Internet-exposure data, we found thousands of forks and more than 4,000 publicly visible servers, alongside growing interest in these tools within underground communities.

The underlying attack techniques, however, are mostly familiar. The real change is how quickly and autonomously attacks can be executed: agents can chain tools and attack stages, work in parallel, and adapt when blocked. For defenders, this makes broad visibility and multiple layers of protection across the attack chain increasingly important. Cato combines existing inline security controls with Agentic Threat Prevention (AGTP), designed to identify attack progression and help stop likely next steps before the attacker reaches its objective.

Agentic Attacks Are No Longer Theoretical – They Are Here

For more than a year, the cybersecurity industry has been asking the same questions: Are autonomous AI-driven attacks really possible? When will they move from research environments into real-world operations? And how much of the threat is real versus hype?

Throughout 2026, controlled testing started to answer that question. OpenAI disclosed models bypassing isolation during cybersecurity evaluations and reaching the internet, while Anthropic reported similar incidents. In July, Cato demonstrated an agentic attack stack reaching Domain Administrator in a controlled Active Directory environment in 40 minutes from a single high-level prompt, with most planning and execution handled autonomously. The capability was no longer hypothetical.

Over the past few weeks, however, the question has changed. We are no longer asking only whether agentic attacks can happen. We are now seeing threat actors actually use agentic offensive frameworks in real operations.

In October, researchers investigating attacks focused on Japan uncovered a CyberStrikeAI environment configured with 44 specialized agents spanning reconnaissance, exploitation, persistence, C2, exfiltration, and reporting. The activity involved at least 19 organizations, including 16 in Japan, with multiple targets processed in parallel. Deep compromise was limited to a smaller number of targets, but the case demonstrated how agentic tooling can automate attack operations at scale.

At roughly the same time, Microsoft observed the China state-aligned actor Storm-0940 using ARTEX to automate attacks against hundreds of organizations globally. Some successful attacks progressed from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in less than three hours. ARTEX was also used during activity associated with the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise, while the FBI later reported that the compromise enabled access to more than 2,250 downstream tenants.

ARTEX is not an isolated case. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported threat actors using other open-source agentic frameworks, including Cairn and HexStrike, during real incident-response engagements. Since late August 2026, they observed these tools being used across multiple stages of the attack lifecycle, including lateral movement, database exploitation, and preparation for data exfiltration.

By November 13, the shift was significant enough for the FBI to publish a FLASH warning that a variety of malicious actors had weaponized ARTEX to automate multiple stages of cyber intrusions at machine speed. The FBI also highlighted financially motivated attacks against South Korean financial institutions that resulted in the exfiltration of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Agentic offensive frameworks have moved from GitHub projects and controlled security research into the hands of real threat actors.

Four Popular Open-Source Agentic Offensive Frameworks We Examined

There are already dozens of AI-enabled offensive-security projects available publicly, ranging from experimental research agents to full multi-agent penetration-testing platforms. For this research, we chose to focus on four popular, free, open-source frameworks that have attracted significant public attention and have also appeared in real-world attacker activity: ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI.

These frameworks are not identical, but they share a common idea: reducing the amount of manual work required from the operator. Instead of executing every step of an intrusion themselves, an operator can provide a goal while the framework uses one or more agents to reason about the environment, select tools, execute actions, interpret results, and decide what to do next.

ARTEX is an autonomous, multi-agent penetration-testing and offensive platform that divides activity across specialized agents and translates high-level objectives into executable actions. Its original GitHub repository was removed in October 2026 following widespread abuse, but the code continued to spread through forks and localized versions. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant have observed ARTEX being used by both financially motivated and suspected espionage actors during real intrusions.

ARTEХ dashboard interface displayed in a GitHub repository, showing system activity, token consumption, active nodes, traffic exchanges, and security findings

Cairn takes a somewhat different approach. Rather than defining a fixed set of penetration-testing roles or workflows, Cairn is designed as a general-purpose state-space search engine. An operator provides a starting point and a goal, while multiple workers explore possible paths toward that goal using a shared graph of facts and intended actions. Penetration testing was the first domain in which the framework was validated, and Cairn has since been observed being operated by threat actors during real incident-response investigations.

Cairn in action with a goal and target, showing its reasoning process and discovered facts during a CTF task

CyberStrikeAI is a broader offensive-security platform combining multi-agent orchestration, MCP-based tooling, knowledge retrieval, attack-chain modeling, a web console, and integrations with a large number of security tools. It also includes capabilities such as WebShell management and built-in C2 functionality. In October 2026, researchers examining attacker infrastructure found one CyberStrikeAI deployment configured with 44 agents, with work distributed across reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, persistence, command and control, exfiltration, and automated reporting.

CyberStrikeAI dashboard in action, showing vulnerability severity, active tasks, tool executions, recent security findings, and system capabilities

PentAGI, developed by VXControl, is a multi-agent penetration-testing framework designed to take a target and goal and break the operation into tasks handled by specialized agents. Those agents can invoke established offensive tools such as Nmap, Metasploit, and SQLmap inside isolated environments rather than requiring the operator to manually coordinate each tool. GTIG and Mandiant have observed PentAGI being abused in the wild, including operations that progressed beyond reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning into active intrusion and persistence.

PentAGI in action during a demonstration by its creator, showing the chat interface coordinating agents to execute assigned web security tasks

We selected these four because they give us a useful sample of the broader ecosystem: they are popular, actively discussed, publicly accessible, and provide enough observable data to study their development and adoption over time.

From GitHub To The Attacker’s Toolbox

One way to understand how quickly these frameworks are spreading is to look at two different signals: developer/community activity on GitHub and Internet-facing deployments.

The GitHub numbers already show substantial interest around the four agentic frameworks we examined. As of November 15, 2026, PentAGI had more than 34,000 stars and 5,300 forks, CyberStrikeAI had more than 8,600 stars and 1,900 forks, and Cairn, despite being created only in April 2026, had already accumulated more than 5,100 stars and 1,000 forks. ARTEX is more difficult to measure because its original repository was removed, but four surviving copies together accounted for more than 10,000 stars and 7,700 forks.

This does not mean that newer agentic frameworks have replaced established offensive frameworks. In fact, the GitHub activity shows very different lifecycle patterns. Sliver remains actively developed, with more than 900 commits and 20 releases during the last 12 months, while Havoc is archived and had only two commits during the same period, despite continuing to gain forks.

GitHub activity only tells us part of the story. We also searched for publicly reachable deployments using open-source intelligence and Internet-search platforms such as Shodan and Censys.

Our searches identified:

These results should be treated as exposure indicators, not confirmed attacker infrastructure, and counts from Shodan and Censys should not be compared directly because the searches used different engines.

The Internet-exposure data shows that these frameworks are not limited to GitHub repositories or research environments – they are already being deployed on publicly reachable infrastructure. But deployment is only one part of the picture.

To better understand how quickly interest in these tools is growing, we also looked at their activity on GitHub. Rather than relying only on stars, we focused on forks and development activity: forks give us an indication of how frequently projects are being copied and picked up by others, while commits help show how actively the frameworks themselves are evolving.

GitHub forks created during the last 12 months:New forks from November 2025 through October 2026:

The difference in recent fork activity is significant. PentAGI recorded 5,297 new forks during the last 12 months, while the surviving ARTEX repositories accumulated more than 5,000. CyberStrikeAI added 1,789 and Cairn 937. By comparison, the established frameworks in our dataset – Mythic, Sliver, and Havoc-added hundreds rather than thousands of forks during the same period.

Forks, however, tell us mainly about interest and distribution. They do not tell us whether a project is actively being developed. To look at that side of the ecosystem, we examined the number of commits made to each framework month by month.

Monthly development activity – last 12 monthsGitHub commits per month from November 2025 through October 2026:

The development activity shows a much more dynamic picture than fork counts alone.

CyberStrikeAI was developed at a particularly high pace through much of 2026, peaking at 476 commits in July. PentAGI also went through a period of intensive development between April and July before activity dropped sharply. At the same time, Sliver shows that established offensive frameworks are far from disappearing: despite being released years earlier, it recorded 906 commits during the last 12 months.

Havoc represents the opposite end of the spectrum. Its repository is archived and recorded only two commits during the period, yet it continued to accumulate forks – showing that development activity and continued interest do not necessarily move together.

ARTEX stands out with a sharp increase toward the end of the period, although its commit history requires additional caution. Because the original repository was removed and our ARTEX dataset combines surviving copies, some of the visible commit history was imported into those copies and predates their creation.

Beyond adoption and development activity, we also looked at where the publicly visible infrastructure for these frameworks is hosted.

Geographic Distribution of Publicly Visible Agentic Framework Servers:

Across ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, and Cairn, our searches identified more than 4,000 publicly visible servers, with the largest concentrations appearing in the United States, China, and Hong Kong.

As a closer look at ARTEX, the following view is based on Shodan data only. It gives a useful snapshot of where publicly visible ARTEX infrastructure is concentrated, but it should not be treated as a complete count. Our broader searches returned higher numbers because they also included other Internet-search engines and data sources.

This is only the infrastructure that was publicly exposed and indexed by Internet-search platforms. The actual footprint could be significantly larger, as private, firewalled, short-lived, or otherwise non-indexed deployments would not appear in these results.

The geographic distribution reflects hosting location only; it does not indicate who operates the servers or whether they are being used maliciously.

Taken together, the data shows an ecosystem moving at different speeds: new agentic frameworks are attracting significant attention and, in several cases, rapid development, while established offensive frameworks continue to maintain their own communities and operational relevance.

We also found signs that these frameworks were attracting attention in underground communities before much of the recent public reporting around their abuse appeared. On October 6, 2026, a user on a dark-web forum explicitly asked for help learning CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike, and PentAGI.

That post appeared more than two weeks before Microsoft’s October 21 ARTEX report, and several weeks before Google/Mandiant’s October 30 research, Eye Security’s November 12 incident report, and the FBI’s November 13 ARTEX warning.

The interest in learning and experimenting with these agentic offensive frameworks was already present in underground communities before they became the focus of widespread public threat reporting.

Old Tradecraft, New Operator

So far, the techniques used by these frameworks are mostly familiar. They scan, exploit known vulnerabilities, steal credentials, move laterally, establish persistence, deploy webshells or C2, and exfiltrate data.

The tools are familiar too. CyberStrikeAI integrates more than 100 existing security tools, including Nmap, Nuclei, SQLmap, Metasploit, Mimikatz, BloodHound and Impacket. PentAGI also relies on established penetration-testing tools, and ARTEX has been observed orchestrating existing offensive tooling during real intrusions.

What is different is the way these tools are used. An agent can take a result from one step, immediately decide what to try next, test several paths in parallel, and change approach when something fails.

The ARTEX incident investigated by Eye Security is a good example. After obtaining API keys, the agents started using them within minutes. When rate limiting blocked the activity, they changed their approach within roughly three minutes. They also modified an existing reGeorg tunnel to work in a load-balanced environment, changed user-agent strings to get around access controls, and tested several ways to escape from a container.

We saw similar behavior in our own Agentic Attacker research. In one run, the agent created custom vulnerability probes after standard probes failed. In another, it changed its collection workflow when the environment did not behave as expected, and it also built an SMB-based path for moving data through an existing foothold.

None of this means that AI is suddenly inventing completely new attack techniques. The bigger change is that it can combine existing techniques, adapt when blocked, and keep moving toward an objective with much less human involvement.

Cato Protection

The fact that agentic frameworks rely heavily on familiar offensive techniques also means that defenders are not starting from zero. Cato already provides multiple layers of protection against the infrastructure, tools, and behaviors used throughout these attack chains, including threat intelligence and reputation-based blocking, IPS protections, malware prevention, and identification of suspicious behaviors such as internal discovery and lateral movement.

On top of these existing controls, Cato Agentic Threat Prevention (AGTP) is designed to address the agentic nature of the attack itself. By correlating activity across the environment, identifying attack progression, and applying inline protections against likely next steps, AGTP helps contain an attack before an autonomous agent can continue progressing toward its objective. In other words, while the attacker may move faster and adapt more frequently, the defensive approach also needs to operate across the full attack chain rather than relying on a single indicator or signature.

What This Means For Defenders

Agentic offensive frameworks are evolving quickly, and the barrier to using them is getting lower. New frameworks continue to appear, existing projects can be forked and modified easily, and increasingly capable low-cost and open-weight models are making these capabilities accessible to a much wider group of operators.

That makes relying on static protections alone increasingly difficult. Defenders need multiple layers of protection and broad visibility across the attack chain – from malicious infrastructure and exploitation attempts to C2 activity, lateral movement, credential abuse, and data exfiltration.

The tools may keep changing, but the goal for defenders remains the same: detect the attack as it develops, understand how the different stages connect, and stop it before the attacker reaches the objective.
