Title: Hackers Impersonate Microsoft Exchange Online Alerts to Trick Users During Microsoft 365 Outage
How to detect stalkerware safely | Kaspersky official blog
Context: During the same period, Kaspersky researchers found 33 previously unknown stalkerware families
Full Text:
As the Coalition Against Stalkerware explains, stalkerware lets someone secretly monitor your private life through your mobile device. Depending on the tool and the access it has, an abuser may be able to view your searches, location, messages and photos, or monitor your calls. These tools are often easy to buy and install, and can run in the background without your knowledge or consent. Their availability does not excuse the person who uses them to abuse you.

Technology has made stalking easier and more dangerous. Recent figures from Kaspersky give a sense of the scale: more than 34,000 people across more than 160 countries were affected by stalkerware in 2024-2025. During the same period, Kaspersky researchers found 33 previously unknown stalkerware families. You can learn more in Kaspersky‘s tech–enabled abuse report.

Stalkerware and other forms of digital monitoring are rarely about a single hidden app. More often, monitoring involves several ways of accessing your information: installed software, account logins, quietly enabled sharing settings, configuration profiles and physical trackers.

Because of this, checking your device is less like running a malware scan and more like a careful investigation — one where the order of your actions matters as much as the actions themselves. The key is not to memorize every menu path, especially as interfaces change. Instead, ask yourself:

How could someone be accessing the information I am concerned about?

Which settings should I check?

What can I document safely?

Which tools can I trust?

Could removing something immediately put me at greater risk?

We’ll guide you through what to look for on Android and iPhone, how to interpret the signs, and — crucially — how to act without making the situation more dangerous. The single most important idea runs through every section: if a check could put you at greater risk, pause and seek help before proceeding.

Ground rules before you check your phone

1. If you might be in danger, do not investigate using the phone you suspect is being monitored

Treat the phone you suspect as if someone may be seeing your screen in real time. Read this guide, look for support, and make plans from a different device the other person cannot reach — a trusted friend’s phone, a computer at a library or workplace, or a new device they do not know about.

2. Do not delete or switch anything off yet

This may feel counterintuitive, but it is important. Removing an app or turning off sharing can alert the person monitoring you. That sudden change may tell an abuser they have been discovered, which could put you at greater risk. Decide whether and when to remove anything only after considering your safety — ideally with help.

3. Save what you find before you change it

Screenshots, app names, settings, and dates can matter later if you ever go to the police or seek a protective order. Capturing evidence first also forces you to look slowly and carefully. Only do this if it is safe to do so.

Four questions to keep asking yourself

As you look through your phone, you will gather a lot of small observations. These four questions can help you make sense of them and avoid rushing to delete something before you are ready.

1. How sure can I be?

A worrying sign is not the same as proof. Some findings are strong evidence; others have ordinary explanations. You can rarely be certain from one clue. A clean app list does not rule out unauthorized account access. A clean security scan does not rule out unwanted location sharing. A factory reset does not help if the abuser can still access your Apple Account, Google Account, email or recovery methods. Look at how the clues fit together, and do not rush to a conclusion.

2. What does it actually look like?

Be specific. Which permissions are turned on? What alerts have appeared? What sharing is set up? Describe what you see before deciding what it means. On Android, warning signs might include an unknown app with location or microphone access, an unfamiliar Accessibility service, or a device admin app that makes removal harder. On iPhone, look for unexpected Find My sharing, an unknown trusted device, unfamiliar iCloud backup activity, a VPN or management profile, or unusual activity in App Privacy Report. An AirTag alert or a privacy alert from a security product may also provide useful clues.

3. Is it open and trustworthy, or hidden?

A legitimate tool should be installed with your knowledge and consent, and do what it claims. Monitoring software may hide, disguise its purpose or resist removal. The key questions are whether you know it is there and have freely agreed to its use. Apply the same care when choosing security tools: do not use just any anti-spyware app you find online. Choose tools from reputable organizations that maintain their software, clearly explain what it can detect, and explain any automatic actions it may take.

4. Can I remove it safely, and is now the right time?

Removal is the last question, never the first. Sometimes the safest and most reasonable answer is “not yet”. Before removing anything, consider whether the action could alert the abuser, destroy useful evidence or escalate the situation. The goal is to protect both your phone and your safety.

The five ways someone can watch you

As we explained above, surveillance may involve several ways of accessing your information, rather than a single malicious app. Searching only for “the spy app” can mean overlooking a compromised password or unwanted location sharing.

Before changing any settings, try to recall exactly what the abuser seems to know and when they first appeared to know it. Was it a message, a photo, a search, a purchase or a meeting? Keep the five main ways someone can use technology to monitor you in mind as you investigate.

1. An app on the phone

This could be dedicated stalkerware or an ordinary-looking app — such as a parental control, anti-theft or phone-cleaning app — misused for monitoring. On Android, start with installed apps, recent installations, permissions, Accessibility services and device admin rights. Some stalkerware tries to hide under a generic name, remove its icon or present itself as a system app. Ask yourself not only “Do I recognize this app?” but also “Does its access match its purpose?”

2. Your accounts

If someone has your Apple Account, Google Account or email password, access to your recovery methods or messaging backups, an active session, or a trusted device, they may be able to see a lot of your information without installing anything on your phone. Unauthorized account access can be easier than installing stalkerware — and easy to overlook.

3. Sharing settings

Built-in features like location sharing, family sharing, and shared photo albums are designed to be convenient — which also makes them easy for someone to switch on without you noticing. Phones are designed to share location, calendars, photos and devices with trusted people. In the context of abuse, those same features can be misused.

4. Profiles and network settings

More technical settings — mobile device management (MDM), VPNs and configuration profiles containing certificates — can control parts of your phone or route its traffic through a network someone else controls. On iPhone, configuration profiles, VPNs and MDM may give another person or organization more control over your device than you realize.

5. A physical tracker

A small Bluetooth tag, such as an AirTag, can be hidden in your bag, car or coat to track where you go. AirTags and other Bluetooth trackers are not phone spyware, but they can be misused to monitor your movements.

You do not have to be a technical expert to check these. The walkthroughs below take them one at a time.

Checking an Android phone

On Android, monitoring often involves an app with permissions that do not match its purpose. It may also use Accessibility services or device administrator rights that make it hard to remove. Go through these checks in order, and write down what you find before changing anything.

Menu names vary by manufacturer. Samsung, Pixel, Xiaomi, Oppo and other devices may label settings differently. If a path does not match your phone, use the search box in Settings to look for apps, permissions, Accessibility, device admin, battery, data usage, VPN or unknown apps.

As you check, pay attention to apps and settings you do not recognize. Ask yourself:

Does this app’s access match its purpose?

Could changing this setting now alert someone or destroy evidence?

Once again, do not rush to change settings. Your safety matters more than completing a routine phone check. Here is how to work through the checks on Android.

Step 1 — Look at your installed apps

A monitoring tool has to live somewhere, so start with the full list. Open Settings → Apps. If your menus look different — phone makers rearrange them constantly — just use the search box in Settings.

Look for apps you do not recognize, apps with generic names (“System Service”, “Sync”, “Device Health”), or apps you do not remember installing. Pay particular attention to anything installed around the time you first suspected monitoring. Stalkerware may use an official-sounding name to avoid attracting attention.

On some Android devices, you can also open an app’s information screen to check its installation source, version, permissions, battery use and data usage. If you cannot identify an app from these details, ask a digital security specialist for help before trying more advanced checks.

Make a note of anything that seems suspicious before changing it. Take a screenshot if it is safe to do so, or use another device to photograph the screen. Note the app’s visible name, icon, package name if displayed, permissions, and whether you can uninstall it. If the Uninstall button is grayed out, the app may have device admin rights or another special access setting, which we will check next.

An unknown app in the list of apps

Step 2 — Check what each app is allowed to do

Next, check app permissions. Open an app’s information screen and go to Permissions, or look for Permission manager under Privacy if your phone has that option. Permissions can help you understand what an app may be able to access, although they do not tell you everything it can do.

Pay particular attention to access to your location, camera, microphone, contacts, SMS messages, call logs, phone functions, files and media, notifications and nearby devices. Depending on the permissions granted, an app may be able to see where you go, what you say, who you talk to, what files you keep, and which alerts or messages appear on your phone.

The practical question is always: does this permission make sense for this app? The thing to watch for is a mismatch: an unfamiliar app that has broad, sensitive permissions it has no reason to need. A flashlight app does not need your microphone and your messages. A “battery saver” or calculator does not need to track your location all day. When an app’s access does not fit what it claims to do, that is one of the clearest warning signs there is.

On newer Android versions, Privacy Dashboard can help you check recent access. Which apps accessed your location, camera or microphone during the period shown? Did the timing make sense? Were you using the app then? This is not proof by itself, but it gives you a timeline and helps you see whether several warning signs form a pattern.

Permission manager helps you find suspicious apps

Step 3 — Check Accessibility and Device Admin

Two Android features deserve a closer look because they grant powerful access that monitoring tools may misuse: Accessibility services and device administrator rights. Legitimate apps may also need these features, so check which app has access and why.

Accessibility services help people with disabilities use their phones. Depending on their capabilities and permissions, these services may be able to read screen content across apps and perform actions on your behalf. A monitoring app can misuse this access to read messages. If an unfamiliar Accessibility service is switched on, investigate carefully.

Use Settings search to look for “Accessibility“. Check downloaded apps or services as well as built-in features. You may rely on legitimate accessibility tools, so the question is not simply whether Accessibility is enabled, but which app or service has access and whether you expect it to.

Device administrator rights let an app enforce certain security policies and can make it harder to uninstall. If an unfamiliar app has these rights on your personal phone, document what you find and consider it when planning any removal.

Use Settings search again to look for “Device admin apps” or “Device administrators“. If something suspicious is enabled, do not immediately turn it off. First ask yourself: would I be safe if the app lost access? Could the abuser notice? Do I need a safer device, legal advice or specialist support before changing anything?

As with every step, document what you see before taking action. Accessibility and Device Admin are not just technical settings; in this context, changing them can affect safety, evidence and escalation.

Check Accessibility and Device Admin apps

Step 4 — Check battery, data, and Play Protect

Battery, data usage and Play Protect are supporting checks. They are useful, but they are not conclusive on their own. A phone can have battery drain because the battery is old. Data usage can be high because of video, backups or normal apps. Play Protect can miss things. So use these checks as part of your systematic approach, not as a single verdict.

Monitoring software often runs in the background, so it may use more battery or mobile data than its purpose would explain — a simple notes app quietly using data around the clock, for instance. Open Settings → Battery. Look for apps using more power than expected, especially in the background, and consider whether you were actually using them.

For data, go to Network, Internet, Connections or Mobile data, depending on the device. Look for unexpected background data usage. Monitoring apps need to send information somewhere, so unusual data can support other findings, especially when it appears together with suspicious permissions, Accessibility access, or device admin rights.

Then check whether Google Play Protect is available, switched on and showing warnings. It is built into many Android devices and may flag known threats. Open Google Play Store → your profile icon → Play Protect. To review scanning settings, tap the settings icon and look for Scan apps with Play Protect. If protection is disabled, consider whether someone may have turned it off to install a monitoring app. Before enabling it or running a scan, remember that Play Protect can automatically disable or remove harmful apps, which could affect your safety or evidence.

Not every Android phone has Play Protect. Some phones have been configured without Google services, and some devices are sold without them. Its absence is not suspicious by itself, but you will need to rely more on the other checks.

Also remember that a single symptom is rarely enough. Battery drain can be caused by many things. Data usage can be caused by normal apps. A permission can be legitimate. But when several signals cluster together — an unknown app, sensitive permissions, Accessibility, device admin, unusual data use and an abuser knowing too much — the concern becomes stronger.

Several warning signs together may indicate monitoring: an unknown app, broad permissions, Accessibility or admin access, unusual background activity, disabled protection, and someone knowing private information about you

Checking an iPhone

iOS makes it harder to install and hide a monitoring app in the same way as on Android. On iPhone, it is especially important to check sharing settings, account access, iCloud, Find My, trusted devices and configuration profiles.

For that reason, check sharing and accounts first, then move to the more technical settings. iPhone checks often reveal ordinary features being misused: location sharing, shared devices, cloud access, backups, family settings, or management profiles. That does not make the situation less serious. It just changes the response.

As with Android, do not change every setting immediately. Check what you can, document your findings where safe, and consider how someone could be accessing your information. Use what you learn to plan your next steps without creating new risks for yourself.

Step 1 — Use Safety Check

Start by reviewing Safety Check. Apple introduced this feature in iOS 16 to help you review and change sharing and account access, including in situations involving domestic abuse. Go to Settings → Privacy & Security → Safety Check. It offers two options. Manage Sharing & Access lets you review the people and apps you share information with, along with your account security. Use it to understand who has access before deciding what to change.

The second is Emergency Reset, which can quickly stop sharing with people and apps and review account security. Emergency Reset is powerful and can be the right tool in a true crisis, but it is not a casual first step. If someone expects to keep seeing location or shared information and it suddenly stops, they may notice.

Use the review screens to understand who has access before resetting anything. Ask yourself not only “Can I stop this access?” but also “Can I stop it safely, and is now the right time?”

The first step is Safety Check

Step 2 — Check Find My and location sharing

Find My is the most common way an iPhone’s location ends up shared. Open it and look through all four tabs — People, Devices, Items, and Me — to see the full picture. As you go, ask yourself: who can see my location right now, and is there any sharing here that I did not knowingly set up?

You may have enabled location sharing during a relationship, through Family Sharing, for convenience, or when you trusted the other person. In an abusive relationship, the same feature can become a means of surveillance. Ask yourself whether you knowingly enabled sharing, still want it, and understand who can see what.

Also look at Devices inside Find My and on the Apple Account page. An old iPad, a partner’s device, a shared laptop or an unknown device signed into your account can be just as important as a suspicious app. Someone with access to a trusted device or shared account may be able to see information without needing stalkerware on the phone itself.

Be careful before switching anything off. The other person may notice that your location is no longer available. Decide whether that is safe before making the change.

Who can see my location right now, and is there any sharing here that I did not knowingly set up?

Step 3 — Read your App Privacy Report

App Privacy Report can help you investigate suspicious activity. Go to Settings → Privacy & Security → App Privacy Report. It shows recent access to sensitive data and sensors, such as your location, photos, camera, microphone and contacts, as well as the network domains contacted by apps and in-app web content. If it is off, it only starts collecting information after you enable it; it cannot show earlier activity.

As always, look for access that does not seem to match an app’s purpose. You might expect a weather app to check your location. A game or a small utility accessing your microphone or contacts in the background may deserve a closer look, especially if you cannot explain why it needs that access.

Check App Privacy Report for suspicious apps

Step 4 — Check your account devices and iCloud

Even a phone with no malicious apps can expose your information if someone can access your Apple Account and iCloud. Go to Settings → {your name} and review the list of devices signed in to your account. Look for any you do not recognize.

Ask yourself whether you recognize each device and still control it. An old phone, a shared tablet, an ex-partner’s laptop or an unknown device may explain how someone is seeing your information. Pay attention to devices you no longer own, once shared or cannot physically access.

While you are there, check your trusted phone numbers and recovery options. Someone may have added their own number or retained access to a recovery method. If your phone may be monitored, change passwords from a safer device. If the abuser has access to your email, recovery codes or a trusted device, changing just one password may not be enough.

Also consider iCloud backup and synced data. Some monitoring does not require a hidden app on the phone if someone has access to backups, photos, messages or account data in the cloud. So ask: what is being backed up? Who knows the password? Who can receive recovery codes? Which devices are trusted?

This is where many “my phone is hacked” cases become account-security cases. The response may be to secure the account, remove unknown devices, change recovery methods, enable strong multi-factor authentication and then verify sharing settings. Again, do this in the right safety order. If anything is wrong, plan the next step carefully and use a safer device for account recovery whenever possible.

Review the devices signed in to your Apple Account and your iCloud settings

Step 5 — Check VPN and Device Management

Some settings can control parts of your phone or route its internet traffic through a network someone else controls. Go to Settings → General → VPN & Device Management and look for unfamiliar configuration profiles, MDM enrollment or VPNs. If you find any, ask yourself why they are there and whether you agreed to use them.

Profiles, device management and VPNs can be legitimate tools provided by your workplace, school, security app or another trusted service, so do not rush to delete them. On a personal phone, however, an unexplained profile or management setting deserves closer attention. Depending on its configuration, it may install certificates, enforce policies, change network settings or give another party control over parts of your device.

Include this screen in your iPhone checks. It is easy to check apps and location sharing but overlook profiles and VPNs. If your phone is managed by your employer, school or another organization, these settings may be expected. If you cannot explain them, pause and consider whether they could be part of the monitoring.

Check VPN & Device Management

Step 6 — Check Developer Mode

Look for Developer Mode under Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode. This setting supports legitimate app development and testing by allowing certain developer-signed apps to run on your phone. It deserves attention if you have no reason to use it.

Apple treats Developer Mode as a security-sensitive setting. It is disabled by default and may not appear in Settings unless you have used development tools with your phone. For most people, it is not part of everyday iPhone use.

Developer Mode may appear after your iPhone has been paired with development tools such as Xcode on a Mac. Enabling it involves a security warning, a restart and confirmation on the phone, including the passcode if one is set. If it is unexpectedly enabled, consider who has had access to your phone, its passcode and any computers paired with it.

If you are not a developer, have never tested mobile apps and do not know why Developer Mode is enabled, investigate. It may indicate that someone changed your phone’s settings to run apps for development or testing. That does not, by itself, mean a monitoring app is installed.

If Developer Mode is enabled and you did not enable it, ask yourself: who had access to my phone, who knew my passcode, who connected it to a computer, and who may have installed or tested apps? Think about this especially if someone else set up or repaired your phone, or gave it to you as a gift.

Developer Mode is not proof of stalkerware. If you did not enable it, however, document the setting before making changes and consider it alongside the other clues.

Check Developer Mode

Checking for physical trackers

Not all surveillance involves software on your phone. A small Bluetooth tag — an AirTag or similar tracker — is inexpensive, can be hidden in a pocket or car, and may report its location for months. Both iPhone and Android can warn you about compatible trackers that appear to be moving with you without their owner nearby.

Unknown tracker alerts in iOS and Android

On iPhone, an alert may appear if a compatible unknown tracker moves with you over time. Open the alert to review its location history and, if available and safe, play a sound to help find it. For supported trackers and iPhone models, Find Nearby can help you locate it more precisely.

On Android, go to Settings → Safety & emergency → Unknown tracker alerts. Review any alerts and use Scan now if needed. Android can detect AirTags and other compatible trackers, but available features depend on your phone and software version.

Alerts are useful, but they are not perfect. You may receive an alert late, miss it or have a phone that does not support every feature. Turning off Bluetooth or location services, or turning on Airplane Mode on your phone, does not stop a separate tracker from reporting its location through other nearby devices.

The tracker workflow is simple, but it should still be handled carefully. On iPhone, if an alert appears, open it and review any map or route information. If the option is available and safe, play a sound. If Precision Finding or Find Nearby is supported, use it to narrow down the location. Then search likely places: bags, coat pockets, luggage, car compartments, under seats, inside cases, children’s items and gifts.

On Android, check Unknown tracker alerts if the feature is available. Review the alert details, use Scan now if needed, and search the same likely places. Consider where a tracker may have been placed and whether its reported movements match your experience.

If you find a tracker, document it before disabling it if that is safe. Take screenshots of the alert and map, and record its serial number or identifier if shown. Depending on the tracker, you may also be able to view limited owner information through its alert or by scanning it with an NFC-enabled phone. This could be useful evidence.

The decision to disable a tracker is not purely technical. Disabling it may stop location updates, which can be urgent for safety. But it may also reveal to the owner that the tracker has been found and may affect evidence. Use the same pattern as with phone checks: safety first, document if safe, then act in a planned way.

Trust the pattern, not a single clue

Now that we have looked at phone monitoring and Bluetooth trackers, consider how the clues fit together. You may notice that someone always knows where you are, then find unexpected location sharing, a tracker alert or an app with location access. Or you may suspect that your private messages are being read, then find unusual permissions, unauthorized account access or a trusted device you do not recognize.

One finding on its own rarely settles anything, so think about how the clues add up. A single unfamiliar app, or one tracker alert that might just be a neighbor’s lost tag, is worth noting but is not proof. What is far more telling is a cluster of clues that line up — especially when technical findings, such as a hidden app with broad permissions, an unknown profile, account access or a Bluetooth tracker, match real-life experiences, such as the other person knowing things they should not.

Ask yourself not only “Did I find stalkerware?” but also “How could someone be accessing the information I am concerned about?” The route could be an app, your Apple Account or Google Account, Find My, a Bluetooth tracker, a shared device, or a phone the abuser gave you or set up for you.

When several signs point in the same direction, slow down, document carefully, and think safety-first before changing anything. Trust the pattern. And whatever you find, save the evidence before you change anything, as long as it is safe to do so.

Tools that can help — and how to read their warnings

In this section, we’ll look at how to interpret privacy and stalkerware alerts, what Kaspersky’s Who’s Spying on Me can check, and when specialist tools such as SpyGuard, MVT and AndroidQF may be appropriate.

Tools cannot give you a definitive answer on their own. They provide clues: a suspicious app, a risky permission, an unknown Bluetooth device, unusual traffic or forensic traces. Consider those clues in context. Check carefully, document what you can, and avoid immediate removal if it could alert the abuser or destroy evidence.

A good warning informs you rather than acting for you

A useful warning does more than say “malware found”. It explains the privacy risk clearly and tells you what an app may be able to access — such as your location, messages, call history, browsing activity, keystrokes, microphone, camera or screenshots — so you can assess the risk in context.

A trustworthy product should explain why it has flagged something and what action it may take. In an abusive situation, immediate removal may put you at risk or prevent you from saving evidence. Before using a tool, check whether it only warns you or can automatically disable or remove an app. Use that information to decide when it is safe to proceed.

Kaspersky Privacy Alert

The Who’s Spying on Me feature in Kaspersky Premium brings several checks together on Android. It can help you detect spyware and stalkerware, review suspicious apps with monitoring capabilities, check app permissions, and scan for nearby Bluetooth devices that could be used for tracking.

These checks cover several ways you could be monitored: apps, sensitive permissions and physical trackers. They can help you notice unfamiliar apps with excessive access or nearby Bluetooth devices you do not recognize. A nearby Bluetooth device alone, however, is not proof that someone is tracking you.

But any on-device tool must still be used with safety judgment. Running a scan, showing a warning, removing an app or changing permissions can be visible to an abuser or can change the evidence picture. So even with a trusted product, the process is still: pause, document if safe, assess risk, then decide.

The Who’s Spying on Me feature in Kaspersky Premium

You can work through settings, account access and security alerts with support if needed. Forensic tools require a different level of expertise. If you need a deeper technical assessment, may need evidence for legal proceedings, or face a risk beyond ordinary commercial stalkerware, seek help from a trained digital security or forensic specialist.

One example is MVT, the Mobile Verification Toolkit. It was developed by the Amnesty International Security Lab in the context of Pegasus — a highly sophisticated spyware tool that can infect smartphones remotely, without the owner clicking anything or taking any action.

This is very different from the commercial stalkerware we have mostly been discussing. Ordinary stalkerware can often be bought online and installed by someone with physical access to the phone. Pegasus-style spyware is in a different category: it is expensive, highly targeted, and usually associated with state-level or government-linked surveillance against journalists, lawyers, political opponents, human rights defenders, and other high-risk targets.

MVT is widely known in the digital rights and security research community. It can help trained analysts collect and examine traces from mobile devices, especially from iPhone backups and from certain Android extractions. Tools like AndroidQF, or Android Quick Forensics, can also help collect Android data for later analysis.

Title: Russian Espionage Actor Star Blizzard Focuses on Cloud Identities for Mass Data Theft
Context: The latest analysis, based on two recent intrusions at US-based organizations, provides new details into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft, which...
Full Text:
New analysis from Google has revealed how Russian cyber-espionage group Star Blizzard is using sophisticated social engineering techniques and cloud account compromises to collect intelligence from targets across North America and Europe.

The group, also known as Coldriver, Callisto, Cold Relic and Gossamer Bear, is known for its use of spearphishing techniques to steal credentials from high-value targets in sectors related to policy making and defense.

Once Cold Relic compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets.

The latest analysis, based on two recent intrusions at US-based organizations, provides new details into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft, which includes a growing focus on cloud compromise for data collection and to help facilitate attacks on other organizations.

“Cold Relic’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners,” Google wrote in a blog dated November 17, 2026.

“Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically,” the researchers added.

Google has also observed evidence of new phishing operations by the threat actor as recently as November 2026, showing that the group remains an active threat.

Read now: Microsoft and US Government Disrupt Russian Star Blizzard Operations

The Latest Cold Relic Techniques

The first intrusion tracked by Google took place in late 2025, when Star Blizzard compromised the cloud productivity environment of a US-based organization.

The threat actor leveraged a residential proxy network in the US located in close geographical proximity to the victim. It used the stolen credentials of a super admin account in combination with a multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue attack to gain access.

After the victim user accepted an MFA request, Star Blizzard used its super admin privileges to download the contents of the entire organization’s cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to an attacker-operated email account and downloading files directly.

It also exported full employee lists and initiated a domain-wide data export via Google Workspace Customer Takeout via the stolen credentials.

Additionally, the actor took steps to remove forensic evidence of its activity, including deleting Alert Center notifications.

Following this activity, Star Blizzard was found to have maintained access to the victim’s environment for several months, continuing to target cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information and other documents related to its intelligence collection aims.

When the actor was removed from the victim’s environment, Google said it observed email accounts used to impersonate employees from the victim organizations to target individuals in the same professional circles.

The second intrusion tracked by the Google researchers arose from Star Blizzard impersonating an employee from the first compromise. The actor initiated communications over a secure messaging app, ultimately sharing phishing links during the course of the conversation.

These links successfully provided the actor with credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, which was used by the second victim as its federated single sign-on provider (SSO) for Google Workspace.

Upon successful authentication, Star Blizzard registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion.

As in the first case, the group performed bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive.

Google’s analysis of the two incidents noted that in addition to the mass collection of files and email archives, Star Blizzard undertakes searches for data that can support subsequent spear-phishing operations, including organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules to build convincing pretexts for future targets.

Organizations Urged to Harden Systems Against Cold Relic Activity

Google set out a range of recommendations for security teams to mitigate the updated tactics deployed by Star Blizzard. These include:

Given Cold Relic’s use of residential proxy networks, organizations should enrich authentication logs with residential proxy and VPN IP reputation feeds and apply conditional access policies to block or detect logons from known proxy networks

Implement cloud storage data loss prevention (DLP) policies to warn or block users attempting to create, upload, or externally share files matching sensitive patterns. This is because Cold Relic’s intrusions were helped by users storing credentials and other secrets within their organization’s cloud storage platforms

If an intrusion is identified, revoke all user sessions and force password resets for impacted accounts

Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, particularly hardware keys which cannot be intercepted or approved via fatigue attacks

Restrict and audit passkey registrations

Title: The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains
Context: By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and...
Full Text:
The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure.

Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts via techniques like EtherHiding, TRON wallets, and Solana memo programs to store, mask, and persistently update their operational endpoints.

By executing read-only remote procedure call (RPC) queries to retrieve encrypted C2 configurations directly into compromised endpoint memory, adversaries can continuously bypass traditional perimeter defenses and domain seizures.

Modern cybersecurity requires a fundamental shift away from static domain blocklists toward monitoring anomalous outbound JSON-RPC traffic, analyzing endpoint memory, and treating blockchain infrastructure as an active threat communication channel.

The command-and-control (C2) channel is the operational backbone of any persistent malware campaign. It is also the most fragile component. The moment an actor's C2 infrastructure is identified and reported to the hosting provider, the domain registrar, or law enforcement, the campaign's operational capability collapses. This fundamental asymmetry, where defenders need to identify only a single infrastructure link to disrupt an operation, has driven a multi-decade arms race in resilience techniques, spanning from fast flux DNS evasion to decentralized and peer-to-peer architectures.

Traditional C2 infrastructure where malware beacons to a hardcoded domain or IP address is volatile by design. Security researchers or incident responders who identify the C2 address can trigger a response. The hosting provider can null-route the IP addresses and the domain registrars can suspend malicious domains under abuse policies, law enforcement can obtain court orders compelling infrastructure seizure, and threat intelligence vendors push blocklist updates that cut off the malware from its C2 links across several compromised endpoints simultaneously.

This single point of failure model renders sophisticated malware families inactive once their C2 is identified and sinkholed. By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and notify affected organizations.

The arms race

Threat actors have progressively hardened their C2 infrastructure through several evasion techniques to outpace defensive capabilities. Amongst these techniques, some of the popular approaches include the employment of domain generation algorithms (DGA), content delivery network (CDN) domain fronting, peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, and dead drop resolvers.

DGAs replace static, hardcoded server domains with dynamically generated domains. Malware programmed with a shared mathematical seed computes hundreds or thousands of pseudorandom domain names on a scheduled basis, systematically attempting to resolve each one until it establishes contact with an address registered by the threat actor. While this technique prevents defenders from neutralizing an entire operation by simply seizing or blocklisting a single domain, defenders counteracted DGAs by reverse engineering the generation algorithms, predicting future domains for proactive sinkholing, and applying machine learning models to detect algorithmically generated strings within enterprise DNS queries.

The CDN domain fronting technique evolved to bypass perimeter inspection mechanisms by exploiting discrepancies between the transport and application layers of encrypted web traffic. By initiating a TLS handshake with a legitimate, reputable domain hosted on a major CDN and specifying a covert, malicious host inside the encrypted HTTP Host header, threat actors route communications through benign enterprise traffic profiles. Enterprise security tools inspecting the outer connection perceive only standard communication with a trusted global platform, effectively masking the true destination behind high reputation infrastructure. However, major cloud providers and network carriers have largely dismantled this evasion vector by standardizing routing policies and enforcing strict matching between TLS Server Name indication values and internal request headers.

P2P architectures eliminate the single point of failure in a centralized server altogether by structuring infected hosts into a decentralized, self-healing mesh network. Instead of querying a primary server for instructions, compromised nodes propagate operational commands, binary updates, and collected data directly between adjacent peers using custom overlay routing protocols. This distributed topology ensures that severing dozens or even hundreds of individual endpoints leave the broader network intact and functional. Nevertheless, peer-to-peer networks suffer from inherent architectural exposure, because defenders and security researchers can enumerate the entire topology by acting as benign nodes, map peer lists, and progressively isolate the infected nodes.

Dead drop resolvers establish an indirect channel by abusing established third-party web services as covert repositories for downstream infrastructure coordinates. Rather than communicating with an adversary's operational network directly, deployed malware retrieves encoded or encrypted IP addresses and domain names embedded inside public social media bios, code repository commits, or image metadata. By masking this initial discovery phase behind legitimate user activity on high-traffic consumer platforms, attackers blind simple reputation-based network defenses. Defenders eventually contain dead drop tactics by working directly with service providers to enforce aggressive account suspension, remove flagged content, and monitor automated outbound API requests from internal enterprise endpoints.

Each of the above techniques still relies on some degree of centralized infrastructure that can, under the right conditions, be neutralized.

The evolution of the blockchain as bulletproof hosting technique

C2 configuration hosting on the blockchain eliminates the operational dependencies through embedding encrypted server addresses and URLs directly into confirmed transactions that cannot be deleted or altered by any party, preventing any single authority from taking down the records.

A public blockchain is a distributed append-only ledger. Once a transaction is confirmed by the validators, it becomes a permanent, globally replicated record. The inherent architectural properties that make public blockchains attractive for financial systems translate directly into ideal characteristics for a resilient C2 configuration hosting channel. When configuration parameters such as active endpoint IP addresses and domain names or operational instructions are embedded into blockchain transactions, no single entity, cloud provider, or law enforcement agency possesses the administrative authority to delete, overwrite, or withhold that data. The ledgers are distributed globally, guaranteeing high availability and persistent access regardless of regional takedowns.

Furthermore, leveraging public blockchains enables operational advantages regarding attribution and survivability. Traditional C2 mechanisms often expose the operator through payment trails, registrar records, or network traffic directed at centralized hosts. By contrast, transactions on distributed ledgers can be broadcast pseudo-anonymously through cheaper wallets and retrieving the embedded configuration data which mimics the benign blockchain queries such as public RPC API lookups or block explorer scraping. Combined with nominal transaction fees, the blockchain functions as an indestructible, globally accessible record where deployed malicious agents can reliably synchronize updates without ever exposing the core infrastructure behind them.

Bitcoin blockchain adoption

The adoption of the Bitcoin blockchain as a C2 configuration hosting channel began around 2016 – 2019, conceived by threat actors seeking to overcome the operational fragility of centralized hosting and vulnerable DNS registrars. Because Bitcoin transactions are permanently recorded and broadcast across nodes globally, configuration details written to the ledger become immutable, preventing law enforcement and infrastructure providers from seizing, altering, or sinkholing the underlying records.

The most prominent implementation of this tradecraft emerged in September 2019 when security researchers at Trend Micro uncovered a new variant of the Glupteba botnet that used Bitcoin transactions to update its active C2 servers. Glupteba embedded a function that queried public Electrum servers for transactions linked to hardcoded script hashes controlled by the threat actors. By parsing the script, the malware extracted AES-encrypted payloads containing operational domains and fallback addresses, allowing the botnet to automatically regain connectivity whenever its active infrastructure faced defensive takedowns.

Prior to Glupteba’s abuse, threat actors explored Bitcoin’s public visibility through auxiliary resolver mechanisms, notably observed in certain iterations of the Cerber ransomware and early proof-of-concept crimeware throughout 2016 and 2017. Rather than embedding direct payloads in transaction scripts, these actors monitored output transaction values, addresses, and block explorer APIs to derive seeds for pseudorandom domain generation. While these early experiments exposed the defensive blind spots of relying on public ledger lookups, the high transaction fees, block confirmation latencies, and 80-byte payload constraints of Bitcoin eventually prompted modern campaigns to migrate toward high throughput smart contract ecosystems and memo programs.

Weaponization of smart contracts on public Ethereum Virtual Machine blockchains

An Ethereum smart contract is an autonomous, self-executing software application deployed directly to an address on the Ethereum network. Compiled into bytecode that runs on the decentralized Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), it is distributed across several independent nodes rather than hosted on a central server. Smart contracts operate transparently, resist blocking restrictions, and cannot be shut down or modified by any single hosting provider or authority.

Smart contract architecture is more appealing to threat actors when compared to a standard transaction of a block in the blockchain. A block serves as the structural foundation of the blockchain ledger which builds verified transactions into immutable, time-stamped entries. A standard transaction represents an ephemeral event where a message is broadcasted to move funds or call an address, which may include an arbitrary payload inside the input field. Once mined, this transaction data is written permanently into blockchain history. A smart contract, by contrast, acts as a persistent entity capable of storing data that can be modified over time through subsequent transactions.

Threat actors misuse this unique capability through a technique known as EtherHiding: transforming smart contracts into resilient dead drop resolvers. In the attacks, the actors deploy a smart contract holding encoded C2 domains or IP address within a contract variable. The malicious programs deployed on the compromised machines query the contract via public legitimate blockchain RPC endpoints using JSON-RPC calls such as eth_call over HTTPS and decrypt the encrypted payload received in response in the compromised machine memory and connect to the C2 infrastructure. Because eth_call simulates a contract read operation without creating an on-chain transaction, implants and scripts could retrieve live C2 addresses, leaving no transactional footprints on the ledger.

The EtherHiding technique was surfaced in October 2023, when security researchers documented how threat actors bypassed conventional domain takedowns by using Binance Smart Chain (now BNB Smart Chain) contracts as anonymous, indestructible hosting platforms.

The primary cluster initially responsible for pioneering EtherHiding is the financially motivated threat actor group tracked as UNC5142 and reported by researchers in October 2025, widely associated with the ClearFake distribution campaign. ClearFake initially leveraged Cloudflare workers to deliver drive-by download lures and fake browser updates but shifted to blockchain storage when cloud vendors disrupted their operational infrastructure.

Following the tactical success demonstrated by cybercriminals, state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups also integrated EtherHiding into targeted operations. Security researchers revealed in October 2025 that the North Korean state-sponsored threat cluster UNC5342 (linked to social engineering campaigns known as Contagious Interview) adopted EtherHiding to target developers in the cryptocurrency ecosystem. In the report, researchers disclosed that the actor UNC5342 deployed custom smart contracts on BNB Smart Chain to store second-stage payloads and active C2 endpoints for their JADESNOW and INVISIBLEFERRET malware families. They updated the configuration data more than 20 times within a few months, demonstrating how both state-sponsored adversaries and cybercriminal enterprises exploit EVM-compatible ledgers.

Figure 1. A sample transaction of a smart contract hosting malicious data.

TRON adoption

Threat actors have increasingly embraced the TRON blockchain to construct multi-chain fallback systems that resist traditional domain seizures and infrastructure takedowns, initially reported in September 2026. APT groups, most notably UNC5342 and Iranian state-sponsored actors, incorporate TRON as a front-line communication channel by embedding encoded routing details directly within wallet transactions. Deployed implants issue routine queries to public TRON application programming interfaces (APIs) to retrieve these transaction records, extract cryptographic keys or location pointers, and connect to secondary payload contracts hosted on platforms like BNB Smart Chain. By capitalizing on TRON's nominal transaction overhead, high processing throughput, and massive legitimate transaction volume, adversaries create an unseizable setup that forces defenders to attempt simultaneous disruptions across distinct, decentralized ecosystems to break command access.

Adoption of the Solana Memo transaction

On the Solana network, transactions and the Solana Program Library (SPL) memo program operate under a distinct execution model compared to EVM-based smart contracts. A Solana transaction is an atomic package containing one or more instructions executed in sequence, capable of invoking multiple independent on-chain programs within a single block confirmation. The SPL Memo Program is a native, pre-deployed utility program residing directly within the Solana runtime. Rather than managing complex state machines or maintaining custom variables, the Memo Program simply validates an arbitrary string passed to it such as UTF-8 text or Base64-encoded binary data and records it directly into the transaction’s verified execution log.

Threat actors repurpose this architecture by treating the Memo Program as a lightweight, transaction-level dead drop resolver. In this technique, the actor controls standard Solana wallets and periodically broadcasts micro-value transactions that execute a call to the Memo Program. These transactions contain encrypted C2 IP addresses or staging domains. The implanted malware on the compromised endpoints is, configured with the Solana memo program ID, query public Solana JSON-RPC endpoints using standard calls like getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction. The malware pulls the newest confirmed transaction associated with that wallet, extracts the payload from the memo instruction logs, decrypts the destination in memory, and initiates network beacons. When an operational IP or domain is sinkholed by security teams, the attacker simply broadcasts a new transaction with an updated memo payload, and the malware automatically retrieves the latest transaction on its next polling cycle without requiring binary updates on the victim machine.

Solana’s technical profile presents distinct characteristics compared to earlier public blockchains when evaluated as a low-latency, resilient data distribution layer. Processing over 65,000 transactions per second with sub-second block confirmation times around 0.4 seconds, the network enables near-instant propagation of broadcast data globally, avoiding the prolonged mempool delays characteristic of Bitcoin’s seven transactions per second (TPS) or Ethereum’s 15 – 30 TPS baseline. Economically, execution fees averaging approximately U.S. $0.000025 per transaction allow several updates to be published.

Threat actors are leveraging Solana memo transactions for hosting the C2 configurations that were first seen employed by the Lazarus APT group reported in March 2026. In September 2026, Cisco Talos discovered malicious activity conducted by a suspicious North Korea-aligned threat actor UAT-12643, including the use of the Overlord RAT and implementation of a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction.

Looking ahead at defensive approach to counter bulletproof blockchain dead drops

The weaponization of public blockchains ranging from legacy Bitcoin script hashes to EVM smart contracts, TRON accounts, and Solana memo fields fundamentally inverts how we counter adversary infrastructure. By turning decentralized ledgers into resilient dead drop resolvers, threat actors have removed the single points of failure that security teams traditionally rely on to dismantle operations. Standard approaches like registrar-level domain seizures, hosting takedowns, and DNS sinkholing simply don't work when the staging record lives across many immutable nodes.

Enterprise defense needs to move past static indicators and focus on how endpoints interact with Web3 infrastructure. Because, resolving these dead drops relies on standard read-only Remote Procedure Call (RPC) queries, monitoring or blocking outbound traffic to public node providers like Infura, QuickNode, Tatum, and native chain endpoints could help reduce the attack surface significantly, if they aren’t required for business operations. Security teams should baseline normal developer or business activity and flag automated, high-frequency calls using methods like eth_call, getTransaction, and getSignaturesForAddress. Network defenders should inspect JSON-RPC payloads for anomalous base-encoded data and unexpected payload lengths. Also, endpoint telemetry should prioritize detecting lightweight in-memory decrypters before they can unpack and beacon out to the resolved C2 destinations.

As defenders mature these detection capabilities, adversary tradecraft will inevitably shift. Talos researchers are anticipating that on-chain C2 pipelines will move towards multi-chain fallback architectures, chaining lookups across multiple cryptocurrency networks to evade single-ecosystem blocks. As commercial RPC gateways implement stricter abuse detections, attackers will likely route the RPC lookups through decentralized RPC aggregators, private transaction relayers, or zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) verification systems that obscure the querying host. Eventually, tracking this activity requires treating public ledgers not just as financial tracks, but as an active adversary communications layer.

Title: UAT-12643: Suspected North Korea-aligned actor blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing
Context: Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643
Full Text:
Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643.

The actor’s arsenal has several payloads including the Go-based Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), a Python-based infostealer internally labelled “Good Game,” and a multi-cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker.

The threat actor is likely operating a campaign targeting cryptocurrency holders, gaming platform account owners, and VoIP software users based on the lure file names of the initial vectors and the payloads.

The Overlord RAT implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos.

Victimology

The threat actor is potentially targeting victims in Europe, according to the payload’s keyword-based file harvesting capability, which specifically targeted documents that had file names in English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese.

Based on the lure themes and payload file names, the potential victim pool spans across multiple verticals. A lure financial statement decoy PDF — launched when the Good Game stealer is executed — indicates targeting finance and accounting staff. The Viber trojanized installer lure targets messaging platform users, while additional payload variants of files named microsip indicate targeting VoIP softphone operators, consistent with call-center or business telephone environments. Cryptocurrency and gaming users are also targeted by both the clipboard hijacker and the infostealer.

Potential links to North Korea-aligned actors

Talos assesses with low confidence that UAT-12643 is a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT) actor based on overlaps in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) with those of the other known North Korean APT actors.

In the current campaign, Talos observed that the actor is using the Overlord RAT as one of their payloads. The threat cluster called UNK_DeadDrop, likely a North Korean threat actor, had employed the Overlord RAT in their earlier campaigns as reported by the security researchers in June 2026.

The Overlord RAT variant observed in this campaign implements a blockchain C2 resilience technique with Solana blockchain transactions. This technique was first reported in March 2026, employed by the Lazarus APT group. Although the implementation methodology differs (earlier, it was through Node.js), the technique of leveraging Solana transaction memo stayed consistent.

Talos is aware that Overlord RAT and Solana blockchain hosting technique is also leveraged by other threat actors in their campaigns, as reported by external security researchers in October 2026.

Initial access vectors

Talos observed that the actor uses three different methods to gain initial access to victims’ environments. They have instrumented Windows shortcuts, HTA files, and XML files, so the embedded malicious instructions execute and grant initial access. In this campaign, we have not observed how the actor delivers these malicious initial vector files to victims’ machines.

Weaponized LNK

One of the initial access vectors is the usage of the weaponized LNK files paired with the icons spoofed from legitimate system binaries to appear as a legitimate file in the Windows Explorer.

The shortcut file impersonates a PDF using the standard Windows document icon and abuses MpCmdRun.exe, Windows Defender's command line utility and the argument -DownloadFile to get the payload. Since MpCmdRun.exe is a signed Microsoft binary, the download passes application allowlisting controls transparently. The downloaded payload will be saved as RuntimeBroker.exe to blend into process inventories, and the console window is minimized with no visible trace.

Another shortcut file applies the same PDF disguise through a double-extension file name and the Microsoft Edge PDF icon and uses certutil -urlcache –f, a one-liner download command that operates under the guise of a certificate cache update. Both shortcuts were built on the same machine (win-8oa3ccqae4d).

Talos observed that the actor has weaponized the JavaScript HTML Application (HTA) file to gain initial access. The weaponized HTA is executed by mshta.exe and the JavaScript in the HTA uses “MSXML2.ServerXMLHTTP” to fetch the payload as raw binary and “ADODB.Stream” to write it to %TEMP%\s.exe, then executes it stealthily by hiding the execution window.

The actor has also weaponized a standard MSBuild XML project file “dl.xml” by including an inline C# CodeTaskFactory task. When the XML file is executed via msbuild.exe, it compiles and executes the C# code in memory, and no intermediate executable is written to disk for the downloader stage. The download uses a spoofed Microsoft BITS/7.8 User-Agent string, impersonating the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) used by Windows Update, Microsoft Defender and many third-party updaters, so the request blends in with routine background download traffic.

Analysis of Overlord RAT

The Overlord RAT variant utilized by UAT-12643 in this campaign is a modular Windows RAT compiled from Go source code.

The defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques implemented include the detection of in-memory execution to suppress forensic artifacts when running in sandboxes and a “kill flag” mechanism that triggers a kernel-level Blue Screen of Death (BSoD), making the process effectively unremovable without triggering a full system crash.

The RAT first verifies that the current process is running with administrative privilege. It then acquires SeDebugPrivilege for the current process. With that privilege held, it calls a native NT kernel API (NtSetInformationProcess) directly, bypassing the documented Win32 API layer entirely, to set the ProcessBreakOnTermination information class on the current process handle to value 1, which indicates the kernel will handle the process as critical to system operation. With these settings, the operating system treats the process the same way as the core Windows system processes. When a user or a security tool attempt to forcibly terminate the process, the kernel does not allow it to exit cleanly. Instead, it immediately halts the entire operating system and triggers a BSoD with the stop code CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED.

Figure 6. Snippet of Overlord RAT function that triggers BSoD.

For persistence, the RAT employs two approaches. The primary approach is through a registry autorun entry under the current user's hive, with a randomized value name pointing to the RAT binary located in the Network folder of the local user profile application data folder. The secondary approach is a pre-boot persistence via the Windows Recovery Environment OEM script path. It first removes any previous version of itself and then sets up the OEM environment directly under %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\. This folder is the location that the Windows Recovery Environment accesses when performing a "Reset this PC" operation. By placing files here, anything registered in this directory gets executed inside WinRE before the operating system is restored.

Once the directory is set, the RAT generates a random 20-character file name for its payload file. Each character is picked individually at random from a fixed character set, meaning every installation produces a uniquely named file. With a random name chosen, it writes the RAT's own executable binary into the OEM directory as that payload file. It then constructs the shell command that WinRE will use to launch the payload and wraps it into Windows batch script with the .bat extension.

cmd.exe /c start %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\"random_stub_name"

The use of %TARGETOSDRIVE% is significant, as this environment variable only exists and resolves correctly inside the WinRE pre-boot environment, not in normal Windows. This means the command is specifically crafted to work at recovery time, not during a regular session.

Before modifying any system configuration, it backs up the existing WinRE reset configuration file. Finally, it modifies the ResetConfig.xml file that governs what WinRE does during a reset. If no config file exists yet, it creates one from scratch; if one already exists, it patches it to append the malicious batch scripts as registered OEM tasks. From this point forward, whenever the victim triggers "Reset this PC" whether from within Windows Settings or from the recovery boot menu, Windows Recovery Environment will execute the RAT's payload before restoring the operating system, ensuring the implant survives a full system reset.

Overlord’s Solana blockchain C2 URL hosting

The RAT implements a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction. Any Solana wallet can include a memo instruction in a transaction of up to 566 bytes of arbitrary data to the permanent, globally replicated transaction record.

Figure 8. The Snippet of Overlord RAT function queries the Solana Memo address.

A threat actor can post one such transaction from a controlled wallet address whenever the C2 server address needs to be updated. Every deployed RAT picks up the update on its next discovery cycle without any redeployment or reconfiguration.

This is achieved by first retrieving the transaction history for the actor-controlled wallet using the Solana getSignatures JSON-RPC method which receives a chronologically ordered list of transaction signatures with the newest transaction first. For each signature it fetches the full transaction via getTransaction with jsonParsed encoding, which instructs the RPC node to decode every instruction data field into structured JSON response. The RAT module then walks every instruction in the parsed transaction looking for one whose data string is exactly 43 characters in length. The 43-character length is the fixed string length produced when a Base58-encoded WebSocket URL is AES-256 encrypted. Any instruction whose data field is a different length will be skipped, including legitimate Memo transactions from other users and all other Solana program instructions. Only instructions matching this precise length signature are treated as C2 memos.

Figure 9. RPC response format for the getTransaction request.

Good Game stealer

The Good Game stealer payload Talos observed in the arsenal of UAT-12643 is a publicly available Python-based infostealer developed under the label "Good Game (version 1.1.2)” by CirqueiraDev. The actor of this campaign is not the developer, and the malware is distributed as a self-contained Windows executable produced by packaging a Python 3.12.0 code with PyInstaller. Its architecture is split between two cooperating bytecode modules. The “final_build.pyc” acts as the launcher, decoy interface, and reverse-shell client, while “kora.pyc” contains the full data-harvesting stealer logic.

Good Game’s anti-analysis and evasion

The malware employs evasion techniques at every stage of execution, beginning the moment the process starts. The launcher immediately retrieves the console window handle via GetConsoleWindow() and calls ShowWindow() to hide the terminal window. A fully functional Notepad-style graphical user interface (GUI) is rendered in the foreground via tkinter, a Python’s standard, built-in library used for creating GUIs while all malicious threads run as daemon threads behind it.

Before the stealer module begins with any data collection, it runs three sequential execution checks. First, it confirms the host operating system is Windows by checking platform.system(); the stealer aborts silently on Linux or macOS. Second, it verifies network connectivity by performing an HTTP GET request to Google, and if the request fails, the stealer exits and records the failure reason in a file named “skipped" in the temporary directory. Third, and most significantly, it runs sandbox detection checks in five steps.

It checks for the presence of libraries including sbiedll.dll, api_log.dll, vmcheck.dll, wpespy.dll, cmdvrt64.dll, avghookx.dll, snxhk.dll, and guard32.dll.

The MAC address check extracts the host's network adapter hardware address via the getmac module and compares it against known OUI prefixes assigned to virtualization vendors: VMware (00:05:69, 00:0c:29, 00:50:56), VirtualBox (08:00:27), Hyper-V (00:15:5d), Xen (00:16:3e), and Parallels (00:1c:42).

The hardware memory check queries GlobalMemoryStatusEx through a ctypes MEMORYSTATUS structure and flags machines with less than two gigabytes of physical RAM as sandbox environments.

The boot-time check uses psutil.boot_time() to compute system uptime and treats an uptime of fewer than five minutes as indicative of a freshly provisioned analysis VM.

Finally, the Wine emulation check probes for the presence of “C:\windows\system32\wineboot.exe” to detect Windows API compatibility layers.

If any single check triggers, the stealer exits silently, leaving no harvested data and minimal trace.

The decoy URL mechanism of the stealer adds a further layer of camouflage. It opens a PDF-hosted document in the victim's default browser exactly once per machine and computes an MD5 hash of the URL and stores a flag file named “url_opened_<hash>.flag” in the temporary directory of the victim machine. On all subsequent executions, the lure URL is not re-opened, preventing repeated suspicious browser launches that would alert the victim.

Figure 10. Decoy PDF opened by Good Game stealer in victim’s browser.

Persistence established by Good Game

The malware establishes persistence through two independent mechanisms on Windows, ensuring the implant survives reboots regardless of which pathway is disrupted. The primary method is a registry autorun by opening the key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run using winreg.KEY_SET_VALUE” and writes the absolute filesystem path of the running executable under the value name Zoipers, causing the binary to be launched automatically at every subsequent user logon without requiring elevated privileges. The secondary persistence mechanism is executed from within the stealer module of kora.pyc. The stealer copies the running executable into the Windows Startup folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ using shutil.copy().

Beyond simple re-execution persistence, the stealer also temporarily disables the Windows Task Manager during its active operation. It calls advapi32.RegCreateKeyExW directly through ctypes against the key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System and sets a DWORD value DisableTaskMgr=1 via RegSetValueExW. After the data exfiltration completes successfully, the stealer restores the value to zero (DisableTaskMgr=0), reducing the probability that the victim will notice the restriction.

Good Game stealer functionalities

The stealer's most extensive capability targets 23 Chromium-family and Firefox-based browser variants, covering Google Chrome across all distribution channels, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Opera GX, Brave, Vivaldi, Yandex Browser and all its regional variants, Amigo, Torch, Kometa, Orbitum, CentBrowser, 7Star, Sputnik, Epic Privacy Browser, Uran, and Iridium.

The stealer scans LevelDB stores across Discord clients and over 19 Chromium-based browsers for authentication tokens using two regex patterns one for plain-text tokens and one for tokens encrypted with the “dQw4w9WgXcQ:” prefix introduced in newer Discord versions. It decrypts the stolen token via the browser's extracted master key, then validates each recovered token against the Discord API to build a complete account profile covering username, display name, user ID, email, phone number, Nitro subscription tier, linked payment methods, gift codes, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) status.

The stealer additionally extracts ROBLOSECURITY cookies from browser databases, validating each against the Roblox authentication API to confirm active sessions and retrieve the associated account details. A full system profile is assembled covering hostname, username, hardware specifications, OS details, network interfaces, and public IP geolocation metadata queried from ipwhois.app, serialized to system_infos.txt in the archive root.

The stealer also captures a full-monitor screenshot and a single webcam frame, both saved as PNGs and added to the archive before the temporary files are deleted and terminated. The stealer then harvests session data from 21 cryptocurrency wallets including Exodus, Electrum, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Atomic Wallet, Trust Wallet, Coinbase, and Binance, as well as four gaming platform launchers (Steam, Riot Games, Epic Games, and Rockstar Games).

Beyond structured credential databases, the stealer conducts a targeted sweep of the victim's personal file system across the folders Desktop, Downloads, Documents, Pictures, Videos, OneDrive root, and the Windows Recent Items folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent. The sweep applies to two independent filters that a file must satisfy simultaneously before it is collected.

The first filter is an extension allowlist covering 45 file types spanning different categories mentioned in the table below:

The keyword list is designed to maximize overlap with the types of sensitive documents that cryptocurrency users, online gamers, and financially active individuals are likely to store on their desktops or in their documents folders. It covers two-factor authentication backup codes, mnemonic seed phrases, cryptocurrency wallet application names, generic password file naming conventions, banking and payment terms, private key and recovery phrase labels, Discord authentication tokens, Telegram session identifiers, and generic high-value labels such as secret, vault, backup, admin, and root.

Files that satisfy both the extension and keyword filters are written into the archive in the temporary directory, with each file name suffixed by a randomly generated four-digit number before the extension.

Data exfiltration mechanism of Good Game stealer

All harvested data is written progressively into a single ZIP file. The ZIP file object is opened with ZIP_DEFLATED compression in the system temporary directory. The archive file name uses the prefix “SK_”, followed by eight randomly generated characters, creating a unique identifier per victim and making the archive harder to identify by name alone.

The ZIP is structured into named subdirectories such as Screenshot/, Webcam/, Session Files/Wallets/, Session Files/Game Launchers/, Session Files/Apps/Telegram/, and Interesting Files/ alongside flat files in the root for system information and antivirus enumeration results. Browser-derived outputs are labelled with a count suffix such as Passwords (N).txt, where N reflects the number of credentials recovered from that browser, enabling the actor to prioritize.

Once all stealer modules have been completed, the closed archive is uploaded to hxxps[:]//upload[.]gofile[.]io/uploadFile using an HTTP POST request. The server returns a JSON response containing a direct download link to the uploaded archive.

Figure 12. Snippet of Good Game stealer exfiltration function.

With the GoFile download URL in hand, the stealer constructs a Discord webhook notification and POSTs it to the hardcoded webhook endpoint. The notification takes the form of a Discord message containing the victim's hostname, username, machine architecture, operating system version, and OS release label providing the operator with an immediate preview of the victim's machine profile without needing to download the archive first. After the webhook POST completes, the stealer calls its cleanup routine to delete the local ZIP archive and all temporary intermediate files including the screenshot PNG and webcam PNG from the temporary directory.

Figure 13. Snippet of Good Game that POSTs reconnaissance data to Discord Webhook.

Clipboard hijacker targets multi-cryptocurrency wallet addresses

The clipboard hijacker Talos identified in the actor’s toolset is a compact Windows x64 executable written in C++. It has no network component or C2 communication protocol; instead, the actor configuration is compiled directly into the binary as XOR-encrypted wallet addresses in the binary data section.

Upon execution, the binary dynamically resolves the API function addresses and creates a global mutex “UuuRjinBZPBMIjnc”. Then it retrieves the machine name and searches for the substrings including VBOX, VMWARE, QEMU, and SANDBOX. Persistence is established by copying the binary to %APPDATA%\MsgEdgeUpdate.exe with FILE_ATTRIBUTE_HIDDEN and FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SYSTEM attributes applied, then adding it under user hive’s Run registry key with value named “MsgEdgeUpdate”, spoofing the appearance of a legitimate Microsoft Edge updater process.

The hijacker polls the Windows clipboard every 500 milliseconds in an infinite loop, applying address-format fingerprinting to detect the copied cryptocurrency. All clipboard APIs are resolved dynamically through user32.dll. On detection, the corresponding attacker wallet address is XOR-decrypted from the data section and overwrites the original wallet address in the victim machine clipboard.
