Title: Optimizely Attack Shows Why Supply Chain Ownership Matters
Context: Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and...
Full Text:
TL;DR

Malicious JavaScript added to Optimizely projects reached sites across multiple industries, including technology, finance, retail, and media.

The injected JavaScript could swap cryptocurrency addresses, capture payment card information entered into website forms, collect some browser-accessible data, and attempt to deliver iOS exploit chains.

Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and secured affected accounts.

Organizations using Optimizely should review project code and account access, investigate relevant logs, and assess potential exposure based on how their sites handled payment and session data.

The Optimizely incident shows how a change in one shared service can reach many organizations through software they already trust.

On November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of websites using Optimizely Web Experimentation. Report URI identified 188 infected snippets across 178 organizations, including major technology, media, retail, financial services, and travel companies.

A Shared Service Became a Shared Risk

Optimizely lets customers add custom JavaScript to their projects. In this incident, malicious code was placed in a project's custom-code field. The altered snippet was then delivered as part of the site's normal Optimizely integration, so the change did not have to pass through each customer's source repository or software build.

An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. Optimizely fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code, secured affected accounts, and added protections against unauthorized code delivery.

This was not a case of attackers changing a customer's application source code or poisoning the CDN cache. The code was added to project settings and delivered as part of a service those websites relied on. An organization can secure its own code and infrastructure while still depending on external services that influence what reaches users.

The Payload Turned Shared Dependence Into Shared Exposure

The injected code used a loader to bring additional JavaScript into the page. Researchers observed multiple loader versions, including one that obscured the external address and another that carried an inline fallback.

That meant blocking one destination alone might not remove every way the code could run.

The payload combined several behaviors:

Cryptocurrency address swapping: The script could replace cryptocurrency addresses in page content and during copy actions, potentially redirecting transfers. Transactions to attacker-controlled wallets were confirmed.

Payment-card skimming: The code looked for card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes submitted through site-controlled forms. It could not access card fields inside cross-origin payment-provider iframes. The available reporting does not establish how many card details were captured.

Browser data collection: The script could send page URLs, screenshots, and cookies available to JavaScript. Cookies marked HttpOnly are not available through document.cookie.

iOS exploit delivery: On Apple mobile devices, the script attempted to load Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. Researchers have not established how many devices, if any, were successfully compromised.

The confirmed cryptocurrency transactions show that at least one part of the operation had financial impact.

These capabilities show why teams need to understand not only what code a service is expected to run, but also what that code can access and how changes to it are controlled.

Integrity and Intelligence Must Cover the Full Path

Component intelligence helps teams identify the software they use, understand its role, and assess its known risks. Artifact integrity addresses a different question: whether the software moving through development and delivery is still the expected artifact. Both matter because organizations need context about their components and confidence in what they build and distribute.

The Optimizely incident exposes a gap between those controls and what happens in production. The malicious code was added through a third-party project setting and delivered to visitors' browsers. It did not need to enter a customer's source repository or change a locally built artifact. A package inventory or artifact check would not, by itself, show whether a vendor-managed script had changed.

That doesn't make component intelligence or artifact integrity less relevant. It means organizations need to understand the scope of each control and account for the code paths it does not cover. Alongside knowing which components enter software and verifying the artifacts teams release, organizations need visibility into the external services that can change code running on their sites.

Software Supply Chain Ownership Is an Operating Model

Organizations using Optimizely Web should consult Optimizely's incident update for current information and use their project and access records to determine whether their sites were affected.

More broadly, this incident shows why responsibility for software inputs and services needs to be shared across development, platform, security, and web teams. Those teams need a common understanding of what their software depends on, how those dependencies reach production, and who is accountable for changes along the way.

Owning the software supply chain means understanding what is being shipped and what external code can become part of the software customers use. Component intelligence, artifact integrity, and runtime visibility each help address a different part of that responsibility. Title: 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat
Borrowed Code, Real Consequences: What OPTIMJACK Teaches Us
Context: 16, 2026, a threat actor exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer accounts
Full Text:
Introduction

On Nov. 16, 2026, a threat actor exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer accounts. Nicknamed OPTIMJACK, this campaign delivered that code to visitors of at least 178 organizations' websites.

The tampered code was delivered directly from the vendor's legitimate content delivery network (CDN), under the vendor's own security certificate.

Enterprises invest heavily in hardening their core web infrastructure. A single compromised third-party tool can undermine that work. OPTIMJACK is a reminder that any vendor script with dynamic execution privileges on your site is part of your direct production code.

Threat actors know that third-party apps are the path of least resistance into lucrative environments. Defenders can respond with a fundamental principle that security engineering has relied on from the beginning: segmentation.

What Happened in OPTIMJACK

On Nov. 16th, 2026, the attacker exploited the vulnerability to place malicious JavaScript in the custom Project JavaScript field of customer accounts.

Because the tampered snippets were served from the vendor's legitimate CDN under its own certificate, at least 178 organizations, including well-known media, technology and financial services brands, unknowingly served the code to their visitors.

Once the code loaded in a visitor's browser, it did three things:

Cryptocurrency wallet swapping: It replaced wallet addresses that visitors copied with the attacker's own

Payment card skimming: It collected card details from checkout forms

Mobile exploit delivery: It attempted to deliver the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits to iPhones and iPads

Optimizely patched the flaw, removed the injected code and secured affected accounts early on November 17.

Trusted Vendors Are the Path of Least Resistance

Websites are not a single monolith. They are dynamic assemblies of dozens of third-party scripts, analytics tags and optimization tools.

That diversity drives speed, but it also introduces new vectors of attack through the software supply chain. When attackers compromise a single trusted vendor upstream, they bypass the perimeter defenses that vendor's customers have built.

The choice of malicious payload also matters. Swapping valid cryptocurrency wallet addresses on a page is a quick and persistent way to direct ill-gotten payments to a threat actor.

Segmentation Is the Strongest Step Available Today

If a third-party script executes on your page, it effectively has the same privileges as your own developers. Organizations need to architect their sites with that assumption in mind.

The best thing security teams can do right now is apply strict segmentation. The goal is simple— a compromised vendor script should never be able to touch sensitive user inputs. Methods of accomplishing this goal include:

Remove non-essential tags from sensitive pages: Strip all non-essential marketing, experimentation and analytics tags from authentication and checkout pages

Isolate payment collection: Place payment collection inside hardened, cross-origin iframes

Segmentation has been a cornerstone of good security engineering since the beginning.

What Affected Organizations Should Know

Even with the flaw patched, affected websites still need to act. Security teams should take these steps now:

Audit all project modifications made while the malicious code was available

Double-check all code that may have been altered during that period

Treat exposed payment data as potentially compromised, including payment card details entered into checkout forms on affected pages

Conclusion

OPTIMJACK is a reminder that any vendor script with dynamic execution privileges on your site is part of your direct production code. One vulnerability at a single vendor allowed an attacker to reach visitors of at least 178 organizations through a trusted, legitimate delivery channel.

Third-party scripts drive speed, but when they execute on your page, they effectively have the same privileges as your own developers.

Administrators of affected websites should start with the cleanup steps above. These segmentation steps will help keep a compromised vendor script away from sensitive user inputs. Isolating and segmenting as much as possible is key to software supply chain security management.

Title: Railway Security Incident: Where Trust Between Services Broke
Context: The attack began with a vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure and moved through several internal systems before reaching encrypted customer environment variables
Full Text:
What you will learn

Railway’s incident shows how a limited-purpose build credential, excess trust between services and a misconfigured OIDC binding led to decrypted secrets, and how to limit decryption access and credential lifetimes.

On November 10, Railway published a detailed report on its October security incident, which exposed customer secrets and led to an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized AI API usage.

The attack began with a vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure and moved through several internal systems before reaching encrypted customer environment variables.

The attacker obtained a credential intended for a limited purpose and exploited weaknesses in trust between services

Railway estimates that environment variables in up to 1.85% of its workspaces, approximately 100,000, could have been decrypted. This represents the maximum potential exposure, not the confirmed number of compromised workspaces. The attacker also obtained linked-account tokens, including GitHub OAuth tokens and AI agent keys, belonging to 1,852 users. Railway has reset those tokens.

The attacker didn't start with a compromised administrator account. Instead, it obtained a credential intended for a limited purpose and exploited weaknesses in trust between services to gain access to increasingly sensitive systems.

From build isolation to internal access

The attacker began creating dummy accounts on October 18. On October 20, it exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's multi-tenant build infrastructure, partially escaping filesystem isolation and reading files from the underlying host.

One of those files contained a credential used by build servers to authenticate to internal systems, including the container registry. The credential was supposed to authorize only operations needed to complete builds.

However, Railway's internal Temporal instance also accepted it as a trusted client. Temporal was used to schedule and run asynchronous tasks, including parts of the build process. Through its APIs, the attacker retrieved stored build histories containing build variables and other information.

The same credential also allowed access to cached repository snapshots. One of the retrieved builds belonged to an internal Railway service, granting the attacker access to a copy of the company's internal monorepo.

The build credential was accepted by a service it wasn't intended to access. The source code then gave the attacker visibility into Railway's internal architecture and additional opportunities to escalate.

The second trust boundary

Railway detected suspicious activity within hours and revoked the compromised build credential that evening. The attacker already had the source code.

Using information found in the codebase, the attacker identified a misconfigured OpenID Connect (OIDC) trust binding in Railway's cloud environment. On October 21, this allowed it to obtain a short-lived cloud credential intended for the company's CI/CD infrastructure.

That credential provided access to additional internal secrets, including an SSH private key and a longer-lived credential that, when combined with internal network access, could be used to read encrypted environment variables from the production database.

The attacker used the SSH key to connect to a machine responsible for orchestration tasks. That machine had access to the production database network and stored another long-lived credential used to decrypt customer environment variables.

The attacker now had the credentials needed to access the production database and decrypt customer secrets. Revoking the build credential stopped that access, but the attacker had already obtained the source code, exposing the next path into Railway's environment.

Encrypted secrets were not enough

Railway protects customer environment variables using envelope encryption. Each environment has its own data encryption key, which is protected by a root key held in an upstream cloud provider's key management service.

The attacker didn't need to break this encryption. It had obtained credentials that allowed it to retrieve encrypted variables from the database and request their decryption through the legitimate key management service.

On October 21, the attacker retrieved encrypted environment variables and decrypted a subset of them. Database logs show that it prioritized AI provider API keys, searching for variable names that matched specific patterns. Another query also matched cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

Railway believes the primary objective was to steal AI provider keys for resale and use in model distillation. The company estimates that unauthorized use of the stolen credentials resulted in approximately $740,000 in losses.

Railway also points to similar thefts disclosed by OpenCode, Warp, Fireworks AI and other platforms between October 6 and 23. It assesses the incident as part of a broader series of attacks targeting platforms that hold AI keys.

Railway reported no evidence of customer repository downloads, customer database access or logins to Railway accounts using credentials stolen during the incident.

Encryption was not defeated, and Railway's per-environment design helped limit potential exposure. But the attacker had obtained credentials authorized to request decryption. The key management service was performing legitimate operations on behalf of a compromised identity.

Did AI change the attack?

Railway describes the incident as a contest of agent speed. According to its report, the attacker used AI models with safety restrictions removed and, based on Wiz's assessment, an orchestration framework similar to ARTEX. The attacker explored multiple paths in parallel, and access to Railway's source code made that process more effective.

The report doesn't establish exactly which actions were autonomous or how much human direction was involved. What it does show is an attack that was dependent on familiar weaknesses: excessive trust between services, a misconfigured identity binding and privileged credentials accessible from compromised infrastructure. AI may have accelerated the attack, but the permissions and trust relationships were already there.

What this means for identity security

The initial build credential was intended for a limited function, but another internal service trusted it more broadly. This is why service identities need the same scrutiny as privileged human accounts. It's not enough to review what a credential was issued for; organizations also need to understand where it is accepted and what those systems allow it to do.

The OIDC misconfiguration is another example of why short-lived credentials aren't enough on their own. The attacker used a temporary cloud credential to retrieve longer-lived credentials and an SSH key. Its expiration time didn't matter much once those credentials were obtained.

The decryption stage also shows the limits of protecting secrets only at rest. Railway's encryption was working as designed, but the attacker had reached a workload with credentials authorized to decrypt customer variables. The most important parts of secrets management are:

limiting which identities can request decryption.

restricting access to specific secrets.

reducing the lifetime of privileged credentials.

Build systems, CI/CD pipelines, deployment tools and orchestration machines also need to be treated as part of the privileged access environment. They may not look like traditional administrative systems, but they often hold credentials that can be used in production.

Railway says it has closed the exploited weaknesses, rotated affected credentials and moved builds to dedicated ephemeral virtual machines. It has also introduced more narrowly scoped credentials, stronger separation between internal services and additional controls around secret decryption.

Why individually protecting credentials isn’t enough

Railway's incident wasn't caused by a single overly privileged account. It was a chain of credentials, each giving the attacker access to another system or another identity.

The initial vulnerability gave the attacker a foothold, but the trust between services determined how far it could go. Even encrypted customer secrets became accessible once the attacker obtained credentials with the authority to decrypt them.

Railway has addressed the specific weaknesses involved. The broader problem is familiar: credentials are often protected individually, while the access they provide across connected systems receives less attention.

Thanks to Railway’s very detailed analysis, every defender has a real attack chain to test their own environment against. That's the kind of openness our industry should reward. If you ever end up in Railway's shoes, publish as they did. The rest of us will be better for it.

Title: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
Context: ” Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first
Full Text:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

1. Start With a Presumption of Innocence–or Negligence

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

2. Look at Status Updates From Organizations That Might Be Involved

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

Full Text:
Report: Online Scams Nearly Doubled in 2026

A new Akamai report using Bolster data found that online scam detections roughly doubled, from about 3.2 million to 6.4 million, during the period studied. They overtook traditional phishing in the first quarter of 2026. The researchers say this signals a "shift toward higher-return fraud tactics focused on direct financial and consumer deception."

"Since MFA has become a baseline security measure, attackers are pivoting toward higher-return scams for faster payouts," the researchers write. "Traditional phishing, however, still grew by 61% by Q2 2026, according to Bolster. Together, these numbers show that while credential theft remains a core driver, threat actors are aggressively expanding into social engineering tactics that can manipulate consumers into direct financial losses."

Threat actors are increasingly using AI to streamline these attacks, allowing them to launch higher volumes of attacks for less effort. "Attackers are expanding their use of AI to create more varied phishing templates, produce multilingual content at scale, and deploy adaptive evasion techniques," the report says.

"These capabilities reduce the cost and effort required to build convincing scams and make campaigns faster to launch, scale, and modify."

Attackers are also using AI as a phishing lure, impersonating popular AI services with malicious websites. "Beyond traditional phishing attacks, adversaries are capitalizing on the boom of generative AI in the workplace," Akamai says.

"This has given rise to 'AI phishing,' which is defined as attacks that include fake sites impersonating major platforms like OpenAI's ChatGPT to pilfer employee credentials. Although AI phishing currently represents only 3.3% of observed activity, organizations should monitor it closely as a critical initial access vector.

"According to our Enterprise AI Usage Risk Report 2026, nearly half of enterprise employees have tried workplace AI tools, though only 18% use them weekly; those figures will likely rise steadily over time. As employee adoption inevitably scales, these low-volume lures will likely transform into high-yield entry points for enterprise compromise."

Adam Bates, Vice President of Product Management, Huntress

Full Defender Ecosystem Visibility Actioned By The Huntress SOC

Huntress has always leveraged Microsoft signals from Defender for Endpoint and Microsoft Defender Antivirus. Now, the Huntress platform has expanded our integration to bring the rest of the Defender suite along.

Your team doesn't stitch these signals together or sort the queue by severity. Our SOC does that, then sends you a report that says what happened and what we did about it.

Expanded Detections to Catch More Attacks

When an attacker replays a stolen session token, no machine in your environment does anything wrong. The target is the account. That's typical of what Defender sees: 85% of medium- and high-severity incidents in a recent two-week period had no device-related evidence at all. So Huntress doesn't wait for a hostname. A Defender incident tells you what Microsoft concluded, but our analysts want to know what else happened. Using Defender's advanced hunting, the SOC can query the raw data in your own Microsoft tenant, going back as far as 30 days. Title: COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise
Context: While Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has tracked and disrupted COLD RELIC phishing campaigns since 2015, recent Mandiant incident response investigations have uncovered...
Full Text:
Written by: Josh Murchie, John Wolfram, Joseph Spero, Peter Ukhanov, Fernando Tomlinson, Jr., Wesley Shields

Introduction

Over the past year, Mandiant has responded to a series of linked intrusions demonstrating how Russian cyber espionage group COLD RELIC (formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057; also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) turns a single cloud compromise into a springboard for ongoing third party compromise and espionage. Most recently, Mandiant investigated a 2026 compromise at a US-based organization where COLD RELIC directly weaponized data, the corporate staff directory, and identities stolen during a late-2025 compromise, which Mandiant also investigated, at a separate US-based organization.

COLD RELIC is a Russian state-sponsored threat group that the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has assessed operates within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). The group is known for implementing sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns with the aim to gain access to information of strategic or political relevance to the Russian government, as well as to leverage compromised access to target compromised individuals’ broader social and professional networks. Once COLD RELIC compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets. While COLD RELIC has largely maintained a low profile, yielding minimal public reporting relative to other Russia-nexus threat actors, it has been highly successful at compromising high-value targets (including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America) while maintaining a consistent operational tempo.

While Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has tracked and disrupted COLD RELIC phishing campaigns since 2015, recent Mandiant incident response investigations have uncovered critical new insights into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft. We are sharing this end-to-end analysis—along with actionable detection and hardening guidance—to help organizations defend against COLD RELIC’s ongoing use of stolen pretexts, localized residential proxies, and cross-cloud identity abuse. As part of our efforts to thwart this threat actor, we issue Government-backed attack alerts when we detect COLD RELIC targeting Google accounts. COLD RELIC remains an active threat; GTIG has observed evidence of new phishing operations as recently as November 2026.

Threat Detail

Over more than a decade of tracking COLD RELIC alongside Mandiant incident response investigations, we have observed the group continually refine how it leverages data harvested from one intrusion to enable follow-on operations against downstream targets. In late 2025, COLD RELIC downloaded a large volume of data from a US-based organization, searching for names, email addresses, and email archives, likely to fulfill broader intelligence requirements. In 2026, Mandiant investigated a subsequent COLD RELIC intrusion at a second US-based organization where phishing URL parameters and impersonation pretexts indicated that COLD RELIC likely leveraged contact and relationship context from the first organization to target the second.

One of the hallmarks of COLD RELIC phishing campaigns is the use of a compromised website as the initial link that will redirect the target to the actual phishing domain. This provides COLD RELIC with a layer of misdirection and hides their phishing domains, while also giving them a chance to fingerprint anyone visiting the link to determine if they should be redirected or not. A COLD RELIC phishing link usually contains a parameter on the end of it with a value that is set by the attacker and often indicates a relationship to a previous victim or what the lure is. For example, a URL might look like these (though this is not always the case):

https://compromised.example.com/some_path/some_file.php?file=<previous_victim_name> https://compromised.example.com/some_path/some_file.php?ref=<lure_name>

Figure 1: Sample URLs incorporating targeted individuals’ names or lure topics

During Mandiant’s incident response investigation at the second US-based organization, responders identified that COLD RELIC initiated contact over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee from the first victim organization. In parallel, GTIG correlated a COLD RELIC redirector URL from the intrusion that had been submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026, whose query parameter referenced the first victim organization.

Case Study 1 - Stolen Credentials to Data Exfiltration

During the late-2025 intrusion, GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise the cloud productivity environment of a US-based organization. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC leveraged a residential proxy network in the US located in close geographical proximity to the victim. COLD RELIC authenticated using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account, in combination with a multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue attack. After the victim user accepted an MFA request, COLD RELIC registered a device model previously unseen within the tenant of the victim organization. COLD RELIC leveraged passkeys, MFA backup codes, and rogue MFA devices to retain access throughout the intrusion.

COLD RELIC used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization’s cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a COLD RELIC-operated email account and downloading files directly. While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, COLD RELIC accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion. COLD RELIC also exported full employee lists and initiated a domain-wide data export via Google Workspace Customer Takeout using Super Admin privileges. Unlike individual end-user Google Takeout, Customer Takeout is an administrative tenant-wide export tool; these requests are logged in Google Workspace Admin audit logs (CUSTOMER_TAKEOUT_CREATED), and administrators can also disable Google Takeout for users at the organizational level.

Following mass data theft and antiforensics activities, COLD RELIC maintained access to the victim organization for several months and performed additional activities including:

Email inbox sync via OAuth to external email clients

Reauthentication using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls

Targeted cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents relevant to COLD RELIC’s intelligence collection requirements

When the threat actor was removed from the victim organization’s infrastructure, GTIG observed COLD RELIC leveraging email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization. These impersonated accounts were used to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles with renewed social engineering attempts.

Case Study 2 - Leveraging Previous Compromise - Initial Approach

During the second intrusion, COLD RELIC demonstrated competency in navigating multi-cloud environments and federated authentication mechanisms. GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a US-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC impersonated an employee of the organization impacted in Case Study 1 to establish a pretext for communications over a secure messaging app. The threat actor ultimately shared phishing links during the course of the conversation. These phishing links, designed to steal credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, redirected the victim to document lures relevant to the ongoing conversation in order to avoid raising suspicion. Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, COLD RELIC registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion.

A redacted and abbreviated version of the social engineering conversation is included below (image generated with LLMs):

Figure 2: Redacted, LLM-generated depiction of observed threat actor social engineering engagement

By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, COLD RELIC increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, COLD RELIC was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive.

Post-Compromise Activity

After gaining initial access to an organization, COLD RELIC registers rogue MFA devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence. Once persistence is secured, COLD RELIC conducts aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations, accessing email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. While COLD RELIC's primary objective post-compromise is mass collection and download of files and email archives, it simultaneously performs targeted queries for specific terms of interest. In particular, COLD RELIC searches for credentials, personnel information, email archives (.pst files), and documents related to their collection requirements. Additionally, COLD RELIC seeks out data that can support subsequent spear-phishing operations, including organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules to build convincing pretexts for future targets.

Beyond seeking out data to support subsequent operations, COLD RELIC also appeared to repurpose the account used in Case Study 2 for follow on targeting. After the compromise, the encrypted messaging application used for the initial approach recorded that the threat actor changed their profile name to a completely new person. GTIG believes this new persona was likely used to continue to target other organizations in the same professional circles in a similar manner to both of the cases documented here.

Outlook and Implications

COLD RELIC’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners. Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically. GTIG will continue to track, disrupt, and expose COLD RELIC infrastructure to protect global cloud users.

Remediation and Hardening

As previously mentioned, GTIG has observed COLD RELIC heavily rely on residential proxy networks in the course of their intrusions. Moreover, the group goes one step further in obfuscating their activities by selecting proxies that geolocate to the same approximate location as their victim users, thereby avoiding impossible travel or other heuristic-based alerting mechanisms. GTIG recommends enriching authentication logs with residential proxy and VPN IP reputation feeds, alerting on sudden residential ASN shifts for privileged accounts, and applying conditional access policies to block or detect logons from known proxy networks.

In some cases, the severity and scope of COLD RELIC intrusions were amplified due to users storing credentials and other secrets within their organization’s cloud storage platforms. This enabled COLD RELIC to pivot to additional accounts or services that it would not have otherwise been able to access, including users’ personal accounts which are typically unmonitored by their employers. Organizations can implement cloud storage Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies, such as Google Workspace’s Security & Data Protection, to warn or block users attempting to create, upload, or externally share files matching sensitive patterns.

In at least one case, GTIG observed that a victim organization identified the intrusion and attempted to remediate COLD RELIC’s access to their cloud tenant via password resets for impacted accounts. However, because the threat actor hijacked sessions and the victim organization failed to also revoke all existing sessions for the accounts in question, COLD RELIC maintained access. In similar circumstances, such as Business Email Compromise (BEC) intrusions, GTIG recommends organizations revoke all user sessions in addition to forcing password resets for impacted accounts.Organizations should implement the following recommendations:

Identity & Multi-Factor Authentication

Enforce Phishing-Resistant MFA (FIDO2 / WebAuthn): Replace SMS, voice, and push notifications with hardware security keys (e.g., Titan Security Keys). Hardware keys are bound to the origin URL and cannot be intercepted by AiTM reverse proxies or approved via fatigue attacks.

Restrict and Audit Passkey Registrations: Monitor identity logs for passkey registrations and rogue device enrollments, particularly on administrative accounts.

Harden MFA Registration: Require existing administrators or out-of-band identity verification to approve new MFA devices or secondary authenticators (such as Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys).

Organizations and individuals may consider enrolling in the Advanced Protection Program.

Session Management & Incident Response

Mandate Session & OAuth Revocation in BEC Playbooks: When remediating suspected account compromise, password changes alone are insufficient. Administrators must immediately revoke all active browser sessions, refresh tokens, and authorized third-party OAuth app permissions across both Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID, and remove any unauthorized passkeys, backup codes, or MFA devices.

Audit Third-Party OAuth Grants: Continuously review authorized third-party applications in Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, flagging unexpected native desktop email clients (e.g., Thunderbird) or external mail services (e.g., Proton Mail).

Network & Infrastructure Controls

Detect & Block Residential Proxy Logons: Restrict administrative access from consumer ISPs, VPNs, and known residential proxy ASN ranges (e.g., AS5650, AS20115).

Cross-Cloud DLP Policies: Deploy Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules across cloud storage (Google Drive, OneDrive, SharePoint) to alert on documents containing sensitive terms (e.g., passwords, roster, .pst) or to restrict mass external file-sharing.

Detections

Observed Activity

MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

Detection Opportunity

MFA Fatigue Attack

T1621: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation

Monitor for MFA Spam: Alert on multiple failed login or MFA challenge events for a single user in a short timeframe, followed closely by a successful authentication from the same IP address.

OAuth Abuse & Mail Sync

T1114.002: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection

T1528: Steal Application Access Token

Unapproved OAuth Scopes: Alert on new OAuth authorizations (Authorize event in GWS OAuth logs) granting broad scopes (e.g., https://mail.google.com/) to non-standard or unapproved email clients like Proton or Thunderbird.

Automated Data Exfiltration Attempt

T1119: Automated Collection

Customer Takeout Initiation: Generate alerts for the creation of any tenant-wide collection or export (e.g., Customer Takeout Created in GWS Admin logs), as this is a technique that can result in data exfiltration of an entire tenant.

Data Theft via Bulk Download

T1530: Data from Cloud Storage

Anomalous Download Volume: Monitor logs for spikes in file downloads (e.g. Download events in GWS Drive logs) by a single user within a short period of time, particularly originating from non-corporate ASNs/IPs or known residential proxy networks.

Data Theft via External Sharing

T1567.002: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

External File Sharing Anomalies: Monitor logs for a spike in documents being shared externally (e.g., GWS Drive User Sharing Permissions Change or Visibility changed to shared_externally), particularly to free email providers (e.g., @gmail.com).

Device & Passkey Enrollment

T1098.005: Account Manipulation: Device Registration

New MFA/Device Enrollment: Alert on new passkey enrollments (e.g., GWS Passkey enrolled events) or device registrations (GWS Device Registered events), particularly when originating from unexpected geographic locations or immediately following an MFA fatigue pattern.

Use of MFA Backup Codes

T1078.004: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts

Backup Code Usage: Monitor logs for authentications with MFA backup codes (e.g., GWS User logs where the Login Challenge Type is Backup code), particularly if it originates from a non-corporate ASN or known residential proxy networks.

Impairing Defenses via Alert Deletion

T1562.008: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Cloud Logs / Alerts

Alert Center Tampering: Alert on any user modifying or deleting security alerts (e.g., Batch Delete Operation Performed events in GWS Admin logs), particularly if the user is deleting alerts related to their own account or critical severity alerts (e.g., GWS Government-backed attack alerts).

Internal Reconnaissance via User List

T1087.004: Account Discovery: Cloud Account

Directory Export: Alert on domain user exports (e.g., User List Download events in GWS Admin logs). While admins may do this legitimately, it should be heavily scrutinized, particularly when performed from unknown devices.

Forensic Counter-Investigation

T1082: System Information Discovery

Admin Log Querying: Monitor logs for users performing audit log queries (e.g., Investigation Query events in GWS Admin logs). Unexpected querying of security, access, or audit logs may indicate a threat actor attempting to perform counter-forensics.

Searching for Passwords & Archives

T1083: File and Directory Discovery

T1552.001: Credentials In Files

Sensitive File Search: Monitor logs for file directory keyword searches (e.g., Item search performed events in GWS Drive logs) containing terms related to archives or credentials such as .pst, .bak, password, cred, or repeated accesses/downloads of documents explicitly titled with credential-related keywords.

Google Security Operations (SecOps)

Google SecOps customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Mandiant Frontline Threats rule pack. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names:

Google Workspace Successful MFA Fatigue Attack

Google Workspace Customer Takeout Initiated

Google Workspace Device or Passkey Enrollment Following MFA Fatigue

Google Workspace OAuth Broad Mail Scope Granted to Unapproved Client

Title: Uncovering GhostMap: The Rootkit Behind Shai-Hulud’s Rusty Cousin
Context: Watching only the installer’s child processes would therefore have missed the actual loader
Full Text:
How does IronWorm install and load GhostMap?

GhostMap runs as part of a larger implant. IronWorm handles installation, service persistence and collection; the rootkit provides concealment and anti-debugging. The sequence below follows the tested npm specimen from installation into those kernel mechanisms. It does not represent a complete infection followed through external command and control.

Figure 1. Two delivery channels with a shared execution pattern. In the compared payloads, installation creates a persistent service. The service loads the GhostMap rootkit component and operates the local collector. The detailed measurements below come from the IronWorm specimen.

Stage 1: IronWorm establishes persistence and loads GhostMap

JFrog documented a preinstall entry that invokes ./tools/setup during installation of [email protected] when lifecycle scripts are enabled. In the AUR channel, modified PKGBUILDs install atomic-lockfile, whose install hook executes its bundled Linux binary.

The npm page for [email protected] was marked as deprecated with the author message: “COMPROMISED via Mini Shai-Hulud worm (TeamPCP). Upgrade to latest.” This is the package author’s attribution in the warning; our analysis does not independently establish who developed or operated IronWorm. The screenshot documents deprecation, not removal from the registry.

Figure 2. Historical npm page screenshot showing the deprecation warning for [email protected] and its reference to Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP).

Our runtime investigation began with the extracted executable, run with root privileges in the lab. In the initial runtime investigation, the specimen copied itself to /var/lib/glugi/glugi, created glugi.service and enabled the service. The executable started by systemd had the same hash as the original sample.

That successor process loaded GhostMap’s eBPF components. Watching only the installer’s child processes would therefore have missed the actual loader. Names varied across runs. One later installation used /var/lib/havebi/havebi. These paths are observed examples, not fixed names that every infection must use.

Stage 2: GhostMap attaches its eBPF programs to kernel events eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) lets small programs run at defined points inside the Linux kernel. A program holds the logic; a hook is where it runs, such as a syscall exit. A link represents the attachment. A map stores data that programs consult or update, and a helper is a kernel function they can call under applicable restrictions.

GhostMap comprised 13 programs, 10 maps and 13 links at an active checkpoint in the IronWorm run. For process hiding, hidden_names holds selected process names. An execution hook can add matching processes to hidden_pids. Another map, scratch, temporarily records the address of a directory result buffer. For socket hiding, hidden_inodes stores socket inode identifiers, which the network concealment programs use to select entries.

Figure 3. Reconstructed terminal view of saved bpftool JSON, filtered for readability. On November 8, hidden_names selected dbus-daemon, hidden_pids held five PIDs and hidden_inodes held inode 23875. Memory evidence linked that inode to the listener on port 8738. Map IDs belong to this run.

Stage 3: GhostMap changes the answer delivered to the reader Linux exposes process information through /proc, a virtual filesystem. Its numeric directory names are process IDs (PIDs). The ps utility lists processes by reading this information.

A syscall is a request from an application to the kernel. The getdents64 syscall returns directory entries in a buffer in application memory. Each record contains a name and a length field, d_reclen, which tells the reader how far to advance to the next record.

GhostMap’s enter_getdents program remembers the buffer address. At sys_exit_getdents64, its exit_getdents program examines the returned records and checks numeric names against hidden_pids. When it finds a selected entry, it uses bpf_probe_write_user to modify the record chain. Increasing the preceding record’s length makes the reader advance past the hidden entry.

The saved map dumps make the selection concrete. We named benign test processes dbus-daemon to exercise the name matching. In the November 8 experiment, hidden_pids included benign test processes 3035 and 3934. Both disappeared from /proc enumeration while their known /proc/PID paths remained accessible. Control processes 3031 and 3930 were absent from the hiding map and remained listed. After the rootkit stopped, the hidden test processes became visible again.

Figure 4. Terminal reconstruction of a comparison computed from the same November 8 snapshots. Benign test PIDs 3035 and 3934 are in hidden_pids and missing from enumeration, but remain directly accessible and return after stopping the rootkit. Control PIDs 3031 and 3930 remain visible.

Hiding is not automatically inherited from a parent. A fork creates a child process; an exec loads a new program into a process. GhostMap’s on_exec hook checks the process’s short kernel name, comm, against hidden_names and adds a matching PID to hidden_pids. In our November 12 test, a fork-only child remained visible even though it inherited the name dbus-daemon. A child that executed a program with that name became hidden, even under a visible parent. A visible child with a parent missing from ps is therefore a useful hunting lead, but not proof of rootkit activity on its own.

Stage 4: One changed byte makes the reader skip a record In a separate experiment on November 10, we captured each directory buffer before GhostMap’s syscall exit hook and compared it with the same buffer delivered to a controlled reader. Matching the thread, buffer address and syscall interval let us identify precisely what changed.

In a controlled directory, the preceding record’s length changed from 32 to 56 bytes. The reader consequently skipped a file whose numeric name matched the hidden process’s PID. In /proc, a record length changed from 24 to 72 bytes, skipping the malware process and the hidden test process.

Each case reproduced three times. Across all six altered buffers, only one byte changed: the low byte of the two byte length field. The hidden records’ bytes remained in the buffer, and the syscall’s returned byte count stayed unchanged.

Figure 5. Terminal reconstruction displaying saved buffer measurements: the preceding record grows from 24 to 72 bytes, causing the reader to skip two PID entries.

The comparison stayed byte identical across 24 calls made before the rootkit started or after it stopped. Actual ps queries also omitted the hidden test process, both with and without our observer running. After the rootkit stopped, ps displayed the process again.

Figure 6. Reconstructed, filtered ps output from the November 10 experiment. While the rootkit is active, only control PID 3821 appears. After it stops, target PID 3820 appears too. The recorded command was ps -eo pid=; filtering was added for presentation. These PIDs belong to a separate run from Figures 3 and 4.

Stage 5: Socket concealment changes two different views Linux exposes socket information through more than one interface. /proc/net/tcp provides a text listing, while socket diagnostic requests over Netlink return structured messages that tools such as ss can interpret. GhostMap targets both paths.

In a separate listener experiment, GhostMap’s hidden_inodes map contained inode 18544, identifying IronWorm’s listener on 127.0.0.1:8738. This is a different run from Figure 3, where that listener had inode 23875; inode numbers are local to the observed socket instance. The listener disappeared from /proc/net/tcp in all three observations, while a benign listener on port 8739 remained visible.

The Netlink path produced a different result. GhostMap changed the listener’s diagnostic message type to NLMSG_NOOP, indicating a no-operation message, but left its port, identifier and listening state in the payload. The tested ss utility still displayed the listener in all three queries, although its process-owner annotation was absent. The corresponding upstream source provides a plausible explanation: its parsing path can read the retained payload without requiring the original message type.

The concealment code ran, but it did not hide the socket from that reader. The result applies to the tested ss package, iproute2 6.1.0-1ubuntu6.4; other consumers may handle the modified message differently.

Figure 7. Terminal reconstruction of the separate listener experiment: port 8738 is absent from /proc/net/tcp but visible to the tested ss utility; control port 8739 is visible in both. The hidden inode in this run was 18544, not the 23875 shown in Figure 3.

Title: Microsoft Warns of Coordinated Phishing Campaign Leveraging M365 Service Outage
Context: “This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog...
Full Text:
Microsoft has identified a “coordinated, high volume” global phishing campaign designed to exploit the recent Microsoft 365 outage.

The campaign was observed on November 13, as the company grappled with rolling out a fix for the tech failure impacting services like Outlook and Teams worldwide.

The outage began on 11.20 EST on November 12 and lasted over 22 hours, with Microsoft confirming that its services were fully restored on 23.15 EST on November 13.

The phishing emails were designed to exploit individuals’ and employees’ desperation to reconnect to M365 services, attempting to entice them into clicking a malicious link and capturing their credentials.

The messages impersonated legitimate M365 service-health notifications. They aimed to create a false sense of urgency by claiming that the recipient’s emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them.

“This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog dated November 16.

There is currently no evidence of credential capture, malware delivery or post-compromise activity emanating from the campaign. However, organizations have been urged to investigate whether any users clicked the malicious links and take immediate steps to mitigate any malicious activity if this did occur.

How the Phishing Campaign Unfolded

The email lures sent during the campaign used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Microsoft said the use of specific sender domain names, such as moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com, were designed to make the messages more tailored and appear relevant to the recipient.

The messages commonly used 24-hour deletion deadlines and call to actions using prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” links to drive immediate action. They also referenced Microsoft services like Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

The body of the messages included fake email conversations positioned to be hidden from the recipient, which appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.

Title: Attackers Pick the Target, AI Does the Rest: Cyber Predictions for 2027
Context: We expect more of the same in 2027: encrypting ransomware as the steady baseline, with extortion-only waves arriving whenever an attacker finds a zero-day in widely used software
Full Text:
Key points

Humans will pick the target, but AI will run most of the attack.

AI credentials will become the new cloud keys.

Shadow AI agents will present a new challenge.

Patching alone will not be enough to tackle modern threats.

Ransomware will break another record, with data-theft waves on top.

The line between spies and criminals will keep blurring.

As the AI juggernaut continues to roll on, in 2027 we may reach a point where cyber attackers need to do little more than pick a target and collect the money, information or access at the end. AI agents will increasingly handle reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft and lateral movement, working at machine pace.

Last year, we predicted that agentic AI would lower the barrier to entry for attackers. Over the past 12 months we have watched that happen, and most of our predictions for 2027 extend what we are already seeing, while one or two go further. As organizations give AI agents standing access to their data, we would not be surprised to see a major breach in which the attacker brought almost no tools of their own, because the victim’s own agents did the work.

Humans will pick the target, but AI will run most of the attack

Until recently, attackers used AI as an assistant, however, increasingly, they are putting it in charge. The “Skynet” agent we reported on in October 2026 wired a large language model (LLM) into the center of an attack tool. The tool had around 74 callable functions covering reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft and botnet control. Its operators described the unattended setting as “Skynet mode” and authorized it to run up to 100,000 steps without human approval.

This is not yet the norm. Most intrusions still have a human at the keyboard making the important decisions. But the direction is clear, and Google’s threat analysts and others have described the same shift from chat-based assistance to agentic orchestration. An agent does not sleep, does not need to be paid and can run many intrusions at once. An operator who once handled one victim at a time could now supervise agents’ activity on dozens.

While agents deployed in most organizations today still run under constrained scopes or human-in-the-loop approvals, they are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks or indirect tool abuse, which could place them under the control of attackers without them even needing to exploit a vulnerability to send the agent rogue. Prompt injection attacks involve the hackers feeding a malicious prompt directly into a LLM that they have gained access to, while an indirect attack involves hackers hiding their payloads or instructions in data consumed by the LLM – such as software tickets, code reviews or web pages that the LLM has been instructed to read. The attackers are essentially tricking the LLM, no vulnerabilities required.

Model poisoning is another way that attackers can potentially interfere with AI agents’ operations. It involves tampering with the data, fine-tuning samples, or open-source weights that an AI uses to learn, so that the AI develops a deliberate blind spot or backdoor known only to the attacker. Security teams are generally so worried about protecting credentials and endpoints, they may not think about whether the intelligence inside the model itself has been compromised. These attacks are also often difficult to detect as the model appears to be functioning normally, and strange outputs may simply be put down to hallucinations.

In 2027 and beyond we expect the human role in many AI-driven cyber attacks to shrink towards choosing targets and collecting the money. Reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft and lateral movement will increasingly be handled by agents working at machine pace, which means the gap between first access and damage will keep closing. Low-skilled attackers will benefit most: capabilities that once needed a team of specialists will be available to anyone who can point an agent at a list of targets. For defenders, the quality of attacker tradecraft will matter less than its volume.

Agents will also change what attackers use. Living off the land, where attackers use tools already present on the victim’s network, has been one of the defining tactics of the past decade. The next version may be living off the AI: attackers turning the victim’s own coding assistants and agents, and the permissions they hold, against the organization. Gartner forecast task-specific agents in around 40% of enterprise applications by the end of this year, and every one of them holds standing credentials and access to data. We would not be surprised to see the first major breach in which the attacker brought almost no tooling of their own, because the victim’s agents did the work.

AI credentials will become the new cloud keys

Attackers learned long ago that cloud credentials were worth stealing, and AI credentials are their newest target. Our recent research on the Aoki infostealer found it harvesting credential and session files for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and other AI coding assistants. Skynet, for its part, scans for exposed AI endpoints and uses them to fund and conceal its operations, leaving the victim to pay for every step.

There is a market for what they steal. Google found that underground prices for AI accounts more than doubled in 2026. Stolen AI access is useful in several ways: free computing power, a way around bans imposed on accounts that have been abused, and a way to strip safety controls from commercial models. Attackers can steal AI access in order to run AI-driven attacks.

In 2027, we expect AI keys to join browser cookies and crypto wallets as a standard target for infostealers, and for the resale of stolen AI access to mature into its own underground business, much as initial access brokers did for network access. Developers will be the main targets. A coding assistant’s configuration files can tie together API keys, source code repositories and cloud accounts, which makes a developer’s workstation one of the most valuable machines in the organization. Many victims will discover the theft through an unexpected bill, not an alert.

AI providers will respond with shorter-lived tokens and tighter controls, as the cloud providers did. Attackers will respond by stealing live sessions instead of static keys. If the history of cloud credentials is a guide, it will take organizations a couple of painful years to treat AI credentials with the same care as the rest.

Shadow AI agents will present a new challenge

As the use of AI continues to become more commonplace across almost all organizations and workplaces, we may see a shift from the traditional issue of “shadow IT” where software, hardware, or other services are used without the knowledge or approval of the enterprise’s IT department, to “agent shadow IT”, where AI tools are being used without the knowledge or approval of organizations’ IT or security departments.

This could be employees using things like AI tools, local models, or unapproved plugins to get their work done faster, without telling their IT or security departments. This is likely to become a bigger issue and has been observed already today where security teams cannot protect what they do not know exists. These unofficial AI helpers often have direct access to company data and code, which may get fed back to whoever is running the AI without restrictions or specialized agreements being in place instructing the AI not to leverage or use the data, leading to this becoming a leak or information disclosure issue.

This could also be a more pronounced issue in markets where the popular, Western AI coding assistants are not legitimately available, leading to those wanting to use them turning to rogue operators. A recent Symantec Threat Hunter Team blog discussed how a grey market relay service was installing the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems and then reconfiguring them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers. This activity was mostly impacting a variety of enterprises across mainland China where many Western AI coding assistants are not officially available.

Of note was that this operation also disabled the CLI's execution sandbox entirely, enabling network access for the write sandbox, replacing the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disabling telemetry and error reporting. While there was no evidence found in this case that the relay operator had abused their level of access, a potential risk is that the configuration it installed would let the operator read every prompt, file, and secret passed through the agent and run commands with the user's full privileges. Given this was not a legitimate service, it’s unlikely any IT or security oversight for this product existed in the organizations where it was being used.

Patching alone will not be enough to tackle modern threats

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) show how short the patching window has become. Both flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Technical details leaked on October 20, 2026, a day before the PHP project released fixes, and public proof-of-concept code followed. Attackers did not need to be clever. They just needed to be early.

Defenders are told to patch faster, but patching is a race against machines that defenders cannot win. Testing and deploying a critical patch takes days or weeks, and for some systems, like those older PHP versions, it never happens. AI is shrinking the patching window. It can increasingly read a patch, compare it with the old code and produce a working exploit in minutes, and it can scan open-source projects for flaws before the fixes ship.

Vulnerabilities are also only part of the problem. Attackers using AI are just as good at finding what has no CVE: misconfigurations, forgotten internet-facing systems, default or reused credentials and over-permissioned identities, and at chaining several low-severity weaknesses into a working attack path. In 2027 we expect more breaches in which no single vulnerability was to blame.

So, we expect the conversation to shift from how fast organizations patch to how fast they can make a threat irrelevant, whether or not a patch exists. Think of it as mean time to mitigate. The answer will lean on controls that do not depend on knowing the vulnerability: behavioral blocking, default-deny application control, tight segmentation and identity protections that stop an attacker using what they have stolen. Patching will still matter. It just may not be enough.

Ransomware will break another record, with data-theft waves on top

Ransomware shows no sign of slowing. There were 3,126 claimed attacks in the third quarter of 2026, the highest quarterly total we have recorded, including the busiest single month, August, with 1,184. Across the first three quarters of 2026 there were 7,777 claimed attacks, 28% more than in the same period of 2025 and already close to the 8,498 recorded in the whole of last year.

The line-up behind those numbers keeps changing. Over the past 12 months, Qilin has been the busiest operation with 1,457 claimed attacks, followed by The Gentlemen with 870, a group that did not feature in our 2025 top 10. Akira (604), Inc (482) and DragonForce (391) follow behind. LockBit, which had struggled to rebuild after the disruption of its operation in 2024, is back with 365.

Data-theft-only extortion is less predictable. It surged in 2025, driven by a handful of mass campaigns, notably Cl0p’s attacks on Oracle E-Business Suite and the Salesforce-related attacks carried out by ShinyHunters, and it fell back in 2026, with 808 identified extortion-only attacks in the first three-quarters of 2026, against 1,187 a year earlier. One campaign against a vulnerability in a widely used enterprise product can add hundreds of victims of these kinds of attacks in a single quarter, making the likely volume of these kinds of attacks harder to predict.

We expect more of the same in 2027: encrypting ransomware as the steady baseline, with extortion-only waves arriving whenever an attacker finds a zero-day in widely used software. Encryption may keep its place partly because it pays better: Coveware found victims paid in only around 15% of cases in the second quarter of 2026 where leaking data was the only threat.

The line between spies and criminals will keep blurring

Many of the threat actors we track no longer fit neatly into a single category. Our research on Jewelbug found a China-based group running espionage operations and a cryptocurrency fraud business from the same infrastructure and the same control panel. On one side it compromised government webmail in the Middle East. On the other, it ran an AI-generated network of fake exchange download pages to target Chinese-speaking crypto users. We assess that the fraud business most likely supplied access, infrastructure and delivery for the espionage.

Warlock, a ransomware operation we wrote about in our Ransomware 2026 whitepaper and blogged about more recently in October 2026, fits the pattern too. Some of its tools trace back to earlier Chinese espionage activity, and ransomware may at times serve to obscure espionage.

We expect this to go further in 2027. Governments that want deniable capabilities have every incentive to let contractors fund themselves through e-crime, and criminals gain tooling, protection or simply tolerance in return. The result is groups whose motives change from one intrusion to the next: espionage on Monday, extortion on Friday.

We expect to see more high-profile incidents in which ransomware turns out to have been a cover for espionage or sabotage, and incident responders will have to start asking what the ransomware was hiding. Attribution will get harder, and the stakes will rise with it. Defenders may need to stop running separate playbooks for ransomware and espionage. Every ransomware incident should include a search for earlier access and for what was taken before anything was encrypted.

What to do about it?

Several of the trends above share one answer: reduce what attackers can do once they are on a network. Behavioral protection, visibility across endpoints and cloud, and governing how AI is used inside your organization matter more than ever when exploits arrive faster than patches. For resource-strapped teams or complex enterprises looking to deepen visibility and correlate signals across their stack, solutions such as Symantec CBX can fill that gap.
