Capabilities and Supported Commands

Due to its highly modular architecture, KUKURAT’s main binary lacks the embedded code required to perform post-exploitation activities. Instead, according to our analysis of the malware's underlying logic and compiled strings, the modules enable features related to data collection and exfiltration, command execution, reconnaissance and lateral movement.

The modules provide the following capabilities:

Screenshots and keylogging

Host and port scanning

Process management – listing processes, killing processes and process injection

File management – uploading, downloading, listing, deleting and executing files

Execution of native shell commands via cmd.exe and PowerShell

Lateral movement via PsExec

Server Message Block (SMB) credential brute-forcing

SOCKS tunneling

Local privilege elevation

Execution of Beacon Object Files (BOF)

Silent mode configuration

KUKURAT’s modular framework facilitates the loading and execution of any arbitrary external module, even if it does not match a pre-existing command handler in the base code. This allows the threat actor to dynamically introduce new capabilities and adapt to shifting operational needs in real time.

See Appendix B: KUKURAT Command Frame Architecture for the full list of KUKURAT commands.

Figure 4 shows a snippet of the KUKURAT code that executes the screenshot module. KUKURAT verifies whether the module is loaded before executing it using the hard-coded parameter capture that is passed to the loaded module. If the loading of the module or the screenshot capture fails, an error message is sent back to the operator.

Deployment of Separate KUKURAT Modules

During our investigation, we observed the attackers using KUKURAT to deploy two additional executables named PsExecService.exe and SecurityGuard.exe. While we could not retrieve SecurityGuard.exe, we successfully recovered PsExecService.exe for analysis.

According to the file's compiled program database (PDB) string, the attackers explicitly classify this binary as an external module of KUKURAT, despite it being compiled as a standalone executable rather than a DLL:

d:\proj\KUKURAT\modules\MyPsExec-master\PsExecService\

This tool is a custom remote execution service that appears may be partially based on the open-source MyPsExec GitHub project. Upon execution, PsExecService.exe registers itself as a local Windows service named PsExec and creates a named pipe called \\.\pipe\PSEXEC. The service natively supports four commands:

Shell execution

File uploading

File downloading

Directory listing

To limit its forensic footprint, the service employs an internal self-destruct timer that automatically uninstalls the service and cleans up its artifacts after five minutes of inactivity.

Spoofing Endpoint Activity: Heuristic Camouflage Engine

KUKURAT introduces a unique heuristic camouflage engine capable of operating across three system axes: network, registry and files. The purpose of this engine is to generate dummy, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage the malware's actual operations. By mimicking normal operational behavior, the threat actor establishes a false baseline, which may significantly affect automated detection and other forensic efforts. The threat actor can toggle each method on or off via the C2 command set_obfuscation:

Network noise generation: KUKURAT generates 10 decoy HTTP requests per operational cycle to randomly selected domains, pulled from a hard-coded list of 15 popular websites using randomly generated URL paths. This camouflages traffic, blending C2 communications into normal web noise.

Registry manipulation mimicking browser activity: KUKURAT mimics legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and then deleting the key. It then opens and enumerates the HKCU\Software\Google\Update\ClientState registry key. The purpose of this sequence is to make the agent's registry operation appear like Chrome crash recovery.

File noise generation: The malware continuously creates temporary files with random names and randomized content inside the system %temp% directory, only to immediately delete them. This technique generates file system noise, masking the agent's file modifications.

While certain elements of this evasion technique have been previously documented across various malware families, KUKURAT distinguishes itself through a highly unique design choice. It can coordinate heuristic camouflage across three separate vectors, while dynamically enabling or disabling each feature at runtime.

The Watchdog Component

In multiple incidents, attackers deployed KUKURAT alongside a separate watchdog executable that ensures the malware remains active.

When KUKURAT’s main binary executes, it creates a dedicated thread to communicate with the companion watchdog component. KUKURAT writes its own active file path to a local named pipe called WINDOW_SEC_WATCHDOG, every three seconds. The companion watchdog process reads this path and pulls a heartbeat message every second. If 15 seconds pass without receiving a heartbeat, the watchdog assumes that KUKURAT has been terminated and automatically relaunches it using the cached file path.

On one occasion, we observed the threat actor deploying this watchdog component into the C:\ProgramData\Cyvera\Ransomware\ directory path. This folder structure was historically associated with Cortex XDR, demonstrating the threat actor’s attempt to lower suspicion by hiding within security-product directory structures.

Comparison of Variants

The investigation identified two distinct variants of KUKURAT, leveraging HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 respectively for C2 communications. Aside from the difference in network transport protocols, the two variants are structurally almost identical except for a few noteworthy code developments that affect the malware's development adaptability and operational survivability:

Command-handling architecture: In the HTTP/2 variant, the threat actor implemented a large, nested If-Else conditional chain inside a single command-handling function. All execution and module-loading logic is embedded directly within those conditions. The HTTP/3 variant demonstrates the transition to an array of function pointers that map to individual commands, creating a standalone function for each execution routine. This design shift enables the malware developers to add or remove capabilities on the fly more efficiently.

Built-in exec bypass command: While KUKURAT is engineered to function as a completely modular malware framework that loads code dynamically, the HTTP/3 variant introduces an explicit, natively coded command called exec. This command enables the attacker to spawn a subprocess directly on the host endpoint via CreateProcessA and pipe the resulting terminal output back to the C2 backend. Because this command does not exist in the HTTP/2 variant, its inclusion suggests that the author sought to provide a built-in survival option: allowing operators to run system commands natively without needing to fetch an external module DLL from the staging server.

Post-Exploitation and Network Propagation

The following section details TTPs used throughout this campaign to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks, gather credentials, transition from Active Directory control to endpoint infection and exfiltrate sensitive data.

Lateral Movement via Domain Log-on Scripts

The threat actor’s most notable method for network propagation involves the manipulation of domain log-on scripts, a stealthy persistence mechanism used to execute code across the environment. In addition, they use well-known tools and remote management protocols such as PsExec, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and Windows Remote Management (WinRM).

After successfully compromising a Domain Controller, the attackers installed malicious log-on scripts. Consequently, whenever a legitimate user authenticated to the domain, the malicious script automatically executed on their local endpoint, triggering the download and execution of the KUKURAT malware.

Figure 5 illustrates the execution of a malicious log-on script that downloads and executes the KUKURAT malware to the infected host, as shown in Cortex XDR.

Figure 5. KUKURAT deployed via a malicious log-on script, as shown in Cortex XDR .

Figure 6 shows that the log-on script persistence technique triggered an alert, due to an uncommon startup process executing with a local or domain user Security Identifier (SID).

Credential Stealing Techniques

Upon gaining initial access, the threat actor employs multiple techniques to harvest credentials including Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) memory dumping and Directory Service Replication (DCSync).

The threat actor also actively used a robust suite of credential-dumping tools, dual-use administrative tools and registry manipulation techniques, including:

Mimikatz and ProcDump

SharpDPAPI, to decrypt DPAPI credentials and secrets

Manually dumping the SAM and SYSTEM registry hives to extract local account hashes

LSASS Memory Dumping

The attackers leveraged a living off the land technique to dump the memory of the lsass.exe process. They misused the native comsvcs.dll Windows utility using the following command.

CmD.exe /Q /c for /f "tokens=1,2 delims= " %A in ('"tasklist /fi "Imagename eq lsass.exe" | find "lsass""') do rundll32.exe C:\windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, #+000024 %B \Windows\Temp\MxA.tar full

Instead of calling the MiniDump function by name, the attackers invoked it via its ordinal hidden index number, #+000024. This evasion tactic is designed to bypass security detection mechanisms that look for the explicit MiniDump string.

Directory Service Replication

To further compromise the identity infrastructure, the attackers executed DCSync attacks to extract password hashes directly from the Domain Controller. This allowed them to simulate the behavior of a Domain Controller replicating user credentials, as Figure 7 shows.

Data Exfiltration

After systematically moving through the network and harvesting high-privilege credentials, the threat actor initiated their primary objective: cyberespionage. Leveraging the PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT malware families, the threat actor attempted to exfiltrate vast quantities of documents back to their C2 infrastructure. Title: The Race to Remediation: Black October Showed that Threat Intelligence Isn’t Enough
Context: Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production...
Full Text:
In a single week in October 2026, security teams faced one serious security incident after another. A certificate authority failed, critical flaws in PHP were disclosed after a broken embargo, a popular open-source AI gateway was compromised, and developer platforms reported thefts of customer secrets. Industry insiders started calling the seemingly steady drumbeat of attacks “Black October.”

Any one of these incidents would have kept a security team busy. Collectively, they exposed a bottleneck that has little to do with any single exploit. Security teams are not short on vulnerability information. They are short on answers: what is affected in our environment, and how can we fix it – fast?

As JFrog CEO Shlomi Ben Haim put it: “A single weak link can cost far more than the fix. For LiteLLM and PHP2Shell, being caught off-guard means money, downtime, and customer trust. The companies that come through well are the ones that know exactly what they are running and can act within hours vs. days. JFrog’s role is to find the problems early, tell customers what to do, and make sure they can precisely determine their exposure.”

Three Pressures That Compound

Three forces explain why answers are getting harder to produce:

Volume: In the AI-accelerated landscape of 2026, based on our count of NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) records, 36,952 CVEs were published in Q3 2026 alone, more than triple the 11,725 published in Q3 2025 (as of November 16, 2026).

Exploitability: A severity score does not say whether a flaw is applicable in your environment. Triage by count alone wastes scarce resources and time.

Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production vulnerabilities within 24 hours, while 74% take between one and seven days. Meanwhile, attackers can use AI to speed up exploitation, chaining together low-severity findings and making repeated automated attempts until one unpatched system gives them an opening.

That is a different kind of weakness, and it needs a different kind of approach. A faster version of the old process will not close it. AI pushes on all three pressures: it surfaces more flaws and drafts more fixes, but maintainers cannot absorb unlimited volume.

The Disclosure Process Wasn’t Built for This

The vulnerability disclosure process was designed around human review cycles. A researcher reports a flaw, a maintainer triages it, a fix is written, and a CVE is published. That rhythm worked when exploitation was also a manual effort. It does not hold up when attackers can automate discovery and exploitation at scale.

Enterprises have also historically depended on upstream maintainers to publish patches on their own timelines, and those timelines are asynchronous with the CVE disclosure window. In an AI-powered threat landscape, that mismatch becomes an exposure gap that attackers can use.

A new ecosystem of patching vendors has stepped in to help close it. These vendors produce signed, backported fixes for the exact versions enterprises actually consume, often ahead of public disclosure.

Why Does Threat Intelligence Alone Leave a Gap?

Threat intelligence describes the outside world, not your software environment. That difference explains why teams with excellent security vulnerability feeds still lose hours after a disclosure. Two gaps open between a published threat and a confident response:

Timing: Public databases trail events. As of October 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) now enriches only a subset of CVEs, and PHP2Shell was being probed days before patches shipped. A process that waits for them is structurally late.

Remediation: Even with timely, contextual intelligence, someone still has to find a trustworthy fix, apply it across every affected artifact (assuming all artifacts are even traceable), and prove it worked. This is where many teams slow from hours to days.

Know Your Exposure With JFrog Threat Hub

Finding problems early and determining exposure precisely is the first half of the job. JFrog Threat Hub, a feature of JFrog Xray, brings JFrog Security Research findings and vetted external advisories into the same single source of truth that holds your scanned artifacts, so a published threat can be matched to your own environment in one step.

Knowing your exposure only matters if you can act on it quickly, which is the second half of the job.

Fortified Defenses Start With One Source of Truth

A month like October does not call for a faster version of the old process. It calls for a different one. In our view, LiteLLM and PHP2Shell showed what separates the teams that come through well: they could see what they run, and they could fix it fast.

Know everything you run

Start with an inventory at every layer: source code, packages, container images, AI models, and agent tooling. A component you cannot see cannot be prioritized or patched. Then verify what you deploy, not only what you wrote, because malicious code can live in built artifacts while the source stays clean. JFrog Artifactory serves as that single source of truth, holding the main artifact types (binaries, containers, AI models, MCP server packages) in one system of record.

Draw on an ecosystem of fix providers

Fix providers often specialize in particular software ecosystems, so drawing on an ecosystem of providers can help broaden coverage. In our view, reducing this risk requires two critical capabilities: high-quality patches across software ecosystems and a control plane designed to automate remediation at the binary level.

Close the loop with zero-touch remediation

A patch sitting in a vendor’s repository does nothing for an artifact already running in production. Artifactory can act as the control plane that ingests each fix from supported partners. JFrog Security can then apply a selected fix according to the customer’s policy and context, and produce a signed evidence chain that can support audit reviews. The goal is a self-healing software supply chain and zero-touch remediation that aims to help customers patch in hours rather than days. For branches past their end of life, migration remains the durable fix.

Ready for the Next Black October?

When the next disclosure lands, what is affected, and can we fix it in hours rather than days? Organizations that can provide a quality answer will weather the next crowded month. Those that cannot will spend it searching.

Move From Disclosure to Fix in Hours

Patching at scale takes a single source of truth, trusted fixes from an ecosystem of partners, and a universal control plane that applies them automatically. See how zero-touch remediation and the self-healing software supply chain work in your own environment: schedule a demo, take an online tour, or start a free trial of the JFrog Platform.

Title: Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline
China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks
Typosquatters Target New Brand Domains Within 24 Hours of Registration
Context: “The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers...
Full Text:
Threat actors are impersonating big-name brands via typosquatting just one day after legitimate domains are created, according to new research from Symantec.

The active campaign, first observed in August, has seen 25 lookalike domains created which resembled authentic domain names used by companies such as Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi.

Every lookalike domain was registered within 24 hours of its authentic counterpart, often before the company even launched the new website.

“The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers who mistype legitimate addresses,” Symantec wrote.

Typosquatting is when malicious actors register domains that are slightly misspelled from a legitimate organization’s domain, such as one letter added or removed. This means that when a user accidently misspells a legitimate site name when typing the address by hand, they could be directed to a typosquatter’s site instead.

The fake websites are designed to closely resemble the organization they are impersonating.

These sites enable a range of follow-on malicious activity, such as directing users to scam sites, installing malware and harvesting credentials.

Attackers Focus on Campaign Sites to Maximize Effectiveness

The Symantec research, published on November 16, found that most of the malicious domains impersonated campaign sites rather than corporate home pages.

These included patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, rebates, claims portals and legal settlements.

Users are more likely to type such addresses by hand as these websites are often displayed on printed mailers, television advertisements, pharmacy leaflets and court-ordered settlement notices.

Campaign sites are also likely to ask visitors for personal information, such as names, addresses, claim numbers or health details, with visitors expecting to hand over such data upon arrival.

The typosquatting campaign focused on clients of two brand-protection registrars, Corporation Service Company (CSC) and MarkMonitor. Each time a large company registered a new domain through one of these registrars, a one-letter lookalike was registered the next day through a China-based registrar.

In one case, used car dealer CarMax registered carmaxclaims[.]com and kmxclaims[.]com through CSC on August 26. The next day, two lookalike domains were registered that removed the ‘s’ from each of the legitimate domains, carmaxclaim[.]com and kmxclaim[.]com.

Other typos used included leaving out other single letters and collapsing a double letter, for example, mywayconnect became mywayconect.

New lookalike domains were registered as recently as November 11, suggesting the campaign is ongoing.

Typosquat Domains Rapidly Monetized Through Ads and Scams

The observed typosquat domains appeared to have several purposes. Some were parked placeholder pages that earned money from pay-per-click advertising feeds, while others were deceptive search portals whose results led to scam blogs, or brand-themed blogs written around the typosquatted name and packed with ads that routed visitors to scam sites.

“This low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal. Advertising networks of this kind can also be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, and a domain that serves ads today could serve a fake claims form tomorrow with a single Domain Name System (DNS) or content change. Visitors who reach these domains are already primed to enter personal details,” Symantec noted.

Given the speed at which attackers published their lookalike domains following the campaign launch, the researchers believe the setup was likely automated.

“The actors’ tooling was not visible to us, but the evidence is consistent with a simple pipeline that watched new registrations, filtered on brand-protection registrars, generated a one-character variant and registered it before the next day was out,” the researchers added.

Title: La Poste Subsidiary Maileva Breach Exposes 22 Million People
Context: Read more on French cyber-attacks: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C Docaposte's statement now called what happened in mid-September "a...
Full Text:
A cyber-attack on La Poste-owned document-sending provider Maileva has exposed the names and postal addresses of 22 million people.

Docaposte, La Poste's digital subsidiary that owns Maileva, confirmed the breach in a November 15 statement.

Maileva sends documents such as payslips, registered letters and invoices on behalf of businesses and institutions.

The firm said that 22 million people who received mailings from Maileva’s business and institutional clients are affected by a leak of identifying information, including first name, last name and postal address.

What Maileva Data Was Exposed

Docaposte said Maileva's clients had been able to tell their customers that some of their data had been compromised, the nature of which is linked to the content of the documents sent. It did not say how many people that covered.

The content of the documents shared on its platform is not held by Maileva, rather it relates to the relationship between Maileva’s clients and the recipients of those documents.

Several thousand Maileva client companies were affected, the company told Cyberattaque.org, which first reported the breach.

Docaposte said affected clients were informed in the days after the incident was identified.

A hospital near Paris, Hôpital Foch, said an attacker could view some payment reminder letters containing invoice numbers, care dates and amounts due, but not the nature of the care or bank details. Meanwhile, a social housing provider in northern France, Flandre Opale Habitat, said exposed information could include names, contact details, client numbers, housing references and invoice amounts.

Dray Agha, senior manager of tactical response at Huntress, said in emailed comments that criminals could use the stolen names and addresses to send targeted fake invoices or payment reminders.

"I strongly advise anyone receiving an unexpected bill to verify it directly with the named organization. You must use official websites rather than the contact details provided in the suspicious letter," Agha added.

Sophisticated Cyber-Attack Hits Maileva

Maileva suspended its platform on September 23 and resumed services on September 29, a six-day outage affecting all clients. At the time, Docaposte described the event as a cybersecurity incident involving attempted unauthorized access to the platform, according to Solutions Numériques.

Cyberattaque.org reported the incident on September 24, when Maileva described attempts against some customer accounts aimed at sending fraudulent mail. No large-scale personal data leak had been announced at that point.

Read more on French cyber-attacks: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C

Docaposte's statement now called what happened in mid-September "a complex cyber-attack," adding that "no data was found to have been altered or destroyed." It said France's data protection authority (CNIL) had been notified, a complaint had been filed and a judicial investigation was under way.

Docaposte did not address whether anyone had claimed the attack or whether the stolen data had been published or sold. Maileva told Cyberattaque.org that notifying affected people was the responsibility of its client organizations.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

TSMC, a major Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer, has confirmed a data breach at an unnamed cloud provider that exposed information about current and former employees. Danish shipping and logistics giant Maersk confirmed unauthorized access and data theft from a legacy system inherited through an acquisition. Japan’s Osaka city government disclosed a data breach exposing more than one million email addresses after attackers compromised a third-party email distribution service. The November 2 attack affected nearly 400 customers of the provider, exposing approximately 77 million addresses and enabling the distribution of fraudulent emails.

ConnectWise, a US-based IT management software provider, disclosed attacks targeting its ScreenConnect remote access platform. Attackers compromised managed service provider environments and deployed malicious remote access tools on at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations. The campaign may have involved the abuse of third-party extensions.

AI THREATS

Researchers analyzed a suspected AI-assisted intrusion targeting a US retailer. After security tools blocked the attacker’s initial commands, the intruder switched to apparently AI-generated scripts. The attacker extracted credentials from SolarWinds Orion monitoring software configuration files and accessed another server within minutes, demonstrating rapid adaptation during the intrusion.

Researchers revealed an autonomous intrusion campaign in which attackers used DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM AI agents against at least 19 organizations during 25 operations. The campaign compromised 10 targets, including semiconductor, defense, and civil-society organizations, exposing credentials and sensitive information, including more than one million personal records.

Researchers uncovered an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, a cyberespionage group targeting Central Asian governments. The attackers used a DeepSeek-powered AI agent to automate reconnaissance, data collection, and evidence removal. Compromised systems included Tajikistan’s railway network and government document infrastructure containing thousands of sensitive files.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Check Point Research has traced attacks exploiting PHP2Shell through the Mobile Access portals of unpatched Check Point Security Gateways. Attackers then exploited CVE-2026-123039 to escalate privileges, achieved persistence, and in some cases wiped a VMware ESXi host. The first wave of attacks targeted Israeli organizations before expanding worldwide, and the tooling shows similarities to China-linked malware.

Microsoft released November security updates fixing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, including an actively exploited Outlook flaw, CVE-2026-124194, that can expose authentication data and enable user impersonation. The release also fixes 48 critical code-execution flaws, including CVE-2026-116928, which could let malicious email attachments run code without being opened.

Google patched CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Chrome’s XML processing component that has been exploited in active attacks. The November security update addresses nine vulnerabilities across supported platforms, including Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android. The fixes address security weaknesses that could enable code execution or bypass existing protections.

Apache has fixed CVE-2026-119618, a critical vulnerability affecting HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely. Successful exploitation could compromise vulnerable servers. Version 2.4.71 addresses the issue.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has identified cyberespionage campaigns linked to CopperDragon, a suspected digital quartermaster to China-nexus threat actors. The campaigns targeted government, military, telecom, and critical infrastructure organizations worldwide. Attackers compromised internet-facing systems and legitimate websites to distribute backdoors and steal sensitive information.

Check Point Research has published its October 2026 threat landscape. Organizations faced an average of 2,550 weekly attacks, down 9% from September but up 32% year over year, while one in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage. Title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
Context: We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered
Full Text:
Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor

Executive Summary

As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks, automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking, the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed.

Key trends over the last quarter include:

Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.

Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse: Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from LLMJacking by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers).

LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO): State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution.

Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution: Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution.

Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild.

At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through proactive disruption of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments.

Multi-Agent Frameworks in Cyber Intrusions

While previous milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now observed multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions.

Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge.

Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks

In addition to the now highly-publicized pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.

GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.

CAIRN: an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US.

CyberStrikeAI: an open source, LLM-native offensive framework which functions as a "single pane of glass" for cyber operations. The core architecture consists of a Go-based backend API acting as a C2 and orchestration server and connects commercial and open-weight LLMs to over 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts to automate end-to-end attack chains.

HexStrike AI: an open source offensive Model Context Protocol (MCP)-integrated harness that enables LLM clients to directly connect to over 150 pre-installed offensive security tools. Operating through a dual-component architecture, the framework wraps standard utilities across reconnaissance, web application testing, exploitation, and binary analysis into callable functions coordinated by more than 12 specialized autonomous sub-agents.

PentAGI: an open source autonomous offensive framework designed to lower technical barriers for entry-level operators running complex campaigns. Between late August and early October 2026, GTIG tracked a threat actor using a customized attack orchestration platform built off of the open source version of PentAGI used to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia.

We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations. These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation.

Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally. Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions. Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.

Figure 2: LLM maturity timeline

Mitigations

Google Security Operations (SecOps) has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework specifically designed to counter the speed and scale advantage of adversaries using LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

Use of Agents in Vulnerability Research and Development

The integration of autonomous LLM agents into vulnerability research and software security workflows has shifted from theoretical experimentation to active operational deployment.

Adversaries are leveraging multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipelines to automate labor-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, such as differential patch examination, dynamic protocol fuzzing, and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization. By chaining these capabilities together, threat actors can dramatically reduce the window between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws. In contrast, searching for zero-day vulnerabilities requires casting a wider net. LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organizations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don't, creating additional verification work for defenders.

For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August.

Figure 3: Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026

In our previous report, we detailed nascent efforts by threat actors surrounding LLM-augmented vulnerability research, including partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation attack sequences.

In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.

More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent, that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

Open source research corroborates threat actor operationalization of fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines. For example, in late August 2026, threat actors exploited two vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers as zero-days that, when chained together, allow for unauthenticated remote code execution: CVE-2026-81578, an authentication bypass flaw; and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe dynamic class loading vulnerability. Using LLMs, security researchers and the cybersecurity company Huntress generated working exploits for the vulnerabilities within a day of disclosure. Greynoise reported a campaign that took place four days after the initial disclosure in which a threat actor likely used LLMs to build and test exploits for these vulnerabilities, assemble a target list, and execute a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations. Greynoise also highlighted the speed of execution, noting that the threat actor expanded an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes.

The PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) also highlight several of these trends. They were discovered using LLM-enabled analysis. Before official patches were released on Oct. 21, 2026, a POC video and early patched code were published. This allowed both researchers and attackers to compare code versions, understand the flaws and attempt to build exploits before the patch became available. In the initial days following the official patch, hundreds of claimed but non-functional POCs, likely generated with the help of LLMs, were published. This proliferation created significant work for the security community to verify or debunk the POCs while monitoring for evidence of confirmed exploitation.

Mitigations

Google continuously invests in AI innovation and research, helping to ensure AI is built responsibly, and that we’re leveraging its potential to automatically find risks. In 2024 we introduced Big Sleep, an AI agent developed by Google DeepMind and Google Project Zero, that actively searches and finds unknown security vulnerabilities in software. Google Cloud employs a defense-in-depth model that combines rigorous code reviews and secure-by-default libraries with continuous, automated scanning using specialized AI agents such as CodeMender to discover, patch, and remediate vulnerabilities before and after release. We partner with the global security community by running a Vulnerability Reward Program and maintaining Project Zero to proactively find and patch zero-day vulnerabilities.

Full Integration of LLMs into Information Operations

GTIG assesses with high confidence that information operations (IO) threat actors have advanced from initial LLM experimentation to full operational integration. Across all tracked categories—state-sponsored groups, including those attributed to Russia, the PRC, and Iran, commercial "Influence-as-a-Service" (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks—adversaries now routinely embed LLMs into their standard tradecraft to produce synthetic media and automate domain network workflows (e.g., LLM-assisted SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of influence content). This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success.

IO Actor Categories

State-sponsored groups are IO actors directly linked to state apparatuses and have traditionally formed the primary baseline tracked by platform defenders and researchers. To preserve plausible deniability, they increasingly rely on third-party commercial contractors to execute campaigns on their behalf.

Commercial IaaS vendors encompass marketing and PR agencies, private intelligence contractors, and offshoots of commercial surveillance vendors, selling services ranging from tailored influence campaigns to turnkey platforms. Tradecraft varies across this ecosystem; intelligence contractors and surveillance offshoots in particular often apply stronger operational security (OPSEC) and more advanced techniques than traditional state-sponsored actors.

Inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are driven by profit rather than ideology. These actors generate a high volume of political clickbait to drive engagement, maximize click-through rates, and boost ad revenue. This combination of political framing and high-volume synthetic content creates a significant frontend perception gap, making IPM network campaigns the most prone to being misidentified as state-sponsored operations.

Table 2: IO actor categories

As automated content generation reduces a primary operational bottleneck, adversaries are increasingly shifting their focus toward leveraging LLMs for infrastructure design, automated distribution pipelines, and anti-detection mechanisms. Specifically, our observations indicate a notable shift toward the commercial development of LLM-enabled, end-to-end IaaS platforms designed to support and automate the full influence campaign lifecycle. The proliferation of these platforms can lower operational overhead for state and commercial actors while increasing the difficulty of detecting coordinated and inauthentic behavior across social media platforms.

The Commercial Development of Turnkey, LLM-Enabled Influence Operations

In August 2026, GTIG investigated threat activity leveraging the Gemini API alongside tools from multiple AI providers to build an end-to-end IaaS platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, primarily across Europe and the Middle East. The platform was engineered to automate the entire IO campaign lifecycle, including persona creation, multimodal media generation, automated content distribution, and interactive posting across platforms. Identified prompts reflected an operational focus on emulating organic grassroots engagement (i.e., “astroturfing”) while evading platform detection rules.

Identified prompts instructed models to adopt localized personas specific to targeted geography, mimicking regional dialects and slang, while incorporating informal phrasing and intentional typos to avoid sounding like an automated tool.

Prompts supporting media generation introduced deliberate camera flaws simulating realistic photos typically captured by smartphone cameras (e.g., making images appear grainy or incorporating uneven lighting changes) and omitted background text to avoid synthetic image markers.

To evade social media platform defenses, operators routed traffic through residential proxies and preserved saved login cookies. This setup was designed to allow automated tools to maintain active, authenticated access continuously, avoiding security checkpoints like CAPTCHAs and login re-verification.

GTIG also detected a separate commercial contractor leveraging the Gemini API—as part of a modular, multi-provider AI architecture—during the development of a turnkey IaaS platform engineered to manage over 100,000 accounts across major global platforms. The platform is architected to combine automated agents, anti-detection and device identifier spoofing tools, and cloud phone farms to operate thousands of inauthentic personas across platforms. Observed prompts indicated the actor’s plan to market the tool to both the actor’s domestic government bodies and foreign clients for influence campaign execution.

To manage large volumes of social media accounts, the platform was designed to run virtual smartphones in cloud environments—disguising each virtual device as a legitimate mobile device—and route web traffic through proxies to bypass automated bot detection and rate limits.

The architecture additionally includes automated fake account creation using disposable email addresses and overseas virtual SMS numbers. To avoid further suspicion, newly-created accounts were configured to undergo an automated aging period, leveraging LLMs to simulate realistic user behavior (e.g., how long a user lingers on a post, scrolling, and interacting with non-campaign content) to establish a history of normal activity before pushing targeted messaging.

Tactical LLM Adoption: Demographic Microtargeting and Content Scaling

Alongside the development of IaaS software suites, threat actors continue to integrate commercial LLM tools into baseline content workflows to overcome linguistic barriers, customize messaging, and scale output. Using commercial models to produce commentary, synthetic personas, and stylized animations at the content layer allows IO actors to improve the credibility and demographic resonance of their campaigns, while enabling IPM networks to mass-produce political clickbait for advertising revenue.

LLM-Enabled Quality Enhancement in Long-Running IaaS Campaign: Since our last report, GTIG observed a long-running IaaS provider tracked since 2019 leveraging LLMs to elevate the baseline quality and volume of its influence operations. Utilizing a proprietary software suite designed to manage thousands of synthetic profiles across major platforms, the provider targeted political discourse in multiple countries. Operators integrated LLM models to produce more convincing virtual personas, as well as academic-style commentary and media focused on political, religious, and civil rights topics. The resulting content was subsequently promoted and amplified across platforms using fabricated Western personas.

Demographic Targeting via Synthetic Content: We have observed threat actors using LLM-generated content to customize context for specific regions and audiences, for example by using synthetic influencer personas to promote policy narratives targeting specific demographics. A separate network posted synthetic, Lego brick-inspired animations and football parodies to satirize global political figures, likely in an attempt to appeal to younger audiences by effectively packaging propaganda in short-video formats consistent with popular internet culture.

LLM-Augmented Inauthentic Political Monetization (IPM): GTIG also tracks a growing trend of IPM actors using LLMs to mass-produce political content. Although their thematic focus, quality, and volume can resemble state-backed IO campaigns, these non-ideological operations exploit societal polarization solely to maximize engagement, click-through rates, and advertising revenue. GTIG has observed IPM operators prompting commercial LLMs to identify lucrative political topics, trending keywords, and high-Cost Per Mile (CPM) niches for ad monetization, while promoting the resulting content via synthetic news anchors that occasionally spoof the likenesses of real journalists and commentators to manufacture credibility.

Mitigations

GTIG collaborates closely with product teams to take action against IO actors across affected Google surfaces under our standard platform policies. Our research and rigorous analysis enables Google teams to make enforcement decisions and to disrupt coordinated IO campaigns. GITG, YouTube, and Google Trust & Safety track and regularly enforce on accounts associated with coordinated IO posting content and commenting. Examples of this enforcement include disruption of YouTube channels, blogs, AdSense accounts, and domains removed from Google News surfaces, as we report on a quarterly basis in the Influence Operations Bulletin.

Beyond enforcement actions, GTIG shares insights with Google DeepMind to harden our platforms and services against emerging tradecraft. This intelligence is used to establish abuse baselines, enhance Gemini’s ability to recognize and refuse misuse, and inform internal policy modifications.

Threat Actors Abusing and Monetizing Access to AI Tools

While compromised credentials have long served as the fundamental bedrock for initial access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement during intrusions, adversaries are increasingly repurposing stolen credentials and compute resources to power unauthorized LLM tooling and autonomous operational pipelines. As access costs, token rate limits, and geographic restrictions present persistent operational hurdles for threat actors attempting to scale LLM capabilities, adversaries are actively harvesting session tokens and platform credentials directly from victim endpoints and continuous integration environments. In tandem with this shift toward hijacking valid credentials for LLMs, underground cybercrime forums and illicit marketplaces have rapidly matured to meet this demand—transitioning beyond generic identity dumps to commodifying verified frontier AI accounts, tokenized API quotas, and targeted infostealer configurations as turnkey utilities for downstream exploitation.

LLMJacking in Incident Response

Throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents where financially motivated actors compromised cloud environments to consume targeted organizations’ cloud compute and/or LLM resource quotas. As seen in the image below, LLMJacking can generate significant usage and billing increases within hours. In some cases, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000 USD. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation.

Figure 5: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests

In November, Mandiant and GTIG described a set of common TTPs we observed across intrusions that affected financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region.

Attack Lifecycle Stage

Description of Observed Tactics

Initial Access

Threat actors frequently used credential theft and session hijacking to gain access to targeted environments, including harvesting valid credentials from public GitHub repositories, and social engineering using deceptive websites to trick users into providing active session tokens.

Internal Reconnaissance & Lateral Movement

Seeking to identify credentials and systems of interest, attackers conducted reconnaissance against internal code repositories, data stores, cloud services, containers, and access logs. In at least one case, a threat actor exploited a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running in an internal container to navigate to additional systems.

Privilege Escalation & Persistence

Threat actors created unauthorized IAM and service accounts or attached administrative policies to service roles. We also observed a threat actor exploit CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that allows an attacker to elevate limited-access inference keys ("Virtual Keys") into full administrative credentials. Privileged service accounts were sufficient to establish persistence without the use of malware.

Complete Mission: LLM Abuse

Inside organizations’ cloud environments, attackers enabled LLM services, including subscribing compromised accounts to pay-as-you-go agreements. To circumvent rate limits, one threat actor used a “burn and rotate” strategy, creating and deleting short-lived service accounts. Other threat actors abused cloud compute resources, provisioning instances with powerful GPUs and requesting quota increases in order to run their own LLM tooling. This included agentic frameworks that a threat actor used to automate further exploitation of the compromised network, as well as open source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure deployed to facilitate the sale of access to the compromised organization’s resources.

Table 3: Common TTPs observed in LLMJacking intrusions

In another investigation, we observed at least two separate attackers seeking to conduct LLMJacking operations. Both actors accessed a targeted environment using the same set of legitimate credentials, which were potentially sold or leaked on underground forums. The first threat actor used legitimate credentials to gain access to the environment, enumerate available LLM services, and query cost and usage information related to the account. On the same day, we observed a set of IP addresses using a common User-Agent, likely a botnet or proxy service, also accessing the environment using the same legitimate credentials. The botnet or proxy service generated millions of LLM API calls in approximately 24 hours before the credentials were revoked. Though the first threat actor returned to the environment, creating service accounts provisioned with permissions to query LLMs, the botnet’s noisy activity caused the compromised credentials to be remediated before this threat actor could execute LLM queries.

For hardening and mitigation guidance for defending against LLMJacking intrusions, please see our blog.

Monetizing LLMJacking through LLM Mixers

Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure. This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.

The LLM Mixer ecosystem mirrors the broader cybercrime marketplace, where specialized threat groups handle discrete phases of the supply chain. While LLM Mixer operators maintain infrastructure and customer fulfillment, for example, operators may partner with separate threat actors who establish initial access to compromised environments, purchase compromised credentials from infostealer operators, or recruit partners to systematically register free trial accounts.

GTIG analyzed numerous LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, and found that most services offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken models that advertise support of malicious cyber activity. Advertised pricing varies significantly across individual mixer platforms and based on the models and types of credentials offered; for example, free trial credentials were much cheaper than enterprise. We observed prices per million tokens range from $0.10 USD to $25 USD. One vendor, APIMart, applies a 5x price increase on both input and output once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Rather than pricing per million tokens, some vendors such as JetNight offer monthly subscriptions at differing prices based on the type of model offered.

Title: Hijacked by Hype: The Weaponization of GTA 6
Context: Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer...
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Lucy Gee and Cameron Sweeney

With Grand Theft Auto 6 scheduled to launch on November 19, 2026, the 13-year wait for the most anticipated video game release of the decade is nearly over.

As legitimate marketing emails from Rockstar Games increase, video game fans are hyped. The anticipation is massive. However, this unprecedented excitement has created a perfect storm for cybercriminals.

Rockstar and its vast cult following have long fascinated threat actors, with the studio famously suffering massive network breaches and high-profile data leaks in recent years. Now, attackers are pivoting those established tactics directly toward the fanbase.

Threat actors are actively capitalizing on gamers' desperation, knowing that heightened anticipation reliably leads to lower critical thinking. By impersonating Rockstar in a massive, coordinated wave of phishing campaigns, they are weaponizing the promise of exclusive early access, fake "leaked" playable copies, or beta tester invitations to actively exploit both everyday consumers and corporate employees.

This playbook aligns directly with findings from KnowBe4’s Phishing Threat Trends Report Volume 8. That research showed planned calendar events drive the highest volume of lure-based attacks, with campaigns landing an average of 21.3 days before the actual date. On top of that, the lifespan of these planned campaigns more than doubled between 2022 and 2026, giving attackers plenty of time to tweak their angles and test out different lures.

The GTA 6 wave illustrates this dynamic in real time. Data obtained from KnowBe4 Defend shows a rapid, strategic escalation precisely within this pre-launch window:

Key Takeaways:

While GTA-themed phishing accounted for just 0.005% of threats in September, general gaming-related phishing emails have since surged by 1,300% compared to the monthly average across the previous six months (March–August 2026).

For the full week starting October 26th, 24 days before the release, GTA-related lures rapidly scaled to make up 9.6% of all phishing volume.

The First Wave: Mass-Market Noise

Predominantly, this surge is driven by high-volume, spray-and-pray commodity lures. These attacks focus on broad consumer appeal, casting a wide net across millions of inboxes in hopes of catching eager gamers off guard.

In the most widespread campaign, threat actors rely on a minimalist payload delivery to bypass security defenses: the email body is left completely blank, containing nothing more than an embedded link. By stripping away text entirely, the message circumvents basic natural language processing (NLP) filters and spam heuristics that search for suspicious gaming keywords.

To evade domain-reputation blocks, the campaign is heavily polymorphic, distributing waves of messages through constantly rotating webmail accounts with random subject lines so that blocking a single sender provides zero defense against the broader campaign.

Anatomy of the Attack

Clicking the link routes victims through a multi-stage lure that heavily borrows the official Grand Theft Auto 6 aesthetic. Initial landing pages are hosted on graph[.]org, which is Telegram’s lightweight, anonymous and login free publishing site. This allows attackers to host malicious content without registering their own infrastructure, making it easy to stand up pages that slip past filters, especially those looking at domain age.

These pages feature Vice City neon styling, AI generated imagery of characters Lucia and Jason, and prominent Rockstar Games branding. The copy leans into themed phrasing like "The wait is over," "Vice City is calling," and promises of an exclusive "$4,000 bonus" using promo code ROCKSTAR.

Once a user clicks the activate prompt, they are redirected to a fraudulent online casino or crypto platform (such as new2026[.]pro) with the promo code pre-applied. The ultimate objective is dual-pronged monetization: tricking victims into registering an account to harvest passwords they likely recycle across gaming and personal platforms, while simultaneously siphoning payment card details or cryptocurrency deposits under the guise of claiming their GTA-themed welcome bonus. While these mass-market lures lack the sophistication needed to directly compromise enterprise networks, their relentless volume acts as a smokescreen, generating endless background noise for SOC teams.

Campaign Telemetry: Commodity Attack Distribution

Top Targeted Regions: United States (47%), United Kingdom (35%), Germany (8%), France (5%), Rest of World (5%)

Primary Target Verticals: Education (39%), Technology (35%), and Finance (15%)

Campaign: 84 attacks on average per campaign, typically peaking on weekends and evenings.

While these commodity attacks lack sophistication, their sheer volume creates a smokescreen designed to overwhelm SOC teams. The real danger lies in what slips beneath the radar: advanced, targeted phishing campaigns, created to weaponize the intersection of personal interests and organizational trust.

The Second Wave: Targeting the Enterprise

Instead of directly impersonating Rockstar Games, these sophisticated attacks pose as employee benefits programs offering a "free Grand Theft Auto 6 Pre-Order" as a corporate perk. Because a free copy of a highly anticipated game is one of the few things that will convince an employee to check a work email on their days off, these campaigns are heavily weighted toward weekends, accounting for 83.2% of the attack volume. This strategy peaked over the October 31 to November 1 weekend, where GTA-related impersonations made up 42.4% of all phishing emails processed.

In this example, the attacker is combining psychological manipulation with technical evasion elements to ensure the attack lands in users’ inboxes and they’re motivated to click. Rather than impersonating Rockstar directly, which users might view with suspicion, the attacker routes the lure through a fake employee benefits program. Framing the game as a corporate perk carries significantly more weight than standard brand impersonation.

The attack also utilizes senses of urgency, claiming the offer closes in 48 hours and is strictly limited to the first 250 employees. This artificial urgency pushes the victim toward a fast, low-deliberation click. To make the attack look legitimate, the banner at the bottom of the email explicitly states that the message was sent to a verified address and does not collect payment information. This pre-answers the recipient's own suspicions, lowering their guard before they even question the email. By tying the lure directly to the real-world GTA 6 news cycle, the attack feels incredibly timely and relevant, blending seamlessly into the broader hype.

Technical Evasion

Clean Authentication Bypass: The attackers use a genuinely owned, look-alike vendor domain rather than a spoofed one. As the domain is legitimately registered to the threat actor, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass cleanly.

Unicode QR Codes: To evade traditional detection, the email uses a QR code rendered entirely out of text block characters (Unicode or HTML tables) rather than a standard image file, allowing it to bypass image QR scanners.

Device Shifting: The ultimate goal of the QR code is to shift the attack off the protected corporate network. By forcing the victim to scan the code with their personal smartphone, the attacker completely bypasses corporate web filtering and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) controls.

These sophisticated phishing emails largely followed the same distribution as the commodity attacks. Campaign sizes, however, are much smaller averaging 20 attacks per campaign.

The Corporate Risk of Personal Lures

This blurring of lines between personal interests and professional environments is exactly what makes these attacks so dangerous. While a fake GTA 6 pre-order might initially look like a standard consumer scam aimed at stealing a personal credit card, the reality is far more severe: these campaigns are explicitly designed to compromise corporate assets. When an eager employee scans a malicious QR code on their unmanaged personal phone to claim a supposed "work perk," the resulting phishing page is rarely asking for their bank details. Instead, attackers are weaponizing this gaming hype to harvest credentials; turning a momentary lapse in personal judgment into a full-scale corporate breach.

Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks

As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer excitement and corporate access. Threat actors targeted human psychology, not a software zero-day exploit. They identified an emotional blind spot of weekend relaxation and genuine excitement and used it to bypass both technical filters and common sense.

Protecting your organization against these hybrid threats requires a layered approach:

Run Contextual Simulations: Train employees on non-traditional lure types. Especially fake HR perks, vendor discounts, real-world events, and corporate benefits delivered outside typical working hours.

Validate Internal Communications: Establish a clear protocol for corporate benefits so employees know legitimate company perks will always appear on an internal intranet or HR portal, never via unsolicited external email links or urgent QR codes.

Teach the "Device Shift" Red Flag: Educate staff that any work-related email asking them to pull out a personal smartphone to scan a QR code is a deliberate attempt to bypass security perimeter controls.

Normalize Healthy Scrutiny: Remind teams that genuine corporate perks never demand urgency. If an offer says “limited to the first 250 employees,” it’s designed to shut down deliberate thinking.

Harden Quishing Defenses: Ensure your email security layer can detect QR codes, including those rendered as Unicode characters or HTML tables, not just as image files.

When real-world hype peaks, critical thinking drops. Ensuring your workforce and security stack are prepared for both the high-volume noise and the targeted signal is the best defense against turning a pop-culture milestone into a network compromise.

Where KnowBe4 Can Help

These attacks rely on natural human emotions to trick your users. Excitement. A sense of urgency. Whether it’s an invitation to click a link or scan a QR code, your users need to be aware of the varied kinds of attacks bad actors are using.

The KnowBe4 Platform and its suite of tools provides the training your users need with the technology-based defenses to help keep attacks from even reaching the inbox.

AI-Native Security Awareness Training

Hype-based attacks need a quick response to ensure your users have the resources they need to spot them. KnowBe4’s suite of AI Defense Agents (AIDA) includes the capabilities to generate custom phishing simulation templates and whole modules in minutes, helping training admins respond to the newest threats.

KnowBe4 Defend: Real-Time Behavioral AI

KnowBe4 Defend uses behavioral AI and natural language processing to analyze email content and context to clearly flag when emails look suspicious. Defend adds a warning banner directly into the email before the recipient opens it. This interrupts the illusion of legitimacy, such as phishing attacks claiming to offer internal company benefits or perks.

PhishER Plus: Automated Threat Response

Once novel threats are identified, either through machine learning or human observation, PhishER Plus uses this information to keep future users from even seeing them. It automatically categorizes threats, provides immediate feedback to reporters, and enables one-click remediation across all mailboxes. Drawing intelligence from 13+ million global users and integrations with leading security platforms, PhishER Plus delivers unprecedented visibility while providing clear decision-making transparency.

Title: Typosquatters Copy Big Brands’ New Domains Within a Day of Registration
Context: Only two pairs did anything else
Full Text:
The name changes were small. Classic typosquatting techniques such as keyboard-adjacent swaps, homoglyphs or hyphen insertion were absent. Instead, the actors favored edits that kept the name readable and plausible, which a hurried reader would be unlikely to notice.

Of the 27 pairs, 15 dropped a plural or possessive “s” (fyzadasavings became fyzadasaving), six left out a single letter (greystarbenefits became greystarbenfits) and four collapsed a double letter (mywayconnect became mywayconect). That makes 25 plain deletions. Only two pairs did anything else. One added a letter (tradealgotcpasettlement became tradealgotcpassettlement) and one swapped a vowel (yourmsdbenefits became yourmsdbenifits).

The dropped plural “s” was the most common edit. Savings became saving, claims became claim and sweeps became sweep. People often say and type the singular form, which may make these the most effective typos. The actors also folded novelty top-level domains (TLDs) back into .com, likely because users default to it; carmax[.]claims became carmaxclaim[.]com and mcdonaldsmedia[.]network became mcdonaldmedianetwork[.]com. A single lookalike could also shadow several authentic domains. For example, carmaxclaim[.]com covered both carmax[.]claims and carmaxclaims[.]com, while yourmsdbenefits[.]com drew three separate variants from two registrars.

Monetization

When queried, the lookalikes served one of three kinds of content. Some were parked placeholder pages that earned money from pay-per-click advertising feeds. Others were deceptive search portals whose results led to scam blogs, or brand-themed blogs written around the typosquatted name and packed with ads that routed visitors to scam sites.

This low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal. Advertising networks of this kind can also be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, and a domain that serves ads today could serve a fake claims form tomorrow with a single Domain Name System (DNS) or content change. Visitors who reach these domains are already primed to enter personal details. Symantec continues to track the campaign’s scope and persistence.

Protection

WebPulse, the collaborative intelligence cloud behind Symantec web security, placed the identified domains in security categories and can catch new variants through shared detection patterns.

For more information on Symantec protection against this campaign, see the Protection Bulletin.
