Title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
Context: To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we...
Full Text:
Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One, Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network.

Key insights

Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure.

Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods.

Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment.

Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour

Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer.

More swarms, fewer giants

Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025:

96% ended in under 10 minutes

98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website

On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad.

Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot. Mirai-classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21.

Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP

The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3.

Meanwhile, DNS amplification surged 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks, exploiting open DNS resolvers in a similar reflection-and-amplification pattern to CLDAP: small spoofed queries, large replies directed at the victim. Other UDP floods climbed from 14.06% to 31.31% of network-layer attacks. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol, which makes it a convenient vehicle for raw volumetric attacks: attackers send large numbers of UDP packets to random or specific ports on the target, forcing the target to check for a listening application and respond, consuming its network and compute resources.

Most-attacked industry

While Media, Production & Publishing remained the most-attacked industry in Q3 2026, its overall share is roughly a quarter of its Q2 level, and the focus has moved across a wider set of industries. Internet rose from outside the top 10 to #6; Consumer Services and Adult Entertainment also climbed in, reaching #8 and #9 respectively.

Most-attacked locations

Geographic surges: Canada and Israel climb the ranks

Adding to an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes, Canada jumped from #16 to #6, driven by attacks against its Retail, Telecommunications, Service providers & carriers, and Marketing & advertising industries.

Israel moved 7 spots to take #10 as a result of sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. While this period was marked by contentious decisions ahead of parliamentary elections and the Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was also a massive, documented surge in hostile cyber warfare targeting Israel this year.

Top 10

The United States was the most-attacked location in Q3 2026, while China was number #2 and Indonesia rose into the top three at 2.93% of total attacks. The U.S.-China pairing at the top is consistent with the first half of 2026, when China finished #1 and the U.S. #2; the countries have traded positions as attention and attacker preferences shift.

Strengthening global defenses and helping to defend the Internet

Cloudflare's network is designed to absorb this kind of growth in DDoS threats. Every service on our network is protected by free, unmetered DDoS protection that runs at every one of our 330+ cities globally, backed by 500 Tbps of network capacity. Autonomy is the point: our systems detect and mitigate attacks without human intervention. And they need to, because as this quarter's distributions make clear, most attacks end long before a human analyst could see the alert, and the largest attacks still regularly exceed 1 Tbps at a cadence measured in hundreds per quarter.

To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we leverage Cloudflare's unique vantage point on DDoS attacks to provide a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for Service Providers.

Over 800 networks worldwide have signed up for this feed, and we've already seen great collaboration across the community to take down botnet nodes. For a continuously-updated view of attack trends across the Internet, visit Cloudflare Radar.

About Cloudforce One

Driven by a mission to help defend the Internet, Cloudforce One draws on telemetry from Cloudflare's global network — which protects more than 20% of the web — to drive threat research and operational response, protecting critical systems for millions of organizations worldwide.

Title: Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing
Context: The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time
Full Text:
Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

The Human Impact of Scams

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.

Title: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework
Context: NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.”

NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session.

In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically.

In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies.

NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows.

Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline.

NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool

The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module.

Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2.

The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc4b8f/main.go), which identifies the project as "nik_panel" and indicates that the implant was cross compiled for Windows from a Linux development environment. Furthermore, the embedded eight-byte hex token matching the build identifier highlights that the threat actor's infrastructure actively tracking and versioning the implants.

Figure 1. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture.

NIK C2 implant evolution timeline

Talos observed that the NIK C2 implant development trajectory spans at least three distinct versions. All binaries observed in the wild were compiled with Go 1.23.4 (which was released in December 2024), placing the entire sample set compiled no earlier than late 2024. The actor has Zeroed PE TimeDateStamp fields and near-epoch filesystem timestamps (manifesting as Nov 29, 1979) are applied consistently across all samples.

We developed a timeline based on the initial sighting dates of NIK C2 implant variants in OSINT.

Figure 2. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline.

The pace of capability addition across the three versions indicates a technically proficient team with prior malware operations experience is actively expanding NIK C2 towards a full-service adversarial framework.

Active NIK C2 server seen in the wild

During our research, we observed that a threat actor hosted the NIK C2 framework on a server at IP address “87.120.196[.]120”, resolving the domain “total-sitevv[.]lol”. The C2 server hosted an SSL/TLS certificate (serial number 7d16381a9de823943b5a0987dbd0f26edf22052b and jarm:"28d28d28d00000000042d42d0000001f361a1bf80ed39a1e352adeb016a07b" ) with the Common Name (CN) set to nik-panel. This CN value matches strings embedded within the implant binary. Observing the NIK C2 infrastructure active in the wild allowed us to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is not merely a proof of concept, but a fully functional, AI-integrated C2 framework.

Figure 3. NIK C2 was observed in the wild during the research period.

NIK C2 implant integrates OpenAI’s API

AI integration is one of the most architecturally distinct features of NIK C2 implant. It constructs a fully formed HTTP request to OpenAI’s production inference endpoint, transmits it from the victim machine IP address, parses the JSON response, and returns the AI-generated text to the actor’s panel. The entire operation from receiving the actor prompt to returning the large language model (LLM) reply is executed synchronously with a 60-second timeout.

The implant begins by extracting three fields from the command payload received from the C2. The first field, identified by the key prompt, is the text the actor wants to send to the AI model. If the prompt string has zero length, the handler immediately constructs an error response and returns without making any outbound network call. The second field, identified by the key api_key is the OpenAI API key to use for authentication. The third field, identified by the key model, specifies which OpenAI model to use.

Figure 4. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

After extracting the three parameters, the implant checks whether the actor supplied an API key. If not, it calls the operating system's environment variable reader with the string OPENAI_API_KEY and uses the victim’s API key. This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications. If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference. OpenAI's billing system will charge the victim's payment method, and OpenAI's access logs will show the victim's API key as the one that made the requests, allowing no trace attributable to the threat actor.

If the actor does not specify a model name, the implant falls back to a five-character default string stored in the binary data section. Decoding the five-character value showed gpt-4 confirming that GPT4 is the default when no model is specified. The actor can override this by passing any valid OpenAI model identifier in the command payload, allowing selection of newer models as they become available without requiring a binary update.

The implant builds the OpenAI API request body by constructing a map with four fields. The first field uses the key model and contains the resolved model name. The second field uses key messages and contains a two-element array of message maps. The third field uses the key temperature and contains a floating-point value read from a constant in the binary data section. The fourth field uses the key max_tokens and contains an integer value also read from binary.

The message array is constructed in the order that the OpenAI Chat Completions API expects. The system message is first followed by the user message. The system message map has the role system and a content string that is exactly 68 bytes long hardcoded in the binary. This 68-byte string is the implant's behavioral instruction to the AI. It defines the model's operational role and response style for the duration of the session. The user message map has the role user and contains the actor's prompt text verbiage. The complete map structure is then serialized to JSON. The JSON message is sent to the URL https:// api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint, through an HTTP POST request.

Figure 5. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

When the HTTP response arrives with a 200 status code, the handler uses Golang's JSON decoder to parse the response body directly into a generic map structure without defining a typed schema. It then navigates the decoded map by string key lookups in the sequence that the OpenAI Chat Completions API response structure defines. The outermost map is queried for the key choices which in a successful response contains an array. The implant checks that this array is non-empty, then accesses its element keys message and content. The string value at key content is the AI model-generated text response.

After successfully extracting the AI-generated content, the handler assembles a result map with four entries. The key status is set to a constant string that reads as generated. The key code is set to the AI model's response text, so that the actor receives the full content of the model’s replies. The key model is set to the resolved model name that was used for the request, confirming which model produced the output. The key usage is set to the raw usage object from the OpenAI response, which contains the prompt token count, completion token count, and total token count. This usage data allows the actor to track how many tokens are consumed per request. The completed result map is ultimately transmitted to the C2 server over WebSocket or through the HTTP fallback C2 address.

Figure 6. AI model response is encapsulated in JSON message and will be sent to C2.

Dual execution modes of NIK C2 implant

Upon execution, the implant inspects its command-line arguments to determine its execution path. The argument watchdog activates supervisory monitoring to relaunch the core process if terminated, the copywatchdog tracks file copy operations, and the absence of either defaults execution to primary agent mode.

In primary mode, it uses a named mutex to enforce single-instance execution, logs a message reading [NIK] Starting, generates a 32-byte cryptographic session key if uninitialized, decodes its obfuscated C2 address, and sets its masquerade name to “svchost.exe” or “simvol.exe”.

After initial setup, the binary records its process ID (PID) in the victim's temporary application folder and executes its persistence and evasion routines. These routines include copying to %appdata%/Roaming/Microsoft/Network with modified access controls, configuring Windows autostart registry entries, and masquerading its process. Finally, it starts the local proxy server, initiates the WebSocket communication loop in a separate goroutine, and enters a continuous heartbeat polling loop on the main thread.

Implant’s C2 command surface overview

The implant command dispatcher module facilitates over 52 commands that are directed by the C2 panel. The dispatcher module uses byte-level string matching to map the associated modules that are launched as concurrent goroutines, allowing multiple operations to run in parallel.

Implant deploys screen-locking ransomware

The ransomware module of the implant operates as a multi-stage attack controller that the actor runs in sequence to prepare, deploy, and retract a screen-locking ransomware payload.

At first, it executes PowerShell to execute a raw disk copy command that reads directly from the physical drive device path (“\\.\PhysicalDrive0”) and writes the first sector, which is Master Boot Record (MBR), to a file named “mbr_backup.bin” in the Windows temporary directory.

Figure 7. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s boot ransomware handler function.

Next, the module constructs a complete self-contained HTML lock screen code entirely at runtime from a hardcoded format string, parameterized with actor supplied Bitcoin and USDT wallet addresses, prices, contact email, timer duration, and custom text from the C2 command message, allowing the actor to fully customize the ransom demands.

Figure 8. Screenlocker HTML code is hardcoded in NIK C2 implant binary.

After generating the HTML code, the binary writes it to the file “lock_screen.html” in the system temporary directory. It then generates a Windows batch script that calls mshta.exe with the path to the HTML file, followed by an infinite loop construct with a five-second timeout between iterations, ensuring that if the user somehow closes the window it reopens within five seconds. This batch file is written to the temp directory as “lock_start.bat”.

The implant then runs a reg add command that writes a registry Run key named “SystemLock” under the current user's autostart path, pointing to a cmd /c invocation of the batch file, so the lock screen is executed on every user's logon. Additionally, a background goroutine is spawned that continuously monitors and relaunches the lock screen process. Finally, the module sends a confirmation response to C2 with the path of the deployed HTML file and the timer value.

The design of this ransomware module is notable for several reasons. It does not encrypt any files, which means it leaves no forensic trail of file modification timestamps or encryption markers. It relies entirely on a screen lock, which is considerably faster to deploy than a file encryption ransomware. The persistence via registry Run key and a self-healing loop ensures the screen lock survives user attempts to dismiss it and survives a system restart.

Figure 9. Desktop lockscreen page of the ransomware deployed by the NIK C2 implant.

Implant’s bootkit preparation feature

The bootkit preparation module of the implant is designed to survey the victim machine's boot firmware environment and then stage a bootkit payload file.

It executes bcdedit /enum, the Windows Boot Configuration Data editor, with the output flag that enumerates all boot entries while hiding the console window. The implant reads the full output and searches for three specific substrings in sequence including EFI, Windows Boot Manager, and Windows Legacy OS Loader. If any of these are found, the boot type is classified as UEFI. The binary also searches for ntldr, the legacy Windows NT loader used by BIOS-mode systems as a fallback. Based on which string was matched, the boot type is recorded as either "UEFI" or "BIOS" as a string of the appropriate length. Separately, the binary runs a PowerShell command invoking Confirm-SecureBootUEFI, which is a built-in PowerShell command that returns to the current Secure Boot state. The output is searched for the string True to detect an enabled Secure Boot and for False to detect an explicitly disabled Secure Boot. If neither is present, the value is recorded as unknown. The result is sent back to the C2, a map containing the boot type classification and the Secure Boot status string.

Then the implant writes a 16-byte placeholder file named “bootkit.bin” to the system temporary directory. The bytes written spell out "NIK_BOOTKIT_PREP" in ASCII, which serves as a staging marker rather than an actual bootkit binary. This placeholder confirms that the target path is writable by the current process, establishes the file location that subsequent operations will reference, and can be overwritten by the actual bootkit binary delivered through the implant's file-upload or file-write command handlers. The path to the staged file is returned to the C2 in response.

Implant’s theft functionality

When the actor issues the theft category commands from the C2, the implant executes the associated goroutines to collect the targeted data into a result map space in the victim machine memory:

WiFi password theft (wifi_steal)

The implant executes netsh commands directly via Go’s exec.Command function by passing arguments as discrete tokens rather than through a shell string. Harvested results are formatted under specific labels: plaintext Wi-Fi passwords appear under Key Content:, saved network names are cataloged under WiFi Profiles: (with missing entries flagged using the per-entry format [%s] not found), and execution failures or absent interfaces return standardized error strings such as [WiFi] no wireless adapter or access denied and No WiFi profiles found.

netsh wlan show profiles netsh wlan show profile name="" key=clear

Browser credential extraction (passwords, quick_steal)

The implant stages targeted browser database files into an archive alongside the Local State file, which contains the AES master key protected by Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI). The implant imports and executes the CryptUnprotectData Windows API to unwrap the AES key and decrypt the databases locally. Otherwise, it exfiltrates the raw encrypted databases to the C2 server for offline extraction.

The implant extracts Discord tokens and session cookies from the levelDB store on the victim machine. The extracted outputs are labelled as === Discord Tokens === and DISCORD TOKENS. The browser session cookies (Discord_Cookies) are extracted from the copied Cookies database.

Cryptocurrency wallet theft (crypto_steal, wallet_export)

Victim’s desktop-based wallets are collected directly from the wallet storage paths. Browser extension wallets are extracted from chromium LevelDB stored by extension ID.

Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance

The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i. The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. Matched data are collected under the label of seed candidates and archived into “browserdata.zip”.

(?i)(seed|phrase|mnemonic|recovery|backup|wallet).*(\.txt|\.md|\.csv|\.dat) (?i)(private|privkey|secret).*(\.txt|\.md|\.key|\.pem)

The implant also performs victim machine reconnaissance by executing the following commands and uses chcp 65001 prefix to force the output in UTF-8 format.

chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & systeminfo chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic os get lastbootuptime /value chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic /namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 path AntiVirusProduct get displayName 2>nul chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & Get-Process | Select-Object Id, ProcessName | ConvertTo-Json -Compress

After all collection paths are complete, the implant assembles all collected data into a single document that looks like a formatted report with clearly labeled sections for each data category such as === CRYPTO ===, === WIFI ===, === BROWSER ===.

Keylogger: Keystrokes livestreamed to C2

The keylogger module of the implant uses a persistent background goroutine that polls all 256 Windows virtual key codes, detecting keypresses via dynamically resolved API calls, and transmits the captured input. When a compromised victim presses a valid key on the keyboard, it is simultaneously streamed live as an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON payload over WebSocket to C2 and also appends to an in-memory buffer capped at 10,000 entries and halved when full to prevent memory leaks. On an actor's dump command, this buffer is concatenated into a single string and returned to C2 via WebSocket or HTTP fallback, ensuring complete data transfer even during network interruptions.

Stolen data exfiltration to C2

Once the archive is assembled, the entire result map is handed to the result transmission routine of the implant. That routine constructs a new JSON object containing five specific fields. It includes the command identifier echoed back from the original command. It also contains the agent's persistent identifier, formatted as ag_<16 hex chars>. The type field is set to the string quick_steal_response. Finally, the data field holds the complete result map.

Once constructed, this object is forwarded to the encryption routine. The routine serializes the object into JSON. It then generates 12 fresh random bytes to serve as a nonce. Next, it encrypts the serialized JSON using AES-256-GCM with a static key derived from a hardcoded seed. It concatenates the nonce, the ciphertext, and the 16-byte authentication tag and Base64-encodes the entire payload. The encrypted payload is placed in a wrapper object under the "e" key alongside the plain-text agent ID, and the wrapper is JSON marshaled into the final payload.

This encrypted payload is then delivered through an available transmission path. The sending routine first checks whether the WebSocket connection is live. If it is, the payload is written directly into a WebSocket text frame on the existing connection, reaching the actor's panel with minimal latency. If the WebSocket is not currently connected, the routine falls back to an HTTP POST request to the endpoint path /api/c2/result on the C2 server, using the same encrypted body format. This dual-path design ensures stolen data is delivered even during WebSocket interruptions, as the HTTP channel remains functional independently of the WebSocket state.

Implant’s C2 protocol

The implant C2 architecture is designed for two independent, simultaneously operating communication channels. The primary channel is a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS. The secondary channel is an HTTP polling loop that posts to a fixed API endpoint at regular intervals.

With the primary channel, the connection begins with a TCP dial to the C2 server address with an eight-second timeout. If the port is not explicitly present in the configured address, port 443 is appended automatically. Once the TCP socket is established, it is wrapped in a TLS session using a custom certificate configuration that pins to a specific certificate rather than validating against the system's certificate authority store. This prevents standard TLS interception proxies from observing traffic.

Immediately after a successful WebSocket handshake but before any command is received, the implant transmits a full system registration message. The implant collects victim data such as the machine hostname, the local LAN IP address, the Windows username from the environment, a user security identifier, the local reverse-proxy port number that was assigned when the embedded proxy server was started, and the detected upstream proxy configuration derived from the Windows registry proxy settings. All of this is assembled into a JSON object and encrypted and sent to the C2.

Figure 10. Snippet of NIK C2 IMPLANT’s C2 communication handler function.

The HTTP polling channel runs independently. Every approximately 250 milliseconds, the agent collects a fresh snapshot of victim state hostname, watchdog status, local IP, username, current timestamp, and system uptime encrypts it in the same wire format and posts it to the /api/c2/update endpoint on the C2 server.

Below table shows the C2 endpoints that the implant communicates:

Endpoint

Purpose

/api/c2/update

Reconnaissance beacon – victim system info

/api/c2/result

Command output exfiltration

/api/c2/screen

Screenshot upload

/api/c2/file_chunk

File exfiltration

/api/c2/rproxy_up

Reverse proxy upstream data

/api/c2/ws

Websocket – actor command channel

Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key.

Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9

The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying.

Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function.

The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result.

Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques

The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow, renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions.

Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module.

Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack, which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command, triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds.

The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET), forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session.

Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script.

Conclusion

The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft.

Title: MR ROBOT Malware-as-a-Service Targets Indian Bank Customers
Context: Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand
Full Text:
A new Android malware-as-a-service (MaaS) operation has been found renting customized banking trojans to criminals targeting Indian bank customers, with one affiliate intercepting 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

The operation, branded MR ROBOT by its operators, was detailed in research published on October 28 by threat intelligence firm CloudSEK. Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand.

The lures are distributed through fake Play Store-style pages and messaging-app links, and impersonate banks as well as utility providers and government services.

MR ROBOT Turns Banking Malware into Subscription Service

CloudSEK said MR ROBOT is not a single actor’s campaign but a multi-tenant crimeware platform. Each affiliate receives its own application ID and can generate Android packages impersonating specific Indian banks.

The platform supports a tiered reseller model with sub-admin accounts, and licenses access for set periods through a control panel identified as version 7.0.

The malware intercepts text messages carrying one-time passwords (OTPs), shows fake screens to harvest banking credentials, card details, PINs and identity information, and can silently enable call forwarding. CloudSEK said this reroutes incoming calls, including banks’ fraud-check callbacks, to a number the attackers’ control.

The storefront, a Telegram bot called APK Shield, offered around 36 lure apps, including bank impersonations and fake apps for utility bills, telecom services, traffic fines and government services.

One Affiliate Intercepted More Than 5400 Text Messages

CloudSEK tracked two affiliates. One affiliate’s panel held around 154 enrolled devices and approximately 3270 intercepted messages, while an exposed Firebase database linked to a second held 153 devices and 5407 messages.

That data was collected between July 16 and 30, 2026, and around 4000 of the messages came from bank and telecommunications short codes. CloudSEK said call forwarding was active on 58% of the devices.

Each build receives a fresh signing certificate and can hide from the Android launcher after installation. CloudSEK said MR ROBOT shares call forwarding and per-customer builders with FatBoyPanel and RedWing, operations previously documented by Zimperium, but its kit, storefront and panel had not been publicly reported.

Read more on Android banking malware: Rokarolla Trojan Combines Banking Fraud With Device Surveillance

CloudSEK advised users never to install bank-branded apps from links sent by text, WhatsApp or Telegram, and urged banks to move customers from text-message OTPs toward app-based or Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication where feasible.

Title: Amatera: How the prolific infostealer works and spreads
Context: ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing
Full Text:
Infostealers have become an established business, with developers who produce and maintain the product and paying customers who run their own campaigns with them. Amatera – which topped ESET’s infostealer detections in Latin America in the first half of 2026 but targets victims worldwide – shows what this professionalization looks like in practice.

Like many other infostealers, Amatera goes after a range of data spanning login credentials, session cookies, tokens, crypto wallet information, messaging data, files, and secrets from development environments. The sheer breadth of the loot shows why infostealers are a mainstay of cybercrime – a single compromise can lead to account hijacking, financial fraud and crypto theft, as well as open the door into the organization where the victim works.

Here’s more about where Amatera came from, along with its business model, capabilities, and distribution.

What is Amatera?

Detected by ESET products as Win/PSW.Amatera, Amatera is a Windows infostealer written in C++ that was first observed in 2024. Since it’s marketed under the malware-as-a-service (MaaS) model, its developers maintain the code, the control panel, and the support infrastructure, while affiliates pay a subscription to use the malware in their campaigns.

Given the similarities in their respective code, Amatera is very likely a rebrand of ACR Stealer. Indeed, the latter has a predecessor of its own: a Sekoia investigation in May 2024 described it as an updated version of the GrMsk stealer, offered as a service on underground forums.

Rebranding – or releasing an updated version of a piece of malware under a new name – is very common across the MaaS ecosystem, particularly among ransomware operators. They sometimes sell the source code when they shut down their operations to avoid being tracked, or they update and rename it as a ‘business strategy’. In some cases, they leak it so that other malicious actors can reuse it. At any rate, by the end of 2024, Amatera Stealer was already on offer for $199 a month, with support via Telegram..

Amatera’s capabilities

Amatera extracts credentials stored in web browsers, along with cookies, browsing histories, form data, and session tokens. It can also search for and grab sensitive documents and files synced with OneDrive or SharePoint – Microsoft reported a surge in attacks on its enterprise customers between late April and mid-June 2026. Separately, Straiker found that the malware also went after cryptocurrency wallet data by manipulating the clipboard.

The malware is also under constant development, and it turns up as the final payload in a wide variety of attack chains. That variety is also typical of MaaS: the developers sell the product, and each affiliate chooses their own way to deliver it.

Amatera has spread via compromised websites, search engine ads, targeted emails, fake documents, SVG files, and ClickFix via fake CAPTCHAs. Indeed, several recent analyses of Amatera campaigns worldwide show that one of its key delivery vectors is ClickFix, a social engineering technique that was first documented in 2024 and was quickly picked up by adversaries to distribute a wide range of malware families.

Often, the victim sees a message that mimics a CAPTCHA check or a browser error and warns them of supposed technical problems that can be fixed by copying a command and running it on their computer. The victim’s own keystrokes then set the compromise in motion. The technique has moved beyond fake CAPTCHAs, however, as adversaries kept the social engineering core of ClickFix with some tweaks:

· AI-fix: Attackers build pages that impersonate legitimate AI services, including Anthropic’s Artifacts, OpenAI’s Canvas, and Microsoft Copilot Pages. The pages contain fake troubleshooting content for non-existent problems.

· CrashFix: A fake ad blocker triggers fake browser crashes and warns of data loss, pushing victims toward a malicious “quick fix.”

· ConsentFix: This variant tricks the victims into handing over their OAuth authorization tokens that open their Microsoft accounts to attackers without any password being stolen.

ClickFix-based campaigns have also used legitimate but compromised WordPress sites, among other methods. Attackers gained access to these sites through weak or stolen administrative credentials or by exploiting vulnerabilities in WordPress themes and plugins.

In Latin America, Amatera topped ESET’s infostealer detections in the first half of 2026, ahead of Formbook, Vidar, Lumma Stealer, SnakeStealer, and Rhadamanthys. ClickFix’s recent growth globally hasn’t been a straight line, however. ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing. Detections fell steeply in the second half of 2025, before more than doubling in the first half of 2026 as attackers adapted the technique to new environments.

Amatera’s affiliates also buy Google ads. The Straiker research mentioned above uncovered dozens of fake install pages that were promoted through paid ads and SEO poisoning and impersonated AI and developer tools, such as Claude Code, NotebookLM, JetBrains, Comet, and Snowflake, and specifically targeted developers who use AI tools. Like AI-fix, these pages piggyback off the credibility of AI brands and share the execution chain with ClickFix.

Risks and consequences of an Amatera compromise

Based on its capabilities, these are some of the potential consequences of falling victim to Amatera:

Compromise of personal or corporate accounts through stolen passwords, cookies, and tokens

Unauthorized access to email and cloud storage

Theft of crypto assets when wallets or recovery phrases are exposed

Infrastructure compromise through SSH keys, FTP credentials, or development secrets

Installation of additional malware

Use of a compromised account for fraud, internal phishing campaigns, or further intrusions

The risk spills over to employers when the victim mixes personal and work profiles in the same web browser. A home computer may hold corporate email sessions, cloud consoles, code repositories, or HR systems. The stolen information eventually becomes a gateway that another actor can buy or exploit days later.

How to prevent and respond to an Amatera compromise

Here are a few tips for staying out of harm’s way, especially in corporate environments:

Remember that no legitimate CAPTCHA, error message, or installation guide will ask you to copy commands from a web page into the Run dialog, PowerShell, or Terminal. A search engine ad is no guarantee that a site is official. That applies equally to pages that look like they belong to a well-known AI service.

Enforce application control rules and reduce the attack surface by limiting the use of system interpreters and binaries outside their normal context.

Monitor PowerShell, Rundll32, WebDAV, unusual scheduled tasks, and the clearing of PowerShell history.

Use phishing-resistant authentication and keep browser sessions as short as business needs allow.

Separate personal and work profiles, and avoid storing secrets in the browser when a managed alternative is available.

Filter newly created sites, cloned installation pages, and downloads initiated from ads when the context doesn’t justify them.

If a compromise is confirmed, isolating the device is only the first step. From a trusted device, revoke active sessions, reset passwords, and rotate API keys, tokens, SSH credentials, and any other secrets present on the system. Also, review access to email, cloud services, repositories, and financial applications. The response must track follow-on activity, rather than stop at the initial host – documented campaigns executed additional payloads, created scheduled tasks, covered their tracks, and used legitimate system tools.

Conclusion

Amatera shows how the infostealer market works today. A developer maintains the product, and other actors distribute it via compromised websites, ads, fake AI tools, emails, or ClickFix instructions. The threat can outlive the malicious file itself, however, as passwords, cookies, session tokens, and confidential documents remain valuable even after the device has been cleaned. Stolen data can fuel both immediate fraud or later intrusions, and the rise in detections in 2026 shows attackers adopting and adapting malicious toolsets at a rapid clip.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform
Context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform appeared first on Cato Networks
Full Text:
Executive summary

Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys were compromised after being generated with insufficient randomness. Attackers could use these keys to forge certificates and impersonate legitimate websites or services to clients that still trust them. An attacker able to intercept a connection could potentially read or modify sensitive traffic.

We have deployed a certificate-trust update through our centrally managed PoP architecture, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Delivering the update through the Cato Cloud removed the need for customers to patch security appliances at individual locations.

What happened?

Intermediate CAs sign certificates used to authenticate websites and services. Compromising their private keys can enable attackers to issue fraudulent certificates for domains they do not control. Organizations can therefore face exposure even when their legitimate certificates come from another provider.

Google and Mozilla received reports on October 17, 2026, and distributed emergency certificate blocks that day.

Mozilla also released updates associated with CVE-2026-113470. These include the certificate block list directly in Firefox and Thunderbird, protecting installations even when automatic block-list updates are disabled or unavailable.

Google found that no website certificates issued through the six affected TLS intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs before its emergency block took effect. CT logs are public records of certificates. Browsers that enforce CT, including Chrome, require valid proof that a certificate has been submitted to these logs before accepting it. Those browsers would therefore have rejected fraudulent certificates from the affected intermediates even before receiving the emergency blocks.

However, this protection does not extend to all software. Some applications, older browsers, or configurations without CT enforcement may have accepted unlogged fraudulent certificates if they still trusted the affected intermediates. The absence of certificates from those intermediates in CT logs before Google’s block therefore does not prove that no attacks occurred.

eMudhra says its root private keys and other intermediate CAs are unaffected. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Business risks

The exposure extends beyond employee browsers. Applications, API integrations, containers, and embedded devices may use independent trust stores or lack effective certificate-revocation checks.

Potential business consequences include:

Credential theft and data exposure: Intercepted connections could expose passwords, session tokens, and confidential information.

Transaction manipulation: Attackers impersonating trusted services could alter business communications or API responses.

Service disruption: Emergency trust removal can also reject legitimate certificates. Google announced a broader root-removal rollout expected on October 27, requiring affected website operators to replace their certificates.

Operational costs: Identifying and updating separate trust stores across applications and infrastructure creates work and opportunities for missed remediation.

These are potential impacts, not evidence of observed exploitation.

Our response: centralized control, global enforcement

The Cato AI-native SASE Platform converges networking and security in a cloud-native service delivered through globally distributed points of presence (PoPs). Our Single Pass Cloud Engine provides integrated security enforcement, while centralized management allows us to deliver updates across our cloud infrastructure. This reduces the coordination and maintenance work customers would otherwise undertake across distributed security appliances.

Centralized operations also support controlled deployment. Our established PoP change-management practices include phased rollouts, validation, monitoring, and rollback capabilities to manage operational risk as the platform evolves.

What this means for our customers

We have centrally deployed a certificate-trust update across our globally distributed PoPs, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Customers do not need to make configuration changes to receive this update.

Analysis of our data lake showed that the certificate chains affected by this update appeared in only a very small proportion of the network flows examined. Based on this limited usage, we expect minimal connectivity impact for customers.

Context: In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid...
Full Text:
By: Intelligence Team, Jacob Malimban

Since September 2026, threat actors have been sending emails that appear to be an invitation to a private Anthropic AI meeting, but are actually attempts to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials. Exclusive access to new AI technology is valuable to many organizations, which is why threat actors use it as a lure in their phishing emails.

Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g. proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization. Employees must stay vigilant, as these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies due to the abuse of legitimate tools like URL shorteners and CAPTCHAs.

Cofense Intelligence consolidates campaign data, including indicators of compromise (IOCs) such as malicious web addresses, phishing email content, and broader campaign context, into Active Threat Reports (ATRs), providing a comprehensive view of identified threats. ATRs contain the full infection chain from the initial phishing link to the final malware file or credential phishing resource. If one ATR IOC appears in the organization, cybersecurity professionals can read the ATR to understand the phishing attack’s impact and mitigations. Each ATR has been curated by a human analyst. This human-vetted intelligence provides context and the campaign information necessary to mitigate future phishing attacks. For this private Anthropic AI preview campaign, actionable intelligence can be found in ATRs 423868, 423866, and 423475.

Key Points

The campaign contains a tantalizing, private offer to preview Anthropic AI technology, which may be enough for employees to click before inspecting the email.

The video teleconference software GoTo Webinar, which is used to send legitimate meeting emails and is usually not blocked by email security technologies, was abused to send a threat actor’s URL instead.

The URL shortener zpr[.]io, which turns long URLs into short links, has been abused to help these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies.

CAPTCHAs, which are tests that confirm a real human is visiting the website, are similarly abused to prevent automated analysis.

Threat actors use subdomains and dashes (-) to obfuscate the malicious URL.

Step 1: The Invitation Email

Figure 1: Anthropic meeting invitation email used in credential phishing (ATR 423475).

Emails in this campaign claim to be an exclusive invitation to see Anthropic’s new AI tool. Many organizations are deciding how AI fits into their business, so a private preview would be very valuable if the email were real. As developments in AI continue to dominate the news cycle, getting a private preview of advancements in Anthropic’s AI is an effective phishing lure.

The phishing email appears to be an abuse of the legitimate GoTo Webinar service. The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com. Threat actors have previously abused that email address and GoTo Webinar’s free trial in 2020. The email also contains a footer with GoTo Webinar branding.

The text in the email contains no obvious spelling errors. The email sender name, however, reads “Austin from nthropic” with the “A” missing from Anthropic. Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign.

The link in the email appears to be generated by Zapier’s URL shortener service. Zapier is a legitimate business process automation company, and their URL Shortener is designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible AI. Unfortunately, this tool has been abused by threat actors during this Anthropic AI Preview campaign. In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid being blocked by email security technologies.

Step 2: The First Checkpoint

Figure 2: Cloudflare CAPTCHA page to hinder automated analysis (ATR 423868).

If the phishing email link is clicked, a CAPTCHA page appears. This Cloudflare CAPTCHA must be completed before the phishing content is shown. This CAPTCHA is the first of two checkpoints that help threat actors block automated scans of their website. Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure because of the CAPTCHA.

Step 3: The Fake Meeting Page

Figure 3: Zoom-spoofing page with Anthropic meeting information (ATR 423475).

After completing the CAPTCHA, a Zoom-spoofing meeting invitation page appears. This brand does not match the GoTo Webinar branding from the email. The page’s Zoom branding is consistent with the “zoom” in the malicious domain, us968web-zoom[.]us.

If the phishing recipient wants to attend the “meeting”, they need to register for the event. They are prompted to register with their work email. Credential phishing occurs when the user clicks on either “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”.

Step 4: The Second Checkpoint

Figure 4: Custom CAPTCHA page to further hinder automated analysis (ATR 423475).

After clicking “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”, another CAPTCHA page appears. This CAPTCHA requires a sliding motion to “unlock” the page. This custom CAPTCHA also appears to be good at detecting and blocking analysis from the most popular VPN services, scanners, Tor browser, and other tools used by defenders.

Because the phishing attack has two distinct CAPTCHAs, automated analysis tools may not be able to follow every step in the credential phishing attack.

Step 5A: The Fake Google Login Page

Figure 5: Google credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423866).

If “Continue with Google” is clicked and the CAPTCHA is completed, the Google credential phishing page appears. Currently, the Google credential phishing page only captures usernames. It is likely that the page is misconfigured as it does not prompt for a password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Google login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

Not only is the phishing page remarkably similar to the legitimate Google login page, but the subdomain is also tricky. Employees who quickly read goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu might not recognize that the URL is not Google.

Step 5B: The Fake Microsoft Login Page

Figure 6: Microsoft credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423475).

If instead of clicking on “Continue with Google”, the user clicked “Continue with Microsoft”, the Microsoft credential phishing page would load. Just like the previous Google Credential Phishing section, the CAPTCHA must be completed (Figure 4) before the phishing content is shown. Unlike the Google credential phishing page, the Microsoft version captures both the username and password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Microsoft login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

The Microsoft phishing page mimics the real Microsoft login page well. It also has a tricky subdomain, where office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com mimics the real office[.]com or sharepoint[.]com domain. Entering credentials into this page exfiltrates them to the threat actor.

Conclusion

This report covers the private Anthropic AI Preview campaign that uses a fake invitation lure, multiple CAPTCHAs, and Google and Microsoft login page replicas. The campaign was very likely designed by threat actors to bypass current email security technologies and tools used by defenders. Once the employee has reached the credential phishing page, they may not be looking for warning signs anymore. The Google credential phishing page only targets usernames, whereas the Microsoft credential phishing page asks for both the username and password. Stolen credentials give threat actors access to a trusted account, the emails stored in it, and a foothold for future attacks against the organization.

Mitigations

Check if the brand remains consistent from the email to a login page. Although organizations can use services like GoTo Webinar to send meetings on their behalf, a GoTo Webinar email is unlikely to redirect to a Zoom event registration page. Searching for small inconsistencies can help identify an email as part of a phishing campaign.

Remind employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry especially now with the use of AI. Note that the URL in the email might not be the same URL as the login page due to URL redirects.

Use Cofense Vision. Vision AI can cluster structurally related messages even when threat actors rotate senders, subjects, URLs, and page elements.

Invest in human-vetted threat intelligence to complement automated feeds. Automated systems are fast but cannot always tell the difference between a legitimate tool being used by IT and the same tool being abused by threat actors, and human analysis adds the context and confidence that AI-based speed cannot provide.

To learn how Cofense combines AI-driven detection, human-vetted threat intelligence, and rapid remediation to identify and stop sophisticated phishing attacks that bypass traditional security defenses, visit cofense.com/platform.

Title: Prediction Markets Emerge as a New Vertical for Traffer Teams
Context: Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since the spring of 2026, Insikt Group has observed multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have quickly adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance. This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.

Artificial intelligence (AI) further accelerates this opportunism by reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events. Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement.

The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities. Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.

Key Findings

AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team supply affiliates with simulated prediction-market websites, administrative panels, payment infrastructure, and promotional support. Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

AtlasCore’s Telegram posts recorded approximately $10.97 million in claimed deposits across its scam offerings between May 2 and September 18, 2026, with the deposits predominantly associated with prediction markets. PolyFucked separately advertises approximately $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures rely on threat actor reporting and remain unverified.

Magnetic Team advertises more than 3,000 simulated traders across more than 5,000 markets to fabricate convincing trading activity. Its code exposes configurable withdrawal-blocking pretexts, forced-loss controls, and pools of up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. AtlasCore similarly exposes settings to force wins or losses and impose individualized withdrawal restrictions.

All three traffer teams advertise or provide AI-assisted victim support. AtlasCore and PolyFucked also supply guidance for AI-generated promotional content, including synthetic influencers and branding, respectively. Magnetic Team’s source code contains indicators of likely AI-assisted development, suggesting AI use may extend to building and maintaining the underlying fraud platforms, although that assessment remains unconfirmed.

Insikt Group identified over 100 unique domains and subdomains associated with AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team, including administrative infrastructure and scam websites likely operated by the teams or their affiliates.

Threat Analysis

AtlasCore

In August 2026, Insikt Group identified a post on a low-tier cybercriminal forum seeking affiliates to join the traffer team “AtlasCore”. The thread was first created on May 15, 2026, by the user “AtlasCore”. The affiliate program was also advertised on a top-tier cybercriminal forum by the user “AtlasCorp” on May 28, 2026. The program includes an offering for prediction markets, as well as more typical traffer scams such as cryptocurrency exchanges and casinos.
